World.title: Ukraine invests in firepower as it inflicts a new Russian casualty record
World.content:
Recent Starlink suspension did not much affect Ukrainian lethality, but Kyiv shows it is losing trust in the US.

Share Ukraine invests in firepower as it inflicts a new Russian casualty record on social media

Ukraine’s military says Russian casualties reached 49,040 in October – a new monthly record.

The General Staff’s estimate of dead and incapacitated Russian troops, as of October 28, comes close to fulfilling Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s goal set in January of at least 50,000 enemy casualties a month by the end of 2026.

Zelenskyy had said that was “a level of destruction of the occupier at which Russian losses exceed the number of reinforcements they can send.”

The previous monthly high of 46,230 was set in September, with both records marking a sharp increase in reported Russian dead and wounded since the summer.

Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert Brovdi called it a “massive industrial slaughter”.

Al Jazeera cannot independently verify casualty estimates by either side. Ukraine’s military says it has video documentation of each strike.

Aerial drones are responsible for most of the casualties Ukraine inflicts, and Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara this week asked his European allies for funding to double drone production next year to about 16 million units.

The goal, he said, was “to scale up joint production of Ukrainian drones in other countries”.

Zelenskyy has said Ukraine could even triple drone production given enough money. Ukraine has decided that mass is the key to winning the war against Russia in terms of firepower.

“We see signs that mass production is preferred over technological sophistication,” said Ukrainian Defence Ministry adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov. “Mass production and simplicity will overcome technology.”



On October 28, the Netherlands and UK took steps to help Ukraine achieve its goal.

The Netherlands said it would provide 500 million euros ($560m) in immediate additional military aid and 1.2 billion euros ($1.34bn) in additional financing.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham upped Britain’s commitments by 10 billion pounds ($13.4bn) over three years, of which 3 billion pounds ($4bn) will be for weapons.

Ukraine announced its Starlink satellite navigation services were back to normal on October 24. “Communication remains stable at speeds exceeding 400km/h,” said the Defence Ministry.

On October 14, Ukraine had reported it was losing control of its drones above about 150km/h (100mph), making it difficult to mount defence against Russian jet-powered drones travelling above 500km/h.

After initially denying involvement, Starlink owner Elon Musk said on October 24 that he had “closed a loophole” that had allowed Ukraine to use Starlink offensively.

But Ukraine appeared to be thinking beyond Starlink and its Pentagon-owned military-grade service, Starshield.

On October 22, Ukraine and Finland announced they were jointly developing an independent sovereign military satellite system. Poland-based ICEYE and Finnish Nokia said they were partnering to realise the system, which would begin to launch satellites in 2028.

Other Europeans may be interested. On October 28, Zelenskyy also discussed satellite technology collaboration with Dutch premier Rob Jetten.

Ukraine said while they lasted, Starlink’s speed restrictions damaged its interception of Russian jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones.

The Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank, said the 10-day outage caused Ukraine’s interception rate to fall from 77 percent to 74 percent.

Yet the rate seemed to be improving regardless.

According to Ukrainian Air Force data, Ukraine managed to shoot down at least 75 percent of jet-powered drones during the week ending October 29.

That was far above the three-month average shoot-down rate of 60 percent for jet-powered drones, suggesting that Ukraine is adapting fast.

Still, many Russian drones are getting through. One struck a train platform in the central city of Dnipro on October 29, killing at least 14 people.

Ukraine is also concerned that the US administration is hesitating about sending ballistic missile interceptors European allies have paid for.



“The artificial and prolonged delays in the delivery of interceptor missiles for Patriot and NASAMS systems, which unfortunately have been occurring recently, are directly helping Russia achieve the goals of its terrorist campaign,” Zelenskyy said, after Russian ballistics hit a university campus in downtown Kyiv on October 27.

The previous day, Khmara had asked European allies to transfer 10 percent of their existing stocks of interceptors as an advance on future orders.

Ukraine struck Russia during the past week, too.

On October 23, Ukrainian missiles destroyed the main microchip production building of Proton-Electrotex in the city of Orel, which makes missile components.

During the week, Ukraine damaged five chemical plants, NAK Azot, Toliattykauchuk, Omskiy Kauchuk, Energiya and Voronezhsintezkauchuk, which make solid rocket propellants used in missiles.

It also damaged the Voronezh Aircraft Company and VSMPO-AVISMA, two factories building airframes or the metals for them.

Notes from underground

Ukraine has also been developing underground warfare, far from the battlefields monitored by drones, planes and satellites.

On October 22, its Khartiia Corps, originally a volunteer unit but now part of the National Guard, announced it had successfully completed an operation to flush Russian infiltrators out of a disused gas pipeline.

The Russians were using the pipeline to move troops from occupied parts of Kharkiv to the front line city of Kupiansk.

“The Russians tried to use underground gas pipelines to move past our positions. Our warriors turned this tactic against the Russians and used this system of underground pipelines against the occupiers with extraordinary success,” said Zelenskyy.

Ukraine’s Operation Veles advanced 15km (10 miles) underground through the pipeline and tunnels to emerge behind Russian positions, said Brigadier General Ihor Oboloenskyi.

Khartiia Corps said it coordinated underground attacks from pipes and tunnels with overland attacks and drones to surprise the enemy from several different directions at once, killing or wounding 100 Russian soldiers and capturing 30.

Russian forces had used the pipelines to evacuate their wounded, too, and were filmed marching Ukrainian civilians among them as human shields, said Viktor Tregubov, United Forces Group spokesman.

Ukraine’s forces besieged the Russians inside the pipeline, said Vladimir Dektyarev, an officer of Khartiia Corps. “Even after they were surrounded, they sat for over a month, until their food ran out, waiting for a command from their command for permission to surrender.”

Veles marked the third operation this year where Ukrainian forces have pushed Russian forces back and reclaimed land.

In the south of the country, too, Ukrainian forces were reported to have liberated three settlements – Peredubova, Komar and Fedorivka – on the Donetsk-Zaporizhia border, expanding an area of reclaimed territory there.

Although the US is still on track to bring Ukrainian and Russian technical teams to the negotiating table on November 10, and Zelenskyy supported a ceasefire on energy infrastructure and grain exports, Russia downplayed expectations.



Russian President Vladimir Putin spoke of Ukraine as “the territory of historical Russia” on October 22, denying the existence of a Ukrainian people and refusing a ceasefire on energy infrastructure.

His foreign policy adviser, Valery Ushakov, said the talks “will not resolve much”.

When Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb held a call with Putin on October 27 – their first contact with him since assuming office – Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov dismissed the conversation as “Europeans’ desire to squeeze into the negotiation process.”

World.title: Italy tightens security as students, unions launch nationwide protests
World.content:
Rallies across the country target living costs, investment in education, and the wars in the Middle East.

Italy has tightened security as tens of thousands of students and unions took to the streets across the country.

Marches were held in dozens of cities nationwide on Friday. Rome, Milan and Naples were among those affected by the protests, which targeted soaring living costs, demanded investment in education and called for an end to the wars in the Middle East.

A large police presence was on hand, as the hard-right government tightened security measures in a bid to control potential unrest seen in Italy and other European states in recent weeks.

In Rome, security was stepped up around the Colosseum, Italy’s most visited tourist attraction, while Milan’s cathedral also received special protection.

A few skirmishes between protesters and riot police occurred at the start of a protest in Turin, with other rallies in Bologna and Genoa.

The USB trade union called for a general strike that attracted large numbers of demonstrators, including truck drivers, taxi drivers and farmers. Rallies in recent weeks have demanded an end to higher fuel prices and rising defence spending.

Unions have also issued a joint call with peers in France, Greece, Spain, Turkiye and Morocco to demand an end to the wars in the Middle East, including the war in Gaza and “an end to the militarisation of ports”.

“Ports must not be used for the transport of weapons, ammunition, military equipment and troops,” the statement said. “Dockworkers do not work for war!”

The government last week agreed on a 175 million euro ($195 million) aid package for truck drivers, farmers and fishermen hit by soaring fuel prices linked to the war in the Middle East.



The prices paid in Italy for food, energy, transport and bills have risen by 68 percent since 2000, while the average wage fell by almost 5 percent.

Measures to support young people and families – such as an annual bonus of 2,500 euros for workers under 30 – have also been inserted into the draft 2027 budget currently being discussed among the various governing parties.

“I hope this can provide answers for young people in general… who feel that the state doesn’t care about them,” Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said at a news conference on Wednesday, stressing that the measures were “not for those who smash windows”.

Following clashes over the weekend of October 17-18 between youth and police in Milan, in which groups of mainly young people looted shops and smashed windows, Meloni toughened laws on public gatherings and eased restrictions on the detention of minors.

World.title: Israel’s opposition may not be able to form a government, but it still could control Parliament.
World.content:
For decades, Israel’s Arab parties have been relegated to the margins of Israeli political life, often sitting on the sidelines while Jewish parties assembled a governing coalition in Parliament and picked a prime minister.

Heading into Israel’s pivotal election on Tuesday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned his supporters that the Arabs were “trying to steal the election,” though electoral officials said there were no reports of widespread irregularities. He repeatedly invoked the specter of Arab voters to galvanize his right-wing base, vowing to keep them out of power.

Mr. Netanyahu’s leading rival, Gadi Eisenkot, largely declined to answer whether he would partner with Arab parties if necessary to topple the Netanyahu government, though he said none met his conditions as potential allies.

But record turnout by supporters of the Arab parties looks to deliver them their largest vote totals in generations, possibly since Israel’s establishment 78 years ago.

Now, the Arab minority represents a political reality that cannot be ignored.

Turnout in the Arab community, which represents about 20 percent of Israeli citizens, appears to have translated into a stunning windfall of parliamentary seats — potentially as many as 19 combined between the two leading parties, Raam and the Joint List alliance. The Arab parties have 10 seats in the outgoing Parliament.

Israel’s future could turn in part on whether Mr. Eisenkot decides to take the political risks of partnering with them. Without their support, Mr. Eisenkot and his alliance will almost certainly fall short of the 61-seat majority required in the 120-seat Parliament to form a new government and end Mr. Netanyahu’s hold on power. Mr. Netanyahu’s alliance also looks to fall short of 61 seats.

Many Israeli Jews have long objected to building a governing coalition that relies on Arab party backing for a majority. Some say a Jewish state should be ruled exclusively by Jews. Some cite national security reasons, questioning whether Arab leaders who see themselves as part of the wider Palestinian people can be entrusted with crucial matters of state.

Those objections became even more acute after the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attacks on Israel and the subsequent rightward shift in Israeli politics. Both Raam and some members of the Joint List condemned the assault, although they have also been highly critical of how Israel has conducted its war against Hamas in Gaza.

The Arab parties for many years were themselves reluctant to join governments that oversaw the Israeli occupation of the West Bank and Gaza. And turnout among Arab citizens has traditionally been lower than Jewish turnout, reflecting doubts about their ability to influence national decision-making.

Raam, a socially conservative party with roots in Islamist politics, has achieved some acceptance in Israel’s mainstream by putting less emphasis on the cause of Palestinian statehood. But the Joint List, an alliance of three smaller parties that includes a joint Jewish-Arab leftist faction and a Palestinian nationalist faction, is seen as more antagonistic toward Zionism.

Initial election results show that the Joint List will be the significantly larger of the two in Parliament.

“Netanyahu knows that without the Arab parties, there’s no majority to unseat him. That’s why he incites against us,” said Yousef Jabareen, the leader of the Joint List alliance in an interview. “The opposition should reject that incitement.”

He added: “The ball is now in Eisenkot’s court. Whoever wants to remove Netanyahu and change his policies — we are ready to cooperate to topple his government.”

Political analysts say the Joint List would be more likely to support Eisenkot from outside the governing coalition, for instance by agreeing to block any no-confidence votes. There is some precedent for this: In the 1990s, then Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin relied on Arab lawmakers to prevent the collapse of his own minority government.

Arab citizens, some of whom identify themselves as Palestinians with Israeli passports, experience a tension that can cut to the heart of daily life. Unlike Palestinians in the West Bank — who live under Israeli military rule — they have the right to vote, and some have held high office, including on the country’s Supreme Court.

But they largely live in separate cities and towns from Jewish Israelis and retain tight familial and historical bonds with Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza. Many view themselves as second-class citizens in the Jewish state, saying they face discrimination in housing as well as neglect in receiving public services.

Before this year, the largest electoral success recorded by Arab parties was in 2020, when they secured 15 seats. And the first — and so far, only — time an independent Arab party joined the Israeli governing coalition was in 2021, when Mansour Abbas, the leader of Raam, joined Mr. Netanyahu’s rivals to unseat him in favor of a short-lived government.

Mr. Abbas has since worked to make his party more acceptable to Israeli Jews. He has recognized Israel’s Jewish character as a fact of life and publicly considered integrating Arabs into the country’s mandatory national service, in particular community service.

In a bold move during the election campaign, he named Jewish lawmaker Yoav Segalovitz — a former senior police officer and centrist Zionist — as the number two on the Raam candidate list.

But if exit polls and initial results are correct, Raam’s support would not be enough to give Mr. Eisenkot’s bloc a parliamentary majority. He would also have to rely on the Joint List to topple Mr. Netanyahu. While political analysts say that Mr. Eisenkot might be willing to bring Raam onboard, he would struggle to keep his bloc with him if he made common cause with the Joint List, even if he wanted to, because this could provoke too much political blowback from many Jewish voters.

“There’s a shift in Arab politics, an attempt to get closer to the Jewish Zionist mainstream. It’s just that the other side is not willing to do so,” said Thair Abu Rass, an expert on Israel’s Arab politics. “There’s no partner on the Jewish side to create an alternative reality.”

World.title: US inmate Christa Pike says she woke up 'confused and in pain' after failed execution
World.content:
US death row inmate Christa Pike has released her first public statement since her botched execution in September.

"There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain," she said in a statement released by her legal team on social media on Friday.

"My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul."

Pike, 50, was discharged from hospital at the end of last month after surviving two lethal injections of the drug pentobarbital, which left her in a critical condition.

She has since been sent back to the prison where she has spent the last 30 years for murdering Colleen Slemmer in 1995.

Pike is thought to be the only person to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.

World.title: Residents leave devastated Russian-occupied Oleshky as evacuation corridor opens
World.content:
The evacuation of the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky is under way, Russian and Ukrainian authorities have confirmed.

A ceasefire, brokered by US First Lady Melania Trump, has been in force in the entire frontline region of Kherson since Tuesday, allowing for the road out of Oleshky to be demined.

Residents of Oleshky who wished to leave had a four-hour window to do so. A convoy of 25 buses was brought in to allow up to 750 people to leave the town until 14:00 (12:00 GMT), along with ambulances for people with limited mobility.

Several hundred people are understood to have decided to stay, despite the widespread devastation and the lack of gas, electricity and running water.

"Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will be given the opportunity to do so safely," Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.

"At the same time, those who decide to remain will be able to stay and will receive all the necessary humanitarian assistance."

Ukrainian territory lies 5km (3.1miles) from Oleshky, but the evacuees will first have to travel into Russian-occupied territory and then to the southern Russian city of Anapa.

They will board a Russian government plane to Gomel in Belarus, and then drive across the border into Ukraine's Chernihiv region.

Others are expected to choose to stay in Russian-occupied territory.

World.title: Prominent Russian newspaper shuts down under pressure from authorities
World.content:
For the last three decades, Novaya Gazeta has been one of the most high-profile independent news outlets in Russia.

Now it's shutting down - and it has accused the Russian authorities of the "murder" of a newspaper.

"They've killed us," reads a statement on the Novaya Gazeta website.

"The newspaper is no more. The Russian authorities and Russian special services have forced the paper to stop its work."

Novaya Gazeta has received an eviction order. Crucially, at the same time, the system that had allowed the paper to receive donations from readers was disabled.

That leaves no way to fund the publication.

Novaya Gazeta had developed a reputation for fearless investigative reporting on subjects such as corruption, human rights violations and abuse of power by officials and bureaucrats - dangerous topics in Russia.

World.title: Spain transport minister says he won't resign over high-speed rail disaster
World.content:
Spain's transport minister says he won't resign over the high-speed rail collision that has left at least 69 people dead.

Ãscar Puente told a news conference in Madrid he had "nothing to hide" while repeating the government's vow to get to the bottom of the disaster, saying many questions needed to be answered.

"My duty right now is not to talk about whether I should remain in my position, but to resolve the problem," Puente said.

The transport minister has been facing calls to step down in the aftermath of the tragedy, including from political rivals, a trade union and demonstrators who protested outside the transport ministry on Wednesday night.

Dozens were killed and many more injured when a state-operated Renfe high-speed train smashed into the back of another stationary train operated by the Iryo company near the town of Urda, in the central Toledo province, on Wednesday morning.

A preliminary report released by transport investigators late on Thursday found the Renfe train was travelling between 160km/h (99.4mph) and 200km/h when the collision occurred, causing its front carriage to become embedded in the tail of the stationary train.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez said earlier on Friday that public trust in Spain's high-speed rail network had been broken and repeated it was "unacceptable" that there had been two similar tragedies within a year.

In January a collision on the same Madrid-Seville route killed 46 people in Adamuz in southern Spain.

Wednesday's tragedy was one of the worst rail disasters in Europe's modern history, and Spain's worst crash since 2013.

Puente said on Wednesday a computer failure at about 08:30 that morning led to the initial halt of six moving trains, including the two trains that subsequently collided.

Leaked audio recordings published in Spanish media revealed conversations between train drivers and a control centre just minutes before the crash.

World.title: Mushroom murderer fails to overturn convictions in Australian court challenge
World.content:
Australia's mushroom killer has failed to overturn her murder convictions on appeal, with the court also ruling that she never be released from prison.

Erin Patterson, 52, was found guilty of murdering three relatives and attempting to kill another when she served them a toxic mushroom-laced meal in 2023. Her life sentence included a non-parole period of 33 years.

In Victoria's Court of Appeal on Friday, three judges threw out her appeal against her convictions and agreed with the prosecution that her sentence was inadequate, as it allowed for the possibility of freedom.

Patterson's crimes were "extraordinarily cold and calculated" and had to be "denounced in the strongest terms," they said.

"We have concluded that the case involved such shocking criminality that it is inappropriate to fix a non-parole period," Justice Stephen McLeish told the court, on the panel's behalf.

After a high-profile trial last year, a jury found Patterson guilty of murdering her in-laws, Don and Gail Patterson, and Gail's sister Heather Wilkinson, by serving them individual portions of beef Wellington containing death cap mushrooms.

Patterson was also found guilty of the attempted murder of Heather's husband Ian Wilkinson, a local pastor, who also ate the toxic lunch at Patterson's home in rural Victoria.

He survived after spending weeks in hospital and has ongoing health issues due to the poisoning.

Simon Patterson, the host's estranged husband, was meant to attend the lunch but cancelled at the last minute, in part due to his belief that his wife had repeatedly tried to poison him over several years.

Patterson was sentenced last September, with the trial judge allowing a non-parole period of 33 years due to the "harsh prison conditions" she would likely face.

World.title: Syrians struggle with soaring prices as crisis challenges post-Assad recovery
World.content:
Last month, protests erupted in squares and streets across Syria. People burned tyres, blocked roads and chanted slogans, angry at the government's decision to raise fuel prices again. It was the largest show of discontent yet since President Ahmed al-Sharaa came to power two years ago.

Speaking on a Syrian TV channel, a man said he still supported the authorities but that his situation had deteriorated to the point where he could no longer afford to buy bread. "Honestly," another said, "we have begun to fear what kind of new decision each morning will bring".

The increase was the latest in a series of measures people blame for a growing cost-of-living crisis. For many Syrians, life, financially, has worsened since rebels led by Sharaa ousted President Bashar al-Assad, ending five decades of his family's brutal rule and more than 13 years of a devastating civil war.

Catapulted to the presidency, Sharaa has, since then, led Syria's transition and efforts to revive a broken economy after a long period of mismanagement, isolation and conflict.

There was never any doubt about how challenging this would be. But as they celebrated Assad's overthrow and their new freedoms, Syrians, perhaps unrealistically, hoped things would quickly improve. That, however, has not materialised, and the handling of the economy has frustrated many here.

From essential bills to basic items, the cost of virtually everything has gone up. And many saw a further and unexpected rise in fuel prices as a sign of a government out of touch with its country. "We don't want roundabouts. Every day they build a new roundabout. People stood by you and are still with you," another protester said, addressing Sharaa, "but this will [make] things explode".

Days later, amid calls for further demonstrations, the increase was revoked.

World.title: Alaska Senate candidate denies knowing about alleged plot to put two Dan Sullivans on ballot
World.content:
Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola has denied she knew anything about an alleged "scheme" that led to two men named Dan Sullivan standing in the Alaska Senate race.

The denial comes as the Trump administration continues to escalate a criminal investigation into the matter, according to US media. The Republican governor of the state ordered an official inquiry earlier this week.

Dan S Sullivan, the incumbent Republican senator running for re-election, and allies have accused the Democrats of trying to confuse voters.

The Alaska race is considered by analysts to be one of the tightest of the upcoming US midterm elections, which will decide which party controls Congress.

"I just want to clear the air," Peltola said while speaking to voters on Thursday. "I knew nothing about any other candidate on the ballot except for me and the incumbent. That is all I have ever known about. I am not interested in tricking voters."

Both Dan Sullivans have been running for the open Senate seat for some time. Still, controversy erupted earlier this week when The New York Times, external reported that Peltola's team worked with people who tried to recruit spoiler candidates in the Senate race.

The Times's report alleged that people connected to Peltola's campaign, as well as senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee (DSCC), worked to try to recruit Dan J Sullivan, a retired teacher who lives in a remote fishing village, to stand in the Senate race.

The paper said it had seen text messages and interviewed 12 people who participated in or were told of the plan, or were would-be candidates who the team tried to recruit. The BBC has not independently verified the reporting.

The Peltola campaign has denied those reports and Sullivan has denied any links to the campaign.

But those denials have not stopped the US Department of Justice and Republicans from attacking Peltola.

World.title: Helicopter carrying six people crashes in northern Indian state
World.content:
A search for survivors is under way after a helicopter carrying six people, including five pilgrims, crashed in the northern Indian state of Uttarakhand, officials say.

Uttarakhand's Chief Minister Pushkar Singh Dhami said the helicopter had crashed near a village close to Joshimath in Chamoli district. Rescue teams have been dispatched to the mountainous area, but the condition of those on board remains unclear.

The aircraft reportedly took off from the Hindu pilgrimage site of Badrinath on Friday afternoon before losing contact.

The cause of the crash is also not yet known. The incident happened amid reports of heavy rain and poor visibility in the region.

Uttarakhand, a Himalayan state which borders China and Nepal, is home to some of Hinduism's holiest shrines and attracts millions of pilgrims every year.

Badrinath is one of four sacred sites on the Char Dham pilgrimage circuit, alongside Kedarnath, Gangotri and Yamunotri. Many devotees travel through steep Himalayan valleys to reach the temples, which are open for only part of the year because of harsh winter conditions.

World.title: WHO raises alarm as 75% of diabetes cases in Africa remain undiagnosed
World.content:
The World Health Organisation (WHO) has revealed that nearly three out of every four adults living with diabetes in Africa are unaware of their condition, warning that delayed diagnosis puts millions at risk of life-threatening complications.

The WHO Regional Director for Africa, Mohamed Janabi, raised the concern in a message shared ahead of the 2026 World Diabetes Day, marked on 14 November.

Mr Janabi said an estimated 24.6 million adults aged 20 to 79 were living with diabetes in the African Region in 2024, according to the International Diabetes Federation (IDF).

He warned that the figure could rise to 59.5 million by 2050, describing the high proportion of undiagnosed cases as the highest globally.

According to him, delayed diagnosis and treatment expose people living with the condition to serious complications, including kidney failure, blindness, cardiovascular disease and lower-limb amputations.

He stressed that early diagnosis and timely treatment could prevent complications, reduce suffering and save lives.

Early diagnosis

Under this year’s theme, ‘Early Action on Diabetes’, Mr Janabi urged individuals, communities, governments and healthcare workers to strengthen public awareness, promote early testing and improve access to affordable diabetes care.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He advised members of the public to watch out for symptoms such as increased thirst, frequent urination, unexplained weight loss, persistent tiredness and blurred vision.

He urged people experiencing these symptoms to seek medical advice and testing promptly, adding that individuals at increased risk should undergo screening even when they show no obvious symptoms.

“Do not ignore these symptoms. Seek testing and medical advice promptly, and encourage family members and friends to do the same,” he said.

Mr Janabi also called on communities to promote accurate information about diabetes and challenge the stigma and discrimination associated with the condition.

He encouraged people living with diabetes to share their experiences and support others in seeking medical attention.

Strengthening healthcare services

Mr Janabi urged healthcare workers to recognise diabetes symptoms early, provide timely testing and ensure compassionate, patient-centred care.

He said the WHO and its partners were supporting African countries to strengthen diabetes services through several initiatives, including the WHO Package of Essential Noncommunicable Disease Interventions (WHO PEN), the HEARTS technical package for cardiovascular disease prevention and management, and HEARTS-D, which focuses on the diagnosis and management of type 2 diabetes.

He also highlighted the Regional Strategy to Address Severe Noncommunicable Diseases at First-Level Referral Health Facilities, known as PEN-Plus.

According to him, these initiatives are designed to improve diabetes services at primary healthcare and first-level referral facilities.

He commended Rwanda for achieving nationwide district-level coverage of PEN-Plus, alongside other countries making progress in implementing the initiative.

However, he noted that significant gaps remained in access to trained healthcare workers, diagnostic services, essential medicines and continuous care.

Call for increased investment

Mr Janabi called on African governments to prioritise diabetes prevention, early diagnosis and continuous treatment within primary healthcare systems and universal health coverage programmes.

He said addressing the challenge would require sustained investment in public awareness, affordable insulin and essential medicines, diagnostic services, trained health workers and reliable healthcare systems.

He also urged development partners, civil society organisations and the private sector to support government-led efforts, particularly in underserved communities.

Mr Janabi reaffirmed the WHO’s commitment to supporting African countries to achieve the 2030 targets of the Framework for the Implementation of the Global Diabetes Compact in the African Region.

He urged people across the continent to recognise the warning signs of diabetes and seek medical attention early.

“Know the symptoms. Do not ignore the warning signs. Seek testing and care early. Encourage others to do the same,” he said.

World Diabetes Day

World Diabetes Day is observed annually on 14 November to raise awareness about diabetes, its prevention, diagnosis and management.

The campaign allows governments, healthcare professionals, communities, and organisations to highlight the growing burden of the condition and the need to improve access to care.

World.title: 2027: PDP says party’s presidential candidate still in race despite backing Tinubu
World.content:
The Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) has said its presidential candidate, Sandy Onor, remains in the 2027 race despite the party’s decision to support President Bola Tinubu under a cross-party political arrangement known as the Rainbow Coalition.

George Turner, the PDP chairman in Bayelsa State, said this during an interview on TVC News’ Beyond the Headlines, as the country prepares for the 2027 general election.

Asked whether the decision to back the All Progressives Congress (APC) candidate meant Mr Onor was out of the race, Mr Turner said: “No, no, no, no, no. He is in the race.”

He said the Rainbow Coalition was not a merger but a political platform that allows participating parties to retain their candidates while supporting agreed candidates at different levels.

“The Rainbow Coalition is a cross-party political platform, with all the political parties coming on board with their candidates,” he said.

Mr Turner said the coalition’s decisions cut across the state assembly, governorship, National Assembly and presidential elections. At the presidential level, he said, the coalition had settled for Mr Tinubu.

“For the presidency, it is President Ahmed Tinubu that is the candidate of the Rainbow Coalition,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He added that the participating parties’ presidential candidates, including Mr Onor, would lead their supporters to back Mr Tinubu. According to him, the coalition announced the decision at its launch in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, two days earlier, after consultations with party leaders and the PDP’s National Working Committee.

Mr Turner said similar political arrangements had been made in the past, citing the APC’s 2015 convention and the support Bola Tinubu, then a leader of the Action Congress of Nigeria (ACN), gave to the PDP’s presidential candidate in 2011.

“The overall interest here is the interest of the people, the interest of the nation, the interest of the various states, and that is what drives the Rainbow Coalition,” he said.

PDP defends position on zoning

Mr Turner also defended the party’s position on zoning, arguing that the South should complete its eight-year presidential tenure in 2027.

“As a nation, we must be concerned about our survival, our unity, what keeps us together and the way we play our politics,” he said.

He recalled the 2013 dispute over zoning, when Atiku Abubakar and five PDP governors left the party after disagreements over the North-South power rotation arrangement. Atiku later returned to contest the PDP presidential ticket in 2019 and challenged former President Muhammadu Buhari’s administration. He also contested the 2023 presidential election.

“Don’t we have conscience? Why do we say one thing in the morning, another thing in the afternoon?” Mr Turner asked.

He argued that fielding another PDP presidential candidate would not guarantee that the person would serve only one term.

“There is no guarantee of doing one term,” he said. “Everything is not politics.”

PDP candidates missing from INEC list

Mr Turner acknowledged that some PDP candidates were missing from the lists published by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC). Still, he maintained that all the party’s candidates met the legal requirements for nomination.

“I can assure you that all our candidates met the requirements of the law, and we follow due process in the nomination of our candidates,” he said.

He said the PDP’s national leadership and INEC were working to resolve the issue, adding that it would be discussed at a leadership meeting in Abuja on Tuesday.

“There is nothing to worry about,” he said.

Mr Turner also defended the PDP’s record in government, describing its 16 years in power as the country’s best period of governance.

“The 16 years of PDP is the best we have had,” he said.

He claimed that Mr Tinubu had approached the PDP for a partnership early in his administration and cited road projects in Abuja as an example of the benefits of cooperation between the parties.

“Who are the biggest beneficiaries of this partnership? Nigerian people,” he said.

APC says PDP support will not slow campaign

Francis Okoye, a member of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, said the PDP’s decision to support Mr Tinubu had made the ruling party’s re-election campaign easier but insisted that the APC would not become complacent.

“Somehow they have made our job easy, but we are not sleeping an inch, because we still have many hurdles to cross,” he said.

Mr Okoye identified the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) and the African Democratic Congress (ADC) as potential challengers, urging APC members not to underestimate the opposition.

“APC members should tell themselves the truth that we have a very strong challenge to cross, even though we have 33 governors supporting us,” he said.

He urged party members to intensify grassroots mobilisation and campaign from door to door.

Mr Okoye said Mr Tinubu deserved a second term, arguing that the president’s economic reforms were beginning to yield results.

“This is a man who has shown capacity, has shown courage in all the reforms he has embarked on,” he said.

He cited the removal of the petrol subsidy, saying it had increased the funds available to state governments. He also claimed that many governors no longer owed workers salaries, gratuities and pensions.

“Today we no longer hear of ASUU strike,” he said, referring to the Academic Staff Union of Universities. He added that students were accessing loans through the Nigerian Education Loan Fund (NELFUND).

Mr Okoye also said the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank and the outgoing president of the African Development Bank had backed the administration’s reforms.

He criticised Atiku for promising to restore the petrol subsidy and failing to offer a credible alternative to the current administration, if elected.

“Whatever he is promising now is what is not going to keep,” he said.

“He has no agenda, has no policy, has no programme to offer Nigerians.”

APC predicts stronger performance in South-east

Mr Okoye predicted that the APC would perform significantly better in the South-east in 2027 than it did in the 2023 presidential election.

“If Tinubu had gotten just five per cent of votes in the South-east in 2023, this 2027 election he will get more than 25 per cent,” he said.

He attributed the expected improvement to the APC’s increased political presence in the region, saying the party had gone from one governor to three. He also cited Anambra State Governor Charles Soludo’s public support for Mr Tinubu.

Mr Okoye rejected the argument that governors could contribute only their individual votes to the president’s re-election campaign, saying their influence extended to political appointees and supporters.

“You can’t say that a governor has one vote when he has appointed more than 200 or 300 SAs or SSAs,” he said. “When you aggregate all these people, you now see that the governor doesn’t have one vote.”

He also rejected criticism that the administration’s reforms had failed to benefit ordinary Nigerians.

“Anybody who says that the reform is not getting to the grassroots is deceiving himself,” he said, citing road projects, student loans through NELFUND and improved pay for soldiers as examples of the reforms’ impact.

World.title: Wike praises Dunamis Church for building pedestrian bridge in Abuja
World.content:
The Minister of the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Nyesom Wike, has commended Dunamis International Gospel Centre (DIGC) for building a pedestrian bridge along the busy Airport Road, Abuja.

Mr Wike ‌‌‍‌‍⁠⁠‍‌‍‌‌‌‍‌‌‌gave the commendation in Abuja on Friday during the inauguration of the pedestrian bridge built at the Church headquarters, the 100,000-capacity Glory Dome, Abuja.

He described the project as an exemplary model of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR).

The minister revealed that while the church applied for approval to construct the facility in 2018, the application was brought to his attention only in February 2026, leading to swift approval within one month.

He described the approval as evidence of President Bola Tinubu’s commitment to good governance, urging members of the Church to support government with proven capacity to respond to the needs of the people.

He said, “Government cannot do everything alone; there is nowhere in the world where government carries every burden. That is why we emphasise comprehensive social responsibility.”

To further encourage community-driven infrastructure, the minister announced that the FCT Administration (FCTA) would defray 50 per cent of the total cost the church incurred in constructing the bridge.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He commended the Senior Pastor of Dunamis, Paul Enenche, and his wife, Becky Enenche, for demonstrating leadership and sacrificing church resources to save lives and enhance human welfare rather than focusing solely on soul-winning.

The minister, however, decried the habitual refusal of many pedestrians to use constructed bridges, choosing instead to risk their lives crossing high-speed expressways.

He warned against continuous public criticism of government actions on social media when enforcement measures were deployed to maintain public order and safety.

Earlier, Mr Enenche, the senior pastor of the DIGC, said the decision to construct the pedestrian bridge was borne out of concern over the frequent fatal accidents recorded along the Airport Road axis.

Mr Enenche explained that “the Church plans to add modern aesthetic coverings, security lighting and transparent side-panels to the structure to protect users from weather elements and boost compliance.”

He urged public-spirited individuals and leaders to live for societal impact and keep eternity in view, emphasising that resources must be deployed for the collective good of humanity.

On her part, the senator representing the FCT, Ireti Kingibe, commended the church for backing its faith with compassionate action.

Mrs Kingibe described the ministry as “a beacon of light” and urged residents and leaders across the territory to unite to build a safer, more peaceful capital.

(NAN)

World.title: Gunmen kill four in Plateau community despite curfew
World.content:
At least four people were killed after gunmen attacked Sabon Angwa community, around Bet/Zat in Barkin Ladi Local Government Area of Plateau State, on Thursday night.

The attackers reportedly stormed the community at about 8 p.m. and opened fire on residents, despite the curfew imposed in parts of the state to contain insecurity.

A resident of Barkin Ladi, Bulus Jok, said the gunmen operated freely for some time, shooting indiscriminately.

“The gunmen struck the community around 8 p.m. despite the curfew in place and started shooting sporadically,” Mr Jok said.

He added that the attack threw residents into panic, leaving four people dead.

Mr Jok expressed concern that the incident occurred despite an early warning reportedly sent to relevant authorities a day before the attack.

“It is very sad, especially as there had been an early warning alert sent to the relevant authorities a day before the attack,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The Publicity Secretary of the Berom Youth Moulders-Association, Rwang Tengwong, also confirmed the incident.

Mr Tengwong condemned the killings, describing the attack as unacceptable and expressing concern over the continued assaults on communities despite security measures.

He urged security agencies to intensify surveillance, strengthen their presence in vulnerable communities and respond promptly to intelligence and early warning reports to prevent further attacks.

The latest incident adds to the series of attacks on communities in Plateau State, raising fresh concerns about the effectiveness of security measures, including curfews, in protecting residents.

Efforts to reach security operatives for official confirmation and further details were unsuccessful as of the time of filing this report.

World.title: Niger Mass Deaths: Probe panel recommends scholarships for victims’ children, N1.4bn compensations
World.content:
The committee that investigated the September deaths of 33 detainees in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) in Niger State has recommended full educational scholarships for the children of deceased victims and N1.4 billion in compensation for bereaved families and survivors.

In its report submitted to the Minister of Interior, Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, on 27 October, the Independent Investigation Committee proposed N30 million for each of the 33 bereaved families, amounting to N990 million, and N10 million for each of the 41 survivors, totalling N410 million.

The committee also recommended full educational scholarships, from primary to tertiary levels, for surviving children of the deceased.

It proposed that tuition payments and living stipends be administered through an institutional trust or escrow arrangement involving the National Human Rights Commission and the Minna Emirate Council to prevent diversion of funds and family disputes.

The report identified three deceased detainees whose wives were pregnant at the time of the investigation: Mu’awiya Abdulkareem, Safiyanu Abubakar and Suleiman Dantala.

It further recommended fully funded medical rehabilitation for all 41 survivors, with priority attention to the nine minors, as well as psychosocial support for survivors and bereaved families.

The committee called for a formal letter of apology from the Minister of Interior to the affected families and survivors on behalf of the Federal Government.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Officers cleared

The committee also recommended the immediate lifting of the suspension of 18 NSCDC officers it said were not found culpable in the deaths.

Among those listed were three deputy commandant of corps – Philips Ajayi, John Agrahau Chagwa, and Obafemi Elvis.

The rest are Stephen Tsado, an assistant commandant of corps; Abdullahi Sale, an inspector of corps, and Annas Lamino Shittu, a chief suprintendent of corps.

It recommended formal commendations and protection as key prosecution witnesses for four officers whose interventions and testimonies it described as helpful. They include Ahmed Abubakar Wushishi, Mohammed Isah Sanusi, Mariam Eteng Nelson and Annas Lamino Shittu.

The committee also recommended disciplinary sanctions against four other officers for what it described as gross management incompetence.

Beyond compensation, the panel called for a formal overhaul of the NSCDC, including improved detention facilities, staff training, supervision and independent inspection of operations.

It recommended the installation of tamper-proof, cloud-backed CCTV cameras in cell blocks, booking areas and corridors, with mandatory video-retention protocols.

The committee also urged the federal government to support the formalisation of artisanal mining and establish a consultative forum involving the NSCDC, miners’ association, traditional councils and local governments to address challenges in the sector.

World.title: EXCLUSIVE: Detainees drank urine, sweat in NSCDC Niger cell before 33 of them died – Report
World.content:
Detainees held in a cell at the Niger State Command of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) drank urine or sweat because they had no access to drinking water before 33 of them died, an investigation committee report has found.

The Independent Investigation Committee, constituted by the Federal Ministry of Interior to investigate the deaths, said the male cell had no running water and its toilet was not functioning.

The report said survivors described extreme heat, dehydration and overcrowding, with detainees unable to move freely inside the approximately 12-square-metre cell.

The Jonathan Kure-led 10-member committee authenticated 33 deaths occuring inside the male cell between 8 p.m. on 16 September and 7 a.m. the following day 17 September.

According to the copy of the report obtained by PREMIUM TIMES, the deceased persons included 14 minors.

The report, which painted a deplorable, harsh condition of the cell, stated that there were 41 survivors.

It found that about 50 male detainees, including children, were confined in the cell, which had a solid metal door and inadequate ventilation.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“The Committee finds that officers responsible for the cells failed to reduce the overcrowding, ignored prolonged cries and banging of the cell door and wall and did not provide emergency help,” the report said.

Under the dehumanising condition of the male cell, the report said, there was “no water” and “toilet not functional”.

It added that “detainees drank urine or sweat.”

The situation in the female cell was barely better. The report said there was also “no drinking water” there, except from relatives. The toilet was also “non-functional but usable with fetched water,” according to the report.

It added that relatives were prevented from bringing food to detainees on Wednesday, 16 September, the committee said.

Warnings ignored

The committee found that medical personnel had warned officers about the danger posed by the overcrowded cell before the deaths.

Mariam Nelson, an NSCDC medical unit personnel, told the committee that she cautioned the cell guards, Usman Ndamaka and Hassan Mohammed, on the evening of 16 September that the overcrowding could cause suffocation.

She said she advised them to leave the metal door unlocked to improve ventilation, but they ignored her warning.

The report said detainees began experiencing symptoms, including eye irritation, burning throats, difficulty breathing, excessive sweating and intense thirst, from around 7:15 p.m. on 16 September.

They subsequently began shouting for help and pleading for water.

An armoury guard, Ahmed Abubakar Wushishi, told the committee that he heard persistent banging and screams from the cell between 1 a.m. and 2 a.m. on 17 September.

He said he approached the night guard, Hassan Mohammed, and urged him to open the cell.

However, Mr Mohammed refused, citing an instruction from his superior, Mr Ndamaka, not to open the door without armed backup because the detainees might be planning an escape.

According to the report, Mr Wushishi said the screaming stopped around 2:30 a.m.

Mr Ndamaka admitted that he had instructed the night guard not to open the cell without armed backup. He also admitted that he did not respond to an emergency call from Mr Mohammed at 10:37 p.m. on 16 September, claiming he was asleep.

He returned the call around 6 a.m. and arrived at the facility at about 7 a.m., when the cell was opened and the bodies discovered.

The committee established that the deaths occurred inside the male cell between 8 p.m. on 16 September and 7 a.m. the following day.

Children among detainees

The report found that 14 of the deceased were minors. It also identified four children under the age of 14 who were recorded during profiling but were nevertheless placed in adult detention cells.

The profiling officer, Abubakar Dabban, admitted that he had recorded four minors under 14 but processed them into the adult detention cells.

The committee said this violated the children’s rights and applicable child-protection requirements.

It also found that adults and minors were detained together in the overcrowded facility.

Cause of deaths

The committee attributed the deaths to acute hypoxic respiratory failure, also known as environmental asphyxia, worsened by heat stress and dehydration.

However, it clarified that the medical conclusion was based on post-mortem examinations of only three available bodies. The other 30 had been buried before the medical team arrived.

The report said the immediate cause of death was lack of oxygen, while the remote causes included failure of duty of care by NSCDC officers, poor detention infrastructure, inadequate emergency medical arrangements and weak institutional supervision.

It rejected the claim that the deaths resulted from a disease outbreak, saying the available medical and forensic evidence did not support it.

The committee recommended prosecution of officers found responsible, including for offences such as murder, criminal negligence, torture and inhuman treatment, where applicable.

World.title: Falana urges Nigerians to look beyond Abuja, hold states, LGs accountable
World.content:
Human rights lawyer Femi Falana has urged Nigerians to look beyond the federal government and demand greater accountability from state and local governments over the management of public funds and delivery of essential services.

Mr Falana made the call on Thursday in Lagos as the keynote speaker at the public screening of LG Billions in the Dark, an investigative documentary on local governance in Osun State produced by DevReporting.

The documentary examines the prolonged crisis over local government leadership in Osun and its implications for public finance and service delivery. It highlights the gap between billions of naira allocated to the state’s 30 local government areas and the poor state of roads, water, sanitation, healthcare and education in many communities.

Mr Falana said the situation is not peculiar to Osun State, arguing that the crisis of local governance is linked to the weakening of local councils and inadequate accountability at the grassroots.

He said many Nigerians had lost confidence in local governments because elections conducted by State Independent Electoral Commissions (SIECs) were often manipulated to favour ruling parties.

“The local government or the State Independent Electoral Commissions in Nigeria conduct the worst elections in Africa, where the members of the ruling party, or rather the ruling party must produce all the chairs and the councillors,” he said.

LG’s finances

Mr Falana also criticised state authorities’ continued control of local government finances, despite the Supreme Court’s July 2024 judgment.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

On 11 July 2024, the Supreme Court affirmed the financial autonomy of Nigeria’s 774 local governments, ruling that allocations meant for the councils should be paid directly to them from the federation account.

Mr Falana said the judgment is yet to fully translate into practice in many states.

“In those days, it was an offence to disobey the judgment of the Supreme Court. In fact, even under the military regime, it was unthinkable,” he said.

“Today, judgments of courts are disobeyed by state governments, federal and even local governments.”

He said citizens should also take responsibility for demanding accountability from public officials rather than leaving governance issues entirely to politicians.

“We have enormous resources in this country, yet our communities remain underdeveloped,” he said. “We cannot continue to focus exclusively on Abuja while ignoring what happens in our states and local government areas. Every citizen has a responsibility to demand accountability.”

Local governments closest to citizens

In her opening remarks, the Vice-Chancellor of the University of Lagos (UNILAG), Folasade Ogunsola, said effective local governments are essential to national development because they are closest to citizens.

Mrs Ogunsola said local councils should play a central role in urban planning and management, particularly as Nigerian cities expand faster than the infrastructure and institutions supporting them.

“They understand their communities, the location of vulnerable populations, the demands of local infrastructure, and the pressures facing neighbourhoods,” she said.

She urged local governments to move beyond basic administration and support local businesses, markets and informal enterprises while improving public spaces and essential services.

Mrs Ogunsola, a professor of Medical Microbiology, said the recent move towards direct funding for local governments is a step in the right direction, although challenges remaint.

Mr Falana also emphasised that citizens should make good use of the Freedom of Information Act (FOI) to obtain information from the government.

He said citizens could ask local governments how much they had received and how the funds were being used.

Accountability at the grassroots

The publisher of PREMIUM TIMES and Chief Executive Officer of the Centre for Journalism and Innovation Development, Dapo Olorunyomi, who chaired the event, described the documentary as an example of accountability journalism.

“Holding public institutions and officers accountable for their responsibilities to citizens is what can make them stay on their toes, and that is what DevReporting did with its documentary,” he said. “And that is accountability journalism.”

The event also featured the unveiling of the Development Reporting Africa Foundation (DRAF), the non-profit arm of DevReporting, and a panel discussion on local governance and accountability.

The panel featured Comfort Idika-Ogunye of Jiti Ogunye Chambers; Moyosore Adebanjo, Executive Chairman of Onigbongbo Local Council Development Area (LCDA), Lagos State; Wale Adedayo, former Chairman of Ijebu East Local Government Area, Ogun State; Vera Amaechi, a lecturer in the Department of Political Science at UNILAG; and Joshua Osiyemi, Head of Tracka at BudgIT.

The panellists called for transparency in local government finances, including publishing budgets and expenditure online in accessible formats. They also urged councils to improve public engagement and sensitise residents about the functions of local governments and how public resources are used.

They further recommended stronger citizen participation, particularly by women, young people and persons with disabilities, and encouraged civil society organisations to take accountability efforts beyond state capitals into local communities.

The panel also stressed the importance of using digital tools to monitor government projects, report failures and track the implementation of public programmes.

The convener and Team Lead of DevReporting, Mojeed Alabi, said the documentary and the launch of the foundation are driven by a shared commitment to improve society through development reporting and accountability.

World.title: Senatorial Race: How I defeated Uzodimma in court – Okorocha
World.content:
Former Governor Rochas Okorocha of Imo State has accused Governor Hope Uzodimma of relying on documents containing alleged irregularities to claim victory in the All Progressives Congress (APC) senatorial primary for Imo West, insisting that he remains the dominant political force in the party in the state.

Mr Okorocha made the allegations during an interview on Arise News’ Prime Time on Thursday, a day after the Federal High Court in Abuja declared him the winner of the disputed APC primary and ordered the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to recognise him as the party’s candidate for the 2027 senatorial election.

The former governor also challenged the legitimacy of the APC leadership structure in Imo State, dismissing those allegedly mobilised against him as political associates of Mr Uzodimma rather than representatives of properly elected party structures.

“Rochas is the APC in Imo State. I was a founding father of this party,” he said. “The structure of APC in Imo State is Rochas. And I gave the name APC.”

The comments signal a renewed confrontation between the two politicians, whose rivalry has shaped the APC’s internal politics in Imo.

PREMIUM TIMES reported on Thursday that Justice Obiora Egwuatu of the Federal High Court ordered Mr Uzodimma to stop presenting himself as the APC’s candidate for Imo West Senatorial District.

The court also directed the APC to forward Mr Okorocha’s name to INEC for publication as its candidate for the election scheduled for 16 January 2027.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The judgement followed a suit filed by Mr Okorocha challenging INEC’s recognition of Mr Uzodimma as the winner of the party’s 18 May primary.

Allegations over primary documents

During Thursday’s interview, Mr Okorocha offered his account of the documentary evidence that formed the basis of his legal challenge, alleging that the records presented in support of Mr Uzodimma’s emergence as the APC senatorial candidate contained some inconsistencies.

He said he obtained certified copies of documents relating to the primary from INEC on 26 July 2026, after making the necessary application and payments.

According to him, the documents subsequently relied upon by Mr Uzodimma were presented to the electoral commission on 22 August, almost a month after he had obtained his own certified copies.

Mr Okorocha questioned the circumstances surrounding the emergence of the later documents, describing them as an afterthought.

He also alleged that there were discrepancies in the dates recorded for the primary election.

He said documents supporting Mr Uzodimma’s emergence indicated that the election was conducted on 16 May, whereas the actual exercise took place on 18 May.

Another inconsistency, according to him, concerned the description of Mr Uzodimma’s emergence as a consensus arrangement despite the existence of competing aspirants and recorded votes.

Mr Okorocha said the governor could not have emerged through consensus when he himself participated in the contest and was credited with votes.

He further alleged that result sheets covering more than 300 polling units across 144 wards and 12 local government areas were completed in the handwriting of one person.

He also claimed that some ward result sheets contained no entries, although documents subsequently presented at the local government level contained collated results.

Mr Okorocha contrasted these documents with the records he said he obtained from INEC, insisting that his own were consistent in their presentation and certification.

He suggested that the discrepancies raised questions about the authenticity of the documents used to support Mr Uzodimma’s nomination.

“All the misinformation on social media about my documents have been put to rest because the court has found out that the documents are genuine and correct,” he said.

Dispute over INEC’s role

Mr Okorocha also challenged the suggestion that INEC had independently determined the outcome of the APC primary in Mr Uzodimma’s favour.

He argued that the commission’s responsibility during party primaries was principally to monitor the exercise and keep records of the outcome submitted by the political party.

He alleged that although the results monitored by INEC favoured him, the figures eventually announced were different from those transmitted to the commission’s headquarters.

He said the party had, at some point, directed that the results should not be announced at the state level but taken to its national secretariat for announcement.

Mr Okorocha said that this created the discrepancy between the results he claimed were recorded during the exercise and the outcome eventually announced by the party.

He also questioned the origin of a letter allegedly submitted to the APC national chairman by the Imo Resident Electoral Commissioner (REC), claiming that it was certified by the party rather than INEC.

According to him, the letter was expected to bear the signatures of both the REC and the Head of Election Monitoring, but only the REC signed it.

He said the document supporting his own claim was addressed to the APC national chairman and certified by INEC.

Mr Okorocha maintained that these differences were part of the evidence he presented to challenge the governor’s nomination.

On challenge to his suit

Responding to questions about why he did not institute his legal action within 14 days of the primary, Mr Okorocha said he could not have challenged a result he believed had already been officially recorded in his favour.

He said he only became aware of the problem on 1 September, when he discovered that his name had been displaced from the records despite having obtained certified copies of the relevant documents from INEC.

He explained that he had no reason to institute proceedings against himself when the documents in his possession showed that he had won the primary.

He subsequently sued INEC, joining the APC and Mr Uzodimma as respondents.

The governor and the APC had challenged the suit on the grounds that it was filed outside the 14-day period prescribed for pre-election matters.

In their responses before the court, they disputed Mr Okorocha’s account of the primary.

A representative of the governor’s election committee had told the court that Mr Uzodimma won the exercise with 230,464 votes against Mr Okorocha’s 1,098 votes.

INEC also maintained in its counter-affidavit that its officials monitored the election and reported Mr Uzodimma as the winner.

Mr Okorocha said he was confident that the facts supporting his case were strong enough to withstand further judicial review, although he acknowledged that the opposing parties retained the right to appeal.

He said he did not expect Mr Uzodimma to challenge the judgement, stressing that the evidence before the court was compelling.

Imo APC leadership dispute

Beyond the senatorial nomination, Mr Okorocha used the interview to challenge the political authority of those claiming control of the APC in Imo State.

He dismissed suggestions that influential party figures were mobilising against him, describing them as individuals appointed by Mr Uzodimma rather than leaders who emerged through recognised party congresses.

“There are no forces, these are what I call the PAs of Hope, that he could put together and say, take chairman,” he said.

He questioned whether the party had conducted congresses to establish the legitimacy of the structures being presented as opposition to him.

“Has there been any election? Was there any congress conducted? There was none,” he said.

Mr Okorocha also questioned the involvement of the Imo State Government in the legal dispute, explaining that the contest was between him and Mr Uzodimma as individuals rather than between two governments.

“What does Imo State Government have to do with the election between me and Hope Uzodimma as a person? It’s not Imo State Government contesting for election, it’s Hope Uzodimma,” he said.

He maintained that his political relationship with the people of Imo State would enable him to mobilise support for the APC and President Bola Tinubu ahead of the 2027 elections.

Uzodimma’s camp rejects judgement

However, the governor’s camp and the APC have rejected the judgement.

The Imo State Commissioner for Information, Declan Emelumba, described the decision as a travesty of justice and said the state government would approach the Court of Appeal to challenge it.

Mr Emelumba also argued that the judgement disregarded judicial precedents on the time limit for instituting pre-election cases and the procedure for presenting allegations of forgery.

Similarly, the APC in Imo State maintained that Mr Uzodimma remained its authentic candidate for the senatorial district, insisting that he won the party’s primary.

The party said its legal department would study the judgement and pursue available legal remedies.

The APC spokesperson, Jones Onwuasoanya, said the APC would determine its next course of action after reviewing the court’s decision.

READ ALSO: APC reacts to court judgement sacking Uzodimma as senatorial candidate

PREMIUM TIMES contacted Oguike Nwachuku, the governor’s Chief Press Secretary, for Mr Uzodimma’s response to Mr Okorocha’s allegations concerning the primary documents, the party’s leadership structure and the possibility of an appeal.

Mr Nwachuku told our reporter he would respond to the allegation. But he had yet to do so as of the time of filing this report.

The dispute is the latest chapter in the longstanding political rivalry between the two men. Mr Okorocha governed Imo from 2011 to 2019 before becoming the senator for Imo West between 2019 and 2023.

Mr Uzodimma, who became governor in January 2020 following a Supreme Court judgement that overturned the result of the 2019 governorship election, is serving his second and final term, which ends in January 2028.

World.title: NDC defends Obi’s single-term pledge, dismisses Okorocha’s ‘gambling’ claim
World.content:
Peter Obi

By Henry Umoru

The National Leadership of the Nigeria Democratic Congress, NDC has thrown its weight behind the single-term presidential pledge by its Presidential candidate ahead of January 16 2027. Peter Obi.

The NDC described describing it as a constitutional commitment to performance, national stability and leadership accountability rather than a political gamble, adding that Obi had voluntarily offered to serve only one term, subjecting his leadership to public assessment based on results rather than political calculations.

The party noted that Nigeria’s experience with an eight-year presidential administration between 2015 and 2023 demonstrated that longevity in office did not automatically translate into improved governance or national development, adding that the period was characterised by rising inflation, naira depreciation, increasing public debt, widespread poverty and insecurity

In a statement signed on Friday by NDC Director-General of the National Presidential Campaign Council, NPCC, Mallam Ibrahim Hussain Abdulkarim, the party disagreed with Okorocha’s characterisation of the pledge as “a four-year gambling”, insisting that the proposal was constitutionally permissible and represented a deliberate commitment to deliver measurable results within four years.

According to him, Section 135(2) of the 1999 Constitution provides for a four-year presidential tenure with the possibility of seeking another term, arguing that the provision does not make a second term compulsory.

The leadership of the NDC was reacting to comments by former Imo State Governor, Senator Rochas Okorocha, during an appearance on Channels Television’s Politics Today, where he described Obi as “a fantastic gentleman; clear in his head” but questioned the viability of his proposed single-term presidency.

The party maintained that Obi’s single-term proposal was designed to shift the focus of presidential leadership from the duration of stay in office to measurable achievements and effective delivery of campaign promises.

Describing the pledge as a performance commitment, He said, “Section 135(2) of the 1999 Constitution provides that a President shall leave office after four years and may seek a further four years. In law, ‘may’ is permissive, not mandatory. A single term is therefore constitutional. It is not a gamble.

“Nigeria already tested an eight-year tenure between 2015 and 2023. The result was rising inflation, a weakened naira, soaring public debt, widespread poverty, and insecurity across the country. That is the real balance sheet of prolonged tenure without performance.

“Peter Obi’s offer is a performance bond, not a gamble. He has pledged to serve one term, to be judged strictly by results, and to hand over power in 2031 in recognition that it is the turn of the North. This is sacrifice for national stability.”

The Director-General noted that Nigeria’s governance challenges were not necessarily the result of insufficient time in office, but the failure of successive administrations to utilise available opportunities to deliver meaningful development.

“Leadership is measured by impact, not duration. Nigeria’s problem has never been insufficient time. It has been the repeated failure to use time well. Mr. Obi proposes to reverse that culture: one term dedicated entirely to delivery,”

Abdulkarim challenged Nigerians to assess the proposal from the perspective of accountability, insisting that a leader willing to limit his tenure despite being constitutionally eligible for another term was making a significant commitment to national service.

“When a man entitled to eight years voluntarily chooses four and invites the nation to judge him by results, he is not gambling. He is sacrificing,” the statement said.

The NDC said that Obi’s proposed single-term presidency should be understood as a time-bound commitment to national recovery and responsible leadership, adding, “This is not a gamble. It is a rescue mission with a deadline.”
