For now, the election has settled the question of how Israelis voted, but not who will govern them. A source familiar with the negotiations concluded: "Whoever manages to forge new partnerships will move forward. Whoever doesn't will remain stuck."

World.title: Dem operative admits Ilhan Omar case has legs as liberal firewall begins to crack: 'I'm not stupid'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A prominent Minnesota Democrat who served in the state's House of Representatives revealed on Thursday he believes the federal probe into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has legitimacy.

It's the latest signal that the political dam may be breaking as scandals and investigations into the congresswoman continue to pile up.

"Democrats should understand that the allegation is almost certainly true—whatever conclusion they draw from that point could vary—and her denials calling it a right-wing, Islamophobic or racist conspiracy are almost certainly not," Joe Radinovich posted on X in reference to the claims that Omar married her brother as part of an alleged fraudulent immigration scheme.

Radinovich, who served as a Minnesota state representative from 2013 to 2015 as a member of the Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party (DFL), added to his post that, in addition to the probe into her immigration status, the investigation into her finances could also be problematic.

OBAMA ADMIN FIRST LAUNCHED THE INVESTIGATION INTO ILHAN OMAR'S ALLEGED BROTHER MARRIAGE

"And then I’d be very, very careful about how I qualified on allegations around her finances—where her defense looks similar and where no meaningful questions have been answered publicly, and where any objective look at the evidence doesn’t look…great," the former state representative said.

Radinovich, a well-connected DFL operative with ties to the party’s state, federal and Minneapolis political establishments, managed Democrat Rick Nolan’s 2016 congressional campaign, ran Jacob Frey’s successful 2017 campaign for Minneapolis mayor and later served as Frey’s chief of staff. He also won the DFL nomination for Minnesota’s 8th Congressional District in 2018 before losing to Republican Pete Stauber.

Briana Rose Lee, a Minneapolis DFL activist who served as an operations director for Omar’s campaign operation, responded to the post calling it a "witch hunt."

"Joe. You aren’t stupid," she wrote. "You know this is a baseless and manufactured witch hunt. I’m actually surprised to see this from you. It’s a new low."

NEARLY 40 HOUSE DEMS SKIP EFFORT TO END ILHAN OMAR IMMIGRATION PROBE

Radinovich stood by his comments.

"You’re right," Radinovich wrote. "I’m not stupid. I believe the Trump DOJ has next to no credibility and that it’s unclear to me the timing of the raid was appropriate—though it’s notable a DC judge signed off on it—but I’m pretty confident this specific allegation is true."

Radinovich’s post is the latest example of the scrutiny surrounding Omar’s legal issues not being confined to conservative media or the MAGA base.

Outlets including the New York Times, MSNBC, NBC News and The Associated Press have reported on evidence suggesting Omar’s marriage and citizenship may have been fraudulent, although no criminal charges have been filed against the Minnesota congresswoman.

Omar's Washington, D.C., home was raided by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) on Oct. 12, 2026. HSI is the chief investigative arm of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). Her passport, phone and computer were seized during the early-morning operation.

Fox News later reported that investigators are in possession of Omar's DNA. Omar's sister, Sahra Noor, voluntarily submitted to questioning shortly after the raid, skipping out on her book tour for a "family emergency."

Sources confirmed to Fox News Digital that the raid stemmed from an investigation into whether Omar or her late father, Nur Mohamed, fraudulently filled out her citizenship paperwork decades ago. The investigation, the sources noted, could lead to the congresswoman's denaturalization.

But questions about whether Omar allegedly married her brother, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, in a fraudulent immigration scheme have also arisen. Omar has been plagued by the accusation for a decade, since she first ran for Minnesota state representative in 2016.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Court filings from the U.S. Attorney's Office in the District of Columbia referred to Omar as "Ilhan Omar Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Omar," suggesting that she shares a surname with the man she married in 2009. Ahmed Nur Said Elmi is a British citizen. Sources later told Fox News Digital that Ilhan Omar is not the Somali-born congresswoman's "real name."

Omar's office has consistently denied the immigration fraud allegation, characterizing it as a right-wing smear. Most recently, she has said that the renewed scrutiny is the product of a political "vendetta" by President Donald Trump.

But Thursday, Fox News Digital confirmed that former President Barack Obama's administration opened a probe into the allegedly fraudulent marriage in 2016. One source told Fox News Digital that the investigation remained open until 2021, when it was closed by the Biden administration. The Times reported that investigators believed the statute of limitations on a potential crime had passed.

Omar's campaign attacked Radinovich in a Friday morning comment to Fox News Digital.

"Joe is a deeply troubled individual whose demons have sadly manifested as an irrational obsession with Congresswoman Omar after managing two losing campaigns against her," the campaign said. "His claims are false, biased, and without any evidence. While he was once seen as a rising star within the party, Joe is now widely recognized as a shill for Republican and Corporate money."

World.title: Texas' red wall facing its biggest threat in decades as Republicans scramble to defend it
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

DALLAS — Democrats see a rare opening in Texas, and James Talarico is giving them their clearest shot in years at turning the state blue. If he pulls off the upset, the former teacher and Presbyterian seminarian could knock the first brick loose in Texas’ red wall.

The polling and fundraising figures help explain why Democrats see that possibility.

To put it in perspective, Talarico’s polling leads are wider than those recorded against Ted Cruz in 2018, when Beto O’Rourke came closer than any Democrat in decades to winning a Texas Senate race. And the enthusiasm on the ground from those who spoke with Fox News Digital backs up the numbers.

DEEP IN TRUMP COUNTRY, A NEW GENERATION REVEALS THE DIVIDE BEHIND TEXAS’ TIGHT SENATE RACE

What's more, Talarico’s campaign raised $64 million from July through September, more than three times Trump-backed candidate Ken Paxton’s $18 million haul over the same period. Since launching his campaign, Talarico has raised more than $146 million.

But Paxton, currently the state's attorney general, has enjoyed Republican outside groups pouring more than $200 million into Texas to support him, nearly all of it bankrolled by Elon Musk, the world’s richest man. Additionally, MAGA Inc., President Donald Trump’s principal super PAC, has spent another $33.7 million on ads backing Paxton, according to AdImpact.

At his Dallas rally on Thursday, Talarico underscored that divide by casting the race as a David and Goliath fight, telling supporters they were his weapon against powerful interests.

"David wasn’t as big or as strong as Goliath. He didn’t have as many weapons, but he had hope. He had faith, and he had a slingshot," he said. "Dallas, you are my slingshot. The people of Texas are my slingshot."

Talarico's momentum has also shown up on the campaign trail.

'That’s a lot of Talafreakos in one room'

Earlier this week, Talarico hopscotched across Texas, stopping in El Paso before holding events in Midland and Amarillo and drawing a larger-than-expected crowd in deep-red Lubbock on Tuesday.

Meanwhile, Trump campaigned with Paxton about four miles away that same night, shifting his rally time so it overlapped with Talarico’s event.

The dueling rallies put the race’s divide on display. Talarico’s campaign said more than 4,000 people signed up for his Lubbock rally, prompting a move to a larger venue.

"I know that we’re not the only show in town tonight, and I appreciate all 4,000 of you that showed up here this evening," Talarico said at the Fiesta Center in Lubbock on Oct. 27. "That’s a lot of Talafreakos in one room."

The Democratic candidate and his supporters have embraced the moniker "Talafreako," a nickname first given to him as a derogatory dig by Republicans and President Trump.

Voters at Talarico’s rallies in Lubbock told Fox News Digital that Trump’s repeated Texas visits signaled Republican anxiety, while Paxton backers remained confident the state would stay red after a costly and contentious primary that saw Republicans divided over Paxton and sitting Sen. John Cornyn, who was ultimately ousted in the May runoff.

"Trump’s in Lubbock? Trump’s in Lubbock, Texas? He’s scared, he is scared," one supporter told Fox News Digital.

Natalie, from Friona, called Trump’s same-day rally a sign Republicans were "nervous."

"I think it’s performative, like to come the exact same day as he is here," she said.

Jenny, from Brownsville, told Fox News Digital outside Trump and Paxton's rally that the race was "not close" and she predicted that "Paxton will wipe the floor" with Talarico.

DUELING RALLIES THRUST DEEP-RED LONE STAR TOWN INTO THE CENTER OF THE POLITICAL UNIVERSE

Beyond the rally crowds, some Talarico supporters in Dallas and Lubbock said Paxton’s past legal controversies and impeachment by the Texas House shaped their views of the Republican nominee.

"We’re here in support of honesty, decency and integrity," Lori, a Dallas voter who has voted Republican in the past, told Fox News Digital. "That’s what we like to see in a candidate, and we think Talarico is all that in one."

George, a lifelong Texan at the Dallas rally, said years of watching Texas politics had become "heartbreaking" and called Talarico "a breath of fresh air."

In Lubbock, Georgia cited several of Talarico’s policies and called him "authentic." She also said his lack of an indictment was a plus, contrasting him with Paxton.

MEET THE VOTERS WHO COULD BREAK THE GOP’S DECADES-LONG GRIP ON A REPUBLICAN STRONGHOLD

Elias, a nurse from Lubbock, described Paxton as a weak leader.



"He had a chance to kind of redeem himself despite his ugly past, but he’s not a man, he can’t stand up for himself. He needs daddy Trump to come and support him."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

With Election Day on Nov. 3, the question is whether Talarico can turn rally crowds and a polling lead into a historic win. A victory would crack the GOP’s decades-long grip on Texas. A loss would leave Democrats still searching for a path to turn the state blue.

– Jayson asks: A buddy of mine writes a mailbag column for a website. He said that occasionally, he will get emails from "psychos" who flip on him for not reading their questions. Have you ever received that kind of junk since starting Screencaps? If you do, do you answer them back, or simply ignore them?

Kinsey: I've never had emailers turn heel because I wouldn't publish their emails, but I've had guys who claimed to be fans and loyal readers who turned out to be total scumbags, especially after I left Busted Coverage and joined Clay Travis here at OutKick. There have been guys who felt like I should've given them freebies that brands used to send to me.

As for a--hole emailers, I like when people write and snap on me. It's great content. Typically, when I reply to their emails, the people disappear.

WARREN SAPP GETS INTO CONFRONTATION WITH FLORIDA STATE FAN DURING TAILGATE, TIM MCGRAW'S BRONZER & DALE ART

This is a career-low and she's playing COLLEGE golf

A quick Google search reveals that Elizabethtown College was having revenue trouble in 2024 when the school cut 13 faculty members. You know what they didn't cut? Women's golf, where members of the team are really killing it out on the links.

Do you let weirdos pick your groceries and dump them into your car?

• Legacy reader Jess in Alabama, who has been emailing longer than pretty much any other OutKick reader, says it's just convenient: The guy who wrote in that only the elderly or disabled should get delivery groceries is forgetting the time in his life with babies. I can get off my lazy ass, but y’all don’t want to see that diaper blowout spill on the aisle next to your shoe or hear the tantrum that happens 1 out of 4 trips. I’ll let the grocery guy pick out a bag of potatoes or mustard or random stuff I grab off the shelf. Then I’ll find time to stock my own meat and fruit when I get a chance. And I am not complaining about my life. I’m very grateful. And very grateful not to ruin your pleasant experience at the grocery store.

SUPERMARKET VOTED BEST GROCERY STORE IN AMERICA AS CUSTOMERS PRAISE MEAL KITS, VARIETY OF OFFERINGS

• Louie in Savannah pushes back on Chris A.'s email: I have been following along with the grocery pick up debate the last few days and have to weigh in, especially after the comment about those that do it are lazy and park in the fire lane.

We use it every week. We are quite able-bodied, just busy as hell.

BABY BOOMERS HATE 10 THINGS ABOUT TODAY'S GROCERY STORES

My wife is the "Food and Beverage Coordinator" in our home and we have been using the Kroger "Click list" just about every week since it became an option years ago. I imagine every store in different parts of the country have varying experiences but there are so many benefits for us to ordering online and picking it up. My wife just submitted ours and I'm picking it up on the way home from work tomorrow. I'll be in the parking lot for no more that 15 minutes total. It's very convenient and actually saves money. There is no impulse buying when you pick it up, only what you ordered. We also aren't bringing our teen and pre-teen sons into the store who are suddenly starving (as always) and now want to throw everything they see into the cart and grab a sushi roll to devour while walking around. As an added bonus, once every two months or so, the store accidentally loads someone else's partial order into the car and there is no way to tell until you get home. It is like a bonus mystery box. We always call to let them know but they always say to keep the items.

Sure, there are issues with produce or other things sometimes but the customer service personnel are always nice and they will throw a $20 coupon into the next order for the inconvenience. Also, beer and wine purchases are allowed as well so that is one fewer stop while running errands.

With as busy as we are in my house with jobs, school and sports, grocery pick up saves a ton of time!

Everywhere is different I am sure but it's a huge benefit for our house.

World.title: Unhinged judge who called Latino attorney a 'White savior' ordered to undergo psychiatric examination

NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Trump-appointed judge was ordered to undergo a psychiatric examination as part of an ongoing judicial misconduct investigation after she called a Latino attorney a "White savior" who was intimidated by "Black excellence" due to his "White mediocrity" during a hearing.

U.S. District Judge Ada Brown of the Northern District of Texas, who is Black and Native American, was temporarily removed from her docket by the Fifth Circuit Judicial Council earlier this month, following a May judicial-conduct complaint filed by attorney Ezra Young, whose permission to practice before Brown had previously been revoked.

The complaint centered on Brown's rhetoric toward Young during his appearance for a show-case hearing, in which he was facing sanctions over allegations from Brown that he shared sealed court filings online. Young represented a Black law professor who sued Southern Methodist University, alleging she was denied tenure because of discrimination. He joined the case in 2022 and appeared before Brown before the judge barred him from practicing in her courtroom.

OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE TORCHES TRUMP ADMIN IN LATEST COURTROOM SHOWDOWN, REFERS ATTORNEY FOR BAR REVIEW

During the April hearing, Brown railed against Young, accusing him of "bullying" the Black attorneys on the case.

"You’re the White savior, come to save all the stupid Black lawyers in Texas who need your help from New York," Brown later said, according to the transcript obtained by Bloomberg.

Brown repeatedly brought attention to Young's skin color, calling him "White presenting" and "fair-skinned" after Brown told her that he was a Latino.

"I think what’s happening here, quite candidly, is you are very intimidated for some reason, Mr. Young, with Black excellence, in light of your White mediocrity. Yeah. Right?" Brown said. "You should write that down. I mean, you — I’m — you look like a White man, right?"

She also called Young a "Chad" which she said is the male version of "Karen."

"It’s someone who calls the manager when they don’t get their way. They stomp their foot when the rules are supposed to apply to them, right?" Brown said.

OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE WITH TIES TO ANTI-TRUMP CONSPIRACY THEORY HIT WITH MISCONDUCT COMPLAINT

Brown also accused Young of sensationalizing the case after reading a news article that quoted his brief and referenced another law professor’s comparison of the Black professor’s treatment in the tenure dispute to a "lynching."

"And so when I read a headline — a sensationalized, very racialized headline that says, ‘it’s like I’ve been lynched,’ and it’s literally got no connection to this case, I have to ask you, Mr. Social Media, Main Character Chad, White Hero, Savior, Loves to Help Black People Be An Ally, where the lynching in this case came from?" Brown said.

The release of the April court hearing transcripts comes as Brown shared with lawyers, judges and several media outlets via email of Young's complaint and her response.

Meanwhile, in a July 28 filing responding to Young's complaint, Brown stood by her conduct.

"I do not believe my demeanor was inappropriate at any time, especially during the candid conversations about race," Brown wrote.

World.title: Binance pledges to cover billions in stolen assets after hack revives crypto fears
World.content:
A record-setting cyberattack targeting the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange rocked the digital assets industry Friday, delivering another blow to a sector already struggling to achieve mainstream adoption.

The exchange, Binance, announced late Thursday that more than $6 billion appeared to have moved through wallets connected to a security breach. Around $3 billion of that had potentially been located and frozen across several exchanges, though it was not immediately clear if those funds were recoverable.

Early Friday, the company said it had set aside $5 billion to make affected users whole, and was working with partners to purchase an additional $1.34 billion to cover the total amount believed to have been stolen.

The hack is the latest setback for crypto, which continues to reckon with a reputation for being too volatile — and too vulnerable to criminal activity — for widespread use. The scale of the hack echoes collapse of crypto exchange FTX, which, though not the result of a cyberattack, caused billions in losses.

The renewed doubts were reflected in Bitcoin’s value Friday, which fell more than 5% overnight to approximately $77,000, accelerating its month-long downturn. Other affected cryptocurrencies fell as much as 9%.

The crypto industry was already reeling from the failure in Congress of the Clarity Act, a bill that would have granted comprehensive legal protections for crypto assets in the U.S.

Despite bipartisan support for the core elements of the legislation, its passage was torpedoed by a battle over conflict-of-interest rules for elected officials, notably President Donald Trump.

The president has disclosed in filings that he earned more than $1 billion from crypto last year.

The Binance hack stands to prolong this reckoning, experts said.

“There will be an imperative for Binance to cover losses not only for its own reputation and value, but I expect there will be a level of co-operation within the space as they look at the collective reputational harm this may, rightly or wrongly, cause to the sector,” Laura Clatworthy, head of digital assets at Edwin Coe said in a statement.

That cooperation was seen in the immediate reaction of other mainstream crypto players.

Crypto firms Tether and Circle, which operate the two-largest stablecoins, worked quickly to freeze assets implicated in the hack.

However, U.S. blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs estimates that $2.4 billion in Bitcoin and Ethereum will never be recovered.

As of Friday morning, the hack’s origins remained murky. The whole heist unfolded in just 20 minutes starting at approximately 4 p.m. ET Thursday.

Binance initially said the attack involved a compromised laptop.

“However, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” ‌it said in a statement on X, without elaborating.

Multiple blockchain analysis firms said the hack had attributes associated with previous operations believed to have been carried out by North Korean actors.

Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said Binance’s investigation had not yet identified the attackers.

At least one prominent tech CEO could not resist making light of the situation. Elon Musk left a “yikes” emoji in response to an X user who noted that the collapsed crypto exchange FTX had initially also told users their funds were safe amid a wave of losses.

Binance co-founder CZ Zhao responded:“Elon, have a lot of respect for you, but bad time to troll. Please stop.”

Zhao noted that his SpaceX shares — the product of a Binance-related $500 million investment in Twitter, were now worth more than $1 billion.

“Would appreciate if you show a little support. Thanks!”

World.title: Trump cancels weekend rallies in Iowa and Kansas in favor of holding tele-rallies
World.content:
President Donald Trump announced Thursday he is canceling his rallies in Kansas and Iowa this weekend, where he had been set to stump for GOP candidates in competitive races, opting instead to do tele-rallies.

The rallies were to have been part of his planned midterm blitz, in which he said he would travel to 35 places across the country to help raise turnout for Republican candidates.

Trump has repeatedly touted what he believes is the positive impact of his rallies on GOP candidates, going as far as to suggest that his presence in battleground states has boosted Republicans in the polls.

But his tune appeared to change Thursday after his cancellations. Trump said he didn’t “feel I have to go to Kansas,” adding that he thinks Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, who’s locked in a tight race with Democrat Adam Hamilton, “is doing well.”

Concerns over high costs connected to the Iran war have helped turn the race into a toss-up in a state that hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate for nearly a century.

Trump, who has campaigned at 25 rallies in the past month, has admitted that the blitz has not been “easy,” saying through a hoarse voice Monday that “God didn’t make your vocal cords to do a rally every day.”

But he insisted Thursday that he felt “perfect” and lashed out at a reporter who pressed him about whether the rally cancellation in Kansas was tied to his health.

“You’ve been following me for two weeks. I feel perfect. You are disgusting. Put yourself in shape. You look like hell,” Trump said to the journalist.

He canceled in Iowa hours after that interaction, after a White House official and a person familiar confirmed that Trump’s appearance was off.

The Republican National Committee said in a news release that the rallies were canceled with the goal of “maximizing opportunities for President Donald J. Trump to speak to voters across the country.”

GOP operatives in Iowa, where all congressional races this year except one are competitive, told NBC News that in-person rallies would have been helpful. Trump’s rally Saturday would have been in Dubuque, in the contested 2nd Congressional District.

“A tele-rally will be helpful in boosting turnout, but an in-person rally would have been really helpful,” an operative said.

Another operative said he “would love to have the president,” but he said, “Iowa’s in pretty good shape.”

Trump is aiming to hold “more than 20” tele-rallies by Election Day, two White House officials said Thursday.

He is still scheduled to hold an event in Daytona Beach, Florida, on Friday. He will be campaigning for Republican Rep. Randy Fine and Sen. Ashley Moody, who are running in races rated solidly Republican by the nonpartisan Cook Political Report.

No events have been announced for Monday.

World.title: Criminal probe launched into alleged noncitizen voting in California
World.content:
The Justice Department has opened a criminal investigation in California as it continues its effort to prove that as many as 20,000 noncitizens are on the state’s voter rolls, a U.S. official confirmed to NBC News on Thursday.

The official said the Justice Department has issued federal grand jury subpoenas to local election officials across the state. It’s unclear how many subpoenas were sent out and exactly who received them.

The New York Times first reported the new subpoenas.

In response to an inquiry from NBC News on Thursday, the Justice Department declined to comment on “leaks about alleged grand jury subpoenas” but said federal courts have said voting unlawfully results in criminal exposure.

The U.S. official told NBC News that receiving a subpoena doesn’t mean a person is necessarily a target, just that the person may have information relevant to the investigation. The official added that the Justice Department rarely subpoenas people it intends to charge with crimes.

The new subpoenas follow a federal judge’s ruling Wednesday to deny the Trump administration’s request to segregate 20,000 mail ballots from alleged noncitizens in California, calling into question the accuracy of the administration’s process to identify such people.

Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder and County Clerk Dean Logan touted the decision Thursday.

“At every step, the U.S. Department of Justice has taken a confrontational, adversarial approach. Election officials are acting in accordance with state and federal law,” Logan said in a statement, adding that “clear court rulings” by both the federal judge and an appeals court have confirmed that.

Last week, Justice Department officials sent letters to 57 of California’s 58 counties warning local election officials to cooperate with federal investigations into illegal voting or face investigations themselves.

The Justice Department expanded the efforts this week, sending similar letters to officials in Washington state and asking its secretary of state to review a list of 400 registrants whom it believes to be noncitizens. It also asked that the state sequester any ballots those people cast.

The Trump administration faced two legal setbacks in the efforts this week when an appeals court denied its request Monday to block California from counting mail ballots from the alleged noncitizens and a federal judge Wednesday rejected its request to segregate those ballots.

The Trump administration has pressured state officials to assist in investigations of allegations of voter fraud for months, having sued 30 states and the District of Columbia for refusing to hand over their voter registration list data.

While noncitizens can appear on voter rolls, it is rare. In addition, newly naturalized citizens are often mistakenly flagged as noncitizens, especially since there is no comprehensive list of U.S. citizens.

Election experts have argued that the Trump administration’s lawsuits rely on flimsy legal arguments, particularly as the Justice Department doesn’t have legal authority to intervene in election certification.

World.title: Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad against Amy Acton’s ends TV run
World.content:
Republican Vivek Ramaswamy’s ad featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton, his Democratic opponent for Ohio governor, is leaving the state’s airwaves, the Ramaswamy campaign confirmed Thursday.

The ad, which debuted last week to wide bipartisan condemnation, is rotating out after completing its intended run, according to the campaign. The campaign has other ads running in the final days of the race.

In the now-completed ad campaign, Donna Arthur — the mother whom Acton says she has not seen since her then-stepfather was charged with raping her as a young child nearly 50 years ago — calls her daughter a liar and urges Ohioans not to vote for her. The ad does not address details of the rape case. But critics panned the Ramaswamy campaign’s decision to use Arthur as a character witness and dredge up painful family history.

“I’m learning things even about my childhood right now that I did not know,” Acton told reporters Tuesday during a campaign stop in Youngstown. “I think it is despicable. … I’m sure someday I’ll unpack everything that I’m learning here. But I’m just grateful to Ohioans and everyone, really so much support and love that we’ve received.”

The Ramaswamy campaign said last week that the ad would be backed by $4 million in airtime. It began as a minutelong spot but was eventually shortened to a 30-second version. Many, including term-limited Gov. Mike DeWine, a Republican who has endorsed Ramaswamy, had called on him to take down the ad.

“Vivek Ramaswamy should never have run his despicable ad in the first place, and it’s totally unsurprising that he took it off the air in the most cowardly way possible, without even the hint of an apology to Dr. Acton, her family, or to the people of Ohio,” Acton campaign spokesperson Addie Bullock said in a statement Thursday.

The Columbus Dispatch first reported that the ad was ending its run.

“It ran to completion, and we’ve put up four other ads,” Ramaswamy said at a Thursday campaign stop, according to the newspaper.

World.title: Christa Pike says there is ‘pain in my mind and in my soul’ one month after her failed execution
World.content:
One month ago, Christa Pike survived what seemed impossible: a lethal injection in which two rounds of the drug had already entered her body. Medics took her from the Tennessee death chamber and she was placed on a hospital ventilator; she regained consciousness days later.

Now, Pike, the sole woman on Tennessee’s death row, says she is healing in a prison medical ward, but that the pain she still feels extends far beyond the physical.

“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain,” Pike, 50, said in her first public statement, which her legal team shared Friday. “My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul.”

Christa Pike appears in court in Nashville, Tenn., on April 12, 2012. Dipti Vaidya / USA Today via Reuters

Pike, who has been on death row for three decades for murdering Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old classmate, was discharged from the hospital and returned to her Nashville prison 10 days after the attempt to execute her Sept. 30 went awry. Her arms were left swollen and bruised after the execution team tried to insert intravenous lines to deliver two rounds of the lethal drug pentobarbital into her bloodstream, her legal team said. Medical experts have suggested Pike’s injuries could have been the result of incorrect needle insertion or the chemical leaking into her tissue.

Before she lost consciousness, she complained that her arm felt as if it was going to burst and that “it burns,” her lawyers said.

“I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger,” Pike said in her statement. “But healing is not the same as being okay.”

On the day her execution was scheduled, Pike said, she walked into the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution at peace and prepared to die after her final days were spent saying her goodbyes to her loved ones. At the execution chamber, she told witnesses that she was leaving them in “loving kindness,” in reference to a Buddhist prayer her spiritual adviser had her recite.

“I had not contemplated life beyond that night,” Pike added, “and I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position.”

A spokeswoman for the Tennessee Department of Correction on Friday declined to comment about Pike’s case, and the office of Gov. Bill Lee could not immediately be reached for comment.

World.title: Tech stocks crushed as Nasdaq tumbles more than 600 points
World.content:
The Nasdaq Composite Index tumbled 610 points, or 2.3%, in early trading on Friday after disappointing earnings reports from Alphabet, Amazon and Intel renewed fears about the prospects for artificial intelligence.

Intel's stock plunged nearly 29% once trading opened, while Alphabet shares continued to wobble after the company's Class A stock slid more than 12% on Thursday, its worst day since the company went public as Google in 2004. The drop erased roughly $500 billion in Alphabet's market value.

"This has been one of the worst tech earnings seasons in memory, with underwhelming results from a slew of very prominent companies," market analyst Adam Crisafulli, head of Vital Knowledge, said in a research note.

The S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average slumped 1.2% and 0.4%, respectively, after the opening bell.

The weaker-than-expected tech earnings reports are heightening concerns that massive investments in AI will not generate the payoff Wall Street expects. Investors are also worried about the debt companies are taking on to finance data center capital expenditures and whether that debt is sustainable.

Investors have been banking on the explosive growth of AI, which has propelled the stock market to record highs, to continue to dominate. However, that sentiment is now under threat. In a report earlier this week, Ulrike Hoffmann-Burchardi, CIO Americas and global head of equities for UBS' Chief Investment Office, advised clients to "diversify beyond AI."

"While we maintain a constructive outlook on the structural growth of the AI theme, high expectations and potentially wide differences in company outcomes underscore the risks of single-stock concentration," she said. "We think investors should ensure their equity portfolios are broadly diversified."

World.title: $6.3 billion Binance hack likely work of North Korea, experts say
World.content:
A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm said a North Korean cyber unit was likely behind an attack that stole $6.3 billion from Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.

Binance said on Friday that deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals were suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two. The company, which worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets, also said it will cover all customer losses.

In a social media post, Binance said that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, while a subsequent probe uncovered additional "points of breach."

Crypto industry analysts say the hack against Binance is the largest cyber heist ever.

What is TraderTraitor?

In a post on its website Thursday, tech security firm TRM Labs attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," TRM said.

"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," the firm said. That would make the hack the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, it said.

In 2025, TraderTraitor also targeted another crypto exchange, Bybit, in an attack resulting in a $1.5 billion loss, according to the FBI.

"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," TRM said.

Jonathan Levin, co-founder and CEO of blockchain research firm Chainalysis, also said on social media that the Binance hack was "likely done" by TraderTraitor.

Analysts believe that TraderTraitor members are part of a wider North Korean hacking unit known as Lazarus Group, which targets multiple institutions across government, finance and other fields, according to the U.S. Treasury Department.

The Justice Department alleged in 2018 that the Lazarus Group was responsible for an attack on Sony Pictures Entertainment four years earlier that leaked a massive amount of sensitive company data online.

Working "around the clock"

Binance said on social media that its "teams are working around the clock to resolve this issue safely and thoroughly. We are working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of these criminals and bring them to justice."

Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.

In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world.

Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as the company's CEO. President Trump pardoned Zhao in 2025.

Zhao posted Thursday on social media that "User funds are safe!" but added that the theft "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that, while he no longer manages Binance, "As a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."

The event, meanwhile, also raises questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.

"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.

Binance said on social media it had "found no evidence of any wallet private key leak" and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

World.title: Christa Pike speaks after botched execution: "Don't know what's next"
World.content:
Christa Pike, who survived a botched execution attempt in Tennessee last month, said Friday that she's been in pain every moment since she woke up confused in the hospital.

Pike said she'd entered the execution chamber having said her goodbyes, adding, "I had not contemplated life beyond that night."

"Several days later I woke up alone in a hospital confused and in pain," she said in a statement dictated to her lawyers. "There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul."

Her statement was released exactly one month after surviving the execution attempt. It is the first public comment she has made since.

Pike, 50, was given two doses of a lethal injection drug, but her legal team confirmed shortly after the failed procedure that, in an unprecedented turn, she was alive and had been hospitalized. One witness, a media attendee, noted she could be heard loudly snoring about one hour after the procedure had started. She was then taken by ambulance to an area hospital.

Pike's attorneys said earlier this month she had pneumonia, a blood clot, couldn't swallow and was unable to move her arms or hands once she regained consciousness in the hospital. One of Pike's attorneys told reporters during a news conference that her hands "looked like if you were to blow up a surgical glove." She was able to begin walking soon after, though, and was discharged back to the prison for further treatment on Oct. 10.

"I don't know why I survived that night. I don't know what comes next," Pike said in the statement Friday. "Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time."

Pike was convicted in 1995 of the brutal murder of her classmate, 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer. Court filings show that Pike, then 18, tortured and killed Slemmer, slashing her with a meat cleaver and box cutter for up to an hour in a wooded part of the University of Tennessee campus, with help from her boyfriend and a friend.

Christa Pike survived a botched lethal injection in Tennessee on Sept. 30, 2026. Tennessee Department of Correction via AP

While other executions have been halted, generally they involved difficulties with finding a vein for the lethal injection. Pike is the only person known to have survived an execution attempt in the U.S. where the drug was administered, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

It is believed Pike's veins may have ruptured before she was injected with pentobarbital, according to court documents cited by The Associated Press. The execution team used about 10 needles and tried several IV sites on both arms, her lawyer said in the filing.

"I am searching for meaning in what happened to me," Pike said. "One thing that has given me strength is the extraordinary love and support I have received from people around the world. I am overwhelmed by the kindness and prayers of people I have known for years and complete strangers who have never met me."

Pike's failed execution has raised questions about the lethal injection protocol in Tennessee. Hers was the second issue this year in the state. Tony Carruthers could not be executed after the execution team members spent more than an hour trying to establish an IV line for the lethal injection. The governor granted a one-year reprieve on his execution.

CBS News reviewed the state's lethal injection protocols going back to 2007 and found that over the years the protocols grew increasingly vague.

It remains unclear what will happen with Pike, even a month after the botched execution. Gov. Bill Lee, who has paused executions in the state through the end of the year, was asked about the next steps for Pike on Wednesday.

"I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts," he told reporters during a press conference.

Pike's lawyers successfully petitioned the court to preserve all evidence related to the botched execution in a hearing on Oct. 7. A follow-up hearing on Oct. 23 was canceled as the judge considers multiple motions in the case. Pike's lawyer, Steve Ferrell, urged the governor to commute her sentence during an interview with "CBS Mornings" days after her botched execution.

"The least that could happen now is that we at least take death off the table and start looking for what the future could be for her," Ferrell, of the Federal Defender Services of Eastern Tennessee, told "CBS Mornings" on Oct. 5.

One-third of Americans back a second attempt at executing Pike, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll from earlier this month.

World.title: Netanyahu's party claims Israel's election was stolen. Now what?
World.content:
Tel Aviv — Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his Likud party alleged Thursday that Israel's election earlier in the week was stolen by Arab-majority parties, helped by foreign funding that amounted to vote-buying, as final results showed Netanyahu's bloc has lost its majority in Israel's parliament, the Knesset.

Israel's Arab-majority parties had their highest turnout ever in Tuesday's election, winning an unprecedented 19 of the Knesset's 120 seats. Their success is one of the main reasons Netanyahu's bloc lost its majority and can't now form a new government.

The final election results show the far-right wing bloc's share of Knesset seats fell from 68 to 53.

Israel's Arab minority, also called Palestinian citizens of Israel, makes up about 20% of the country's population.

"Israel's elections have been stolen," Netanyahu's Likud party declared in a statement Thursday, claiming "an attack on democracy aimed at leading to a foreign takeover of the Knesset, the Islamization of Israel, and the overthrow of the right-wing government to cause a withdrawal and defeat of the IDF (Israeli military) on all fronts — first and foremost, Iran."

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks to supporters after polls closed in a national parliamentary election, at the Likud party headquarters in Jerusalem, Israel, Oct. 28, 2026. Amnon Gutman/Bloomberg/Getty

The four parties that make up the main bloc opposing Netanyahu won 48 seats, so they would need some support from the Arab parties to try to form a coalition government, assuming none of the lawmakers currently aligned with Netanyahu's bloc defect.

The heads of Israel's two biggest Arab parties, which collectively won 19 seats, have said they would be willing to help the main opposition bloc oust Netanyahu from power.

Most of the Jewish-led parties that oppose Netanyahu vowed before the election not to rely on support from Arab parties to form a government, however, leaving a question mark over whether they might now be willing to cooperate to build a coalition to unseat the incumbent prime minister.

"No basis to the claims regarding a systematic compromise"

The Shin Bet, Israel's internal security agency, said it had opened an investigation into possible foreign influence in the election, but the scope of that investigation has not been made clear.

"An investigation of this type is also focused and bounded, and does not cast aspersions or place blame on an entire sector that went out to vote democratically and legally," the agency said in a Thursday statement.

The Acting Director-General of the Central Elections Committee, Din Livne, said in a letter to a committee member on Thursday that "there is no basis to the claims regarding a systematic compromise of the integrity of the elections."

Israel media reports said one of the allegations the Shin Bet investigation would consider was whether Qatar had sent money to Arab parties in order to increase turnout among Arab Israeli voters.

Qatar's foreign ministry has denied the accusation.

"We categorically deny allegations that Qatar has interfered in Israeli elections or funded any activities intended to influence their outcome," ministry spokesperson Majid Al-Ansari said. "Qatar should not be used as a scapegoat for the political failures of certain Israeli politicians."

"An improper influence operation?"

While vote counting is now officially complete, the election results must still be certified and sent to President Issac Herzog before a new parliament can be sworn in and the process of forming a new government begins.

Gadi Eisenkot, head of the centrist Yashar party and the top candidate to replace Netanyahu as prime minister, said he was worried that Netanyahu could be using the allegation of a stolen election to justify delaying or disqualifying the results.

"Netanyahu, who has accustomed himself to dealing with reality through lies, consciousness engineering, and the spreading of chaos, is leading alongside his partners an improper influence operation on the Israeli public aimed at delaying the publication of the election results on time and creating fictitious delegitimization of the activity of the 26th Knesset," Eisenkot said Thursday in a social media post.

Former Israeli military chief and Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot gestures as he addresses supporters at an election-night rally in Tel Aviv, Israel, in the early hours of Oct. 28, 2026. Tomer Neuberg/Middle East Images/AFP/Getty

Once the new Knesset is sworn in — even without a new government decided on — Eisenkot's bloc, along with the Arab parties, could begin passing laws given that they will control a majority in the parliament.

Netanyahu, who President Trump endorsed enthusiastically, will remain in his post as a caretaker prime minister until a new government is formed. If the parties cannot negotiate to form a new coalition government, then the country would have to hold the election all over again, and Netanyahu would remain the prime minister in the interim.

World.title: Pope Leo becomes first pontiff to vote in a U.S. election
World.content:
Pope Leo XIV has become the first pontiff to vote in a U.S. election. The Vatican confirmed Friday that the American-born pope submitted a mail-in ballot in his native Chicago ahead of November's midterm elections, citing his longstanding belief in civic participation.

The pope, formerly Cardinal Robert Prevost, "has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen, whenever he was eligible to do so," the Holy See press office said.

"The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," the Vatican said in a statement.

The Chicago Sun-Times first reported Leo's vote, quoting the chief of staff at the Will County clerk's office, who said the pope, registered at a New Lenox address, requested a mail-in ballot on Oct. 3. This was just days before his recent lung cancer surgery.

The pope has been recovering and resuming his activities at the Vatican after being released from the hospital Oct. 17 and is moving ahead with plans for a trip to South America next month.

Pope Leo XIV arrives to lead his traditional Wednesday General Audience in St. Peter's Square. Stefano Costantino/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images

Last month, Leo told a general audience at the Vatican that the faithful should leave behind "all passivity and indifference" toward current events.

"We cannot remain as unengaged spectators; rather, we must listen with our hearts, allow ourselves to be challenged, and become involved," the pope said on Sept. 2 in St. Peter's Square, according to the Catholic News Service. "With Christ and sustained by the power of his Spirit, believers are called to take on the burdens of their brothers and sisters, especially those who are crushed by injustice, discrimination and violence."

The pope has a long history of civic engagement in the U.S., the Vatican said, confirming that during his nearly two decades as a missionary then bishop in Peru, Leo voted whenever he was eligible. He holds U.S. and Peruvian citizenship.

According to records from the Illinois State Board of Elections, the pope, as Robert Prevost, was registered to vote in Cook County. The Associated Press reports he previously voted in five primary elections since 2000 — on the Democratic ballots in 2008 and 2019 and Republican ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016.

Illinois has closed primaries, which means voters must declare a party preference to receive a ballot. No such declaration is required in general elections.

The pope submitted ballots in every general election since 2000, except in 2020 and 2022, the AP reported, citing Illinois election records.

World.title: Blockchain intelligence firms link North Korea to $6.3B hack on Binance
World.content:
Blockchain intelligence firms link North Korea to $6.3B hack on Binance

toggle caption i Matt Slocum/AP

A U.S.-based blockchain intelligence firm says a North Korean unit was likely behind the hack that impacted more than $6 billion on Binance, the world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange.

Binance said it worked with blockchain partners to freeze roughly $3 billion in affected assets. It said Friday that it was beginning to recover assets for users.

The cryptocurrency exchange said deposits were unaffected, while withdrawals have been suspended and are expected to resume in the next day or two. It said it will cover all losses.

The company said on X that an initial investigation suggested the incident may have involved a compromised laptop, but that a subsequent investigation uncovered additional "points of breach."

Sponsor Message

TRM, in a post on its website Thursday, attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as North Korea's elite hacking unit. "We make this judgment with high confidence," the firm said.

"An attacker moved approximately USD 6.36 billion out of Binance wallets on ten blockchains, most of it in about 20 minutes," TRM said. That would make the hack the largest cryptocurrency theft on record, it said.

In February last year, another cryptocurrency exchange, Bybit, suffered a $1.5 billion hit when it was hacked. The FBI said North Korea and TraderTraitor were responsible for the hack.

"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," TRM said.

Blockchain analysis company Chainalysis also believed the Binance hack was "likely done by DPRK group TraderTraitor," its co-founder and CEO Jonathan Levin wrote on X. DPRK stands for the Democratic People's Republic of Korea, North Korea's official name.

Asked about the potential ties to North Korea, a Binance spokesperson said only that the company is "working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice."

Experts say North Korea has turned to crypto hacking and other illicit cyber activities as a source of badly needed foreign currency to support its troubled economy and fund its nuclear program in the wake of tough U.N. sanctions and other difficulties.

Sponsor Message

In December 2022, South Korea's spy agency said North Korean hackers had stolen an estimated 1.5 trillion won ($1.1 billion) in cryptocurrency and other virtual assets in the past five years, more than half of it in 2022 alone. It said North Korea's capacity to steal digital assets was considered among the best in the world.

Changpeng Zhao, also known as CZ, founded Binance in 2017. In 2023, he pleaded guilty to a felony linked to failing to prevent money laundering on the platform, and stepped down as the company's CEO. U.S. President Donald Trump pardoned Zhao in 2025.

Zhao posted Thursday on X that "User funds are safe!" but added that the theft "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that while he doesn't manage Binance anymore, "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."

The event, meanwhile, also raises questions about why stronger approval controls were not in place, said Kok Tin Gan, cofounder and CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab.

"This looks like one signature that gave the attacker a never-expiring, full-access token to a Binance hot wallet," he said, referring to cryptocurrency wallets that hold users' "private keys," or unique authorizations, digitally and which are connected to the internet.

Binance said on X it had "found no evidence of any wallet private key leak" and that the company would release more technical details when its probe is complete.

World.title: Why is the Cheesecake Factory at the center of the latest culture war?
World.content:
Why is the Cheesecake Factory at the center of the latest culture war?

toggle caption i Kayla Bartkowski/Getty

They say there's no such thing as bad publicity. If that's true it's been a golden week for the Cheesecake Factory restaurant chain.

The furore began when former President Obama, stumping for Democrats in Ohio this week ahead of the midterms, joked about President Trump's White House refurbishments, saying they looked "like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory. Just gold everywhere."

The late Iraqi dictator was known for building lavish palaces, with gold walls, cabinets of gold-plated rifles, a golden throne and of course plenty of depictions of the man himself.

Trump is also well-known for his love of anything gilded and Obama joked he'd been "supergluing gold medallions to the mantel in the Oval Office," while also paving over the Rose Garden and "building a ballroom that's bigger than the White House."

toggle caption i Sue Ogrocki/AP

And the Cheesecake Factory? The beloved U.S. restaurant chain was started in 1978 by David Overton, whose mother reportedly made a fine cheesecake, and now has 218 locations across the country and an annual revenue of $1.03 billion.

Sponsor Message

But it's as well known for its kitschy decor as its food, with The Atlantic writer Elaine Godfrey describing it in an article this week "as if ancient Egypt and Tuscany had a baby in Las Vegas."

Obama first made the "home renovations" remarks at the political rally on Saturday, where he also portrayed the Trump administration as out of touch with ordinary Americans suffering from a cost of living crisis and the economic consequences of the president's war in Iran.

Obama said the Trump administration had resulted in "two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption" and that those at the helm were not "serious people."

toggle caption i Hadi Mizban/AP

The administration was quick to respond, with President Trump defending his taste, saying: "I've taken care of the White House, I've fixed it with the finest artisans in the world."

"The White House was in terrible shape. The White House is now in the best shape it's been since 1792," he told reporters when asked about Obama's quip, adding that Obama was "not a smart guy."

The official White House X account posted a photo of the Cheesecake Factory's famously large menu, saying "Since we're talking about The Cheesecake Factory... The only thing bigger than the menu is the list of President Trump's accomplishments."

Sponsor Message

Allegations of elitism

Vice President Vance reacted by accusing Obama of being out of touch with ordinary Americans. "Obama, without even trying to be, just can't help himself for being super elitist," he wrote on X.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent also sought to capitalize on the backlash, having lunch at a Cheesecake Factory near the White House on Monday. He ate a French Dip Cheeseburger and told journalists afterwards: "I had a great meal, always have a great meal, and I would just tell the Martha's Vineyard set to give it a try," in an apparent reference to the Obamas who are known to holiday on the exclusive island.

toggle caption i Mark Schiefelbein/AP

On the topic of taste in decor, Bessent, who used to manage a hedge fund, also made an apparent jibe about the new Obama Presidential Center in Chicago.

"This is the man who built the museum [that] looks like Darth Vader's tomb," he added.

Obama was undeterred, taking up the theme again at a rally in Georgia on Wednesday, and saying that he was surprised that instead of hitting back on his criticisms about policy and corruption, the White House was more upset about the Cheesecake Factory remark.

"The president wasn't even mad about the Saddam Hussein comparison! That part didn't bother him," said Obama.

"They mobilized a whole of government response to that joke. Not to inflation, but to that joke. The White House even called the Secretary of the Treasury. This is the man who is in charge of the economy. The person who's supposed to be figuring out how to make your life more affordable," he added.

"The guy who's supposed to be figuring out how to lower inflation. And reduce interest rates. They told him he should hold a press conference in front of the Cheesecake Factory."

Sponsor Message

Obama also stressed he had been a proud patron of the restaurant for many years.

"I am the father of two daughters. Do you think I could have survived their childhood without going to the Cheesecake Factory?"

toggle caption i Mariam Zuhaib/AP

Later in the week, restaurants and affordability came up again. Trump told supporters at a political rally in Texas that they could spend the $5,000 he's promised every adult citizen if the Republicans keep Congress on dining out at his Mar-a-Lago club in Florida.

"The problem is that for $5,000, the most you'll be able to buy is a hamburger and maybe a small dessert," Trump joked.

"I'm not even sure you could buy that," he said, before rescinding the advice: "No, don't go there. That's not a good place if you're price-conscious."

World.title: Binance flags 'potential security issue,' says approximately $6.3 billion impacted
World.content:
Binance flags 'potential security issue,' says approximately $6.3 billion impacted

toggle caption i Matt Slocum/AP

LOS ANGELES — Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange, said Thursday it's investigating reports of a potential security issue as its founder said the incident "does look like a hack on Binance." The company said late Thursday the estimated total impact was at more than $6 billion, which could be one of the most significant of such security incidents on record.

It wasn't immediately clear the extent of the damage hackers might have been able to cause, and Binance had not explicitly confirmed that funds had been pilfered. The company said its teams are "working around the clock" to resolve the issue.

"Rest assured that user funds are completely safe," a Binance spokesperson said in a statement.

"Our security teams are reviewing all relevant information with urgency, and we will provide updates through official Binance channels as soon as we have verified information," the statement continued.

Sponsor Message

The company wrote on its X account that the estimated total impact sat at around $6.3 billion. It said it has worked with blockchain partners to freeze affected assets, with roughly $3 billion frozen on-chain so far.

"Binance's initial investigation suggests that the security incident may involve a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop, which allowed an attacker to gain access to a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions," the company wrote.

"We have found no evidence of any wallet private key leak," it added.

Binance said it will share more technical details once the investigation is complete and when the facts are "fully verified."

"Our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets," the company wrote in a separate post earlier Thursday.

Binance also said all deposits and withdrawals are temporarily suspended while it conducts security checks, freezes funds and works with law enforcement.

Stablecoin providers Tether and Circle each said they froze funds Thursday in response to the incident.

Jeremy Allaire, co-founder and CEO of Circle, wrote on X that the company had frozen the equivalent of more than $800 million in currency associated with the incident "in coordination with law enforcement." Tether CEO Paolo Ardoino said on X that the company froze the equivalent of more than $1.5 billion in currency related to "a potential Binance exchange hack."

Sponsor Message

The price of bitcoin dropped 3.2% Thursday evening to under $79,000.

Binance was founded in 2017 by Changpeng Zhao, who in 2023 pleaded guilty to a felony related to his failure to prevent money laundering on the platform and stepped down as CEO. President Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.

Zhao posted on X on Thursday that "User funds are safe!" but added that the incident "does look like a hack on Binance." He added that while he doesn't manage Binance anymore, "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."

Zhao was released from prison last year after being sentenced for violating the Bank Secrecy Act. He was the first person ever sentenced to prison time for violations of that law, which requires U.S. financial institutions to know who their customers are, to monitor transactions and to file reports of suspicious activity. Prosecutors said no one had ever violated the regulations to the extent Zhao did. Zhao and Binance have been key supporters of some of the Trump family's crypto enterprises.

Behind the story

by Rob Stein , NPR's science desk correspondent and senior editor

Mary Long/Getty Images

I've been doing stories about the organ transplantation system for decades. One of the most fundamental guiding ethical principles in organ donation has long been the "dead donor rule." That rule, stated simply, says: Organs should only be retrieved for transplants from a person who is dead, and death should never be accelerated to try to boost the chances their organs will be usable. To make sure that's the case, there's long been a strict firewall between the doctors and nurses trying to save patients in the hospital, and the organ retrieval teams standing by to try to procure their organs.

But over the years, I've heard many stories from family members who nevertheless felt pressured to donate their loved one's organs. So when I got a tip that the Organ Procurement & Transplantation Network, which runs the nation's organ system, was planning to relax that firewall, I instantly knew that was a big story.

I rushed to confirm the documentation that the network's board of directors had indeed endorsed the change, which would go into effect Nov. 18. I then reached out to bioethicists and others for their reaction to this major change. The revision was part of a set of new policies designed to boost donations and improve patient safety. Those changes were spurred by disturbing revelations about mistakes, including patients literally being wheeled into the operating room to remove their organs when they were still alive. Some of the changes were praised as improving safety. But many bioethicists and even some transplant surgeons and patient and organ donation advocates say relaxing the firewall between care and organ retrieval teams is dangerous. The fear is it could lead to families and caregivers discontinuing treatment too soon, and deepening distrust in the organ donation system.

World.title: The two most interesting risks to Anthropic
World.content:
The two most interesting risks to Anthropic

You're reading a newsletter from The Indicator from Planet Money. Once a week, we curate our favorite stories and insights on business, finance, economics and why they matter. Subscribe here to get it in your inbox every Friday.

A TILE GAME is giving a boost to Chinese factories. Our very own Jennifer Pak reported that Chinese manufacturers have not had the easiest few years with U.S. tariffs and the war in Iran pushing up costs. Well, the aged game of Mahjong is giving them a surprising boost. That's because it's having a moment in the U.S. and some entrepreneurial citizens in China are enjoying the benefits. Mahjong sets can sell for like $300-$400 in the States … and want to know how much they cost to make? ~$30. One businessman said he used to make the game primarily for Chinese consumers. Now, every set is exported to the U.S.

toggle caption i Justin Sullivan/Getty Images North America

Coming up:



The risks to Anthropic's (and AI's) business

Why we're saying 'buyout' and not 'layoff'

How young people are doing with AI summaries

New's We're Watching

The two most interesting risks to Anthropic - U.S. Securities & Exchange Commission

What to Know: Anthropic gave the world 94 pages of risks to its business (slash the entire AI economy) in its IPO prospectus aka the S-1. It wouldn't be Anthropic if they didn't discuss the "existential risks" to humanity and society several times. And isn't that an important risk to disclose? Another that stood out: the AI boom has a glaring point of failure. The majority of advanced semiconductor manufacturing is concentrated in one place, Taiwan, and if anything were to happen there, it could disrupt the entire AI economy. Think earthquake, Chinese military action, blockades. But I want to focus on a different risk, because it is FASCINATING!

Sponsor Message

toggle caption i Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images North America

Committing to the past at a premium: Anthropic is worried about aging out of the tech that's powering its AI, while paying the same prices. What does that mean?! AI companies have to lock into pricey contracts for all sorts of softwares, hardware, data center, and squadrons of GPUs. But technology is advancing quickly right now. New GPUs, for example, could come along that can do the same amount of work for way less money. Then Anthropic is stuck like CHUMPS in a contract paying a premium for old hardware, while some competitors may be doing more for less.

Why buyouts and not layoffs? - The Wall Street Journal

What To Know: Microsoft offered buyouts to 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its staff this week. And doesn't that sound better than "Microsoft laid off 60,000 employees this week"?? Skydance ALSO offered a buyout to employees on Monday, though it's not clear how many would be eligible. And here at NPR, we've been a fan of the term buyout too. So what's the real difference in offering a buyout versus just laying off staffers?

The difference: Morale? Morale. There's something about a "mega-layoff" that doesn't inspire worker confidence. A "buyout" not so much. Really? Ok, I guess. The WSJ reported the focus in C-suite land is on the ratio of employees to AI agents inside companies. Companies have to find ways to pay for the ever-increasing costs of AI … and you know … actual human workers expect to be paid.

Andy Challenger, Chief Revenue Officer of Challenger, Gray & Christmas, a consulting firm, told the Journal that it can help staffers emotionally by making it a little easier to let go. It also tends to motivate older staffers to retire a little bit early, which may be the company's goal.

Today's Indicator

There are more bots than humans online. Here's what that means

If you HAVEN'T listened: I never thought I'd yearn for the days when the internet felt wholesome. Where you could go to blogs and random sites and make friends across the world. Well, more than half of internet traffic now comes from non-humans, aka bots. They're pouring into the digital veins of the World Wide Web, ignoring a lot of ads, generating all kinds of comments, nonsense and what have you. One interesting takeaway: this shift from human-to-bot traffic changes the business model of the internet. If humans let bots do their shopping for them, then ads suddenly become less useful. And if ads don't pay out for websites, then who pays for them?
