In Our Spare Time

Producer Corey Bridges is playing through NPR's gaming coverage

Just last week I completed the campaign for Gears of War: E-Day and I thought it was excellent. I've never been a huge Gears of War fan, but this game was absolutely gorgeous and super fun to play. Xbox has had it pretty rough in recent years, so it's encouraging to see them churn out a game of the year quality product like this.

toggle caption i RICCARDO MILANI/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images/AFP

I've also been playing the new Nintendo Switch Sports Resort entry which I highly recommend to people who were fans of Wii Sports back in the day. And then finally, I've been preparing for the Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake by actually trying to progress in my year-old Breath of the Wild save. All I gotta say is, my backlog is looking more daunting than ever.

NPR put out its "Best Games of 2026" list. NPR is one of more than 150 outlets polled in The Game Awards, which has yet to be released.

World.title: Candy prices got you scared stiff? What to know about the cost of Halloween this year
World.content:
Candy prices got you scared stiff? What to know about the cost of Halloween this year

toggle caption i Stephanie Scarbrough/AP

For people stocking up on candy this Halloween, it's a spooky season in the grocery store — and not in a fun way.

Prices for candy, the most popular Halloween purchase, and gum have risen 7.7% in one year and are up more than 18% in two years, according to the latest federal data. That's higher than the average rate of food inflation during that time.

One major culprit: chocolate. Drought and heavy rains in places like West Africa have hurt cocoa harvests in recent seasons and pushed up prices worldwide.

Global cocoa production is now rebounding, but that isn't much help to consumers preparing to hand out candy to peckish trick-or-treaters this weekend, according to David Branch, sector manager with the Wells Fargo Agri-Food Institute.

"The candy on the shelves right now — chocolate candy — that cocoa was purchased in 2025," he said. And last year's cocoa prices were high.

Sponsor Message

Still, rising consumer prices aren't expected to scare people away from celebrating the holiday, with the National Retail Federation estimating consumers will spend $13.5 billion on Halloween this year. That's a 3% annual increase and sets a record: $115 per person, which is 55 cents more than last year.

Hair-raising cocoa prices are moderating

There was a surplus in the global supply of beans earlier this year, and cocoa prices have come down from their recent highs..

Yet Branch said consumer chocolate prices are "sticky," meaning they won't fall even when cocoa prices do because of the lag time in production. Manufacturers are also dealing with higher prices on other ingredients like sugar, pricier fuel costs due to the war in Iran and costlier imports subject to U.S. tariffs.

Enna Grazier, who owns the New Hampshire small-batch chocolate company Enna Chocolate, said she is facing a slew of higher costs, including a 50% tariff on some of the holiday packaging and ingredients she planned to purchase from Canadian suppliers.

"I've had to look elsewhere or get creative with some of my packaging needs for this holiday season, and that's super frustrating," Grazier said. "It's meant that I can't plan as far out, or the plans that I did make were disrupted and we've had to pivot and change."

Sponsor Message

Some candy makers have ushered in a flavor shift in recent years. Companies are offering more gummy and sour candy, and launching products that don't use pricier chocolate, such as KitKat's marshmallow-flavored Witch's Brew and Reese's White Ghosts coated in white creme.

Still, consumer demand for chocolate hasn't melted away. According to data from the market research firm Circana, which tracks purchases in U.S. supermarkets, chocolate candy sales have been increasing for several years running. However, shoppers have been buying less chocolate candy over the same period, which means people are paying more for chocolate and getting less of it.

World.title: 'Affordability? For who?' Voters decide between helping homeowners or public services
World.content:
'Affordability? For who?' Voters decide between helping homeowners or public services

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

JACKSONVILLE, Fla. – The ramp was steeper than she expected, but Rachel Dues was not going to stop. Not mere steps away from what she believed to be the most important thing she would do this year.

Dues, 54, gathered herself then pushed hard, propelling the wheelchair that carried her injured niece to the polls.

"You're gonna get in there. I don't care how," Dues said, her voice breathless with effort. She was speaking as much to herself as she was to her niece, 21-year-old Rochelle Covington, who asked to come along to vote.

Sponsor Message

"By any means necessary," Dues said, giving the wheelchair another shove.

For Dues, this year's midterm election feels existential. Gas prices have soared, her rent is up, and some days it feels like simply buying groceries or paying her electricity bill could push her over budget.

While political candidates all over the country have paid lip service to issues of affordability, here in Florida, the question of how to make life more affordable is literally on the ballot.

A massive property tax cut has been put to voters in the form of Amendment 3, a ballot measure that asks Florida residents to vote on increasing the amount of money that can be exempted from homestead taxes. The proposal would increase the allowable amount from $50,000 to as much as $250,000 over the next two years, cutting billions of dollars in revenue from local governments' budgets. If the measure passes, some jurisdictions could functionally eliminate all non-school homestead property taxes over time.

That could mean thousands of dollars in annual savings for some homeowners — something supporters have called a game-changer for Florida residents stretched thin by a strained economy. But in an already tax-averse state — Florida famously does not have individual income or estate taxes, among others — local governments have limited revenue streams from which to pull funds for public services, and property taxes have been a lifeline.

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

Critics have cautioned that the proposed tax exemption will have dire consequences: cuts to public services and infrastructure, eroded social safety net programs and a domino effect that could drive up costs elsewhere should city and county governments attempt to recoup lost revenue.

Sponsor Message

"One of the things our members are always knocking on doors and asking is: affordability? For who?" said Steven Johnson, an organizer with grassroots nonprofit Florida Rising, which organizes residents to get involved in political action on state and local issues.

Florida isn't the only place where politicians have explored ways to cut, or even eliminate, property taxes — 11 states have reined in property taxes so far in 2026, according to an analysis by the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities. But Florida's proposal, which is more expansive than many others, puts the question directly to voters.

How they vote, experts said, could set the stage for what's to come in Florida and around the nation.

A disabled veteran, Dues works as a notary and closing agent on home sales. For her, she said, the Amendment 3 vote is personal.

"Lucky for me I'm a resourceful person, but I rely on things like food pantries and other services to get by," Dues said. "Now I'm wondering, what am I going to do if they get rid of all that? What can I do?"

The impact

Since it was introduced, Florida's proposed Amendment 3 has been pitched to voters as an affordability fix for homeowners.

While the state already has laws limiting how much can be taxed of a home's assessed value — and how much that amount can grow each year — this amendment would, in some cases, virtually eliminate all property taxes due on a homeowner's primary residence.

Backers like Florida's Republican governor, Ron DeSantis, and the Florida Realtors trade association have said property taxes have grown out of control and local governments are flush with excess revenue as a result.

"Homeowners have funded the incredible increase in revenue that is now at record growth, and as property values have increased that growth has translated into significant revenue gains for local governments," said Margy Grant, the CEO of Florida Realtors, which as of the end of October put $19.5 million into the 'Vote Yes on 3' campaign. "This is about making sure that Floridians who want to stay in their homes and are seeing this rising cost get to stay in their homes."

toggle caption i Joe Raedle/Getty Images

In the campaign to persuade Floridians to vote yes, ads highlight just how expensive daily life has gotten.

Sponsor Message

"Everything keeps going up!" the Vote Yes on 3 website exclaims. "Cost of living. Inflation. PROPERTY TAXES. What if there was a SOLUTION that could help?"

"Florida families are paying more for nearly everything, whether it's groceries, fuel, insurance, utilities and housing," Grant said. "This is tax relief money that stays in a Floridian's pocket instead of going to the government."

Property tax revenue collected by local governments in the state has nearly doubled from around $32 billion in 2019 to almost $60 billion in the last fiscal year, according to the governor's office. Much of that growth, experts said, was driven by a post-pandemic real estate boom with out-of-state residents moving in and low interest rates driving new property sales.

The question of how law enforcement, fire and emergency medical services will be affected by these potential tax cuts have fueled headline-grabbing debates across the state. Some public officials have insisted emergency services will be able to weather any cuts, while others, including the Florida Sheriffs Association, warned they would suffer.

Amendment 3 proponents said these warnings have been overblown.

"That is just a talking point of the opposition," Grant said.

Sen. Rick Scott (R-Fla.), who supports the measure, wrote in a post on X that "every county has waste to cut," and argued that the amendment would force local governments to eliminate waste rather than essential services.

But local leaders said services other than police, fire and EMS are likely to be hit even harder: Funds for libraries, public transportation, infrastructure, homelessness prevention, small business supports, after-school programs for kids and more could be eliminated.

toggle caption i Bob Self/Florida Times-Union/USA TODAY Network via Reuters

The amendment was put to voters "very, very quickly and without understanding the unintended consequences," said Mike Weinstein, Jacksonville's chief administrative officer and a former state legislator. "There's a small segment of homeowners that will benefit from this. But the majority of people — renters, business owners, everyone else, and even many homeowners — won't see any benefit from this amendment at all." (The amendment would limit which homeowners qualify for the increased exemption based on when they purchased their home.)

According to an analysis by the state's Office of Economic and Demographic Research, the amendment would cut local revenue in the state by nearly $12 billion on a recurring basis. In Jacksonville, the Florida Policy Institute found , that could mean losing as much as $372 million over the next five years.

Sponsor Message

"Our budget here is $2 billion. A billion comes from property taxes," Weinstein said. "So, mosquito control, road surfacing, libraries, parks, all will be affected. And so will police and fire."

Weinstein, a Republican, said in lieu of funding things like parks and libraries, fixing roads or clearing trash, the city may instead have to channel resources toward opening a "very big" complaints department.

Getting out the vote

Maggie Fernandez, 68, is exactly the kind of person who might benefit from Amendment 3. She owns her own home. Her husband is retired.

But in recent weeks, Fernandez has spent her nights and weekends in the lead up to Election Day phone banking and knocking on doors to get her neighbors to vote the amendment down.

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

"Sure, I might see some relief in taxes," Fernandez said. "But overall this is going to hurt local services. It's going to hurt people who are worse off than we are."

Fernandez signed up to do voter outreach with Florida Rising. On a recent weekday evening, she was one of more than a dozen volunteers who packed into the progressive nonprofit's office and hit the phones. All told, organizers said, they made nearly 1,500 calls that night.

With early voting already underway in Florida, Fernandez said she felt a renewed sense of urgency to get the "vote no" message out.

She dialed number after number — 111 in one night — leaving messages and urging those who answered to consider how Amendment 3 might hurt their neighbors in the long run.

Down the hall, Dues was also making calls.

When a woman answered halfway through the evening, Dues scrambled for her script.

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

"Amendment 3 may lead to cuts on local services like flood prevention, road maintenance, public transportation and housing assistance and that's what it doesn't tell you when you see those commercials on TV," Dues said. "It doesn't tell you any of that, it just makes you think it's this great amendment."

Sponsor Message

The woman on the other line said she'd be voting no.

Dues exhaled as she hung up the phone.

'People don't know'

Dues doesn't need to work hard to picture how the amendment might affect her daily life. She thinks about it constantly: On her drives across town as she calculates the amount of gas it might take to get home; on her regular visits to food pantries, where she gathers enough bread and eggs and frozen meat to make it through the month.

Will the food banks be able to operate if they lose city funding, she wonders. Will relief programs that help renters like her pay for utility bills or avoid eviction disappear?

In her work as a closing agent, Dues sees how much people are paying to become homeowners in Florida, and, she said, she feels for anyone who is struggling to make ends meet.

But she's done her research and practiced her pitch. Whenever she gets the chance, she tells homeowners that the affordability Amendment 3 promises isn't all it's cracked up to be.

"When I first heard about it, I was like, oh that's great. That'll really help people," Dues said. "But then I learned more about it and it felt like a bait and switch. It might be great for some people, in the short term, but in the long run, it's going to do a lot of harm."

If local lawmakers shift the financial burden into other taxes homeowners could end up paying more in other places, she tells friends and colleagues.

toggle caption i Malcolm Jackson for NPR

Renters like her, she says, may absorb increases put to landlords or commercial properties. And any programs that exist to help people survive won't necessarily be there to help anymore.

The amendment needs the approval of a supermajority — 60% or more — to pass.

Sponsor Message

On a recent morning outside a church on the west side of Jacksonville, Dues got in line to register for the food bank. She needed a few staples, she said, to carry her through the end of the month.

"Are you voting?" she asked the woman working the sign-in desk.

The volunteer squinted up at her.

"You know to vote 'no' on Amendment 3, right?" Dues pitched, taking a number.

Dues said she's never been more nervous before an election.

"It's kind of scary to me that people don't know" about the amendment, she said.

Looking around the crowd gathered for boxes of bread and other pantry items, Dues shook her head.

"How do they expect poor people to be able to live as regular people?" she wondered aloud.

The number in her hand read 104. All around her, the crowd was still growing.

World.title: This American importer is suing Trump to end some tariffs on Canada
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Inside a sprawling refrigerated warehouse, tucked into an industrial neighbourhood not far from New Jersey's Newark Airport, you'll find a new front in the U.S.-Canada trade war.

It's the headquarters of Gellert Global Group, a third-generation, family-owned food distribution company that is suing the Trump administration over its 50 per cent tariffs on certain Canadian goods and seeking refunds.

In one of his first broadcast interviews since launching the lawsuit, Thomas Gellert, the company's CEO, says he felt he had to do something.

"We can't sustain a tariff like this on these products for much longer," he said during an interview with CBC News on the floor of the warehouse in Elizabeth, N.J.

Gellert Global Group imports roughly $80 million US worth of Canadian cheeses every year, including Celebrity goat cheese produced by Mariposa Dairy in Lindsay, Ont. It also imports a range of Canadian-produced brie and camembert products.

"Customers are not going to take price increases. Everyone is sort of beat down and tired from inflationary pressures," he said, confirming that his company is eating the cost of the tariffs for now.

Thomas Gellert, CEO of Gellert Global Group, stands inside the company's refrigerated warehouse in Elizabeth, N.J. His company is suing the Trump administration over its 50 per cent tariffs on certain Canadian goods. (Katie Simpson/CBC)

Gellert tried to get exemptions for these products in meetings with American lawmakers and diplomats, including U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra. In those conversations, he says he highlighted the fact that American-produced milk is being used for some of the cheese products hit by tariffs, arguing that, in the end, the policy is hurting U.S. farmers too.

Those lobbying efforts were not successful. And with no Canada-U.S. trade deal appearing to be on the horizon, Gellert decided he had to take legal action.

"Frankly we don't have time to wait for things to settle on their own," he said.

"We have a business here to run."

The lawsuit was filed by the Liberty Justice Center, a non-profit, non-partisan legal advocacy organization. It is the same organization that successfully challenged Trump's IEEPA tariffs, which were struck down by the U.S. Supreme Court earlier this year.

"We felt like our job wasn't done if the President keeps putting illegal tariffs on different countries," said Sarah Albrecht, the chair and CEO of the Liberty Justice Center.

Tariff technicalities

The Trump administration imposed this round of tariffs after trade talks with Canada broke down in August.

The duties are applied through Section 338 of the U.S. Tariff Act, also known as the Smoot-Hawley Act, a Depression-era law that had never been used before for tariff purposes.

The law gives the president the power to impose tariffs of up to 50 per cent on imported goods from a country that has discriminated against the U.S.

The Trump administration has argued that Canada's decision to retaliate against previous rounds of U.S. tariffs amounts to discrimination. It specifically cited the banning of American alcohol products by certain provinces, protections for the Canadian dairy industry and measures related to the auto sector.

In a statement released the day the lawsuit was filed, the Liberty Justice Center said Section 338 cannot be used as an "all-purpose authorization for the executive branch to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises."

Among the arguments the group is making, it says there's a disconnect between allegations of discrimination by Canada and the products Trump is targeting with the tariffs. It also says the Trump administration illegally rushed the implementation of some of the tariffs. And it claims Trump does not have the authority to impose tariffs in this way.

"No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required," Albrecht said.

Initially, the tariffs applied to roughly $28 billion worth of Canadian goods, with targets including cement, road salt, hockey sticks and other items. However, the list has been adjusted twice to remove some products and add others.

Some of the changes were made at the request of Republican Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, as she finds herself in a tough re-election race. She has sought exemptions for products important to businesses in her home state, as the trade war with Canada is proving unpopular there.

WATCH | Trump shifts tariffs on Canadian goods as he hints at trade deal; Carney remains cautious: Trump to lift some tariffs on Canada before U.S. midterms | Duration closed caption 2:41 Ahead of the U.S. midterms, the Trump Administration is lifting 50 per cent tariffs on some Canadian products but adding them to others. The President also suggested a trade deal may be close, but Prime Minister Mark Carney was more cautious.

Experts mixed on strength of Trump's tariff justification

Since the tariffs were first announced, legal experts have offered varying opinions on whether the measures would survive a legal challenge.

"There's a good chance it could get reversed," said Ryan Majerus, a trade lawyer and partner at King & Spalding International Trade Group.

"I think the administration may have a tough time identifying the reasons why these particular products or these particular actions by Canada are discriminatory."

Lawyers for the Trump administration will have to make the connection, Majerus says, between the alleged discrimination and why the U.S. tariffs offset that discrimination.

"The fact that there have been adjustments [to the product list] since they've been put in place ... I think it may undermine their claim as well," he said.

However, the Trump administration is expected to put up an intense defence.

"I think they can make some creative arguments on how they're able to kind of invoke the authority broadly," Majerus said.

"It's a bit of a blank canvas in terms of how the courts are going to look at this."

A display of Celebrity goat cheese and other Canadian cheese products. Gellert Global Group says U.S. tariffs on Canadian goods are threatening its business and the Canadian producers it works with. (Katie Simpson/CBC)

Fears of losing shelf space

If there isn't a resolution by next year, Gellert says his company will have to reassess how it handles the tariffs and whether it is sustainable to keep importing these Canadian goods.

"If we stop selling a product — to get back on the shelf would be very difficult," he said.

"We don't want to lose shelf space."

He also says that if these Canadian products are not available to U.S. consumers, there aren't readily available American alternatives to replace them.

"There is not enough goat milk in the United States to support demand," he said.

"And the existing goat cheese factories that are here, even if they're importing frozen curd, they don't have the capacity. So that's the reason why we work with our Canadian partners."

The goat cheese issue specifically weighs heavily on Gellert. He says he worked closely with the family that owns Mariposa Dairy and encouraged them to invest in production to grow their business.

"I do feel some sort of sense of personal responsibility to that community, that we've encouraged them to build up infrastructure to help support the business — and now that's at risk," he said.

"If we stop buying, they start culling goats. It's not something that can be brought back again."

World.title: Christa Pike says she's in 'constant pain' since surviving execution attempt
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Convicted murderer Christa Pike says while she continues to get stronger, she has been in pain since surviving a botched execution in Tennessee last month.

"My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts," said Pike in a statement that was dictated to her legal team and released Friday.

"I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn't just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul."

Pike survived two doses of the drug pentobarbital as the state tried to execute her on Sept. 30 for the 1995 stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. Pike was 18 when she tortured and killed Slemmer with her boyfriend, becoming one of the youngest women to be sentenced to death in the U.S.

The slaying involved the perpetrators carving the shape of a pentagram in the victim's chest and taking a chunk of her skull as a souvenir.

The execution attempt initially left Pike unconscious and on a ventilator, with severe arm injuries. She was hospitalized but has since returned to the prison where she was serving her sentence.

Pike is the first person known to have survived being injected with a full lethal dose of execution drugs.

"I am recovering, and I know that I am getting stronger. But healing is not the same as being OK," she said.

"There hasn't been a moment since that night when I haven't been in pain," Pike said.

In her statement, Pike said she had walked into the execution chamber "prepared to die" and had "made my peace."

"I had also told the people in the room and who were there to witness my execution that I was leaving them in loving kindness."

Instead, she said, she woke up several days later "alone in a hospital confused and in pain."

"I had not contemplated life beyond that night, and I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position."

Pike said she has received "extraordinary love and support" from people around the world.

"To know that so many people care about me, that they see me as a human being whose life matters, is something I cannot fully put into words. It is humbling, and it has touched me more deeply than I can explain."

'Don't know why I survived'

Pike also thanked the first responders, doctors, nurses and hospital staff who cared for her.

"I don't know why I survived that night. I don't know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time."

Pike's attorneys have urged Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to reduce Pike's sentence to life imprisonment. Lee told reporters earlier this week that, "I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts."

Following the unsuccessful execution attempt, Lee halted further executions for the remainder of the year and ordered a comprehensive third-party review to determine exactly what occurred.

Meanwhile, a Tennessee judge has ordered that all evidence from the attempted execution be preserved so a full investigation can take place.

World.title: 'You can't just get out': How 2 boys were recruited into the drug trade at the age of 12
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Kai was 12 years old when he began to warn his mother he might not make it home.

"[If] I don't make it home by four o'clock, just know that I got snatched and somebody put me in their car and kidnapped me," he would tell her.

His mother, whom CBC's the fifth estate is calling Aria for her protection, moved her family to another city when Kai was a boy to disconnect from his father, who had a criminal past and street associations.

She enrolled Kai, whose name has also been changed for his protection, in community centres and drop-in spaces in Winnipeg to keep him busy and away from trouble

But Aria believes those spaces exposed her son to people who would exploit him.�

Watch the full documentary, "Missing Boys: Lured into Danger," from the fifth estate on YouTube or CBC-TV on Friday at 9 p.m .

She believes some staff abused their positions, allowing gang members to manipulate her son and coerce him into the drug trade — sending him thousands of kilometres away from home.

Fifth estate host Mark Kelley, left, sits down with a boy who was recruited by a gang when he was 12. He says he has been sent out of town to sell drugs more times than he can count. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

Kai said men in their 20s and 30s presented themselves as people he could trust.

"People call it grooming, people call it using. There's many words for it, but it's just being taken advantage of because you're innocent," Kai said.

For the last two years, the fifth estate has investigated the disappearances of young Black boys from the Greater Toronto Area (GTA) who are groomed and lured into drug trafficking networks in Ontario cities as far away as Sarnia and Thunder Bay, and sent further north into Indigenous communities like Ginoogaming, a First Nation.

Now, the fifth estate has heard directly from boys who live this dangerous life and say they were sent across the country to sell drugs, revealing a network that reaches even farther.

We now know of this activity taking boys as young as 12 as far west as British Columbia, as far north as Yellowknife and as far east as Halifax — places where drugs are sold at exponentially higher prices — up to 10 times the price in some cases.

The business of going OT

In an interview with CBC's the fifth estate, Kai recounts his first trip out of town, also known as “going OT,” when he was 12.

"You don't know what's in those bags. You don't know what you're delivering for people … you just think, 'I'm helping the older guy, because I want to be cool like him,'" he said.

Kai said the older men picked him up, told him where he would stay and expected him to sell drugs. He was left in a remote community eight hours north of his home in Winnipeg.

LISTEN: The Missing Boys: When It All Went Wrong

Kai said he did not fully understand what he was getting into. He had to figure it out in a place where he did not know anyone and his family was out of reach.

"You're not telling family members," he said. "Because not only do they not know where you are, you don't know where you are."

The first trip taught him more about what he calls the rules of "the game," where the three outcomes are freedom, jail or death.

And he says he was forced to gamble for the gangs.

"You can't just get out ... whoever sent you there is expecting you to come back with a prize," Kai said. "And if you don't come back with anything … God forbid something happens to you."

Now 14, Kai has made more trips out of town than he can count.

WATCH | Sent north by gangs: On the front line of the drug trade | Duration closed caption 0:49 Kai, not his real name, 14, says he has been sent by gangs to remote northern communities where drugs can sell for 10 times the price.

Jamal, another teenager whose name has been changed for his safety, started going OT at 12. He had been away from home for more than a week and his mom reported him missing.

The now-18-year-old who lives in the Toronto area said he has been sent to communities in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Ontario.

Jamal's farthest trip took him to Yellowknife. He was even convinced to pay his own way.

Like Kai, Jamal said it was in Grade 7 when he was first approached to work for a gang. His family had spent a year bouncing between houses and he grew close to older people in his neighbourhood who were often around his cousins.

"I always just had the respect and looked at them like an older role model," he said.

Jamal said those role models could offer him an escape from the instability at home.

"If things were stable at home, I wouldn't really have a reason to go outside," he said.

Jamal said the adults he worked for were selling drugs bought internationally — and worked with cartels.

Then Jamal tells the fifth estate how the boys cross the country — a key piece of information — as many families are baffled as to how their boys are boarding planes and driving to remote locations when they are too young to have a driver's licence and don't have identification.

Jamal said fake names and identification are provided for them.

"It doesn't even matter who you are, how young you are. You can go anywhere in Canada," he said. "It's actually quite easy."

The adults behind the operation

The fifth estate previously found adult traffickers use the boys as disposable mules and legal shields that often take the fall when police make drug busts.

A 2026 federal Justice Department report found that the proportion of Black youth in correctional supervision in Nova Scotia, Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia remained at around 12 to 13 per cent from 2019 to 2024. That's almost two times more than their combined share of the population for that age group, across all four provinces.

Black boys often face well-known socio-economic challenges including high unemployment , and bias within justice and educational systems that can make them more vulnerable to the pull of organized crime.

"Many of these youth[s] are exploited … they're seen as disposable to the people who are running these networks," said Winnipeg police Insp. Josh Ewatski.

Winnipeg police Insp. Josh Ewatski tells the fifth estate the drugs supplied by gangs have been linked to international cartels. Young boys are often used for street-level dealing so gang members don't have to expose themselves to violence or being arrested. (Oliver Walters/CBC)

In May, Ewatski led a team involved in what police called Manitoba's largest drug bust. Investigators seized 525 kilograms of cocaine, methamphetamine and fentanyl in Winnipeg.

Those arrested included people associated with Canada's highest ranks of organized crime including the Hells Angels, Wolfpack Alliance and a Mexican cartel.

"Most of the drugs of cocaine and methamphetamine will come from Mexico up to the U.S. and into Canada," Ewatski said.

He described a sophisticated network where multiple drug trafficking organizations are working together to move drugs into remote communities.

He says it's associates of these international criminal networks who are recruiting and using boys.

Ewatski said boys are used for street-level dealing and to work in stash houses. He said they often don't know who they are working for.

"These kids are used so [those running the networks] don't have to expose themselves to being arrested or being shot."

Leaving a gang can be just as dangerous. Ewatski said some boys become trapped by debts they are told they owe their recruiters.

“If they're out, they're going to be out in a violent way," he said. "Possibly even dead."

Denny Heathen, a reformed gang member, now counsels youth and leads prayer circles in his community of Prince Albert, Sask. (Shelley Ayres/CBC)

Denny Heathen spent much of his 20s working for a gang in Prince Albert, Sask. He said some recruiters targeted boys between 15 to 18 and told us that the boys who were targeted had a look of desperation.

"They wanted purpose," Heathen said.

Recruiters offered attention, money and the promise of protection, presenting themselves as brothers or older mentors.

"These are puppets," he said. "You just got to make them feel like they're appreciated, like they are going to be taken care of."

WATCH | A price for getting out: What it takes to get out of a gang | Duration closed caption 0:24 A former gang member tells boys in the drug trade that getting out will come with a price.

Kai remembers the grooming process well.

“You're a little kid in a community centre trying to play basketball and then you see these guys … walking around with the large prize in their hand."

The prize was money — an amount that felt impossible to a boy too young to get his first job.

During his interview with the fifth estate, Kai pulled out a thick stack of $100 bills to demonstrate how quickly money could influence a boy to sell drugs.

"All it takes is this and you're influenced."

He said the amounts involved can be enormous in First Nations communities where an oxycodone pill can sell for $200.

"That substance that is being put in these boys' pockets and these boys' hands to go deal over the province … people will do anything for."

The boy who never came home

On March 27, 2025, Jay'siiah Webb-Long walked out of his family's home in Brampton, Ont., carrying a single duffel bag that appeared nearly empty.

Doorbell camera footage provided by the family to the fifth estate shows the 15-year-old placing a single box in the recycling bin on his front porch, scanning the street before disappearing out of frame.

His story made national headlines.

Jay'siiah Webb-Long, 15, was last seen outside his home in Brampton, Ont. on March 27, 2025. (Saskatchewan RCMP)

"Somebody had sent me photos after his disappearance," said Shenice Long, his mother.

"She had sent photos of him holding stacks of money. So, at that point, I said, 'OK, somebody has sent him far out … to make money.'"

Long said she remained in contact with her son for weeks after he left home. But he would not tell her where he was.

Jay'siiah's family told the fifth estate they are frustrated with action from Peel Regional Police and the RCMP in Saskatchewan, citing for example that it took Peel police eight weeks to alert the public that Jay'siiah was missing.

Long said police used a phone number she never had for her son to trace his location to Pelican Narrows, Sask., a northern community about 3,000 kilometres from his home in Brampton. This number only surfaced when the public alert came out and a young woman came forward.

"I heard of Saskatchewan, but … I don't have family there. I don't know anyone there," Long said.

In July 2025, Saskatchewan RCMP took over the file as a homicide investigation. They didn't alert the public of this shift until September 2025.

Police told the family a search was delayed by winter weather. In the spring, investigators told the family they planned to search near Pelican Narrows — led with cadaver dogs.

Pelican Narrows, Sask., a community of about 4,000 and located about 500 kilometres north of Saskatoon, is part of the Peter Ballantyne Cree Nation. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

On May 13, human remains were found near a sewage lagoon just outside the community. An autopsy confirmed two days later that the remains belonged to Webb-Long.

RCMP believe his death was a homicide. The investigation is ongoing and no charges have been laid in connection with his death.

Missing — and not always reported

In 2024, 322 male youth were reported missing to Toronto police. Statistics Canada data shows Black boys account for almost half of those missing, despite representing less than 10 per cent of the city's population of that age group.

The fifth estate has found not every family reports their youth missing. In the case of Jay'siiah Webb-Long, his mother didn't file a formal report until three weeks after he had left home. She told the fifth estate she had called Peel Regional Police after 48 hours but they dissuaded her because she was still in contact with him.

"One youth missing is too [many]," said Christene Lewis, who is a violence intervention specialist and works with families in Toronto and surrounding areas. She supports many families who have youth that go missing and go "OT." It's a life she knows because she lived it.

"I come from the gang culture," Lewis said. "I come from feeling isolated, I've come from feeling like the streets were more loyal to me than my own family was."

Christene Lewis, a violence intervention specialist, works with families in Toronto and surrounding areas who have youth who go missing. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

Lewis said some parents hesitate reporting their child missing because they fear their kids will be treated as runaways rather than young people at risk. Others feel shame and embarrassment.

Lewis said there is also a breakdown of trust between marginalized communities and police.

"They don't feel like the police even care."

Lewis's advice to parents: Always report a missing kid and keep following up.

"If they didn't hear you the first day, call the next day," she said. "Don't give up."

WATCH | Parents urged to be vigilant: A message for parents of missing kids | Duration closed caption 0:30 A woman who works with the families of missing kids says they should stay vigilant and always report to police.

Aria remembers when it first became clear her son had gone to a First Nations community to sell drugs.

"He was telling stories like he came back from camp," she said.

He would leave home sporadically, returning home with designer clothing and money.

Aria said she has also had the windows of her home shot at three times.

Now, when Kai goes missing, she reports him and collects evidence that might help police locate him.

"This is not something you make peace with," she said. "This is something that's wrong."

'Nobody's just going to let you go'

Jamal said the people who recruited him continue to contact him and tell him he owes them money.

''They're going to keep texting you, telling you that they got this opportunity … nobody's just going to let you just go."

Kai has also tried to leave. He spent the summer away at camp and returned determined to get out of gang life.

"Now that I realize what kind of hell on earth is like … I never want to go back there," he told the fifth estate in August.

But Aria said the messages continued.

She found text messages about Kai from a sibling that read: "I will not be returning your little bro" and "he's my slave.”

She believes the messages are proof her son is being trafficked.

Aria, a Winnipeg mother whose name has been changed for protection, worries gangs will never loosen their grip on her son. (Ousama Farag/CBC)

Kai left home again the night before he was set to start Grade 10. He returned home and left again several times.

Aria fears that even if Kai manages to break free from the gangs, they will continue to chase and manipulate him, tempting him with money and a sense of belonging.

Kai is facing drug trafficking charges.

"This monster exists and it's going to exist on his path as a young man, as an adult," Aria said. "I don't think that this monster ever goes away."

World.title: Carney points to EU's strong belief in democracy as political winds shift for 2 largest members
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney is hosting European Union leaders in Montreal on Friday as he looks to deepen ties with like-minded leaders in the face of an increasingly protectionist United States.

But the rise of nationalist political forces in Europe could make that more difficult in the years to come.

The 21st Canada-EU summit, which wraps Friday, is aimed at forging a stronger alliance between Canada and the 27-member bloc in the face of an unpredictable and volatile White House.

On Thursday, both Carney and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen stressed the two sides' shared values as they pitched an "alliance for the future" based on deeper trade and security ties.

But shifting political winds on the continent could test that alliance, notably in France and Germany — heavyweights within the bloc.

In France, presidential hopeful Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally is leading in polls ahead of the spring 2027 election. Le Pen, an advocate for strict immigration limits, has criticized the EU-Canada trade pact.

While in Germany, the far-right and isolationist Alternative for Germany (AfD) continues to gain ground in regional parliaments and national polls.

Asked Thursday if he has concerns about dealing with a potentially different political makeup, Carney praised the EU's adherence to democratic values.

WATCH | Carney on new partnership: Canada forging 'alliance for the future' with EU as an 'associate member,' Carney says | Duration closed caption 0:48 On the margins of the Canada-EU summit on Thursday, Prime Minister Mark Carney told a roundtable meeting that Canada and the European Union are in the process of forging a new 'alliance for the future, with Canada as an associate member.' Carney earlier told reporters the proposed partnership's 'name doesn't matter.'

"One of Europe's strengths is democracy, freedom and a core belief in the rule of law. There will always be different governments, governments of different stripes in Europe," he told reporters.

"Over the course of decades, the European Union has continued to develop, and strengthen, throughout, and be enriched by the national democratic processes of those countries."

Carney also downplayed the notion he was looking to secure commitments with the EU before the French election.

"We're not tying it to any political cycle, but to the fundamentals of what they deliver … for Canadians," he said.

Despite some objections from EU members, von der Leyen has pitched making Canada the first associate member of the bloc. Carney has welcomed a more expansive alliance across the Atlantic.

That appeared to anger U.S. President Donald Trump who said if he interpreted the move as a "hostile act," he might stop trading with Europe "on many things."

Asked earlier this week about the summit potentially attracting retaliation from Trump or right-wing leaders in Europe, a senior Canadian government official told reporters the gathering isn't directed against anyone but reflected deep interests between Canada and the EU.

Joint statement expected

As the two-day summit winds down, the Canadian and European sides are expected to release a joint statement on Friday with a number of new commitments.

A draft version of the statement seen by CBC News commits to reinforcing "a predictable trade environment," deepening collaboration in critical mineral supply chains, countering cyberattacks and continued support for Ukraine.

Both sides are also promising to launch negotiations toward deeper participation in Erasmus, the European Union's student and youth exchange program.

World.title: Dead humpback whale that was struck by ferry towed to First Nation for ceremony
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

WARNING: This story contains graphic images of a dead whale.

A dead humpback whale that was struck by a B.C. Ferries vessel has been towed to a Squamish Nation village for a cultural ceremony.

The whale, identified as Notcho (BCX1700), was seen floating off Gambier Island on Monday night after being struck a week earlier in the same area.

Ferry passengers say they felt a collision with a whale on Oct. 18 while travelling on the Queen of Surrey, travelling between Langdale Terminal on the Sunshine Coast and Horseshoe Bay in West Vancouver.

The Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO) said the collision happened between Grace Point and Keats Island.

Aspen Wing and her son watched as a humpback whale was struck by a ferry leaving the Langdale terminal on the Sunshine Coast on Oct. 18, 2026. (Submitted by Aspen Wing)

Paul Cottrell, a member of the DFO’s marine mammal response team, said they found the whale on Tuesday and confirmed it was the same whale that was struck.

He said Notch’s fluke and peduncle were missing from the rest of its body.

The DFO and the Canadian Coast Guard have now towed the whale's bloated carcass from West Bay near Gambier Island to the village of Xwemelch’stn (Capilano) in West Vancouver.

Chairperson Sxwíxwtn Wilson Williams of the Squamish Nation said whales are considered sacred relatives with profound cultural and spiritual importance.

"There’s a deep connection historically, [and] having whales coming back through our waters means a lot to our people," Williams said.

The dead humpback whale was found by the Grace Islands off B.C.'s coast, according to the Marine Education and Research Society. (Emily Ashton)

The Canadian Coast Guard contacted Williams about the whale, and the Squamish Nation quickly assembled a team.

"We have an elder that has travelled down from the far west of [Vancouver] Island that has experience in harvesting whales," Williams said.

Whale skin and bones can be used for regalia, he explained, and could even be used in part of education and school curricula.

"We're looking at providing time for community members to come down, maybe having the little ones' school come down as a field trip," Williams said.

The dead whale is seen floating on the shore near Burrard Inlet off Squamish Nation’s Xwemelch’stn (Capilano) village. (Squamish Nation)

Notcho is now at the the village on the shore in Burrard Inlet.

"A lot of people that reached out today want to go down and just share a song, drum, and sing and share a prayer," Williams said on Thursday.

Chairperson Sxwíxwtn Wilson Williams of the Squamish Nation is seen on Oct. 29, 2026. (Alanna Kelly/CBC)

The Squamish Nation is planning to hold a private cultural ceremony, and is asking the public for privacy.

"Being on site was challenging today because our hearts go out to the loss of life, and you can feel the power of such a beautiful mammal," Williams said.

The DFO is conducting a necropsy and collecting samples to determine the whale's exact cause of death, and the results are expected to take months.

World.title: Yes, Halloween candy is expensive this year — but some sweets are scarier than others
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A haunted house, but it's just your grocery bill after buying Halloween candy this year.

If you're feeling spooked stocking up for trick-or-treaters, you're not alone. The price of confectionery, which includes candy, has climbed steadily over the past six years, according to Statistics Canada monthly inflation numbers, rising 28 per cent since January 2020.

That's about four percentage points higher than the overall inflation rate for all consumer items during that time period. And while confectionery prices last month did dip slightly compared to September 2025, overall, some Canadian consumers are still experiencing sticker shock.

"Apparently Halloween candy is nearly $30 per box this year??" one person wrote on X last week, along with a photo of a store display of packages of 100 candy bars that were on sale for $13.99, but that are regularly $27.99 — a price CBC News confirmed at several Canadian retail locations, including Calgary Co-op and Save-On-Foods.

"I'm in Canada, and normally you could find a sale where the 100 packs of mini chocolates would go on sale for $10. The cheapest I found was $12," another consumer posted on Reddit Tuesday.

"Given the prices of the traditional Halloween candy, I went full size."

Still, some treats are trickier than others. And new data from the Agri-Food Analytics Lab at Dalhousie University in Halifax suggests that the treat with the biggest price hike this year isn't actually sweet, but salty.

The average price of chips and savoury snacks in October jumped about 18 per cent compared to last year, the data states. A pack of 40 small bags cost, on average, between $12.97 and $12.99 — about $2 more compared to 2025.

The October data provided to CBC News out of Dalhousie comes from the lab's review of grocery and pharmacy flyers in Vancouver, Calgary, Toronto, Montreal and Halifax, supplemented by online retail listings. It doesn't include tax or loyalty rewards.

September confectionery data from Statistics Canada — the most recent available — shows that even though prices have increased steadily since 2020, they are down 2.9 per cent this year, relative to September last year.

"Last year, we had the impact of the tariffs on sugar and confectionery, which is a big part of the reason prices were up dramatically [in 2025]," Michael von Massow, a food agriculture professor at Ontario's University of Guelph, told CBC News.

"Except for things like potato chips, which have no sugar or chocolate."

Chocolate levels out, thanks to sales

According to the Agri-Food Analytics Lab's October data, gummy candies (like Sour Patch Kids) were next on the list of price increases, with the price of a box of 90 sweets up 8.4 per cent compared to last October, followed by packs of chewy candies (like Skittles and Starburst), up about 6.5 per cent.

On the bright side, the price of pressed-sugar candies like Rockets was essentially unchanged.

The same went for boxes of chocolate treats, which had jumped as much as 30 per cent earlier in October, but have since levelled back out thanks to last-minute flyer sales, notes Sylvain Charlebois, the director of the Agri-Food Analytics Lab.

Cocoa prices have more than doubled over the past few years due to poor weather and disease in West Africa, which supplies more than 70 per cent of the world’s cocoa, according to The Associated Press.

A quick search of Toronto stores on Thursday showed a pack of 100 Nestlé assorted mini bars and candies on sale for $13.99 at Food Basics, Metro and Shoppers Drug Mart, and $15 at Loblaws — overall savings of about $9.

In Montreal, a bag of 100 Hershey assorted mini chocolate bars was on sale for $15.99 at Metro, down from $21.99. In Vancouver, the same bag was on sale for $11 at Loblaws, down from $20. No Frills in Dartmouth, N.S., had the item for $12.99, down from $18.99.

In other words, you can breathe a sigh of relief if you're just here for the peanut butter cups.

Still, watch out for shrinkflation, cautions Charlebois.

The tactic where companies quietly reduce the weight or volume of a product, but not the price, affected Halloween candy last year, when CBC News discovered two major candy makers had reduced the weight of several Halloween chocolate bar variety packs by as much as almost 17 per cent.

"Package size matters as much as the sticker price. A cheaper bag isn't necessarily a better deal if it contains fewer treats," he told CBC News.

WATCH | Is chocolate more expensive than it used to be?: Is chocolate way more expensive than it used to be? | Duration 2:31 The weather is causing chocolate to get pricey. Extreme rain can kill cacao flowers and pods before they get a chance to develop. New research says rain is responsible for recent downswings in production, with climate change increasing the chance of similar such events in the future.

Is it the candy, or everything else?

A few new reports from the U.S. also show rising Halloween candy prices — and sluggish sales.

U.S. candy prices have been climbing faster than inflation for several years. As of September, candy and gum prices were up 44 per cent over a five-year period, according to government data reported by The Associated Press.

In the U.S., the items that saw the biggest price increases compared to 2025 were Mondelez sour gummy candy variety packs (up about 40 per cent), followed by five different types of Hershey variety packs, including both chocolate and non-chocolate bundles, according to an analysis by Groundwork Collaborative.

Halloween candy is displayed for sale at a Giant grocery store on Oct. 22 in Dundalk, Md. (Stephanie Scarbrough/The Associated Press)

And U.S. Halloween candy sales fell 6.7 per cent in the month ended Oct. 17 compared to the same period last year, according to NielsenIQ, a market research firm. That wasn't necessarily because candy is more expensive, but because, well, everything is.

"I think what you're seeing now is a consumer that's spending so much additional money on fuel and housing and clothing and food," Chris Costagli, a vice-president of food thought leadership at NielsenIQ, told The Associated Press.

On Thursday, chocolate maker Hershey also warned that the rising cost of living might be spooking U.S. customers, rather than candy prices themselves.

That sentiment was echoed by some Canadian consumers on Reddit. Some posted in a Halifax subreddit that they didn't think candy prices were actually that bad this year.

"It's not the candy for us, it's everything else," one person commented.

"Sale prices are actually the best I've seen in a while," another person wrote in a subreddit for Burlington, Ont., last week.

"Regular price, the candy is absolutely ridiculous, I agree. But I've managed to buy about 300 pieces plus probably 40-50 full sized bars for, spitballing, around $100? I think even a little under that."

World.title: Quebec launches investigation after Montreal police officer allegedly deleted domestic violence video from evidence
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Montreal police say the Quebec Crown prosecution's office is investigating an officer alleged to have committed misconduct and obstruction involving a case of domestic violence in 2025.

In a statement, police said the report surfaced during the investigation into Station 39 in Montréal-Nord, which has been at the centre of a major racism scandal since June.

Police also said the complaint originated within the police force.

The statement from police didn't include many more details, but Radio-Canada learned that the officer is facing allegations of destroying a video on the smartphone of a woman who was a victim of domestic violence.

According to Radio-Canada, a police duo — one man and one woman — responded to a residence in Montréal-Nord following an emergency call from a woman saying she had been a victim of domestic violence.

The alleged victim reportedly opened her phone to give video evidence of the abuse to the officers. As the male officer watched the video, he reportedly recognized the alleged aggressor and deleted the video in front of his police partner. She then later reported the actions of the officer to two sergeants on duty.

Radio-Canada learned that female officer had to escalate her concerns within the SPVM because her concerns were ignored by her supervisors.

In its news release, the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) said the investigation into the officer is ongoing and that they have reassigned the officer to administrative tasks.

He will not hold a public-facing role until the investigation ends, the SPVM said.



"My confidence has been shaken by several police officers who cast a shadow — a serious shadow — on the exceptional work of other officers," said Mayor Soraya Martinez Ferrada.

In a separate case, Montreal police have also said that an officer from Station 21 in downtown Montreal has been suspended for alleged racist and discriminatory acts related to the probe regarding Station 39.

Montreal police chief Fady Dagher will provide an update this afternoon on the allegations surrounding the Station 39 investigation.

"The police chief has a lot of explaining to do to the citizens of Montreal today, with yet another incident having just occured," said Martinez Ferrada.

"He has a duty to restore trust with the public, and I expect that to be his focus in the coming days."

Yves Francoeur, the president of the Fraternité des policiers et policières de Montréal, the union representing police officers in Montreal, told Radio-Canada it would not comment until they review the entire file.

In June, a 16-member patrol unit from Station 39 was suspended following allegations of discrimination and misconduct.

Those allegations included cutting locs from people's hair during police interventions and collecting them as trophies.

World.title: How drones and DNA testing are being used to hunt down invasive wild pigs in Manitoba
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Thermal drones and environmental DNA testing are showing promise in strengthening Manitoba's fight against invasive, destructive and disease-carrying wild pigs.

Squeal on Pigs, a public awareness campaign aiming to stop the spread of the invasive Eurasian wild boar and cross-bred pigs across the province, says eradication is within reach. It warns the invasive animal poses major risks, including spreading African swine fever, and wreaking havoc on agricultural land and ecosystems.

"We've got a real chance of being able to get rid of them, if we're persistent," said Wayne Lees, Squeal on Pigs program co-ordinator.

The program is organized by Manitoba Pork and gets funding from the federal and Manitoba governments.

The group logged 240 confirmed wild pigs spotted provincewide last year, as removal efforts increased.

Wild pig population control has been an ongoing issue since the 1980s, but Lees believes two key technologies — thermal imaging drones and environmental DNA testing of water samples — are pushing the province closer to being free of wild pigs.

He highlighted Alberta's rat control program as a proven model that shows years of sustained, targeted efforts can eradicate an invasive species from a province.

Wayne Lees, Squeal on Pigs program co-ordinator, says the program logged 240 confirmed wild pigs provincewide last year. (Chelsea Kemp/CBC)

Strides in technology are making it easier to track the pests. Thermal drones allow teams to survey dense and inaccessible terrain more easily, while DNA testing helps hone in on potential groups of the animals.

"We're making progress.… If we're diligent and maintain our efforts, we will be able to eradicate them from Manitoba," Lees said.

"Maybe in a decade we won't need to talk about this anymore."

Spruce Woods Provincial Park, about 140 kilometres west of Winnipeg, remains a major hot spot and a key target for eradication.

"It's an island of bush land surrounded by agriculture," Lees said. "The wild pigs can go in there and hide out, and then they've got a feed source."

African swine fever

The primary disease threat posed by the animals is African swine fever, which is highly contagious and fatal to both commercial and wild pigs, Lees said.

The disease, which poses no threat to humans, is currently not in Canada.

Lee warns that if the disease ever takes hold in wild populations, it could spread to commercial herds, devastating Manitoba's hog industry.

Manitoba developed a response plan to cull and dispose of hundreds of thousands of pigs if an outbreak should occur.

Cassidy Klima, executive director of Animal Health Canada, said Manitoba is leading the charge when it comes to eradicating the invasive species. The national organization brings together industry and governments to prepare for and manage foreign animal disease outbreaks.

If African swine fever spreads to Canada, wild pigs could severely jeopardize food security and pork production, Klima said.

Cassidy Klima, executive director of Animal Health Canada, is optimistic about getting rid of wild pigs. (Chelsea Kemp/CBC)

She pointed to recent outbreaks in Europe damaging pork industry exports as an example, including an outbreak in Finland that the Canadian Food Inspection Agency reported in August.

"If African swine fever gets into our commercial herds, it can really decimate our food, our pork sector," Klima said.

"If we don't safeguard against that, no one else will."

The wild pigs originated from commercial wild boar farming in the 1980s. Klima said that in many cases, farms would shut down and release the animals into the wild.

Provincial regulation now prohibits wild boar farming to prevent further population expansion. A 2025 regulatory change under the Wildlife Act and the Exotic Wildlife Regulation banned importing or possessing the animals.

For now, Klima said she's optimistic for the future.

"Eradication is a true potential in Canada," she said. "We have a national strategy. We have a lot of people invested in seeing this through."

A group of wild pigs can leave a trail of destruction. (Submitted by Ryan Brook)

But declining population density presents challenges, making remaining groups of wild pigs harder to find, Klima said. That makes public awareness critical.

While the nocturnal wild pigs are rarely spotted directly, their environmental impact is stark, she said. A group of the animals, called a sounder, can leave trails of destruction across farms and pastures while devastating native ecosystems.

"They're not native to Canada.… they don't really fit into the environment," Klima said. "They just create a lot of damage."

Eradication efforts focus on capturing and euthanizing entire groups to stop population growth, Lees said. Sounders usually include mature breeding females and their offspring.

Manitoba's harsh weather climate also helps slow reproduction rates compared with warmer southern regions such as Texas, he said.

World.title: How the B.C. Conservatives toppled David Eby: Anthony Koch
World.content:
Article content

An election no one expected has produced one of the most remarkable political stories — and political comebacks — in recent Canadian history. The snap election gamble by B.C. Premier David Eby backfired spectacularly on the NDP, producing instead a massive majority government for the B.C. Conservatives. So how did the Conservatives — a party which seemed to be falling apart at the seams just a couple of months ago — turn the table on Eby’s opportunism and finally oust the NDP from power? In this interview, Rob Breakenridge speaks with Anthony Koch, a veteran conservative strategist who played a key role in the B.C. Conservative campaign. We’ll look at the circumstances that led to Eby’s fateful election decision and how it jolted the Conservative party toward unity. We’ll also look at the impact of Lorne Doerkson, B.C.’s premier-designate, and how his humble, down-to-earth image — coupled with a focused conservative message — helped to carry the day.
