World.title: Tabasco residents prepare to contain the damage caused by climate-change-induced coastal erosion
World.content:
As the Gulf of Mexico encroaches on the Tabasco coastal plain, some communities are working to recover natural barriers that protect the coast from erosion.

Residents of Barra de Santa Ana — a sandy strip of land separating the Gulf from the Carmen-Pajonal-Machona Lagoon System — have received training from Eni Mexico (the Mexican subsidiary of an Italian multinational energy company) and UNESCO to revegetate coastal dunes.

Climate change and the resulting rise in sea level threaten Santa Ana and other coastal communities and has resulted in the erosion of 85% of the 30 kilometers of coastline between Boca de Santa Ana and Boca de Panteones.

Up to 3.5 meters of shoreline are lost each year, prompting the development of the Dunas Vivas project (Living Dunes), which includes a temporary paid-work scheme to carry out its activities.

The project is part of a plan to reduce disaster risk and strengthen community resilience through science-based solutions and sustainable management of natural and cultural heritage. Community participation is critical to these restoration processes, ensuring ownership and long-term continuity.

With the additional help of local universities, ejido authorities and government officials, a 30-member brigade selected by the community was given a crash course in strategic planting to rebuild the vegetative barrier and the installation of sand catchers made from organic materials (to facilitate dune formation).

Additionally, the brigade will operate botanical nurseries and collect the germplasm (seeds, plant tissues, pollen, DNA, etc.) needed for the controlled propagation of species ideal for revegetation.

Coastal dunes are among the main natural defenses against hurricanes and storm surges, while also protecting communities, infrastructure and mangroves.

El Heraldo de Tabasco newspaper reported that the state has 50,044 hectares of mangrove forest, but large stretches of these coastal intertidal zones have scarce vegetation.

Government mapping of the area last year identified 2,179 hectares of disturbed mangrove compared to 406 hectares in the 2020 assessment.

A January 2026 report outlined the vulnerability of the Tabasco coast and the problems affecting the areas between the Gulf and lagoons.

In August 2026, a report prepared by the Navy warned of critical levels of erosion in El Alacrán, near La Machona Lagoon, as well as in Barra Santa Ana and in Paraíso further to the east.

With reports from UNESCO, Prevention Web and El Heraldo de Tabasco

World.title: Cartel roadblocks paralyze Matamoros after arrest of Gulf Cartel leader’s son
World.content:
Alleged cartel members set up roadblocks in Matamoros, Tamaulipas, on Monday after federal forces arrested a high-level criminal target in the northern border city.

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch confirmed Thursday afternoon that Axel Alfredo Cárdenas Rodríguez, son of a Gulf Cartel leader known as “El Contador” (The Accountant), had been detained earlier in the day. El Contador is José Alfredo Cárdenas Martínez, nephew of Osiel Cárdenas Guillén, a former Gulf Cartel leader and founder of Los Zetas criminal organization.

Como resultado de trabajos de inteligencia militar de @Defensamx, Fuerzas Especiales del Ejército Mexicano y de la @GN_MEXICO_ detuvieron en Matamoros, Tamaulipas, a dos personas, entre ellas Axel Alfredo “N”, alias “Axel”, identificado como segundo al mando de la célula delictiva “Ciclones”. Axel Alfredo “N” está relacionado con homicidios, secuestro, extorsión y tráfico de drogas, armas y personas hacia Estados Unidos. También es señalado como responsable de la agresión contra integrantes de @SSPCMexico, ocurrida el pasado 17 de mayo, en la que lamentablemente perdió la vida un compañero y varios más resultaron heridos. Su memoria y el compromiso de quienes arriesgan la vida para proteger a la ciudadanía nos obligan a continuar las investigaciones hasta detener a todos los responsables. No permitiremos que esta agresión quede impune. Durante la acción se aseguraron armas, cargadores, cartuchos, droga y un vehículo. Ambos detenidos fueron trasladados por la @FuerzaAereaMx a la Ciudad de México. — Omar H Garcia Harfuch (@OHarfuch) October 29, 2026

On Thursday afternoon, the Tamaulipas government’s security spokesperson’s office announced the arrest of a “priority target” on social media, but didn’t identify the suspect.

“In Matamoros, federal forces detained a priority target linked to an organized crime group,” the office said, adding that the suspect “was extracted from the area” prior to being turned over to “the relevant authorities.”

“As a result of these events, blockades have occurred at various points in Matamoros and Río Bravo,” the office said, referring in the latter case to a border municipality and city west of Matamoros.

“The public is advised to exercise caution, avoid the affected areas, use alternate routes, stay informed through official channels and follow the instructions of security authorities.”

🚨 La ciudad fronteriza de #Matamoros, Tamaulipas, registra bloqueos y quema de vehículos tras la detención de un integrante del Cártel del Golfo. La policía de Brownsville, Texas, informó que los puentes internacionales están cerrados por un “incidente de seguridad. 📹 Especial — La Silla Rota (@lasillarota) October 29, 2026

Blockades were also reported on the highway between Matamoros and Reynosa and the highway between Matamoros and Ciudad Victoria. The newspaper Reforma reported that main roads in Matamoros — located opposite Brownsville, Texas — were blocked.

“To block traffic, the criminals used public transport and cargo vehicles, as well as vehicles from which they had forced the drivers out,” Reforma reported.

In addition, “alleged organized crime accomplices … threw tire spikes on avenues in Reynosa and in the area around the [city’s] airport,” the newspaper wrote.

In addition to roadblocks, gunfire was reported in Matamoros and other parts of Tamaulipas, where criminals reportedly clashed with security forces.

Early Thursday afternoon, the Brownsville Police Department announced on social media that all international bridges between Brownsville and Matamoros were “closed due to an active security incident in Matamoros.”

However, later in the afternoon, it said that all bridges had “resumed normal operations.”

The Tamaulipas Ministry of Education canceled classes in Matamoros for students who start school in the afternoon (turno vespertino) in order to “protect the physical safety of school communities.”

The Gulf Cartel, one of eight Mexican criminal groups that the U.S. government has designated as foreign terrorist organizations, is one of the two main criminal groups that operate in Tamaulipas, the other being the Northeast Cartel.

According to the think tank and media organization Insight Crime, the Gulf Cartel is “one of Mexico’s oldest criminal groups, but it no longer operates as a unified organization.”

“… The Scorpions and the Cyclones are the most powerful factions. From the border, these groups smuggle migrants and drugs into the United States, move weapons and cash into Mexico, and operate complex extortion schemes,” Insight Crime says.

According to a report by the El Economista newspaper, Cárdenas Martínez is the leader of the Cyclones, while his son — who was detained today — is second-in-command.

With reports from Reforma and Aristegui Noticias

World.title: Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas, who helped end decades of one-party rule in Mexico, dies at 92
World.content:
Listen to this article

Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas Solórzano, a three-time presidential candidate, a central figure in Mexico’s democratic transition and son of former president Lázaro Cárdenas del Río, died in Mexico City on Wednesday. He was 92.

The cause of Cárdenas’ death was not immediately clear. He reportedly passed away in the Ángeles Metropolitano Hospital in the Roma Sur neighborhood of the capital.

President Claudia Sheinbaum and former President Andrés Manuel López Obrador acknowledged Cárdenas’ death in social media posts on Wednesday night.

Sheinbaum called him “a man of steadfast principles who transformed the political life of our country.”

López Obrador said Cárdenas was “a precursor of the democratic movement in Mexico’s recent history.”

“Without him, the country’s political reality would be different,” he wrote.

La presidenta Claudia Sheinbaum encabeza la guardia de honor ante el féretro de Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas, histórico líder de la izquierda mexicana, acompañada por la familia del fallecido político. Más información en López-Dóriga Digital https://t.co/rSlCjtnTUo — Joaquín López-Dóriga (@lopezdoriga) October 29, 2026

Cárdenas is credited with helping to end the Institutional Revolutionary Party’s decades-long rule in Mexico, which spanned much of the 20th century. He was a member of the PRI for more than 30 years, but left the party in 1987 and ran in the 1988 presidential election as the candidate for the National Democratic Front, a coalition of left-wing parties. Cárdenas is widely believed to have won that election, but the PRI’s Carlos Salinas de Gortari was declared the winner.

He would go on to contest the 1994 and 2000 elections as the candidate for the Democratic Revolution Party (PRD), which he co-founded. The 2000 election was won by the National Action Party (PAN) candidate Vicente Fox, who became the first president of Mexico from outside the PRI or its predecessors in 71 years.

The early years

Cárdenas was born in Mexico City on May 1, 1934, exactly two months before his father, Lázaro Cárdenas, won the 1934 presidential election with more than 98% of the vote. His mother was Amalia Solórzano Bravo, who, like his father, was a native of Michoacán.

Cárdenas was not yet four years old when his father nationalized Mexico’s oil industry on March 18, 1938. Lázaro Cárdenas is best remembered for that historic decision, but also oversaw significant land reform, redistributing millions of hectares to small-scale farmers, or campesinos.

Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas spent his early years living at Los Pinos, the erstwhile residence of the president of Mexico. The New York Times reported that “[a] boyhood friend, José J. Altamirano, remembered the young Cuauhtémoc pushing toy trucks around his father’s feet there.”

Cárdenas was educated at private schools before enrolling in a civil engineering degree at the National Autonomous University of Mexico (UNAM). He graduated from UNAM in the mid-1950s and worked as a civil engineer before starting his long political career.

Cárdenas wed María Celeste Batel in 1963 and they remained married until her death in 2021. The couple had three children.

A political life

Cárdenas was a member of the PRI from 1954 to 1987. During that period, he served as a federal senator for Michoacán (1976-80) and governor of Michoacán (1980-86).

While in those positions, he was critical of the federal government’s economic decisions — Mexico’s so-called neoliberal period began in 1982 — and the “dedazo,” the colloquial name for the practice in which the sitting president handpicked the PRI’s next presidential candidate.

Before he left the PRI, Cárdenas, Porfirio Muñoz, Ifigenia Martínez and others founded the Corriente Democrática (Democratic Current), a progressive and reformist faction of the PRI.

The 1988 presidential election

Cárdenas had hopes of representing the PRI at the 1988 presidential election, but President Miguel de la Madrid chose Salinas de Gortari — a free trade advocate — as the party’s flag bearer.

Having left the PRI, Cárdenas stood as the candidate for the National Democratic Front, which was backed by the Mexican Socialist Party and the Authentic Party of the Mexican Revolution, among other parties and organizations.

His message of economic nationalism resonated with voters, and early results on the night of the 1988 election showed that he had a significant lead over Salinas. However, later in the night, election officials claimed that the electoral computer system had broken down and they stopped reporting results. Before midnight on July 6, 1988, Salinas was declared the winner with almost 51% of the vote compared to Cárdenas’ 31%, according to the official, but highly questionable, results.

De la Madrid admitted that the results were rigged in his 2004 memoir.

The New York Times reported that Cárdenas’ “sway over the Mexican people was so great that he could have, with a few words, set off a bloody civil war after obvious fraud in the 1988 presidential election robbed him of the victory that many believed was his.”

“But instead of whipping up their anger, he convinced his followers that they could launch a true revolution, not by taking to the streets but by returning to the polls.”

“Se cayó el sistema”. La elección presidencial de 1988 marcó para siempre la trayectoria de Cuauhtémoc Cárdenas. La interrupción del flujo de información, las denuncias de fraude y el triunfo oficial de Carlos Salinas de Gortari abrieron una de las mayores polémicas electorales de México. Así fue aquella histórica elección. @renzochiquito nos cuenta https://t.co/beFZrZj8VB — Azteca Noticias (@AztecaNoticias) October 29, 2026

Cárdenas seeks the presidency again

In 1989, Cárdenas, Porfirio Muñoz, Ifigenia Martínez and Andrés Manuel López Obrador founded the PRD, which became Mexico’s main left-wing party.

Cárdenas represented the PRD at the 1994 and 2000 presidential elections, finishing third in both.

In between his second and third presidential bids, he served as mayor of Mexico City between 1997 and 1999, having won the first direct election of the capital’s head of government, a position previously filled by presidential appointment.

President Sheinbaum used the Mexico City mayorship as a springboard to the presidency, but that wasn’t the case for Cárdenas. Fox took the presidency for the PAN in 2000, which, along with Felipe Calderón’s victory in another controversial election in 2006, left the PRI out of power at the federal level for 12 years. The once-dominant party wouldn’t return to the national halls of power until Enrique Peña Nieto took office in late 2012.

While he didn’t rise to the national leadership position he appeared to be destined for, Cárdenas “was, in a real sense, one of the midwives of Mexico’s democratic transition,” according to University of California political scientist Kathleen Bruhn.

He helped turn the PRD into a competitive political party after the long 20th-century hegemony of the PRI. The party won elections in Mexico City and various states before its recent demise as a result of its poor showing in the 2024 federal elections. Cárdenas left the PRD in 2014, 25 years after co-founding the party, due to differences with its leadership, but he will forever be linked to the party that was Mexico’s preeminent leftist force until the emergence last decade of the National Regeneration Movement, or Morena, which has ruled Mexico since late 2018.

Symbol of the Mexican left

The La Jornada newspaper described Cárdenas as a “symbol of the left in Mexico” and a “historic leader” of the national leftist movement.

“Cárdenas left a profound mark on contemporary political history by leading the most significant rupture of the PRI in the decade of the ’80s, the … Corriente Democrática, and by opening a new stage for the Mexican left,” reported the Mexico City-based daily.

“… He became closely associated with the emergence of an electoral left, the call for free and competitive elections, and the transformation of the Mexican political system. He also supported causes such as those of the EZLN [the Zapatista Army of National Liberation] and the defense of energy resources and national sovereignty,” La Jornada wrote.

El Universal reported that biographers have defined his ideology as “rejection of neoliberalism, defense of the state in strategic sectors, especially energy, austerity, national sovereignty and laicism.”

Cárdenas’ autumn years

Cárdenas remained engaged in Mexican politics in the later years of his life. He spoke out about the need to combat organized crime groups and retake territory they control, and voiced concerns about issues such as low economic growth, the militarization of public security and insufficient funding for education and healthcare.

“I’m very concerned about the situation we’re living, the situation that the country is going through,” he said during a meeting with a cross-party group of senators in 2022. He made those remarks while his former PRD colleague, López Obrador, was in office. Like Cárdenas, AMLO contested three presidential elections, but, in contrast to his political associate, won on his third attempt.

In 2011, Cárdenas, at the age of 77, was awarded the Belisario Domínguez medal, the Mexican Senate’s highest honor, in recognition of his political career and contributions to public life. Among those contributions are several books he authored.

Cárdenas is survived by his three children Cuauhtémoc, Camila and Lázaro Cárdenas Batel, and his grandchildren. Lázaro, governor of Michoacán between 2002 and 2008, is President Sheinbaum’s chief of staff.

With reports from La Jornada, Reforma, El Economista, El Universal and The New York Times

World.title: After a surprisingly strong start, Chipotle plans more restaurants in Nuevo León and Mexico City
World.content:
Chipotle, the U.S. fast-casual food chain inspired by Mexican and Tex-Mex food, plans to open more restaurants in Mexico after its first branch in the country exceeded expectations.

Mexico’s first Chipotle restaurant opened in July 2026 in the border state of Nuevo León, in the high-end municipality of San Pedro Garza García, part of the greater Monterrey area.

Alsea, a Mexican company that operates the U.S. brand, said it plans to open between three and four additional locations in Nuevo León during the first quarter of 2027, while also preparing for its entry into Mexico City that same year.

According to Alsea CEO Christian Gurría, the public’s positive response to the first restaurant exceeded the “honeymoon effect” associated with the initial excitement surrounding an opening.

“Now that our operation is consolidating and the flow of customers is stabilizing, we remain above [expectations],” Gurría said during a call with analysts cited by Bloomberg Línea.

Chipotle arrived in the country after other Tex-Mex food chains tried—and failed—to establish a market there, including U.S. fast-food mainstay Taco Bell, which attempted to expand into Mexico in the 1990s and the 2000s.

Gurría attributed the favorable reception of Chipotle to a combination of price, quality, and portion size. According to Bloomberg Línea, the bowls, burritos, and salads on the Mexican menu cost between 150 and 200 pesos (US $7.98 and $10.64).

The expansion of Chipotle is part of the renewal of Alsea’s portfolio in Mexico, which also includes preparations for the arrival of Raising Cane’s, a U.S. chain specializing in breaded chicken tenders. According to Gurría, the brand’s first branch is set to open in the first quarter of 2027.

Beyond Mexico, Alsea operates and develops restaurant and coffee shop chains in other parts of Latin America and Europe. Its portfolio includes brands such as Starbucks, Domino’s Pizza, Burger King, Vips, Chili’s, Italianni’s, P. F. Chang’s, and The Cheesecake Factory.

According to Alsea’s latest financial report cited by specialized media Merca 2.0, Starbucks remains one of its largest-scale operations with 1,983 coffee shops across 12 countries, including 976 located in Mexico.

The company operates more than 4,800 units across 12 countries, and trades on the Mexican Stock Exchange.

With reports from Bloomberg Línea and Merca 2.0

World.title: Mexico City Grand Prix: Everything to know for the year’s premier motor sports event
World.content:
Formula 1 — the world’s most popular motorsport series — is in Mexico City this week for the 21st race of its 2026 season.

Widely viewed as one of the most vibrant, high-energy and uniquely festive spectacles on the F1 calendar, the Mexico City Grand Prix is expected to attract 400,000 fans to the Autódromo Hermanos Rodríguez this weekend.

For most in Mexico, Guadalajara native Sergio “Checo” Pérez is the star attraction of this year’s F1 event and will be competing in his 10th Mexico City GP. Checo — who missed last year’s race after being released by Red Bull following the 2024 season — will be racing for Cadillac, a constructor in its first year of competition.

Helping make his return to his home country extra special, Cadillac announced on Wednesday that it had signed Checo to a contract extension, keeping the six-time Grand Prix winner with the team through the 2029 season.

Checo has another reason to celebrate. Sunday’s race will be his 300th F1 race, making him the seventh driver in history to reach that number. As if getting to achieve that milestone at home is not enough, Checo also made a special appearance in the capital on Wednesday.

Driving a modified Formula 2 car, Pérez rumbled along the Paseo de la Reforma avenue in front of an estimated 100,000 onlookers. He burned rubber while performing donuts near the Diana roundabout, then stopped at the Angel of Independence Monument to acknowledge the fans.

“I know some of you have been here since last ​night. I really appreciate it,” Checo told the crowd. “You guys are one of the main reasons I ​came back.”

The what, when and where of the F-1 weekend

For those planning on attending the F-1 race, the Hermanos Rodríguez circuit is inside the Ciudad Deportiva de la Magdalena Mixhuca public park located at the eastern terminus of the Viaducto Río de la Piedad (Viaducto Miguel Alemán). It can also be reached by Metrobus (Line 2) and Metro (Line 9).

Tickets are available via the Official Mexico GP Website, the Formula 1 Official Ticket Portal or through verified secondary resale markets like StubHub.

As for the event, drivers will take two practice runs on Friday, while the third practice run and qualifying take place Saturday.

The Mexico City GP, featuring 71 laps of the 4.3-kilometer (2.6-mile) track, begins at 2 p.m. Sunday.

Of note, Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli, 20, could become the youngest champion in series history by finishing in the top nine.

Also competing is five-time Mexico City GP winner Max Verstappen (2017, 2018, 2021, 2022, 2023). Sergio Pérez was Verstappen’s teammate from 2021 through 2024.

With reports from The Associated Press, Reuters, The Straits Times and Grand Prix 247

World.title: MND Local CDMX: Rent reforms, a viral Tesla crash and possible Cowboys game
World.content:
Mexico City is tackling a range of issues this week, from housing affordability and suspected dog poisonings to a dramatic car crash caught on camera. Meanwhile, Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones has teased a future NFL game in the capital, adding to the growing buzz around U.S. sports in Mexico.

Let’s get into it.

Morena’s housing bill aims to curb rent hikes and gentrification

The ruling Morena party and Mayor Clara Brugada put forth a framework on Oct. 22, aimed at stabilizing Mexico City’s ongoing housing rental affordability crisis.

Dubbed the Law on Tenant Relations and Fair, Reasonable and Affordable Rents, the reforms include capping rent increases, prohibiting excessive requirements to obtain a rental, creating an official government office tasked with handling tenant-landlord relations, and building more affordable housing.

In a news release, the administration said the bill is aimed at “curbing gentrification and guaranteeing the right to housing.”

According to the mayor’s office, roughly 2 million people rent their homes in the capital, representing a 54% increase over the past 15 years. Rent, meanwhile, “frequently exceeds 30% of the family income,” a benchmark set by the United Nations in 2020, with prices in some high-demand areas skyrocketing between 100% and 200% over the past decade.

Mexico City’s government already passed a 2024 law capping rent increases relative to inflation. However, the new legislation goes a step further, barring landlords from raising a property’s rent when it changes from one tenant to another. There is an exception for landlords who undertake significant renovations to a property.

Other reforms included in the legislation

A Bill of Rights protecting renters from excessive rental requirements and discrimination. A Tenant Relations Ombudsman tasked with providing free legal advice and resolving disputes. A Digital Registry of Contracts and a one-year lease requirement. A Social Support Office for Evictions, tasked with ensuring the eviction process is “peaceful and respects human dignity.” An affordable housing project that aims to build 80,000 new units alongside 120,000 improvement and expansion projects in low-income neighborhoods. A Public Housing Observatory tasked with monitoring land prices and rental prices across Mexico City’s 16 boroughs.

According to the International Business Times, Morena is gathering signatures for the bill, which it will present to the Mexico City Congress as a show of public support. The proposal is currently being considered by the joint Housing and Administration and Justice committees.

Authorities investigate suspected dog poisonings at Parque España

We reported on this in Mexico News Daily’s regular coverage. However, some stories are so important, we felt it prudent to reiterate here: Authorities are investigating suspected dog poisonings at Parque España in the capital’s Condesa neighborhood.

Simply put, if you or someone you know is a pet parent in the capital (cat walkers, we see you too), please be aware and spread the word.

In a news release published Oct. 27, the Attorney General’s Office of Mexico City announced it is launching an investigation and preventative measures after several dogs became fatally ill while spending time in the park, which features a popular off-leash dog area.

According to the AG’s office, the Citizen Security Ministry (SSC) was called to a nearby veterinary clinic that was treating the dogs. The SSC subsequently canvassed the park and found a blue pill wrapped in a piece of sausage. The pill, which is currently being investigated, has not been definitively linked to the suspected poisonings.

The case is being treated as potential animal abuse and cruelty. While the park is still open, the dog run and children’s areas were closed for cleanup.

“Citizens are urged to report any situation that could put the integrity of animals at risk to 911 or to the SSC Secretary’s Contact Unit, at telephone 55 5208 9898,” the Attorney General’s Office wrote in its news release, “as well as through the accounts @SSC_CDMX and @UCS_GCDMX.”

Tesla crash in affluent Mexico City neighborhood goes viral

A viral video of a shocking car crash in western Mexico City is making the rounds, roughly a week after the incident.

According to video obtained by U.S. media outlet TMZ, a Tesla careens off the road in Cuajimalpa, smashes through a gate and part of another structure before launching off a side patio and ultimately landing somewhere off-screen.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by TMZ (@tmztv)

A time stamp on the footage, taken from what appears to be a home surveillance video, dates the incident to Oct. 19. The incident occurred in Cuajimalpa’s affluent Lomas del Chamizal neighborhood.

International Business Times reports that the cause of the crash, as well as the condition of those involved, is unknown.

Dallas Cowboys tease future game in Mexico City

With the NFL’s first Mexico City series game of the season less than a month away, Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones suggested his team could soon be coming to the capital.

During a post-game interview with ESPN’s John Sutcliffe on Monday, Oct. 26, Jones was asked, on a scale of one to 10, about the likelihood of the Cowboys playing at Mexico City’s Estadio Azteca (also known as Estadio Banorte).

“One,” Jones said several times before catching his mistake and changing his answer to an emphatic 10. “We’re coming,” he added.

Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott doubled down on the enthusiasm, telling Sutcliffe a game in Mexico City would be “exciting.”

“I know the atmosphere would be electric,” Prescott said. “Viva Mexico!”

U.S. sports have had something of a moment in Mexico as of late.

Ticket demand for the Nov. 22 Week 11 match-up between the San Francisco 49ers and Minnesota Vikings was extraordinary, with some 840,000 fans registering to get a highly coveted seat, as Mexico News Daily previously reported.

Meanwhile, NBA Commissioner Adam Silver suggested last week that Mexico City could be considered for a future league expansion, telling the Pat McAfee Show, “It’s a shorter flight from New York to Mexico than from New York to Los Angeles, so you can see why we’d be interested.”

Drew Pittock serves as Mexico News Daily’s features director. He is based in Mexico City. Have an idea for a feature story or unique event in CDMX? Send an email to drew.pittock@mexiconewsdaily.com.

World.title: Mexico in Numbers: How does Mexico’s education system compare to other countries?
World.content:
Last week, we published Part 2 of the MND Mexico Well-being Series, which focused on eight education indicators, including expenditure on education as a percentage of GDP, average class sizes in primary and secondary schools and Mexico’s scores in the 2025 PISA tests.

This “Mexico in Numbers” article is a condensed version of that report — a concise presentation of the key data, complemented by visual features.

As we have previously noted, the MND Mexico Well-being Series — a collection of articles on a range of topics related to well-being — draws on the most recent internationally comparable data, as well as data from the past decade, to assess the state of well-being in Mexico today, and to see what has changed in Mexico during the eight years that the ruling Morena party has been in office.

Without further ado, let’s take a look at the key data from Part 2 of the series.

* The data in this article comes from the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development’s Education at a Glance 2026 report and the OECD’s PISA 2025 Results report.

Early childhood education enrollment rates

Just 4% of two-year-olds in Mexico were enrolled in early childhood education programs meeting International Standard Classification of Education (ISCED) criteria in 2024, compared with an OECD average of 50%, placing Mexico last among 30 countries assessed.

Enrollment among children aged 3 to primary-school entry was 75%, versus an OECD average of 90%, ranking Mexico 42nd of 46 countries.

Both rates declined from 2015, when they stood at 5% and 79%, respectively, widening Mexico’s gaps with the OECD averages.

Expenditure on education as a percentage of GDP

Mexico’s government spent the equivalent of 2.9% of GDP on education in 2023, below the OECD average of 4.2%, ranking it 39th of 42 countries, or fourth-lowest.

Mexico’s spending on education fell from 4.4% of GDP in 2015 — when it matched the OECD average — a decline of 1.5 percentage points.

Educational attainment rates

In 2025, 40% of Mexicans aged 25–34 lacked an upper secondary qualification, down from 55% in 2015 but still well above the OECD average of 12%, leaving Mexico fourth-worst among 47 countries.

Tertiary attainment among the same age group rose from around 21% to 29% over the decade.

In 2025, 28% of young men and 30% of young women held tertiary qualifications — 12 and 24 percentage points below the respective OECD averages — ranking Mexico 39th of 45 countries for both sexes.

Teacher qualifications

In 2024, 82% of preschool teachers, 92% of primary teachers and 87% of lower secondary teachers in Mexico met national minimum educational attainment requirements. Mexico exceeded the OECD average only at primary level, by four percentage points, while trailing it by five points at preschool level and two points at lower secondary level.

All three rates declined between 2017 and 2024, falling by five, five and six percentage points, respectively.

Average class sizes in primary and lower secondary education

Mexico’s primary school classes averaged 23 students in 2024, while lower secondary classes averaged 25 — both two students above the respective OECD averages. Mexico’s classes were larger than those in 30 of 38 countries assessed at primary level and 27 of 38 at lower secondary level.

Since 2015, average primary class sizes increased by one student, while lower secondary class sizes fell by three.

PISA scores

Mexican 15-year-olds scored below OECD averages in all four areas assessed in PISA 2025: reading (408 points), science (414), mathematics (388) and computational problem solving (453), with gaps ranging from 47 to 75 points.

Mexico ranked equal 52nd of 90 countries and jurisdictions in reading, equal 63rd of 91 in science and equal 64th of 90 in mathematics.

Since 2015, Mexico’s average reading score fell by 15 points, its math score declined 20 points and its science score dropped two points. Nevertheless, the gaps between Mexico’s scores and OECD averages narrowed as OECD scores declined more sharply between 2015 and 2025.

Students’ exposure to bullying

In 2025, 19.5% of Mexican students aged 15 and 16 reported being bullied at school at least a few times a month, just below the OECD average of 19.6%. Mexico had the 38th-lowest bullying rate among 88 countries and jurisdictions.

Mexico’s bullying rate declined from 20.2% in 2015 — a fall of 0.7 percentage points — allowing it to move from above to slightly below the OECD average.

NEET rate

In 2025, 19% of Mexicans aged 18–24 were neither employed nor in education or training (NEET), five percentage points above the OECD average of 14%, giving Mexico the joint ninth-highest rate among 41 countries. The rate was 29% for young women, compared with 10% for young men.

Mexico’s overall NEET rate fell from 23% in 2015, narrowing its gap with the OECD average from seven to five percentage points.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: LP in Mexico City, 22 November 2026
World.content:
File photo, 2011. The entrance steps and name sign of the Auditorio Nacional on Paseo de la Reforma in Mexico City, where LP plays on 22 November 2026. (Photo: Nacho Facello, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

MEXICO · MUSIC

Key Facts Date and time Sunday 22 November 2026, 7 p.m. Mexico City time (8 p.m. US Eastern); doors open two hours earlier.

Venue Auditorio Nacional, Paseo de la Reforma 50, Polanco, Mexico City; 9,564 seats.

Tickets Venue box office without service charge, or Ticketmaster Mexico with a commission; up to eight per person.

Prices MXN 880 to MXN 2,590 (US$47 to US$138) by seating zone, as listed by the venue.

Getting there Metro Line 7 or Metrobús Line 7 to Auditorio station; parking costs MXN 270 (US$14).

LP, the Los Angeles-based singer-songwriter behind the 2017 hit “Lost On You”, plays the Auditorio Nacional in Mexico City on Sunday 22 November 2026 at 7 p.m. local time as part of the All Is Not Lost Tour. Seat prices run from MXN 880 (US$47) to MXN 2,590 (US$138), and tickets are on sale at the venue box office and on Ticketmaster Mexico.

The show is one of four Mexican dates on LP’s tour listing, which also shows Monterrey on Friday 20 November, Zapopan near Guadalajara on Wednesday 25 November and the Tecate Comuna 2026 date in San Andrés Cholula, in the state of Puebla, on Saturday 28 November. The same hall hosts the singer Hayley Williams four days later, on Thursday 26 November, according to the venue calendar.

Who Is LP and Why This Tour Matters

LP is a Los Angeles-based singer-songwriter whose official biography says the 2017 folk ballad “Lost On You” reached No. 1 in 18 countries. The same biography says LP has played sold-out shows in more than 150 cities, with 3,000 to 20,000 tickets per show, which puts the 9,564-seat Auditorio Nacional inside that range.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 71.4 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The artist’s website lists a release called Room 12 as out now, and the venue prints the tour name, All Is Not Lost, on its event page. The tour listing shows 15 dates between 2 and 28 November, 11 of them in Europe and 4 in Mexico, so the Mexican shows close the listed run.

Mexico City is the only one of the four Mexican stops on a Sunday, which matters for travelers planning around the working week. The venue says its 9,564 seats sit in five sections that are reached through 26 doors spread over three floors.

File photo, 2023. A concert by the Argentine singer Tini Stoessel at the Auditorio Nacional, showing the hall’s stage (not LP). (Photo: MJVV27, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

We send a confirmation link first, and the same address then receives The Rio Times Brief, our daily briefing. Unsubscribe with one click at any time; see our privacy policy. Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

Tickets, Prices and Sale Rules

The Auditorio Nacional lists five price zones for the show: Preferente MXN 2,590 (US$138), Luneta MXN 1,890 (US$100), Balcón MXN 1,520 (US$81), Primer Piso MXN 1,180 (US$63) and Segundo Piso MXN 880 (US$47). Dollar amounts use the Bank of Mexico’s daily reference rate, known as the FIX rate, of MXN 18.8148 per US$ for Thursday 29 October 2026, the latest rate published.

The venue says tickets bought at its box office carry no service charge, while purchases on Ticketmaster Mexico include a commission for the ticket company. The venue page does not say whether the listed prices already include that commission, so compare the final total at checkout.

A buyer can purchase up to eight tickets per person, and refunds are given only if the event is canceled or postponed. The box office on the venue forecourt takes cash, credit cards and debit cards, and a second box office inside the hall serves attendees from two hours before the show.

The regular box office opens Monday to Saturday from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m., and on Sundays and holidays it works from 11 a.m. until 6 in the evening. The venue recommends buying tickets as early as possible.

The hall has 24 spaces for wheelchair users and a companion on the first floor, and its elevators are reserved for wheelchair users, older adults and pregnant women. The venue also lists a ramp on the west side of the building, near the parking entrance.

Getting to the Auditorio Nacional

The Auditorio Nacional stands at Avenida Paseo de la Reforma 50 in the Polanco neighborhood, beside Campo Marte, in the Miguel Hidalgo borough of Mexico City. The venue says visitors can arrive on Metro Line 7 or Metrobús Line 7, and both lines stop at the station called Auditorio.

The hall opens two hours before each show and closes two hours after it ends. For the 7 p.m. start, that means the building opens around 5 in the afternoon.

Parking at the venue costs MXN 270 (US$14) per event, is paid at the pay stations inside the building, and the lot has limited space. The venue warns that no employee will ask for payment in advance and that visitors should not follow anyone who offers to lead them to another lot.

Bicycle parking is free, and the venue’s parking page lists event-day rates of MXN 180 (US$10) self-service or MXN 210 (US$11) with valet at the Hyatt Regency (Campos Elíseos 204) and the Presidente InterContinental (Campos Elíseos 218). The Hyatt rate is valid only on the day of the event and close to showtime, and the ticket must be shown at the valet window.

What to Bring and What to Leave at Home

The venue bans food, pets, photo and video cameras, selfie sticks, laser pointers, audio recorders, weapons, sharp objects, flags on poles and anything that blocks the view, such as banners, signs, flowers and balloons. Backpacks, suitcases, strollers and bulky items must be left at the free cloakroom on the east side of the lobby, in front of door 1.

Cash machines of the banks BBVA and Banamex stand on the east side of the lobby, and the hall has food and drink stations on each level. Food may not be taken into the hall, so plan to buy snacks at the stations or eat before arriving.

Safety and Entry Tips for US Visitors

The State Department rates Mexico Level 2, exercise increased caution, in an advisory dated 29 May 2026, citing terrorism, crime and kidnapping. It advises US citizens to follow the restrictions placed on its own employees, which include not traveling between cities after dark and not waving down taxis on the street.

For the ride home, the advisory points to dispatched vehicles from regulated taxi stands or app-based services such as Uber or Cabify, and it advises avoiding travel alone, especially in remote areas. The hall sits on a main avenue, so book the return ride through an app or the hotel before the show ends.

The US Embassy in Mexico issued demonstration alerts for Mexico City covering 10, 13, 21 and 26 October 2026, and the 26 October alert warned of transportation protests that could disrupt the highways into the city. Check the embassy’s alerts page on the day, and enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) to receive security updates.

Mexico City stays on UTC-6 all year, while US clocks fall back on Sunday 1 November 2026, so the 7 p.m. start equals 8 p.m. in New York and 5 p.m. in Los Angeles. Entry rules and stay limits are set by Mexico’s National Migration Institute (INM), so check its website before booking flights.

What It Means for You

The cheapest seat, at MXN 880 (US$47), is the entry price for an LP concert in a 9,564-seat hall, and buying at the box office avoids the commission that Ticketmaster adds. A Sunday evening show also fits a weekend trip that ends before the working week.

Travelers who want more to do around the concert can read the guide to what to do in Mexico City in November and follow the Mexico coverage for security and transport news. Fans who also want the Monterrey or Zapopan dates should check the tour listing, because those shows use different venues and sellers.

What Is Not Known

The venue page does not say whether the listed prices include the Ticketmaster commission, and neither the venue page nor the tour listing shows a sold-out label for the show as of 30 October 2026. No opening act has been announced on the pages reviewed for this guide.

Neither the venue nor the tour listing publishes a set length or a running order, so the end time is unknown. The pages also do not say whether a US broadcast or livestream is planned.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where is LP playing in Mexico City?

LP plays the Auditorio Nacional on Sunday 22 November 2026 at 7 p.m. local time, which is 8 p.m. US Eastern. The venue opens two hours before the show.

How much are tickets and where can I buy them?

The venue lists seats from MXN 880 (US$47) to MXN 2,590 (US$138), sold at its box office without a service charge or on Ticketmaster Mexico with a commission. Buyers can purchase up to eight tickets per person.

How do I get to the Auditorio Nacional?

Take Metro Line 7 or Metrobús Line 7 to the Auditorio station, or park at the venue for MXN 270 (US$14) per event. The address is Avenida Paseo de la Reforma 50 in Polanco.





Sources: Auditorio Nacional, LP event page (venue), 30 October 2026; Auditorio Nacional, frequently asked questions; Auditorio Nacional, seating; Auditorio Nacional, parking; Auditorio Nacional, access policies; Auditorio Nacional, cloakroom and services; Auditorio Nacional, recommendations; LP, official tour page, 30 October 2026; LP, official biography; Bank of Mexico, FIX exchange rate, 29 October 2026; US State Department, Mexico travel advisory (Level 2), 29 May 2026; US Embassy in Mexico, alerts page, 30 October 2026; US Embassy in Mexico, demonstration alert, 26 October 2026.

On the 4-hour chart the latest candle took 1.9% off gold and 2.3% off silver, and silver has lost 4.4% in three 4-hour candles. Hourly readings of the Relative Strength Index, a gauge of how stretched a move is, are 17 for gold and 15 for silver; anything below 30 counts as oversold.

Two, Five and Seven Days

Period Gold Silver Mon 26 Oct +0.5% -0.0% Tue 27 Oct +1.2% +1.1% Wed 28 Oct +0.2% -1.0% Thu 29 Oct -1.2% -3.7% Fri 30 Oct (10:38 a.m. ET) -3.3% -5.7% Two days (since Wed close) -4.4% -9.1% Five sessions -2.6% -9.0% Seven sessions -5.7% -14.7% Since 19 Oct open (9 sessions) -7.0% -14.6% Spot prices, weekday closes; Friday at 10:38 a.m. ET. Source: Rio Times market data (RT).

The losses grow with every session: silver fell 1.0% on Wednesday, 3.7% on Thursday and 5.7% on Friday, and gold has lost 4.4% in two days. Over five sessions silver is down 9.0% and gold 2.6%; over seven sessions silver has lost 14.7%, or US$8.48 an ounce, and gold 5.7%, about US$236.

Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

Both trade below their 50-day and 200-day moving averages. On the daily chart the RSI is 30.0 for gold and 23.0 for silver, a deeply oversold reading for silver.

Since 19 October

Measured from Monday 19 October, when gold opened at US$4,184 and silver at US$57.38, silver has lost 14.6%, or US$8.38 an ounce, in nine sessions and gold 7.0%, or US$294. From the highest prices since then, gold at US$4,190 that Monday and silver at US$58.60 on 20 October, silver is down 16.4% and gold 7.2%.

Compared with the close of Friday 16 October the losses are 14.1% for silver (US$8.02) and 6.7% for gold (US$278). Most of it has come in the last six sessions: silver was still above US$57 on Wednesday 21 October.

Why It Is Happening

The main driver is the Federal Reserve. It held its rate at 3.75% to 4.00% this week, but two policymakers, Lisa Cook and Michelle Bowman, voted for an immediate increase, and futures markets now price roughly an 85% chance of a hike in December.

Higher expected rates make interest-bearing assets more attractive than metals that pay nothing, and the 10-year Treasury yield, near 5%, and a stronger dollar add to the pressure. Silver falls faster because more than half of its demand is industrial and its market is smaller, so leveraged traders move it harder.

Has This Happened Before?

Yes, and much worse: on 30 January 2026, days after the records, silver fell 24.2% in one session and gold 10.5%, and silver lost about 32% in the seven sessions to 6 February. A silver drop of today’s size has occurred about 20 times since 2022, most recently on 14 October (5.5%), 28 September (5.4%) and 10 September (5.6%).

Even since that January crash there have been deeper slides: in March 2026 silver lost 22% and gold 14.5% in nine sessions, and in June silver lost about 18% and gold 10%. The current slide, with silver down 14.6% and gold 7.0% in nine sessions, is a serious one but not the largest of the year.

What is different is the combination: losses that grow day after day, a steepening intraday curve, and daily oversold readings in both metals at once. Silver’s 14.7% loss in seven sessions is among its five worst such stretches in the data and was last exceeded on 25 June 2026 (17.6%); gold’s 5.7% was last exceeded on 2 September (6.3%).

What Would End It

Accelerating drops of this shape are typical of forced selling, such as stop-loss orders and margin calls, and they often end in a sharp rebound. Gold trades about 2.2% and silver 3.7% below their 20-period hourly averages, which is stretched enough for a bounce.

A bounce would not change the trend, though, until prices recover the 4-hour 20-period average, about US$4,005 for gold and US$52.3 for silver. The Fed’s December meeting is the decisive date: a hike would deepen the slide, while a signal of a pause could spark a strong rebound.

What It Means for US Readers

For investors in gold and silver funds, coins or bars, the losses since the January peaks are now about 30% in gold and almost 60% in silver. Falling prices can look like a bargain, but an oversold market can stay oversold, and nothing in the chart yet marks a bottom.

Miners and jewelry buyers feel the move too: miners’ margins shrink with the metal price, while buyers of jewelry and coins see lower prices. Anyone who holds metals as a hedge against inflation should note that the market is pricing tighter policy, which works against them.

What Is Not Known

The Friday closing prices are not yet set, because the figures here are a 10:38 a.m. ET snapshot and final settlements may differ. How much of the move comes from algorithmic selling, forced liquidation, margin calls, options or physical flows has not been established.

Sources: Rio Times market data (spot prices, daily archive since 2022); Federal Reserve decision and futures-market pricing as reported; Treasury yield data. This is news, not investment advice.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is silver falling more than gold?

Silver is a smaller market and more than half of its demand is industrial, so it reacts more to rate expectations and to leveraged trading. That is why silver lost 5.7% on Friday against 3.3% for gold.

Is this the worst sell-off in precious metals?

No. On 30 January 2026 silver fell 24.2% and gold 10.5% in a single session. What stands out now is that the losses grow every day and both metals are oversold at once.

How far have gold and silver fallen from their records?

Gold is about 30% below its peak of about US$5,596 on 28 January 2026, and silver almost 60% below its peak of about US$121.6 on 29 January. Both are far below their 200-day averages.

What would signal the sell-off is ending?

A recovery above the 4-hour 20-period average, about US$4,005 for gold and US$52.3 for silver, would be an early sign. A signal from the Fed that it will pause would be the stronger one.

World.title: Costa Rica National Symphony in San Jose, 13 November 2026
World.content:
File photo, 2014. The facade of the Teatro Nacional de Costa Rica in downtown San Jose at dusk. (Photo: CZmarlin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

COSTA RICA · CLASSICAL MUSIC

Key Facts Date Friday 13 November 2026, 8 p.m. (9 p.m. in New York); repeat Sunday 15 November, 10:30 a.m.

Venue Main Hall, Teatro Nacional de Costa Rica, Avenida Segunda, Calles 3 and 5, San José.

Tickets Teatro Nacional box office and official website; online sales run until two hours before the start.

Prices From ₡2,220 (US$4.90) in the side gallery to ₡10,000 (US$22.07) in front-row boxes, before fees.

Program Freitas Branco’s Paraísos Artificiais, Korngold’s Violin Concerto and Debussy’s La Mer, per the orchestra’s season programme.

Costa Rica’s National Symphony Orchestra plays the 11th concert of its 2026 season on Friday 13 November at 8 p.m. in the Main Hall of the Teatro Nacional in downtown San José, with a repeat on the morning of Sunday 15 November. Seats run from ₡2,220 (US$4.90) to ₡10,000 (US$22.07) before the theatre’s service fee.

The theatre’s own concert page lists Pedro Oliveira Neves as guest conductor and Fernando Muñoz del Collado as violin soloist. The orchestra’s season programme names the works as Paraísos Artificiais by Luís de Freitas Branco, the Violin Concerto by Erich Wolfgang Korngold and La Mer by Claude Debussy.

The Concert at a Glance

The concert belongs to the season series of the Orquesta Sinfónica Nacional, which the theatre’s 2026 announcement calls the orchestra’s 86th season. The same announcement says the Teatro Nacional continues as the official home of the orchestra.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Costa Rica ranks 9th of 14 with 36.5 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (75); weakest: military means (0). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB). See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The Ministry of Culture and Youth, which runs the theatre, says its anniversary programme closes with the 10th season concert on Friday 30 October. The theatre’s calendar lists the 11th concert two weeks later, on Friday 13 November, and gives a second performance of the same concert on Sunday 15 November.

The theatre’s page gives the Friday concert as running from 8 p.m. to 10 p.m. Costa Rica time and the Sunday repeat as running from 10:30 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. local time. The country keeps the same clock all year, six hours behind UTC, so Friday’s start is 9 p.m. in New York and 8 p.m. in Chicago and Sunday’s start is 11:30 a.m. in New York, because US clocks return to standard time on Sunday 1 November.

This guide condensed into 3 printable pages with tick boxes and the key official links. Email address Get the PDF Free. We send a confirmation link first, and the same address then receives The Rio Times Brief, our daily briefing. Unsubscribe with one click at any time; see our privacy policy. Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

The Program and the Players

The theatre’s page names two works, Paraísos Artificiais, a symphonic poem by Luís de Freitas Branco, and a concerto for violin in D major. The orchestra’s official 2026 season programme, published by the Centro Nacional de la Música (the state music institute that runs the orchestra), identifies the concerto as Korngold’s and adds Debussy’s La Mer, the sea-inspired orchestral work, to the same evening.

Pedro Oliveira Neves is billed as guest conductor, while the theatre’s listing for the 9th season concert on Friday 9 October names Andrés Salado Egea as the orchestra’s titular conductor. Fernando Muñoz del Collado is the violin soloist for both performances, and neither page gives a biography for either guest.

The theatre lists the Main Hall as the venue for this concert. A second, smaller stage, the Teatro Vargas Calvo, is the theatre’s chamber space for Costa Rican plays and is not the venue for this concert.

Tickets, Prices and Discounts

The theatre sells tickets at its box office and on its official website, and its purchase terms allow online sales until two hours before an event. Tickets bought online can be collected at the box office until the concert starts, with the buyer’s official ID, the card used and the purchase number.

The price list has eight tiers, the same for Friday and Sunday, with Luneta at ₡8,130 (US$17.94), Butaca at ₡7,690 (US$16.97) and boxes (palco) in the stalls and in rows 2 and 3 at ₡7,240 (US$15.98) each. Front-row boxes cost ₡10,000 (US$22.07), while the gallery costs ₡3,820 (US$8.43) in the first row, ₡3,330 (US$7.35) in the center and ₡2,220 (US$4.90) at the sides.

Each ticket carries a service fee on top of the listed price, and the theatre does not publish the amount. The page lists 30 percent off for students and older adults and 50 percent off for holders of a card it calls Brete, and it grants free entry to what it calls the IMAS population, a reference to the state social-aid agency Instituto Mixto de Ayuda Social.

Purchases are final, because the terms allow no changes, refunds or cancellations unless the theatre itself cancels, in which case the refund is 100 percent. One transaction is limited to 8 tickets, and the terms tell buyers to choose seats with age and health in mind because some areas are hard to reach.

The box office is open from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. and takes calls at (506) 2010-1142 and 2010-1143. The theatre’s online sales run through bank card payment platforms, so a card is needed for an online purchase.

The National Theatre and Getting There

The Teatro Nacional opened in 1897, is listed by its own institution as a national historic monument and marked its 129th anniversary in October 2026. The building stands on Avenida Segunda between Calles 3 and 5 in downtown San José.

The theatre also uses the basement of the Plaza de la Cultura, a public square where it scheduled free anniversary concerts for Sunday 18 October. The theatre runs under the Ministry of Culture and Youth, whose minister in October 2026 is Jorge Rodríguez Vives.

The theatre lists six parking lots around the building, four to the north and two to the south, and runs a free minibus to them from one hour before the show and again when it ends. The visit page lists parking but no bus directions, and Costa Rica’s main airport, Juan Santamaría International (SJO), lies in Alajuela, outside the capital.

The tourism board says the departure tax is included in most airline tickets, and travelers whose tickets leave it out pay US$29 per person, in dollars, colones or by card. Neither the theatre’s pages nor the tourism board’s airport page gives a taxi fare to the theatre, so visitors should confirm the fare with a driver or their hotel before the ride.

Entry, Safety and Money for Visitors

The Costa Rica Tourism Board lists the entry rules as a passport that can be read electronically, proof of funds of at least US$100 per month of stay and a return or onward ticket. The US State Department’s Costa Rica page says authorities may permit stays of up to 180 days without a visa but are not required to, and the tourism board adds that the immigration agent sets the final permitted stay at entry.

The US State Department rates Costa Rica Level 2, Exercise Increased Caution, because of crime, in an advisory dated 2 April 2026. It says petty crime is common throughout the country and that violent crime also affects tourists.

Visitors going to an evening concert in downtown San José can lower the risk by arranging the ride home before the show, keeping phones and wallets out of sight and using the theatre’s free minibus to the parking lots. The tourism board describes May to November as the green season, so a rain jacket is sensible even though the Pacific side treats November as a transition month.

This article converts at the midpoint of the central bank’s reference rates for 30 October 2026, as published through the Finance Ministry’s indicators service, which were ₡450.80 to buy and ₡455.44 to sell one US dollar. That is ₡453.12 per US$1, so a ₡10,000 ticket costs US$22.07, and the dollar figure moves with the exchange rate on the day of purchase.

More at the Theatre in November

The theatre’s calendar also lists a concert by the Portuguese fado guitarist and singer Ângelo Freire on Wednesday 25 November, from 7 p.m. to 9 p.m. in the Main Hall. General admission is listed at ₡4,000 (US$8.83), and students and older adults pay ₡2,500 (US$5.52), although the page showed no ticket button on 30 October.

Guided tours in Spanish and English cost ₡3,500 (US$7.72) for foreign visitors, and children under 12 enter free. The visit page lists daily hours of 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., and the theatre’s lunchtime program runs on Tuesdays at 12:10 p.m. through November.

Two other San José events fall in early December: the Nutcracker ballet at the Teatro Melico Salazar on 4 December and the Festival of Light parade on 12 December. More Costa Rica coverage sits on the Costa Rica hub, and a cost of living guide for San José covers longer stays.

What It Means for You

A visitor in San José on Friday 13 November can hear the national orchestra in a hall from 1897 for as little as ₡2,220 (US$4.90) plus the service fee. The most expensive tier, front-row boxes, costs ₡10,000 (US$22.07).

Buying early matters for the better tiers, because the theatre’s pages do not show how many seats remain and online sales end two hours before the concert. Bring official ID, the card used for the purchase and the purchase number if the tickets are collected at the box office.

What Is Not Known

The theatre’s page lists only two of the three works in the orchestra’s season programme, and the programme was published in February 2026, so the order of the works is not confirmed. Neither source says whether there is an interval or when the doors open.

The service fee per ticket, the number of seats still available and any dress code are not published on the theatre’s pages. The Brete card discount and the free entry for the IMAS population are listed without conditions, so the box office is the place to confirm who qualifies.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much are tickets for the National Symphony concert in San José?

Tickets range from ₡2,220 (US$4.90) in the side gallery to ₡10,000 (US$22.07) in front-row boxes, before a service fee. Students and older adults get 30 percent off.

Where do I buy tickets and when does the sale close?

Buy at the Teatro Nacional box office or on its official website. Online sales run until two hours before the concert starts.

Do US citizens need a visa for Costa Rica?

The State Department’s page says authorities may permit stays of up to 180 days without a visa but are not required to. Travelers need a passport, proof of funds of US$100 per month and a return or onward ticket.

World.title: Coquimbo Unido vs O’Higgins Final, 14 November 2026
World.content:
File photo, 2023. A grandstand outside Estadio Santa Laura in the Independencia district of Santiago, the venue now listed for the Copa de la Liga final. (Photo: Carlos yo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

CHILE · FOOTBALL · SANTIAGO

Key Facts Date Saturday 14 November 2026, 6:30 p.m. in Santiago (4:30 p.m. EST), as listed by the seller.

Venue Estadio Santa Laura, Independencia district, Santiago, Chile.

Tickets Puntoticket, the official seller: 5,750 to 40,250 pesos (US$5.79 to US$40.52), service fee included.

Stakes The first Copa de la Liga champion earns a 2027 Copa Libertadores place under the league rules.

Entry US citizens need no visa for stays of 90 days or fewer; the stadium requires an identity card.

Coquimbo Unido and O’Higgins, two Chilean football clubs, are scheduled to play the first Copa de la Liga final on Saturday 14 November 2026 at Estadio Santa Laura in Santiago, with kickoff at 6:30 p.m. local time, which is 4:30 p.m. EST. The match has already been moved twice, so the date and venue below are the seller’s listing as of 30 October.Tickets are on sale at Puntoticket, a Chilean online seller that names the National Association of Professional Football, known as the ANFP, as producer, from 5,750 pesos (US$5.79) for children to 40,250 pesos (US$40.52) in the mixed sector.The winner of the new cup earns a place in the 2027 Copa Libertadores, South America’s top club tournament, under rules the association approved in December 2025.

How the Final Was Moved Twice

The association first set the final for Saturday 18 July 2026 at 6 p.m. at Estadio Elías Figueroa in Valparaíso. On 13 July it rescheduled that match because of an approaching weather front, heavy rain and early warnings from Senapred, Chile’s national disaster prevention and response service, and proposed Saturday 17 October at the same time and place.

The final was then set for Friday 16 October at 8:30 p.m. at the Claro Arena stadium in the Las Condes district of Santiago. On 13 October the association announced its suspension after the Metropolitan Presidential Delegation, the national government’s office for the Santiago region, did not authorize the match because of the weather front and a flash flood known as an aluvión in Las Condes.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Chile ranks 3rd of 14 with 63.6 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (86); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (38). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The delegation also did not approve the association’s alternative of playing at Santa Laura, citing security observations it had raised about that stadium, the association said in the same statement. Ticket buyers were told to claim refunds of the full amount, service fee included, through Puntoticket, and the association said the new date and venue would be announced in due course.

The seller now lists the final at Santa Laura on Saturday 14 November at 6:30 p.m., with a presale for each club’s supporters having opened on 23 October at 4 p.m. Chile time. The association’s own news page, as of 30 October, carries no statement naming the new date, so the seller’s listing is the only published confirmation of the new date and venue.

Email address Get the PDF Free. We send a confirmation link first, and the same address then receives The Rio Times Brief, our daily briefing. Unsubscribe with one click at any time; see our privacy policy. Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

Who Is Playing

Coquimbo Unido, from Coquimbo in northern Chile, was founded on 30 August 1958 and plays its home games at Estadio Francisco Sánchez Rumoroso, according to the association’s club page. The association says the club won the 2025 Liga de Primera, Chile’s top league, before the 2026 season began.

In January 2026 Coquimbo Unido beat Universidad Católica 8 to 7 on penalties after a 0 to 0 draw to win the Supercopa Lanco, which the association called its first trophy as Chile’s super champion and the first for a northern club. Its goalkeeper, Diego Sánchez, saved two penalties in the shootout and scored one, and the association noted that he took part without gloves.

O’Higgins was founded on 7 April 1955 and plays at Estadio El Teniente, according to the association’s club page, which lists one top-division title, one Supercopa and one second-division title. Neither club’s squad for the final is described here because the association has not published team lists.

The New Cup and What the Winner Gets

The Copa de la Liga is a new tournament for 2026 contested by the 16 clubs of the Liga de Primera, and its opening match was Universidad de Chile against Deportes La Serena on Friday 20 March at six in the evening. The association said every match of the cup would be broadcast by its television partner.

The trophy, 65 centimeters (about 26 inches) tall and weighing 2 kilograms (about 4.4 pounds), is silver-plated bronze made in a workshop in the Lo Espejo district of Santiago, according to the association. Its design is inspired by the Torres del Paine, the mountain peaks of Chilean Patagonia, with three columns that also refer to the cup being the third tournament of the Chilean season.

Under the rules the association approved in December 2025, the champion of the Copa de la Liga 2026 takes the third Chilean place in the 2027 Copa Libertadores. The first two places go to the top two clubs in the 2026 league table, and the fourth goes to the winner of a one-match playoff.

Tickets and Prices

Puntoticket lists nine price points for the final across sectors named Pacífico, Andes and Galería, with sectors assigned to Coquimbo Unido and O’Higgins supporters. The mixed sector, Pacífico Mixto, costs 40,250 pesos (US$40.52), the Andes sectors cost 18,400 pesos (US$18.53) and the Galería sectors cost 9,200 pesos (US$9.26).

Children aged 4 to 12 pay 5,750 pesos (US$5.79) in the four club sectors, and the seller says the total price includes its service fee. Dollar figures use the observed dollar of 993.22 pesos per US$1 that the Banco Central de Chile, the country’s central bank, showed on its website on 30 October 2026.

Sales are online only through e-tickets, each ticket is tied to one Chilean tax and identity number called a RUT and to a single entry, and the seller says the national identity card is mandatory to enter the stadium. A damaged card or one with an unreadable barcode or chip means no entry, and misuse of an e-ticket can bring a ban from the club’s future matches.

The seller’s terms say purchases are not refundable, except that when an organizer cancels an event the seller refunds buyers, and when the date, time or place changes the organizer sets how and when money is returned. Because this final has changed date twice, a buyer should expect the same risk again and keep the purchase confirmation.

Getting to Santa Laura and Staying Safe

Estadio Santa Laura is in the Independencia district, north of central Santiago, at Julio Martínez Prádanos 1365 according to the seller’s listing. The seller advises arriving early to avoid lines and says every person entering needs a valid ticket.

The US State Department’s Chile page says public transportation is generally regarded as safe and that a prepaid BIP card is needed for buses and the subway in Santiago. It adds that ride-share applications and taxis with orange and yellow license plates are generally safe to use, while unauthorized taxi services have led to theft.

The department rates Chile at Level 2, exercise increased caution, in an advisory dated 19 August 2026 that cites crime, unrest and health. It says petty crime is common, large demonstrations can occur in Santiago with little notice and can disrupt buses and the metro, and the risk from Andes hantavirus is extremely low for most travelers.

Match days add crowds, and the State Department’s country page warns that small bags and purses have been stolen from crowded tourist locations, the Santiago subway and taxis. A visitor going to a football match should carry as little as possible.

Visas, Time Zone and Money for US Visitors

US citizens need no visa for a tourist stay of 90 days or fewer, according to the State Department’s Chile page, which says the traveler receives a Tourist Card valid for up to 90 days. The page adds that the passport must be valid for the period of the stay and have at least one page for the entry stamp.

Chile is on summer time in November, three hours behind Greenwich time, so the 6:30 p.m. kickoff is 4:30 p.m. in New York once US clocks go back on Sunday 1 November. That makes the gap with the US East Coast two hours on 14 November.

The seller’s page does not list accepted payment methods or say whether a foreign passport can replace the Chilean identity card, so a US buyer should confirm both with the seller before paying. The seller’s prices already include its service fee, so the figure shown is the total for the ticket.

What It Means for You

For a US visitor the match is a one-night chance to see a domestic cup final, with prices from US$5.79 to US$40.52, but the identity-card rule and the history of postponements make it a risky purchase for anyone booking flights. A traveler who is already in Santiago on 14 November should buy through Puntoticket only and keep flights and hotels flexible until the association confirms the date.

Other events in the city are listed in a guide to what to do in Santiago in November 2026, and a guide to the cost of living in Santiago helps with budgeting. Long-stay readers can compare neighborhoods in a guide to the best places to live in Chile for expats, and more coverage is on the Chile news page.

What Is Not Known

The association’s own site carries no statement naming 14 November or Santa Laura, so it is not known whether the Metropolitan Presidential Delegation has now authorized the stadium it questioned on 13 October. The seller’s page does not say how many seats are left or what the stadium’s capacity is.

The seller does not say whether a foreign passport can replace the Chilean identity card at the gate or whether a foreign buyer can register without a RUT. The sources also do not name the match officials or a broadcaster for viewers outside Chile.

Whether the rules for the 2027 Copa Libertadores places have changed since December 2025 is not stated on the pages read. The forecast for the day is not yet available, and the sources do not say whether the winner will receive a ceremony at the stadium.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is the Copa de la Liga final in Santiago?

The seller lists the final between Coquimbo Unido and O’Higgins for Saturday 14 November 2026 at 6:30 p.m. at Estadio Santa Laura. That is 4:30 p.m. EST.

How much are tickets for the Chilean cup final?

Tickets run from 5,750 pesos (US$5.79) for children to 40,250 pesos (US$40.52) in the mixed sector at Puntoticket. The seller says the prices include its service fee.

Do US citizens need a visa to see a football match in Chile?

US citizens need no visa for a tourist stay of 90 days or fewer, according to the State Department. The seller separately requires an identity card at the stadium gate.

World.title: Soda Stereo Returns With a Dead Singer
World.content:
File photo, 2025. Aerial view of the Palacio de los Deportes, the domed arena in Mexico City’s Iztacalco district where Soda Stereo plays on 23 November 2026. (Photo: ProtoplasmaKid, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

MEXICO · LIVE MUSIC

Key Facts The event Soda Stereo, the Argentine band that shaped Spanish-language rock, brings its Ecos tour to Mexico City.

When Monday, 23 November 2026; the start time is not yet published.

Where Palacio de los Deportes, the Copper Dome arena in the Iztacalco district, opposite the Foro Sol stadium.

Tickets On sale at Ticketmaster Mexico, the seller the band and promoter OCESA link to; prices are not published.

Getting there Metro Line 9 to Velódromo station, the Metro stop the venue lists; Metrobús stop Goma.

In Plain English OCESA is a Mexican live-entertainment promoter, and its own website lists the Palacio de los Deportes among the venues it operates. Ticketmaster Mexico is the ticket seller that both the band and OCESA link to for this show. Ecos is the name the band gives its 2026 tour, and its Spanish tagline describes Gustavo Cerati, Zeta Bosio and Charly Alberti meeting again through technology. Cerati, the band’s late co-founder, died on 4 September 2014.

Soda Stereo, the Argentine trio whose songs defined Spanish-language rock from the 1980s, plays the Palacio de los Deportes arena in Mexico City on Monday, 23 November 2026. The band’s own tour page lists the night with a ticket link, and the promoter OCESA, which lists the arena among its venues, shows the same date.

The night is a return, because the band’s site also lists three April 2026 shows at the same arena, on Tuesday 14, Wednesday 15 and Thursday 16 April. Tickets for November are on sale through Ticketmaster Mexico, while no price list or start time appears on the pages of the band, the arena or the promoter.

What the Ecos Show Is

Soda Stereo formed in Argentina in early 1982 from the union of Gustavo Cerati, Zeta Bosio and Charly Alberti, and its own history page calls it one of the most important and influential bands in the history of Argentine and Latin American rock. The same page records that Cerati fell into a coma in May 2010 during a solo tour and died on 4 September 2014.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 71.4 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The band’s site presents Ecos as a concert in which Gustavo, Charly and Zeta meet again through technology, in a show it says transcends time. How Cerati appears on stage is not described on the official pages, so the staging is left open here.

An earlier project on the history page, called Gracias Totales, is described as a tribute in the company of musician friends from around the world, meant to evoke Gustavo with love and respect. The official pages do not say whether such guests join the 2026 nights.

The history page says the 2007 reunion tour, Me Verás Volver, brought 22 concerts and more than one million spectators, and that a Cirque du Soleil show built on the band’s songs sold more than 1.5 million tickets across the Americas in 2017 and 2018. Those are the band’s own figures.
