This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The Band’s Return to Mexico City

Mexico has a long place in the band’s story, because the history page lists it among the countries of the 1997 farewell stadium tour that ended on 20 September 1997 at River Plate in Buenos Aires. The plan for the 2007 reunion also named Mexico among its stadium stops.

In 2026 the band’s site lists three nights at the Palacio de los Deportes in April, followed by two nights at the Auditorio Telmex in Guadalajara and two at the Auditorio Banamex in Monterrey. Monday, 23 November is therefore the fourth night at the Mexico City arena this year.

The same list shows arena dates in the United States in September 2026, in San Jose, Los Angeles, Las Vegas, New York and Miami, all now among the past shows. US fans who missed those nights still have Mexico City and several Latin American cities left this autumn.

Before Mexico City the Ecos tour stops in Honduras, El Salvador, Costa Rica, Nicaragua and Panama, as this guide to the Central American dates explains. After it, the band’s calendar shows Bogotá on Thursday 10 December and Medellín on Saturday 12 December.

The Venue and How to Get There

The Palacio de los Deportes, known as the Domo de Cobre or Copper Dome, was designed by the architect Félix Candela and opened for the 1968 Olympic Games, according to the venue’s own site. It stands on Río Churubusco in the Granjas México area of the Iztacalco district, opposite the Foro Sol stadium.

The venue lists Velódromo as its Metro station and Goma as its Metrobús stop, and it has an on-site car park with limited spaces and a variable price. Velódromo is on Line 9, the brown line, and the transport guide of the Mexico City Grand Prix organiser, which covers the same sports district, says a Metro ride costs 5 pesos (US$0.27) at the Banco de México rate of 18.8148 pesos per US dollar on 29 October 2026.

The same guide gives Metro hours of 5 in the morning until midnight, so a Monday show that ends late may leave only taxis and app rides for the trip back. It puts a Metrobús ride, on the city’s bus rapid transit system, at 6 pesos (US$0.32).

The venue’s rules, which can vary by event, ban backpacks, umbrellas, professional cameras and outside food and drink. Clear plastic bags up to 30 by 15 by 30 centimeters (about 12 by 6 by 12 inches) and small clutches up to 11 by 16 centimeters (about 4 by 6 inches) are allowed.

Tickets and Prices

The band’s tour page marks the 23 November show as available and links to Ticketmaster Mexico, and the OCESA event page carries a general-sale button to the same seller. The OCESA page shows only placeholder text in its weekday and show-time fields, so the start time is not yet published.

No price list appears on the band, arena or OCESA pages, so no ticket price is quoted here. The seller’s own page shows the current prices and service fees, and the arena’s FAQ says its Gate 7 box office sells tickets without service charges, with hours of 11 in the morning to 5 in the afternoon, Tuesday to Saturday.

Tips for US Visitors

Mexico’s immigration institute (INM) lists a 2026 fee of 983 pesos (US$52) for the document that records a visitor’s stay without permission for paid work, in its table of charges for arrivals by air. The Canadian government’s travel advice, updated on 19 October 2026, adds that arriving visitors complete a digital Multiple Migration Form online, so US travelers should carry a valid passport and confirm the form and the fee with their airline before departure.

The US State Department’s Mexico advisory, issued on 29 May 2026, is Level 2, Exercise Increased Caution, and cites terrorism, crime and kidnapping. It tells US citizens to follow the restrictions that apply to US government employees, who must rely on dispatched vehicles from regulated taxi stands or app-based services such as Uber or Cabify, may not wave down taxis on the street and may not travel between cities after dark.

The Canadian advice adds that the Mexico City Metro is often very crowded and a popular place for pickpocketing, and that credit card fraud occurs in taxis hailed on the street, including licensed ones. It also notes that demonstrations occur frequently in the capital and that earthquakes occur, particularly in Mexico City.

Mexico City lies 2,240 meters (about 7,350 feet) above sea level, and the Canadian advice warns that high-altitude illnesses can be life-threatening. The city keeps UTC minus 6 all year, so on 23 November it is one hour behind US Eastern Time, and a show starting at 9 in the evening there would start at 10 in the evening in New York.

Visitors pay in pesos, and at the Banco de México rate of 18.8148 pesos per US dollar on 29 October 2026, 100 pesos is US$5.31. The rate moves daily, so the dollar figures in this guide are rounded and dated.

What It Means for You

For a US fan the practical steps are to buy only through the seller that the band and promoter name, to book a bed within reach of Metro Line 9 and to plan the trip home before the Metro closes at midnight. The band’s September 2026 US arena dates are over, so a trip to Mexico City is now a way to see the Ecos show this year.

Travelers should enroll in the State Department’s Smart Traveler Enrollment Program and save the US Embassy’s emergency number before leaving. The embassy lists +52 55 2579 2000 from inside Mexico and +1 202 501 4444 for calls from abroad.

More event dates, holiday closures and neighborhood advice are collected in the guide to what to do in Mexico City in November 2026. Wider reporting on the country sits on the Rio Times Mexico page.

What Is Not Known

The show’s start time, door time and ticket prices are not published on the band, arena or OCESA pages, and it is not confirmed how many seats remain. The official sources mark the night as on sale, but only the seller can confirm live availability.

How Gustavo Cerati appears in the Ecos staging, which musicians join Zeta Bosio and Charly Alberti and what the set list contains are not described on the official pages. Whether extra Mexico City nights will be added after 23 November has not been announced.

Frequently Asked Questions

When does Soda Stereo play Mexico City in 2026?

Soda Stereo plays the Palacio de los Deportes on Monday, 23 November 2026. The start time has not been published.

How do I buy tickets for Soda Stereo in Mexico City?

Tickets are on sale through Ticketmaster Mexico, the seller linked by the band and by the promoter OCESA. The arena’s own FAQ lists a Gate 7 box office that sells tickets without service charges, Tuesday to Saturday.

How do I get to the Palacio de los Deportes?

Take Metro Line 9 to Velódromo station, which the venue lists as its Metro stop, or the Metrobús to Goma. The Metro closes at midnight, so plan a taxi or app ride home after a late show.

World.title: Fado Singer Camane in Lima, 19 November 2026
World.content:
File photo, 2014. The facade of the Teatro Manuel A. Segura in central Lima, where the Camané concert is scheduled. (Photo: Juan José Pacheco Ibarra, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

PERU · MUSIC · LIMA

Key Facts Date Thursday 19 November 2026, 8 p.m. in Lima, the same as 8 p.m. EST.

Venue Teatro Manuel A. Segura, Jirón Huancavelica, Cercado de Lima, Peru.

Tickets Teleticket, the official seller: S/25 to S/120 (US$7.27 to US$34.88) from 1 November.

Program Exhibition at 4 p.m., film at 5 p.m., talk at 6:30 p.m., then the 80-minute concert.

Entry US citizens need no visa for tourist stays under 90 days; passport valid six months.

Camané, the Portuguese singer whom the festival’s own biography calls “the voice” of fado, performs in Lima on Thursday 19 November 2026 at the Teatro Manuel A. Segura. The concert is the evening highlight of the Festival Fado Lima and starts at 8 p.m. Lima time, which is 8 p.m. EST because Peru keeps the same clock all year and US clocks go back on Sunday 1 November.

Tickets are on sale at Teleticket, the seller the festival links to, at S/25 to S/120 (US$7.27 to US$34.88) from 1 November, after a presale that ends on Friday 30 October. The festival’s program adds an exhibition, a film and a talk on the same afternoon at a second venue, the Sala Alcedo.

A Fado Festival Comes to Lima

The Festival Fado Lima is the Lima edition of an international fado festival that, according to the description on the seller’s page, began in Madrid in 2011 and is now in its 16th edition. The same text says the festival has appeared in 21 cities in 15 countries on four continents.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Peru ranks 5th of 14 with 54.7 points. Strongest pillar: military means (71); weakest: future resources (37). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

This year’s theme is “El fado y los barrios”, or fado and the neighborhoods of Lisbon, and the whole program is built around it. The festival’s website lists Everything Is New as co-producer, while the seller names MACBA Comunicaciones SAC as the event’s organizer.

Fado was inscribed in 2011 on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity kept by UNESCO, the United Nations cultural agency, which is the same year the festival began. UNESCO describes it as a performance genre incorporating music and poetry that is widely practiced by communities in Lisbon.

UNESCO says fado is usually performed by a solo singer, traditionally accompanied by a wire-strung acoustic guitar and the Portuguese guitarra, a pear-shaped cittern with twelve wire strings. It adds that fado is performed professionally on the concert circuit and in small fado houses, and by amateurs in neighborhood associations in the older parts of Lisbon.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Peru expat life Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Who Is Camané

The festival’s biography says Camané first met fado almost by chance, listening to his parents’ record collection while recovering from a childhood illness, and won Lisbon’s Grande Noite do Fado at age 13. It dates his first album, Uma Noite de Fados, to 1995 and says a partnership with the producer and composer José Mário Branco lasted until Branco’s death.

The biography lists albums from Na Linha da Vida in 1998 to Horas Vazias in 2021, which it calls his latest album of original songs. It says he will present his new work in Lima, but neither the festival nor the seller names the new album or any of the songs.

Among his honors the festival lists the Amália Rodrigues award in the best fado performer category, the Premio Tenco and the Premio Europa David Mourão Ferreira, plus several Latin Grammy nominations. It says he has performed in countries including the United States, Canada, Mexico, Argentina, Chile and Peru.

The Full Evening Program

The festival’s program for Thursday 19 November starts at 4 p.m. with an exhibition called “El Fado y los Bairros”, curated with the Fado Museum, at the Sala Alcedo. At 5 p.m. the same venue shows the 75-minute film “Do Bairro” by Diogo Varela Silva.

At 6:30 p.m. Ângelo Freire gives a 50-minute talk titled “La Calle y el Fado”, or The Street and Fado, at the Sala Alcedo. Camané’s 80-minute concert follows at 8 p.m. at the Teatro Segura, which puts the end of the show at about 9:20 in the evening if it starts on time.

The seller’s page gives an approximate duration of four hours for the event and says it may begin at eight in the evening. The festival and the seller do not say whether the exhibition, film and talk are free or need a ticket, and the seller’s price table lists only theater seats and an add-on.

Tickets and Prices

Teleticket lists eight sectors at the Teatro Segura, from the stalls, called Platea, and the lower boxes to galleries on the second and third floors, where the upper tier is known as the Cazuela. The seller states that its prices include its service fee, so the figure shown is the total for the ticket.

From 1 November until 19 November, or until the seats run out, the regular prices are S/100 (US$29.07) for the Platea, S/120 (US$34.88) for the lower boxes, S/60 (US$17.44) for the central gallery and S/35 (US$10.17) for the lateral gallery. All three Cazuela sectors cost S/25 (US$7.27), and the wheelchair stalls cost S/70 (US$20.35).

The presale, which runs from 14 August until 30 October or until stock runs out, is cheaper at S/70 (US$20.35) for the Platea, S/84 (US$24.42) for the lower boxes and S/17.50 (US$5.09) for the Cazuela. A buyer who acts by Friday 30 October therefore saves up to S/36 (US$10.47) per seat compared with the regular price.

Peru’s national disability council, known as CONADIS, has its own price of S/80 (US$23.26) for the Platea and S/96 (US$27.91) for the lower boxes, valid for one ticket per accredited person who shows the CONADIS card at the door. The seller limits purchases to 10 tickets per customer and says e-tickets can be downloaded from two days before the event.

Getting to the Theater and Staying Safe

The Teatro Manuel A. Segura stands on Jirón Huancavelica in the Cercado de Lima district, and the front of the building carries the inscription “Teatro Principal Manuel A. Segura”. The seller says guests are searched at the door and that food, drinks, lighters, sharp objects, glass or metal items, aerosols, laser pointers, drones, selfie sticks and professional cameras are not allowed.

The seller recommends the concert for anyone over 14, and children from 12 may enter with a responsible adult, with both paying for a seat in the same sector. Entry after the time printed on the ticket is subject to the organizer’s rules.

The US State Department rates Peru at Level 2, exercise increased caution, in an advisory dated 4 September 2026 that cites crime, unrest, kidnapping and terrorism. It says petty theft, muggings and other violent crime often happen even in daylight hours and that the risk of crime increases at night.

The department’s Peru country page advises travelers to use app-based taxis, phone-ordered taxis or hotel-affiliated services rather than hailing a taxi on the street. It also says robberies have occurred on routes to and from Lima’s airport, so keeping bags out of sight in the car is the safer habit.

Visas, Time Zone and Money for US Visitors

US citizens need no visa for tourist stays of less than 90 days, according to the State Department’s Peru country page, which also says the passport must have six months of validity at entry and one blank page for the entry stamp. Border officials set the length of stay at arrival, so visitors should check the stamp before they leave the airport.

Lima is five hours behind Greenwich time all year, so the 8 p.m. start is 8 p.m. in New York once US clocks go back on Sunday 1 November. Peru has no seasonal clock change, so the gap with the US East Coast changes only when US clocks move again in March.

Dollar figures in this guide use the US Treasury’s reporting rate of S/3.44 per US$1 for 30 September 2026, the latest official rate the Treasury lists for the sol, so card charges at checkout can differ slightly. The seller’s page does not list its accepted payment methods or say whether foreign cards work, so a US buyer should test the checkout well before 19 November.

What It Means for You

For a US visitor already planning a trip to Lima, the concert is a dated, low-cost cultural evening, with seats from US$7.27 to US$34.88 at the regular price and a presale price that ends on 30 October. The seller says it is not responsible for tickets bought outside its official channels, so Teleticket, the seller the festival links to, is the safe place to buy.

The afternoon exhibition, film and talk make the day a short introduction to fado for readers who do not know the genre. Budget travelers can plan the rest of a stay with a guide to the cost of living in Peru, and long-stay readers can compare neighborhoods in a guide to the best places to live in Peru for expats.

After the concert, a taxi ordered by phone or app is the option the State Department recommends over hailing one on the street. More coverage of the country is on the Peru news page.

What Is Not Known

Neither the festival nor the seller publishes a setlist, the name of Camané’s new album or the musicians who will accompany him. The theater’s capacity and the number of seats still available are also not published.

The festival does not say whether the exhibition, film and talk at the Sala Alcedo are free or need a ticket. The seller also lists a meet-and-greet add-on, but its description, a book signed by the artist, appears to belong to another event, so this guide does not treat it as part of the Camané offer.

The seller’s page gives the duration as four hours, while the festival lists an 80-minute concert, so the end time is an estimate. The seller lists no sales period for 31 October, between the end of the presale on 30 October and the start of regular sales on 1 November.

Frequently Asked Questions

When is Camané playing in Lima?

Camané plays on Thursday 19 November 2026 at the Teatro Manuel A. Segura, with the concert at 8 p.m. local time. That is 8 p.m. EST.

How much are Camané tickets in Lima?

Regular prices from 1 November run from S/25 (US$7.27) to S/120 (US$34.88) at Teleticket. The presale price, which ends on 30 October, starts at S/17.50 (US$5.09).

Do US citizens need a visa to attend a concert in Peru?

US citizens need no visa for tourist stays of less than 90 days, according to the State Department’s Peru page. The passport must have six months of validity at entry.





Sources: Festival Fado Lima, Camané page; Festival Fado Lima, program; Teleticket event page, 30 October 2026; UNESCO, Fado, urban popular song of Portugal; US State Department travel advisory feed, Peru, 4 September 2026; US State Department, Peru country page; US Treasury, reporting rates of exchange, 30 September 2026.

World.title: US$22 Tickets Fund Colombia Quake Rebuild
World.content:
File photo, 2024. A warm-up before a match at the 2024 FIFA U-20 Women’s World Cup, seen from the stands of the Estadio Olímpico Pascual Guerrero in Cali. (Photo: CalinkaPF, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons)

COLOMBIA · FOOTBALL

Key Facts Date and time Friday 13 November 2026, 7 p.m. Colombia time (7 p.m. US Eastern); doors open at 3 p.m.

Venue Estadio Olímpico Pascual Guerrero, San Fernando neighborhood, Cali, Colombia.

Tickets Official seller TuBoleta only, online; general sale opened 8 a.m. Friday 30 October; limit four per person.

Prices 70,000 to 380,000 Colombian pesos (COP), or US$22 to US$120, service fee included, by stand.

Purpose Charity match: gate money funds relief after the 10 August 2026 earthquake.

Colombia’s senior men’s national team plays Chile in a friendly at the Estadio Olímpico Pascual Guerrero in Cali on Friday 13 November 2026, with kick-off at 7 p.m. local time. General ticket sales opened at 8 a.m. on Friday 30 October through TuBoleta, the official seller, with prices from 70,000 Colombian pesos (COP), or US$22, to COP 380,000 (US$120).

The match is a charity game, because the Colombian Football Federation (FCF) says all gate receipts go to rebuilding after the earthquake of 10 August 2026. An earlier report on this match was written before the federation named a seller or prices, so this guide carries the confirmed ticket details.

Why Colombia vs Chile Matters

The FCF announced on Monday 14 September that Colombia would play Chile twice in the November FIFA window, the stretch of the calendar when clubs release players to national teams. The first match is in Cali, and the return match is on Tuesday 17 November 2026 at the Estadio Nacional in Santiago, with its kick-off time still to be confirmed.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The Cali game is a benefit match, and the federation says the money raised at the gate will support reconstruction and assistance in the areas hit by the quake. The ticket seller TuBoleta has pledged an extra contribution of its own, and the federation thanked the Cali mayor’s office, led by Mayor Alejandro Eder, for its support.

A magnitude 7.4 earthquake struck western Colombia on Monday 10 August 2026, centered 4 km (2.5 miles) south-southwest of San José del Palmar, according to the US Geological Survey (USGS). The USGS rated the event red, its top alert level, and the Cali city government says the quake hit Cali itself, while a separate report on the national quake fund covers the state side of the rebuilding.

For the stadium, the night is a homecoming of sorts, because the Cali city government counts it as the ninth match of the senior men’s national team at the Pascual Guerrero. The first was a 2-2 draw with Mexico in April 1962, and the last was a 1-1 draw with Denmark on 24 January 1999.

On the pitch, Colombia played three friendlies in a 16-day camp that ended on 6 October, including a 1-1 draw with Mexico in Baltimore on 26 September and a 2-0 win over Peru in Miami on 6 October under coach Néstor Lorenzo. The FCF describes the November friendlies as preparation for the 2030 FIFA World Cup as well as a chance to raise money for the quake zone.

Free download · Expat checklist Get the free checklist as PDF Moving to Colombia 2026: the step-by-step checklist. This guide condensed into 2 printable pages with tick boxes and the key official links. Email address Get the PDF Free. We send a confirmation link first, and the same address then receives The Rio Times Brief, our daily briefing. Unsubscribe with one click at any time; see our privacy policy. Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

Tickets, Prices and Sale Rules

TuBoleta lists four prices by stand with the service fee included: West (Occidental) COP 380,000 (US$120), East (Oriental) COP 250,000 (US$79), and the North (Norte) and South (Sur) ends COP 70,000 (US$22) each. Dollar amounts use the official representative market rate (TRM) of COP 3,166.91 per US$ in force on Friday 30 October 2026.

A delivery charge of COP 2,000 (US$0.63) for the TuBoleta Pass app is added once per purchase. The service fee is already inside each price: the West ticket, for example, is COP 332,500 (US$105) plus COP 47,500 (US$15) in fees.

Sales ran in three steps: customers of the bank Bancolombia had two presale stages of 2,000 tickets each on Wednesday 28 and Thursday 29 October, and the general sale of 24,041 tickets began at 8 a.m. on Friday 30 October and runs until stock is gone. TuBoleta says the general allotment can include blocks held for sponsors, partners and the organizer that go on sale if unused.

Tickets are sold only on the TuBoleta website, with no box office, sales points or call center, and every ticket is delivered digitally in the TuBoleta Pass app. A buyer can purchase at most four tickets, and each person must show an individual ticket in the app at the gate, with exceptions for minors and older adults.

Card holders outside Colombia must use the separate international-card channel on TuBoleta, which is open from the start of the general sale, while Colombian credit cards and PSE, the national online bank-transfer system, use the national channel. Wheelchair users must buy through a dedicated reduced-mobility channel, and only in the section set aside for them.

Children need their own ticket and an adult, with a minimum age of 3 in the West and East stands and 5 in the North and South ends. Doors open at 3 p.m. local time, four hours before kick-off, and the stadium bans weapons, hallucinogens, liquor and smoking.

The sale page warns that demand can exceed supply and that a virtual queue controls access during peak sales. Buy only from the official TuBoleta page, because the federation says there is no other sales channel.

Getting to the Stadium and Around Cali

The Estadio Olímpico Pascual Guerrero is in the San Fernando neighborhood of Cali, the main city of the Valle del Cauca department in southwestern Colombia. Cali’s international airport, Alfonso Bonilla Aragón, has been run by Colombia’s civil aviation authority, Aerocivil, since 1 September 2025.

The State Department bars its own employees in Colombia from hailing taxis on the street or using any form of public transportation, so many visitors prefer rides booked by a hotel or through a ride app. Download the TuBoleta Pass app and sign in with the purchase e-mail before leaving the hotel, because tickets are digital only.

The west stand was closed after the earthquake because nearby buildings were damaged, and on Thursday 8 October the city’s local football commission cleared it to reopen for the 11 October club match, with entry through the north and northwest gates. For that match the city’s risk-management office limited the second level to 50% and kept the third level for journalists, and the city pages do not say whether limits apply on 13 November, although TuBoleta now sells tickets on all three levels of the west stand.

Entry Rules and Safety for US Visitors

US citizens do not need a visa for tourist stays of 90 days or less, the State Department says, and the passport must be valid at entry and for the whole stay. Colombia’s migration authority, Migración Colombia, grants a free tourist permit of up to 90 days at the border checkpoint after an interview with an officer.

Migración Colombia offers an optional, free online form called CheckMig that can be filed up to 72 hours before travel and speeds up the interview. Anyone carrying more than the US$10,000 limit in cash on entry or exit must declare it and prove where the money came from.

The State Department rates Colombia Level 3, reconsider travel, in an advisory dated 31 March 2026, and its do-not-travel list covers the department of Valle del Cauca excluding the city of Cali. That wording makes Cali itself an exception, so visitors planning road trips outside the city should read the advisory first and check the Colombia coverage for security news.

The advisory warns that street crime can turn violent and tells victims not to resist, and it says earthquakes are common across the country. For seismic updates it points travelers to the Servicio Geológico Colombiano, the national geological survey, and enrolling in the State Department’s Smart Traveler Enrollment Program (STEP) brings embassy security updates.

Colombia has no daylight saving time and keeps UTC-5 all year, and US clocks fall back on Sunday 1 November 2026. From then on, 7 p.m. in Cali equals 7 p.m. in New York, Miami and Washington, and 4 p.m. in Los Angeles.

What It Means for You

A fan in the United States can buy directly from TuBoleta with a card issued outside Colombia, and a Friday evening match fits a long weekend that ends before the working week. The cheapest ticket, at COP 70,000 (US$22), also helps the quake fund, because the federation says all gate receipts go to reconstruction.

Travelers should plan a Friday arrival in Cali, read the State Department advisory again the day before departure, and enroll in STEP so that embassy alerts reach them. Those who want to see the city’s recovery can read the report on rent aid for quake families in Cali before they go.

What Is Not Known

The federation has not published a broadcast or streaming plan for the United States, and the pages reviewed for this guide name no television partner. It has also not said how many fans the west stand will admit on 13 November or which players Colombia and Chile will call up.

The kick-off for the return match in Santiago on Tuesday 17 November 2026 was listed as to be confirmed in the federation’s 14 September announcement and on its calendar. The amount TuBoleta will add to the relief effort has not been published either.

Frequently Asked Questions

When and where is Colombia vs Chile in Cali?

Colombia plays Chile on Friday 13 November 2026 at the Estadio Olímpico Pascual Guerrero in Cali, with kick-off at 7 p.m. local time. Doors open at 3 p.m.

How much are tickets and where do I buy them?

Tickets cost COP 70,000 (US$22) to COP 380,000 (US$120) with the service fee included, and the only official seller is TuBoleta online. General sale opened at 8 a.m. on Friday 30 October.

Do US citizens need a visa to attend?

No, the State Department says US citizens need no tourist visa for stays of 90 days or less, and the passport must be valid for the whole stay. The free online CheckMig form is optional.

World.title: Bogotá, Colombia Explained 2026
World.content:
COLOMBIA · CITY GUIDE

Key Facts The city Colombia’s capital, with a projected 7,945,996 residents in 2026 and 20 localities, as of October 2026.

The economy 25.4 percent of Colombia’s output in 2025, COP 471.2 trillion (US$148.8 billion), growing 3.5 percent against 2.6 percent nationally.

Who runs it Mayor Carlos Fernando Galán as of October 2026, with the national government of President Abelardo De La Espriella based in the capital.

Jobs Unemployment was 7.9 percent in June to August 2026, against 8.5 percent nationally.

Getting around Metro Line 1 was 83.73 percent built at 30 September 2026, and commercial service is planned for March 2028.

Security The US travel advisory for Colombia is Level 3, reconsider travel, dated 31 March 2026; Bogotá is not on the do not travel list.

For visitors US citizens need no visa for stays of 90 days or less, and the passport must be valid for the whole stay.

File photo, 2020. The Primate Cathedral of Colombia on the Plaza de Bolívar in central Bogotá, with green hills rising behind it. (Photo: Bernard Gagnon, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Bogotá, the capital of Colombia, has a projected 7,945,996 residents in 2026 and produced 25.4 percent of the national output in 2025, according to DANE, the national statistics department. As of October 2026 the city is led by Mayor Carlos Fernando Galán, its first metro line was 83.73 percent built at the end of September, and the capital is the seat of the Presidency and the Congress.

Download the PDF checklist

Why Bogotá Matters

Bogotá celebrates its birthday every 6 August, marking its founding in 1538, which made 2026 the city’s 488th anniversary, the city government says. The founding took place in what is now La Candelaria, the historic center that holds the Plaza de Bolívar and the Primate Cathedral of Colombia.

DANE projects 7,945,996 residents for Bogotá in 2026, up from 7,391,056 in 2018, the year of the last national census. The same projection series shows the city peaking in 2026 and then shrinking slowly to 7,112,442 residents in 2050.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.9 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

DANE counts Bogotá as a unit of its own beside the 32 departments, which are Colombia’s regional divisions, and the city shares a metropolitan region with the department of Cundinamarca. The 2025 Multipurpose Survey covered the capital and 21 Cundinamarca municipalities, among them Soacha, a neighboring city of about 870,000 people.

La Candelaria also houses the seats of national power, because the city government lists the Presidency, the Congress, the Palace of Justice and the mayor’s office there. Readers who follow the country can find more in the Colombia coverage.

File photo, 2008. Bogotá seen from the Monserrate hill above the city. (Photo: Jair Hernández Q., CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

How Bogotá Is Governed

Carlos Fernando Galán is the mayor of Bogotá as of October 2026, and the city government calls the office the Alcalde Mayor, the top local post. He presented the city’s results on 26 October 2026 at a regional meeting held to draft the National Development Plan 2026 to 2030, the roadmap of President Abelardo De La Espriella’s four year term, which the National Planning Department, known as DNP, is preparing.

Below the mayor the city is divided into 20 localities, each with its own local mayor’s office, from La Candelaria in the center to the rural locality of Sumapaz in the far south. The city government’s pages list Sumapaz at 78,095 hectares with 3,275 residents, while La Candelaria covers 1,830 hectares and has 18,143 residents.

The city negotiates its biggest projects with the national government, and Galán said on 28 October 2026 that the money for Metro Line 1 and for the New Calle 13 road in the west of the capital is assured. He added that President De La Espriella has stated that the Line 1 funds will be delivered as agreed with the city, after the national government announced budget adjustments.

The Economy of Bogotá

DANE puts Bogotá’s gross domestic product in 2025 at COP 471.2 trillion (US$148.8 billion), which is 25.4 percent of the national total, in its preliminary departmental accounts of 3 July 2026. Dollar figures in this guide use the official exchange rate, the TRM, of COP 3,166.91 per US$1 for 30 October 2026, so the dollar value is a conversion at that rate and not at the 2025 average.

The capital’s economy grew 3.5 percent in 2025 in volume terms, faster than the 2.6 percent national growth, and DANE says trade, transport, lodging and food services, public administration, education, health, arts and finance explain the result. Bogotá, Antioquia and Valle del Cauca together hold nearly half of Colombia’s output, and the six biggest economies account for 67.3 percent.

DANE counts 52,695,952 people in Colombia in 2025, so Bogotá’s 7,942,867 residents are about 15 percent of the population while the city produces 25.4 percent of the output. DANE also lists Bogotá among the departments whose output per inhabitant is above the national figure of COP 34.9 million (US$11,020).

In the June to August 2026 quarter DANE counted 4,339,900 employed people in Bogotá and 373,000 unemployed people, which put the unemployment rate at 7.9 percent against 8.2 percent a year earlier and 8.5 percent nationally. The participation rate of the working age population was 70.0 percent in the capital against 64.2 percent nationally, and the underemployment rate, which counts people who want to work more hours, fell from 7.5 to 6.0 percent.

The 2025 Multipurpose Survey, presented by the district planning secretariat, the metropolitan region and DANE from a sample of more than 80,000 households, found that monetary poverty in Bogotá fell to 22 of every 100 people, beating the city’s own 2027 target. Multidimensional poverty, which measures lack of access to education, health, work and housing, fell from 5.6 percent to 3 percent.

The same survey shows that 55.1 percent of Bogotá households rent, up from 43.6 percent in 2017, and that the average household has 2.71 people. The average age of residents rose from 34 years in 2017 to 36 years in 2025, and 80.2 percent of households have an internet connection.

Getting Around Bogotá

Metro Line 1 will run 23.9 kilometers with 16 stations from Bosa in the south to Calle 72 on Avenida Caracas, and 10 of the stations will connect directly to TransMilenio stations. The city’s metro company, Empresa Metro de Bogotá, reported on 28 October 2026 that the project was 83.73 percent complete at 30 September 2026.

The elevated viaduct is 93.02 percent built, with 18,836 meters done, while the stations and access buildings are 49.26 percent complete and the Bosa depot is 95.10 percent complete. Of the 30 trains, 22 had arrived in Colombia by late October 2026, 21 were running dynamic tests on the depot tracks and the viaduct, and the company expects all 30 to be built and shipped from China before the end of 2026.

The tests are required for commercial operation, which the company plans for March 2028, and the city also plans to extend Line 1 to Calle 100 and to build lines 2, 3 and 4. Readers can follow the project in the coverage of the Metro.

File photo, 2018. Articulated TransMilenio buses on Avenida Caracas in Bogotá, seen from above beside brick apartment towers. (Photo: Mariordo (Mario Roberto Durán Ortiz), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

TransMilenio is the city’s bus rapid transit system, and passengers use the TuLlave card, which can be recharged through the TransMiApp and through digital wallets with NFC on a phone. Temporary stations on the Caracas Centro trunk line have changed as Metro works advance, so the city asks riders to learn which station and platform serve their route at peak hours.

Private cars face the pico y placa driving restriction from Monday to Friday between 6:00 a.m. and 9:00 p.m., and the plates allowed on the road alternate by day. The city publishes a calendar for each week, and in the one for 26 to 31 October 2026 cars with plates ending in 1 to 5 could run on odd numbered days and those ending in 6 to 9 and 0 on even numbered days, with no restriction on Saturday.

Bogotá received 119,463 regular flights and 15.3 million air passengers from January to August 2026, which is 5.2 percent more flights and 3.7 percent more passengers than a year earlier, according to the city’s tourism institute. A total of 36 airlines linked the capital with 57 cities in 29 countries, and Colombia as a whole moved 39.4 million air passengers in the eight months, up 4.6 percent, the civil aviation authority Aerocivil says.

The three intercity bus terminals moved 10,645,040 passengers from January to September 2026, 0.3 percent more than a year earlier, and the Salitre Central Terminal handled 53.7 percent of them. The Northern Terminal handled 31.2 percent and the Southern Terminal 15.1 percent.

Neighborhoods and Localities

La Candelaria, where the city was founded, has 18,143 residents and holds the historic center around the Plaza de Bolívar. Santa Fe, which the city describes as part of the traditional center, includes the Centro Internacional business area, the Avenida Jiménez commercial strip, El Rosario University and the San Victorino market district.

Chapinero, in the center north, is known for its music culture, its restaurants and its nightlife, and it also has a rural area in the eastern hills. Teusaquillo, in the center west, is known for Victorian style architecture, the Simón Bolívar park, the National University campus and the El Campín stadium.

Usaquén, in the far northeast, is called the land of the sun by the city government and is known for wood carving, weaving and a weekend flea market near its founding plaza. The city’s pages list about 502,000 residents there, against 1,348,372 in Suba, a large locality with wetlands and an Indigenous council, and more than 1,250,000 in Kennedy in the southwest.

In the south, Ciudad Bolívar is one of the city’s largest localities and has the city’s first TransMiCable, a cable car line. Kennedy grew along main avenues such as Las Américas, where the capital’s first airport, the Techo aerodrome, operated from 1930 to 1959.

File photo, 2010. Bogotá at dusk, seen from above, with the lights of the city spreading toward the horizon. (Photo: Jorge Díaz, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Security and Public Order

The Bogotá police, the Attorney General’s Office and the district security secretariat work together on operations against homicide, sexual crimes, theft and drug trafficking, and the city government publishes the results. It asks residents to report emergencies on the 123 line.

President De La Espriella and Mayor Galán led Operation Kratos on the night of 27 October and the early hours of 28 October 2026, a joint action with the city police, the Attorney General’s Office and the Army’s 13th Brigade that produced 172 arrests and 114 raids in Bosa, Los Mártires, Santa Fe, Usme and other localities. The city government says 10 criminal gangs involved in extortion, homicide, drug trafficking, kidnapping and theft were dismantled, and the people arrested will be handed to prosecutors.

Galán said he believed no operation of that size had been carried out in Bogotá before, and he credited the coordination between the national government, the city, the judiciary, the police and the Attorney General’s Office. Further security in Bogotá is covered in a separate report.

The US State Department rates Colombia at Level 3, reconsider travel, because of crime, terrorism, civil unrest, kidnapping and natural disasters, in an advisory dated 31 March 2026. It names Arauca, parts of Cauca and Valle del Cauca, Norte de Santander and the border strip with Venezuela as do not travel areas, and Bogotá is not on that list.

The advisory warns that street crime occurs throughout Colombia and can quickly become violent, and it tells victims not to resist. It also names landslides as a risk in mountain cities such as Bogotá and Medellín, so travelers should read the full advisory before they go.

Bogotá in 2026

Bogotá received 1,334,279 foreign travelers from January to September 2026, 5.5 percent fewer than in the same months of 2025, and 53.9 percent of them gave tourism as the reason for the trip. Venezuela, the United States, Mexico, Spain and Ecuador were the main origins and together made up 53 percent, based on records of Colombia’s immigration authority analyzed by the city’s tourism observatory.

Hotel occupancy in the capital reached 57.5 percent in August 2026, 8.3 points above the national average of 49.2 percent, and tourism supported an average of 132,096 jobs a month from June to August, up 17.4 percent. The city’s tourism institute says Bogotá has beaten the national occupancy rate in 95 percent of the months measured since February 2022, helped by business trips, congresses and fairs.

On 27 October 2026 the city’s water utility opened the tender for the Canoas wastewater treatment plant, which the mayor calls the largest in Colombia and the answer to a promise that is 30 years old. Four prequalified bidders are in the race, and the utility expects to award the contract around the middle of 2027.

Events fill the city calendar, and a separate guide lists what to do in Bogotá in November 2026 with venues. The city government also publishes a cultural agenda and a daily mobility report on its website.

What It Means for US Readers

The State Department’s Colombia page lists no visa requirement for stays of 90 days or less, and it says the passport must be valid at the time of entry and for the whole stay. The US Embassy is in Bogotá at Calle 24 Bis, number 48 to 50, according to the department.

Prices are in pesos, and the official rate of COP 3,166.91 per US$1 on 30 October 2026 means COP 1,000 is worth US$0.32. The United States is one of the five main source countries of foreign visitors to the capital, with Venezuela, Mexico, Spain and Ecuador.

For US companies the draw is scale, because one quarter of Colombian output is produced in Bogotá, while the risks are crime and congestion. Background on the country is in the explainer on Colombia’s history, and the Metro, the tourism data and the security operations above are the items to watch.

What Is Not Known

March 2028 is the company’s plan for commercial operation of Metro Line 1, and it is not known whether the remaining 16.27 percent of the work, including stations that are 49.26 percent complete, will be finished on time. The mayor says the money is assured and the national budget adjustments do not affect it, but it is not known whether later budget decisions will change that.

DANE’s population figure is a projection built on the 2018 census, so the true size of the city is an estimate, and DANE’s own labor survey uses a larger base of 8,137,200 residents for June to August 2026. The projection also has the city peaking in 2026, which later data may change.

Foreign arrivals in Bogotá were 5.5 percent lower from January to September 2026 than a year earlier, and it is not known whether the September gains in event and business travel will last. The Canoas plant contract is not expected before the middle of 2027, so the benefit for the river is not known yet.

Frequently Asked Questions

How many people live in Bogotá?

DANE projects 7,945,996 residents for 2026, the latest official projection as of October 2026. That is up from 7,391,056 in 2018, and the projection shows the city peaking in 2026.

Is Bogotá safe for US tourists?

The State Department rates Colombia at Level 3, reconsider travel, and Bogotá is not on its do not travel list. Street crime occurs throughout the country and can quickly become violent, so the department tells victims not to resist.

Who is the mayor of Bogotá?

Carlos Fernando Galán is the mayor as of October 2026, and the city government calls the office the Alcalde Mayor. The mayor’s office is in La Candelaria, the historic center, where the city government also lists the Presidency, the Congress and the Palace of Justice.

Do US citizens need a visa for Bogotá?

The State Department’s Colombia page lists no visa requirement for stays of 90 days or less. The passport must be valid at entry and for the whole stay.

When will the Bogotá Metro open?

The Empresa Metro de Bogotá plans commercial operation of Line 1 in March 2028. The line was 83.73 percent complete at 30 September 2026.

How big is the Bogotá economy?

DANE puts Bogotá’s 2025 output at COP 471.2 trillion (US$148.8 billion), or 25.4 percent of the national total. The city’s economy grew 3.5 percent that year, against 2.6 percent nationally.

World.title: Costa Rica Gas Prices Jump Sharply as Regular Fuel Becomes More Expensive Than Premium
World.content:
Drivers in Costa Rica will soon be paying considerably more at the pump after the public services regulator approved yet another round of fuel price increases, including a 12.38% jump in regular gasoline that will make it more expensive than premium fuel. The Public Services Regulatory Authority (ARESEP) approved the adjustment a couple of days ago, with the new prices announced yesterday. Regular gasoline will increase by ₡89 per liter, climbing from ₡719 to ₡808, while premium gasoline will rise by ₡42, from ₡764 to ₡806.

That creates an unusual situation at Costa Rica’s gas stations. Regular gasoline, traditionally the cheaper option, will cost ₡2 more per liter than premium, while diesel will also reach ₡808 following an increase of ₡23. The higher prices have been approved but will not take effect until the regulatory resolution is published in the official government newspaper, La Gaceta. Under the resolution, the new rates begin the following day. An exact implementation date had not been confirmed as of Friday morning.

At the new price, filling a 40-liter (10.6-gallon) tank with regular gasoline will cost ₡32,320 (about $71), up from ₡28,760 (about $64) today, an increase of ₡3,560 (about $8) per fill-up and with regular. Drivers filling a larger 60-liter (15.9-gallon) tank will pay ₡5,340 more than before.

For those who commute daily, operate delivery vehicles or regularly travel between Costa Rica’s major cities, the additional expense could quickly add up. The increases are not limited to gasoline and diesel. Households that use propane gas for cooking will also face higher costs, with the price of a standard 25-pound cylinder rising by ₡549, from ₡7,172 to ₡7,721.

ARESEP estimates that approximately 53% of Costa Rican households use this type of cooking gas. Restaurants, small food businesses and other commercial establishments that depend on propane will also be affected. The regulator says the adjustments reflect rising international fuel costs, which have been influenced by instability in global energy markets.

Costa Rica imports all of its finished petroleum fuels, making domestic prices especially sensitive to changes in international supply, shipping costs and the exchange rate between the colón and the U.S. dollar. Energy officials pointed to disruptions involving oil shipments from the Middle East, declining global inventories and higher refining and transportation costs. Diesel supplies have faced particular pressure as demand and supply conditions fluctuate internationally.

The latest adjustment was calculated using fuel purchases made by the Costa Rican Petroleum Refinery (RECOPE) between September 11 and October 8. The exchange rate also played a role. ARESEP used an average rate of ₡456.66 per dollar for the new calculation, compared with ₡450.41 in the previous adjustment. Because fuel purchases are made in dollars, that difference increases the amount paid in colones even when the international price of a product remains unchanged.

For Costa Rican businesses, higher fuel prices can create expenses that extend well beyond the cost of filling a vehicle. Transportation companies, agricultural producers, delivery services and businesses that distribute goods throughout Costa Rica depend heavily on diesel and gasoline. When those costs rise, companies may face pressure to adjust their operating budgets or eventually pass some of the increases on to customers.

Tourism operators could also feel the effects. Rental car companies, shuttle services and tour providers frequently travel long distances between Juan Santamaría International Airport, the Central Valley and popular destinations such as La Fortuna, Manuel Antonio, Tamarindo and the southern Pacific coast.

Tourists coming here and are renting cars will find the same regulated fuel prices as Costa Rican motorists. However, any increase in tour prices, transportation fares or rental rates would depend on decisions by individual businesses and where applicable, additional regulatory approvals.

The latest adjustment comes after earlier fuel increases in October, adding to transportation expenses as Costa Rica approaches the busy end-of-year holiday and tourism season. The approved changes also highlight how fuel prices can move differently depending on the type of petroleum product. Although regular gasoline is typically cheaper than premium, international market conditions and the formulas used to calculate domestic prices can occasionally reverse that relationship.

For those who don’t have a diesel car, once the new rates become effective, premium gasoline will actually be slightly cheaper than regular gasoline, but you should still follow the fuel specifications recommended by your vehicle manufacturer. The regulator’s decision covers nearly two million vehicles circulating in Costa Rica, including private cars, motorcycles, buses, trucks and other commercial transportation.

While our government regulates retail fuel prices, those prices are reviewed periodically and can increase or decrease depending on the cost of imported petroleum products and other factors included in the pricing formula. For now, drivers have a short period before the latest adjustment takes effect. Once the new prices are officially published and implemented, a liter of regular gasoline and diesel will both cost ₡808, marking another increase in the cost of getting around Costa Rica.

World.title: Heading Out for Halloween in Costa Rica? Expect More Police on Patrol
World.content:
Heading to a costume party, a beach bash or a masquerade parade this Saturday? Expect to see more police than usual. Costa Rica’s national police are stepping up patrols across our country for Halloween and they will concentrate on the places where crowds gather. The Public Security Ministry said officers will focus on cemeteries, churches, shopping centers and the streets around bars hosting costume parties.

The goal is to prevent vandalism, spot unauthorized parties and head off trouble at large gatherings. When the national police first outlined the plan, it said it would deploy 1,500 officers from today through Sunday. The ministry’s latest statement, issued yesterday, did not give a number of officers.

Because halloween falls on a Saturday, many parties start Friday night, and that three-day window is meant to cover them. Why cemeteries and churches? Police said incidents in past years, including vandalism and rituals at cemeteries, are the reason officers will patrol them through the weekend. César Anchía, deputy director general of the national police, outlined the weekend operations.

If you’re going out, expect police at the party too. Themed Halloween events and other mass gatherings will see preventive checks and patrols at venues and meeting points. Part of the aim is to catch parties held without permits. Shopping centers, which draw families in costume on Halloween, are also on the patrol list.

If you’re driving, watch for the Caravana del Payaso, or Clown Caravan, a Halloween ride that draws hundreds of motorcyclists. Police will watch the route and the gathering points, and the ministry said highway patrols are meant to prevent crashes. Give riders room and allow extra time where the caravan passes.

Taking kids trick-or-treating? Police are asking parents to stay with their children and keep them in sight the whole time they go door to door. Before you head home, make sure the car you get into is the ride you actually booked. Lat night, the Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) said it had detained four men suspected of drugging and robbing people outside bars and nightclubs in San José.

According to the OIJ, one of the suspects allegedly posed as the ride-hailing driver victims had requested, then offered them drinks laced with a sedative. Investigators said other members of the group then withdrew cash and moved money out of victims’ accounts and spent it on goods and services, including fuel.

Saturday is also Costa Rica’s National Masquerade Day, when towns celebrate with giant-headed mascareros, cimarrona bands and dancing in the streets. Police said those community events fall under the same security operation. In beach towns, Halloween runs all weekend. Tamarindo has costume surfing, parades and beach parties on the calendar. Big crowds also draw thieves, so keep valuables with you and out of parked cars, where a rental can be emptied in minutes. In an emergency, call 911.

Halloween has grown steadily in Costa Rica alongside our own masquerade tradition, blending a centuries-old holiday with local customs. Authorities are betting that a visible police presence will keep this year’s celebrations safe for everyone who takes part.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Cambronero Bridge to Reopen
World.content:
The Cambronero bridge on Route 1 is scheduled to reopen Tuesday, November 3, restoring traffic through a stretch of the Inter-American Highway closed since a truck damaged the structure in September. The reopening is planned for noon, nearly two weeks ahead of schedule. The bridge is at kilometer 71, on the road connecting San Ramón, Alajuela, with Esparza, Puntarenas.

The crossing has been closed since the night of September 7, when a tractor-trailer struck the modular steel bridge. Crews had to dismantle parts of the structure, replace damaged components and remove and reinstall the bridge deck. Before those repairs could begin, workers built a support tower to hold the bridge’s weight while damaged pieces were removed. Some parts of that temporary support had to be manufactured specifically for the work.

Additional work will continue after the bridge reopens, but those remaining tasks are not expected to interrupt traffic. Drivers should slow down and use caution around crews at the site. The reopening will restore passage through Cambronero while preparations continue for a permanent solution to the ground instability affecting this section of Route 1.

Bids for that project are under review, with construction expected to begin in early 2027. The planned work includes stabilizing the slope, removing the modular bridge and restoring the road’s two lanes. A possible third lane is also being studied, but it has not been approved for construction.

World.title: Tamarindo Celebrates Halloween Weekend With Costume Surfing, Parades and Beach Parties
World.content:
Tamarindo is getting ready for a Halloween weekend that promises everything from surfers riding waves in costumes to trick-or-treating, costume contests, live music and beach parties. The popular Guanacaste destination will host the fifth annual Tamarindo Halloween Fest, with its main celebrations taking place this Friday and Saturday.

Organized by the Tamarindo Development Association (ADIT), the festival brings together local families, tourists, businesses and community organizations for two days of activities designed to offer something for just about everyone. There will be events for children, contests for pets, a nighttime running race and plenty of entertainment for adults looking to celebrate Halloween at the beach.

The celebration has grown since it began in 2022, with Tamarindo’s hotels, restaurants and local businesses joining the festivities. Organizers hope the event will also bring more people to the community before Costa Rica’s busy tourism season gets underway. This year, Halloween falls on a Saturday, giving everyone a full weekend to enjoy the celebrations without having to rush home the next morning.

The main family activities begin Friday at 5 p.m. with a costume parade through downtown Tamarindo, starting near Hotel Tamarindo Diria and continuing toward Parque Oneida, where much of the evening’s entertainment will take place. Children and adults are encouraged to dress up, with costume competitions planned for kids and families. Even dogs will have their chance to compete, as organizers invite pet owners to bring their four-legged companions dressed in Halloween outfits.

The Friday celebration will feature a crazy hair competition, trick-or-treating, music and activities for younger children. The traditional Payasos Los Alegres will also join the parade, bringing a touch of Costa Rican entertainment to the festivities. For those who prefer something a little scarier, Journey School will operate a haunted house at Parque Oneida beginning at 6 p.m. Admission to the haunted house carries a fee, with proceeds supporting scholarships for students at the school.

Those looking for food will find local vendors participating in the Tama Market, offering a variety of dishes and refreshments throughout the evening. A dance competition will add another element to the celebration, with participants performing routines inspired by Halloween characters and popular horror-themed entertainment. Organizers are encouraging groups to put together their most creative performances for a chance to win prizes.

Friday will also feature a recreational 5-kilometer (3.1-mile) race organized by Tama Run. The event combines exercise with Halloween fun, rewarding runners who show up wearing the most creative costumes. After the family celebrations, Tamarindo’s nightlife will take over. Crazy Monkey will host its Haunted Paradise party on Friday beginning at 9 p.m., featuring several DJs and three stages with dancehall, reggaeton and electronic music.

The festivities continue Saturday morning with a free Halloween reading event at the Tamarindo Children’s Community Library. From 10:30 a.m. until 12:30 p.m., children can enjoy themed stories and collect candy. One of the weekend’s most unusual events takes place Saturday afternoon when surfers head into the Pacific Ocean wearing Halloween costumes.

The costume surfing event is scheduled from 3:30 p.m. to 4:30 p.m. in front of Witch’s Rock Surf Camp, bringing together local surfers, instructors, residents and visitors for an afternoon of waves, music and prizes. Participants will be judged in different categories, adding a playful twist to a sport that has helped make Tamarindo one of Costa Rica’s best-known surfing destinations.

Several local surfing organizations are participating, including the Tamarindo Surf Association, the Tamarindo Sports Committee and the North Pacific Surf Association. For anyone who would rather watch than paddle out, the beach will provide a chance to see surfers attempt to catch waves while dressed in costumes not normally associated with the ocean.

Saturday evening will bring another round of parties and competitions. Sharky’s is planning a Halloween celebration with $1,500 in costume prizes, while Iguana Surf and NAIA restaurant will hold a sunset gathering featuring music and additional costume contests. A pickleball tournament organized by 15 Love Tamarindo is also part of the festival’s activities, with prizes that include a two-night hotel stay for two people.

Beyond the entertainment, the festival is intended to support Tamarindo’s tourism businesses during a traditionally slower period of the year. Hotels including Pasatiempo, Mar Rey, Hideaway Costa Rica and Las Guapas are offering special accommodation promotions, with some deals extending into November.

Restaurants and shops are also participating, giving everyone more reasons to spend the weekend in town. Several beachwear and fashion retailers have announced discounts ranging from 10% to 70%. Elizabeth Cole, president of the Tamarindo Development Association, said the goal is to make the community a destination people associate with Halloween celebrations in Costa Rica.

The combination of beaches, restaurants, nightlife and family entertainment makes Tamarindo well suited for a festival that appeals to different age groups, while providing additional business for local merchants ahead of the high season. Although many of the community activities are free, some attractions, races and private parties may require advance registration or paid admission.

Anyone planning to attend should check individual event details, particularly for nighttime entertainment and competitions with limited participation. The main family celebration at Parque Oneida runs from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m. Friday, while the Saturday program offers activities from the morning through late evening.

For travelers already visiting Guanacaste, Halloween weekend provides another reason to spend time in Tamarindo. And for those living in Costa Rica who want something different from the usual Halloween party, watching costumed surfers catch waves in the Pacific might be difficult to beat.

The complete schedule, registration details and any last-minute changes are available through the Tamarindo Development Association’s official website and its social media accounts.

World.title: Costa Rica’s Native Stingless Bees at Center of Supreme Court Fight
World.content:
Costa Rica’s tiny native bees have become the center of a legal battle that could affect beekeepers, honey producers and efforts to protect some of the country’s most important pollinators. The Constitutional Chamber of the Supreme Court (Sala IV), has agreed to review a challenge against government regulations that limit the commercial use of native stingless bees. The case raises questions about whether the rules are protecting biodiversity or making it unnecessarily difficult for people who have raised these insects for generations.

Costa Rica is home to 58 recorded species of native stingless bees, but regulations introduced in November 2025 allow commercial production without additional scientific studies for only two species. Anyone hoping to commercially produce honey, wax or other products from the remaining species must first provide scientific evidence showing that doing so will not threaten their survival.

The legal challenge was accepted last week following a complaint filed by Yandry Johanna Alvarado Castro. The lawsuit questions several provisions of the Executive Decree which regulates facilities where stingless bees are raised and managed. Unlike the familiar European honeybee, Costa Rica’s native stingless bees lack a functional stinger. Many are much smaller, and some live in colonies inside hollow trees, fallen logs and other natural cavities.

Two of the best-known species are the mariola (Tetragonisca angustula) and soncuano (Scaptotrigona pectoralis). Both are included among the species permitted for commercial production under the regulations. Their honey is produced in relatively small quantities and has long been valued by Costa Rican families, particularly in rural communities where raising native bees has been passed down through generations.

The practice is known as meliponiculture, a type of beekeeping that focuses on stingless bees rather than the imported honeybees commonly used in large-scale commercial honey production. But these insects do much more than produce honey. They pollinate native plants and agricultural crops, helping forests regenerate and supporting the reproduction of vegetation throughout the country.

That ecological importance is one reason the government introduced the regulations. Officials say the rules are intended to protect native bee populations, prevent overexploitation and preserve genetic diversity. However, beekeepers and researchers have questioned whether some of the restrictions are supported by sufficient scientific evidence.

One of the most controversial measures limits commercial operations to 30 colonies and noncommercial operations to just five. The legal challenge argues that these limits fail to consider differences between species, regional environmental conditions and the availability of food sources.

A beekeeper working in the humid forests of Limón, for example, may face very different conditions from someone maintaining colonies in the dry forests of Guanacaste. Critics argue that applying identical limits to both operations may not make sense without additional research.

The regulations also require beekeepers to maintain minimum distances between their colonies and agricultural operations using pesticides. Depending on the size of the bee species, those distances range from 500 meters (1,640 feet) to 3.5 kilometers (2.2 miles). Even greater distances are required in some circumstances, including where aerial spraying takes place.

Although the intention is to protect bees from potentially dangerous chemicals, the lawsuit questions how those distances were established and whether they are practical for small farmers and rural families. Researchers at the National University’s Tropical Bee Research Center (CINAT) have also raised concerns about the scientific basis for the restrictions.

Of the 58 native stingless-bee species recorded in Costa Rica, researchers have documented 20 species being maintained in managed colonies. That is considerably more than the two species covered by the regulation’s simpler commercial approval process. Specialists agree that native bees need protection but have warned that more information is required before deciding how many colonies should be allowed or which species are appropriate for commercial production.

For traditional beekeepers, the rules could have financial consequences. Some families maintain several species and depend on the sale of small quantities of honey and other products to supplement their income. Others raise bees primarily to preserve traditional knowledge and maintain healthy populations of pollinators on their properties.

The National Chamber of Stingless Beekeepers has previously called for additional species to be included in the regulations, particularly the jicote gato (Melipona beecheii) and jicote barcino (Melipona costarricensis). The organization and other critics argue that overly restrictive rules could discourage beekeepers from registering their operations and push some producers into the informal market.

Another concern involves potential penalties. The lawsuit challenges provisions that refer violations to Costa Rica’s Wildlife Conservation Law, arguing that beekeepers could face legal uncertainty over activities involving insects that naturally move between managed colonies and the surrounding environment. The case now moves forward in the Constitutional Chamber, where judges will examine whether the disputed rules comply with Costa Rica’s Constitution and environmental protections.

The court has given the Attorney General’s Office and the ministries of Environment and Energy and the Presidency 15 days to respond to the legal challenge. Importantly, accepting the case does not mean the judges have ruled against the regulations. The existing requirements remain in effect while the court considers the arguments.

Beekeepers also face a registration deadline in November 2026, when the 12-month period established under the regulations is scheduled to expire. The dispute comes at a time when Costa Rica is already confronting broader concerns about the survival of native bees. Earlier this year, the Constitutional Chamber ordered authorities to enforce a nationwide ban on insecticides containing fipronil after a separate case involving damage to bee colonies in Lepanto, Puntarenas.

The complainants in that case reported losing at least 24 native bee colonies and serious damage to hundreds of additional hives. The ruling highlighted the risks that agricultural chemicals can pose to pollinators and reinforced the importance of protecting native insects that play an essential role in Costa Rica’s ecosystems.

For now, the latest legal dispute presents a difficult question for authorities: how to protect native bees without placing unnecessary burdens on the people who raise and care for them. With dozens of native species, a long tradition of small-scale beekeeping and an economy closely connected to agriculture and conservation, Costa Rica has considerable interest in finding the right balance.

The Supreme Court’s eventual ruling could help determine how the country manages its native bees for years to come, affecting not only honey producers but also the forests and farms that depend on these small but valuable pollinators.

World.title: Costa Rica’s President Invites Pope Leo XIV to Visit in 2027
World.content:
President Laura Fernández formally invited Pope Leo XIV to visit Costa Rica during a private audience at the Vatican, proposing a trip in 2027 that would make him the first pontiff to set foot in the country since John Paul II in March 1983. Fernández delivered the invitation in a letter and handed it to the pope in person at the Apostolic Palace. In it, she extended what she called a fraternal and respectful invitation on behalf of the people and government of Costa Rica, describing the country as a land where work and peace prevail.

The letter ties the proposed visit to two anniversaries Costa Rica will mark in 2027. One is the 203rd anniversary of the declaration of Our Lady of the Angels, known here as La Negrita, the patron saint. The other is the 180th anniversary of the Constitution recognizing Catholicism as the official religion of the state.

No date has been set and the letter leaves the timing to the pope, and Fernández offered to coordinate preparations for an eventual pastoral and official visit through the Vatican’s Secretariat of State and the Apostolic Nunciature in San José. The Vatican has not said whether the pope will accept.

Fernández also presented the pope with a replica of the Virgin of the Angels and coffees from several Costa Rican growing regions. It is not the first time Costa Rican coffee has reached Leo XIV. Speaking to Catholic media after the meeting, Fernández said she had invited the pope to come and greet La Negrita, and that it would be very special for Costa Rica to receive a pope again after 1983. She said the conversation lasted about 30 minutes, that she told him Costa Ricans had been praying for him, and that she felt at home.

She added that the pope appeared in good spirits and in good health following a recent medical procedure, though she said the two did not discuss his recovery directly. The Holy See Press Office said in a statement after the audience that Fernández also met with Cardinal Pietro Parolin, the Vatican secretary of state, and Archbishop Paul Richard Gallagher, secretary for relations with states and international organizations.

According to the statement, those talks highlighted good relations between the Holy See and Costa Rica and between the state and the local Church and covered social and political issues in the country and the region, particularly security and migration. Fernández said she discussed with the pope the situation of Nicaraguan migrants, the largest migrant group in Costa Rica, as well as cooperation with the United States on people going through deportation proceedings.

On security, she said her government pairs investment in education, health and support for young people with measures against organized crime, including efforts to stop inmates from directing violence from inside prisons. The audience came two weeks after Fernández toured El Salvador’s CECOT mega-prison, and as Costa Rica moves inmates into its own maximum-security facility, the CACCO.

Bishop Bartolomé Buigues of Alajuela, vice president of the Costa Rican Episcopal Conference, said closer engagement between the Church and civil authorities is of great importance. The bishops’ conference thanked the president for promoting the meeting. The Vatican stop opened Fernández’s third official trip abroad since taking office in May, following visits to El Salvador and Colombia. Her schedule in Rome also includes a meeting with Italian President Sergio Mattarella.

She then travels to Madrid for the 30th Ibero-American Summit of Heads of State and Government on Nov. 4 and 5 and is scheduled to return to Costa Rica on Nov. 6. A papal visit would carry particular weight in a country where devotion to La Negrita draws pilgrims from every province to the Basilica of Our Lady of the Angels in Cartago each August. John Paul II’s 1983 stop, part of a tour of Central America, remains the last time a pope visited the country.

World.title: 46 US Veterans Tried Ayahuasca in Costa Rica, Where Rules Remain Murky
World.content:
Forty-six American military veterans and first responders spent a week at an ayahuasca retreat in Guanacaste in September, hoping the Amazonian brew would ease trauma they carried home from combat zones and emergency scenes. Their accounts, published Wednesday by the New York Post, describe former Army Rangers and Navy SEALs weeping in ceremony tents and returning home calmer.

The stories are moving. They also land in a place where the Ministry of Health has spent nearly two years warning the public against therapeutic ayahuasca use, while the best-known center that serves it holds a ministry authorization the ministry itself tried, and failed, to cancel.

The retreat ran from Sept. 5 to 12 at Rythmia Life Advancement Center near Tamarindo, in the area of Santa Cruz, spanning the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks. It was organized with The Coming Home Project, a nonprofit founded in 2021 by Navy SEAL veteran Nate Brown to combat veteran suicide, and funded largely by the Birds Eye View Project, a Texas veterans charity, according to the organizers.

The Post put the group at 46, while a September press release from the organizers said 47 took part. Days combined yoga, individual and group counseling, classes and meditation, with ayahuasca ceremonies held at night in tents. Rythmia and Coming Home reviewed each participant’s medical history, medications and mental health beforehand, the Post reported.

The need behind such efforts is stark. A 2026 Department of Veterans Affairs report counted 6,488 veteran suicides in 2024, an average of nearly 18 a day. Participants described the week as a turning point. A 44-year-old firefighter and former Army Ranger, identified only as Dave L., told the Post that the constant inner conflict he lived with had grown much quieter since he returned home. He stopped short of calling a single retreat a cure.

Jeff McNairy, Rythmia’s chief medical officer and a psychiatrist, told the paper that trauma is the condition he considers ayahuasca best suited to treat. He said roughly half the participants vomited on any given night, a reaction the center describes as a psychosomatic release of trauma.

What the coverage does not include is outcome data. No standardized symptom scores, follow-up assessments or comparison group were reported for the group. Rythmia advertises a self-reported success rate above 97% among more than 23,000 guests since 2016, a figure drawn from its own guest surveys rather than independent clinical measurement.

The broader research is promising but young. An observational study run with the nonprofit Heroic Hearts Project followed 58 veterans who attended ayahuasca or psilocybin retreats in Peru and Jamaica between 2021 and 2024. Its research director, neuroscientist Grace Blest-Hopley, has said more than 80% of those who entered with PTSD no longer met the diagnostic criteria afterward.

The study’s published averages were more modest, with PTSD symptom scores falling about 26% among the ayahuasca group. Researchers at the University of Texas are now studying how brain responses in combat veterans change after ayahuasca treatment. None of this yet amounts to the large controlled trials regulators require before approving a treatment.

The risks are well documented. About 70% of users experience acute nausea and more than half report unsettling psychological effects, according to research cited by the Post. Combined with common SSRI antidepressants, the brew can trigger serotonin syndrome, which can be fatal, and it can provoke prolonged psychosis in people with underlying psychiatric vulnerabilities.

Those medications and histories are common among veterans with PTSD, which is why screening matters as much as the ceremony itself. Costa Rica has no law written for this industry. In January 2025 the Ministry of Health issued a health warning on ayahuasca and ibogaine, urging the public not to consume or promote either for therapeutic purposes, not to join rituals that use psychoactive substances for healing, and to report anyone offering them.

The ministry said no product based on either plant holds the sanitary registration it requires. Rythmia is the exception, and an awkward one. The center promotes itself as the world’s only medically licensed ayahuasca center, with a round-the-clock medical team that McNairy said includes five doctors and 12 registered nurses.

According to a February 2025 opinion from the Attorney General’s Office (PGR), the Ministry of Health told Rythmia in July 2022 that it could keep using ayahuasca for therapeutic purposes on a temporary basis until a regulation was issued. In October 2024, Health Minister Mary Munive asked the PGR to endorse annulling that authorization.

The PGR declined and said the ministry’s request contained extremely serious errors, including a failure to identify which rules the authorization violated, and noted that no regulation governed or banned ayahuasca when the permission was granted. It is not clear whether the ministry has revisited the case since.

Elsewhere, safeguards vary widely.
