A study published in January in JAMA Network Open interviewed representatives of 49 publicly advertised psychedelic retreat organizations, most of them based in the United States. About seven in 10 worked with a licensed health professional or someone trained in emergency response, but only about two-thirds had such a person present at retreats even some of the time.

By one estimate, Costa Rica hosts about 80 psychedelic retreat centers, some 60 of them offering ayahuasca, making it the second most popular destination for this kind of travel after Peru.

The consequences of thin oversight have already been felt here. Lauren Levis, a 40-year-old social worker from New Mexico, died in August 2024 after taking iboga at Soul Centro, a retreat in Paquera on the Nicoya Peninsula. Her brother has said she collapsed in a shower after an all-night ceremony, and that an electrocardiogram taken before the retreat showed marked abnormalities, yet she was allowed to attend.

Judicial investigators sent their findings to prosecutors in March 2025, nearly eight months after her death. A Norwegian woman died after taking ibogaine at another facility near Liberia in 2014. The veterans’ relief may prove genuine, and researchers are working to measure how much of it lasts. For now, the safeguards around ayahuasca in Costa Rica depend largely on the operators who serve it.

Researchers who study the retreat industry advise anyone weighing one to ask for a written medical screening that covers heart conditions, psychiatric history and every medication, a medical professional on site rather than on call, a clear emergency plan with transport to the nearest hospital, and straight answers about the legal status of what is being served. Medical experts also warn that safely tapering off antidepressants can take six to 12 weeks under supervision, far longer than many retreats allow.

World.title: All Three VIP Lounges at Juan Santamaría Airport Close Sunday
World.content:
If you are flying out of Juan Santamaría International Airport this Sunday, Nov. 1, plan on waiting at the gate. All three VIP lounges at Costa Rica’s main airport will be closed that day, and one of them has no date to reopen. The closures start Saturday, Oct. 31, and each lounge is on a different schedule. BAC Credomatic said the special hours are the result of an operational adjustment scheduled by the airport’s management and outside the bank’s control.

Here is how each lounge is affected:

Lounge BAC closes at 6 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 31, two hours earlier than usual. It reopens at 4 a.m. Monday, Nov. 2. That is 34 hours without service.

closes at 6 p.m. Saturday, Oct. 31, two hours earlier than usual. It reopens at 4 a.m. Monday, Nov. 2. That is 34 hours without service. VIP Santamaría , next to Gate 5, closes for Sunday, Nov. 1, only.

, next to Gate 5, closes for Sunday, Nov. 1, only. VIP Lounge Costa Rica, the Mastercard lounge that also operates as the Copa Club, closes Saturday, Oct. 31, until further notice.

That last closure is the one to watch. If you usually get in with a Mastercard card or a Priority Pass membership, you will lose that option for an open-ended period. The lounge’s own notice gives no reopening date, and Priority Pass now lists it as temporarily closed from Oct. 31 until further notice.

Aeris, the company that runs the airport, has not said what the adjustment involves. Asked whether the lounges would change operators, the company said it recognizes the lounges as an important part of the airport experience. It added that any official information will be released through its own channels.

The lounges normally open from 4:30 a.m. to 8 p.m. Priority Pass also lists VIP Santamaría as undergoing renovation work, and warns that space may be limited even when it is open. Nothing announced so far affects flight schedules. If you were counting on lounge food or a quiet place to work this weekend, eat before you head to the airport and bring a charged phone and laptop.

Check with your bank or lounge program before you leave home, since access rules differ from one lounge to the next. If you are heading to the United States, you will also need to sign a new passenger form starting Nov. 3. The lounge closures come a week after a power failure disrupted the airport’s control tower. From Monday, the BAC and VIP Santamaría lounges are expected back on normal hours. The Mastercard lounge may stay closed well beyond that.

World.title: Onion and potato prices went up!
World.content:
Onion and potato prices went up!

By Zoila Palma: Consumers in Belize are paying more for several staple vegetables, with onion and Irish potato prices recording the largest increases among selected produce items listed in the latest data from the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB).

The data show that the price of one pound of onions increased by 10.2 percent, rising from $3.05 to $3.36. Irish potatoes also recorded a notable increase of 10.7 percent when compared to September 2025, with the price per pound climbing from $3.14 to $3.48.

Corn prices rose by 8.3 percent, with a pack of three increasing from $5.64 to $6.11. Meanwhile, the price of one pound of carrots increased by 4.5 percent, moving from $3.00 to $3.13.

World.title: Clothing, cleaning supplies and household services become more expensive
World.content:
Clothing, cleaning supplies and household services become more expensive

By Zoila Palma: Belizeans paid more for clothing, household cleaning products and certain domestic services in September 2026, according to the latest Consumer Price Index report released by the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB).

The report shows that clothing and footwear prices increased by 3.1 percent compared to September 2025. The increase reflected higher prices for clothing for both males and females.

Meanwhile, furnishings, household equipment and routine household maintenance costs rose by 2.5 percent. The SIB attributed the increase mainly to higher prices for household cleaning and maintenance products, including laundry bar soaps, liquid detergents, soap powders, dishwashing liquids and bleach.

The cost of domestic and household services, including lawn-cutting services, also increased during the month.

World.title: Dining out costs more as restaurant and café prices rise
World.content:
Dining out costs more as restaurant and café prices rise

By Zoila Palma: Eating out became more expensive in Belize in September, with prices for restaurants and accommodation services rising by 4.3 percent compared to September 2025, according to the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB).

The increase occurred alongside a 4.3 percent rise in the food and non-alcoholic beverages category, as households also paid more for groceries, including poultry, vegetables, sugar, fruit and certain beverages.

Higher transportation costs, including fuel and passenger fares, further contributed to the overall increase in consumer prices.

World.title: Higher light and water bills push cost of living higher
World.content:
Higher light and water bills push cost of living higher

By Zoila Palma: Belizeans are paying more for electricity and water, with rising utility costs contributing to a 4.4 percent increase in housing-related expenses in September 2026, according to the latest Consumer Price Index report from the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB).

SIB noted that electricity costs increased due to a rise in the price per kilowatt-hour and the introduction of the Cost of Power Adjustment (COPA) during the year.

These increases added to the financial pressure on households already dealing with higher prices for everyday goods and services.

Water bills also climbed over the 12-month period. A household consuming 4,500 gallons of water per month paid $91.13 in September 2026, compared to $86.38 in September 2025, representing an increase of $4.75.

In addition, home rental costs rose by 2.3 percent compared to September last year.

World.title: Electricity, water and rent push housing costs up by 4.4%
World.content:
Electricity, water and rent push housing costs up by 4.4%

By Zoila Palma: The cost of maintaining a household in Belize increased in September, with housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels recording a 4.4 percent rise compared to September 2025, according to the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB).

The SIB’s September Consumer Price Index report identifies higher electricity costs as a major contributor to the increase.

The report attributes the rise to an increase in the price per kilowatt-hour and the introduction of the Cost of Power Adjustment (COPA) during the year.

Water bills also increased over the 12-month period. For a household consuming 4,500 gallons of water per month, the cost rose from $86.38 in September 2025 to $91.13 in September 2026, an increase of $4.75.

Home rental costs were also higher, increasing by 2.3 percent compared to September of last year.

The combined increases in electricity, water and rent contributed to the housing category becoming one of the leading drivers of Belize’s overall annual inflation rate of 4.7 percent.

World.title: Belizeans pay more for chicken, vegetables, sugar and fruit as food prices keep rising!
World.content:
Belizeans pay more for chicken, vegetables, sugar and fruit as food prices keep rising!

By Zoila Palma: Belizean households continued to face higher grocery bills in September, as food and non-alcoholic beverage prices increased by 4.3 percent compared to September 2025, according to the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB).

The SIB’s latest Consumer Price Index report indicates that prices within the food subcategory rose by an average of 4.6 percent.

Among the products recording increases were poultry, which became 5.9 percent more expensive, and vegetables, including onions, sweet peppers, habanero peppers and cilantro, which rose by an average of 5.0 percent.

Sugar recorded one of the most notable increases, with white and brown sugar prices rising by 18.0 percent. Fruit prices increased by 10.6 percent, while bread and bakery products rose by 1.8 percent compared to the same period last year.

Non-alcoholic beverages also became more expensive, recording a 3.0 percent increase. The report attributed this largely to higher prices for instant coffee, which rose by 13.5 percent, and fruit and vegetable juices, which increased by 4.8 percent.

Food and non-alcoholic beverages were among the three main categories driving Belize’s overall annual inflation rate of 4.7 percent in September 2026.

World.title: Transportation more expensive as fuel prices keep soaring
World.content:
Transportation more expensive as fuel prices keep soaring

By Zoila Palma: Motorists and commuters in Belize faced higher transportation costs in September, with the category recording a 10.7 percent increase compared to the same month in 2025, according to the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB).

The SIB’s September 2026 Consumer Price Index report shows that diesel recorded the largest increase among the listed motor vehicle fuels.

The average price per gallon climbed from $11.92 in September 2025 to $15.69 in September 2026, an increase of $3.77. Regular gasoline increased by $1.76 per gallon, rising from $12.01 to $13.78, while premium gasoline rose from $13.21 to $14.62, an increase of $1.40.

The cost of passenger transportation services also increased significantly, rising by 15.2 percent over the year.

The report attributed this increase to higher bus and taxi fares, as well as rising international airfares. These increases contributed to transportation being one of the leading drivers of Belize’s overall inflation rate of 4.7 percent in September.

World.title: SIB September report: Everything gane up!
World.content:
SIB September report: Everything gane up!

By Zoila Palma: The cost of living in Belize continued to rise in September, with consumer prices increasing by 4.7 percent compared to September 2025, according to the latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) report released by the Statistical Institute of Belize (SIB).

The report shows that the All-items CPI rose from 120.5 in September 2025 to 126.2 in September 2026, reflecting higher prices for goods and services regularly purchased by households.

The leading contributors to the increase were transportation, food and non-alcoholic beverages, and housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels. Together, these three categories accounted for approximately three-quarters of the overall rise in consumer prices.

The transportation category recorded a 10.7 percent increase, driven primarily by higher fuel prices and passenger transportation costs.

Food and non-alcoholic beverages rose by 4.3 percent, while housing-related costs increased by 4.4 percent, reflecting higher electricity charges, water tariffs and home rental costs.

Other categories also recorded increases, including health services, which rose by 6.4 percent, and restaurants and accommodation services, which increased by 4.3 percent.

Clothing and footwear prices climbed by 3.1 percent, while furnishings, household equipment and routine household maintenance costs rose by 2.5 percent.

World.title: A year in limbo
World.content:
Velecia Ewen shows the two mattresses on the floor that her family of five has been sleeping on in the Petersfield High School teachers’ cottage where they have been living after Hurricane Melissa last October. (Photo: Anthony Lewis)

One year after Hurricane Melissa devastated Westmoreland and left dozens of families homeless, several displaced residents remain stuck in an emergency shelter, their frustration mounting as promised relief remains elusive.

More than a dozen people, mostly families, are still housed in the teachers’ cottage at Petersfield High School, where they were relocated after initially taking refuge in the main school building.

For Velecia Ewen, a displaced resident of Pullet Lane, and others sharing the cramped shelter, the desire to move on with their lives is growing increasingly urgent.

Full story on Pages 6&7

World.title: Adam Stewart honoured for giving
World.content:
Sandals and Beaches resorts Executive Chairman Adam Stewart responding after receiving the International Achievement Award at the American Friends of Jamaica’s 2026 Hummingbird Gala on October 16 in New York. Stewart was recognised by Town and Country Magazine for Sandals Foundation’s funding of projects that touch on hurricane relief, conservation, education, animal welfare, and health care in the islands where Sandals Resorts operate.

JAMAICA’S Adam Stewart, executive chairman of Sandals and Beaches resorts and the ATL Group, has been named among an impressive list of individuals recognised by Town and Country (T&C) Magazine as Philanthropists of the Year.

The awards were presented at the 180-year-old magazine’s 13th annual Philanthropy Summit held at Hearst Tower in New York City on Tuesday, October 27, 2026.

Introducing the awardees, T&C said they were chosen for philanthropic gestures ranging “from nine-figure donations to small acts of kindness”.

“A transformational gift is always a welcome one, but what does that mean, exactly? That’s the question at the heart of this year’s philanthropy issue. How does an act of generosity, or service, change the world, or someone’s life, or even someone’s day?” stated T&C, the oldest continuously published general-interest magazine in the United States which has a digital audience of 5.8 million to 11.3 million unique monthly visitors.

Stewart was recognised for Sandals Foundation’s funding of projects that touch on hurricane relief, conservation, education, animal welfare, and health care in the islands where Sandals Resorts operate.

The magazine noted that this year the American Friends of Jamaica Foundation honoured Stewart, who is president of Sandals Foundation, for his work.

Reacting to the T&C award, Stewart said: “I am deeply honoured to be recognised among Town & Country Magazine’s philanthropists of the year alongside the remarkable list of honorees.

“This recognition is particularly meaningful because at Sandals and Beaches Resorts and across the ATL Group we know that success is measured not just by what we achieve, but by the difference we make in the lives of others in the islands we call home. Our actions speak louder than words when we make decisions that impact our countries and our communities.”

Added Stewart, who is also executive chairman of the Jamaica Observer, “Our 20,000 team members across the Caribbean region are the heart of our organisation who show up every day creating magical moments for our customers. So, when the region needs us it’s our duty to respond. And in times of need we, and the Sandals Foundation, do extraordinary things because they are the right things to do.

“I share this recognition with our entire organisation in celebration of a commitment to making a meaningful and lasting difference in the lives of the people who call these beautiful Caribbean islands home.”

Founded in 2009 by Stewart as the non-profit arm of Sandals Resorts International, the foundation has impacted more than 1.5 million people across the Caribbean. Because Sandals Resorts covers all administrative costs, 100 per cent of public donations to the foundation go directly to community, education, and environmental projects.

The list of philanthropists recognised by T&C also include:

* Colombian singer, songwriter, and dancer Shakira who helped pledge US$1.25 million to assist the rebuilding of schools following the 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck Colombia in August this year.

* American flim-maker George Lucas and his wife Mellody Hobson, who pumped US$1 billion into building the new Lucas Museum for Narrative Art in Los Angeles.

* American artiste Beyoncé, who gave US$2 million to the Studio Museum of Harlem to celebrate her 45th birthday.

* Gail Gallie’s the Nat, which focuses on the natural world, funding restoration and education projects.

* The Michelangelo Foundation for Creativity and Craftsmanship, which is the force behind the international craft showcase Homo Faber.

* Seattle’s Jon and Kim Shirley, who spent upwards of US$10 million restoring Alexander Calder’s Mountains and Clouds sculpture, which is on public display in the Hart Senate Office Building.

* The Tang family, the Lauder family, and Jen Rubio and Stewart Butterfield, who all made transformative gifts to New York City’s Metropolitan Museum of Art, securing its future.

* Architect Moshe Safdie, who “is bringing his flair for socially responsible design to restoring Brooklyn’s Pacific Library, the borough’s first Carnegie library”.

* Olivia Walton, who as chair of Crystal Bridges Museum of American Art, has helped make Bentonville, Arkansas, a cultural destination.

* American film-maker Eric Goode, a wildlife conservationist who goes beyond merely featuring endangered animals on television.

*ABC News correspondent Bob Woodruff who, after being seriously wounded in Iraq 20 years ago, founded the Bob Woodruff Foundation which has, under the leadership of CEO Anne Marie Dougherty, funded US$228 million in health care, housing, and employment services for veterans.

On announcing the awards, T&C invited its readers to join it “in celebrating and studying those who have most impactfully funded new programmes and new museum wings, as well as others who saw a fellow citizen’s need and tried to fix it, or those who, through simple acts of kindness, offered us a reminder of the good in the world that remains, despite it all”.

World.title: Hauto takes talent to big screen
World.content:
Content creator Hauto is the mastermind behind the film..

Jamaican content creator Hauto is betting on the talent of his fellow social media personalities as he makes his film-making début with Rivalry, a crime drama that brings some familiar faces from TikTok into a new creative space.

Officially released on Wednesday, October 28, the film follows rival gangs battling for control of Kingston, with drugs, guns, and the criminal underworld fuelling a power struggle that soon attracts the attention of law enforcement.

But beyond the violence and high-stakes drama lies a bigger ambition for Hauto: To prove that the talent entertaining Jamaicans on their phone screens can make an equally compelling impression on film.

The project, which features TikTokers Swiiss Lee, Deeman, Emmy, Jakes, Jimbo Dee, and artiste Top Banks, among others, was initially conceived as a single full-length movie. However, financial constraints forced production to stop midway, prompting Hauto to split the story into two parts. With the first instalment completed, the team is preparing to move into production on the second.

Despite the change in plans, Hauto believes Rivalry offers something fresh to the local entertainment landscape.

“Although some will say the topic and the themes are the same, you’ve never seen TikTokers take on film like this. This is us coming together as a community to showcase our talent beyond social media. The vibes, the energy, won’t be anything the industry has seen before,” he told the Jamaica Observer’s Splash.

The first instalment establishes the day-to-day operations of the rival gangs and introduces the players in their dangerous world. In the second, the conflict is expected to intensify as the rivals begin taking more aggressive action against each other.

For Hauto, the idea came together organically, with the writing flowing naturally once he began fleshing out the initial concept. Casting, however, required a more personal approach.

Having spent years interacting with content creators on the app, he said he had become familiar with their personalities and individual strengths, allowing him to envision how they might translate to the screen.

“Most of the persons in the film are folks I see and communicate with every day on the app, so when mi get the idea, mi analyse everybody personality and mi know exactly what dem capable of, and that’s how I put all the roles together,” he explained.

While some of the cast members were initially shy in front of the camera, Hauto said they grew more comfortable as filming progressed and they became immersed in their characters.

“I saw it in them, it’s hard to explain, but what I envisioned came through,” he said.

Working with a cast whose members have their own online schedules and commitments was not without its challenges. Hauto admitted that coordinating filming sessions and getting everyone on set, on time, could be frustrating. Nevertheless, he said their willingness to take direction and prepare for their roles made the experience worthwhile.

“They’re easy to work with and they follow instructions very well. When the cameras are rolling and you say, ‘Action!’ they’re ready. They know what they’re doing. They got their lines, learnt them, and they did well,” he said.

Hauto is aware that moving from social media to film may invite scepticism, particularly from those who question whether online personalities possess the acting ability required for a full production. His response is simple: “Give the project a chance.”

“Before you knock us and knock the project and say we talentless, give us a chance. This might shock you and you might actually see that the yutes dem have talent and all they need is a chance to show what dem capable of,” he said.

That opportunity comes at a considerable personal cost. Hauto revealed that more than $2 million has already been spent bringing Rivalry to life, with the production financed out of pocket through revenue generated by the various media outlets he operates online.

It is a significant investment for a debut project, but one he considers worthwhile given his confidence in the cast and his desire to create more opportunities for Jamaican creatives.

“What I really want is for this to put us on the map, and for me to break new grounds in the creative industry. My plan is to become a young, Caribbean Tyler Perry. I want to start mass-producing local films using local talent,” he said.

The ambition builds on an interest in entertainment that dates back to his school days. Hauto recalled being the class clown, often using humour to get people laughing. He had also been creating social media content since high school, recognising early that entertainment was the direction he wanted to pursue.

Now, he hopes to turn that experience into something more expansive; moving from creating content for digital audiences to developing film projects that can sustain a wider creative ecosystem.

For now, Rivalry is being distributed independently, allowing the team to retain the proceeds from sales. Hauto said the possibility of approaching a distribution company to purchase the film’s rights could be explored in about a year, but the immediate focus is on getting the production directly to viewers.

The film is available for purchase at US$28.99 through southsideent.gumroad.com/rivalry.

“We took you off Netflix and brought you to TikTok and now you watch our streams. We’re taking you away again, but this time to a website to watch us in a different light,” Hauto said.

With Rivalry, he is hoping audiences will look beyond the online personae they already know and recognise a different side of the creators they have come to follow.

For him, the film is not simply a new venture, but the beginning of a larger plan to build a platform for local talent and expand the possibilities for Jamaican storytelling.

World.title: CONCRETE THREAT
World.content:
The National Water Commission has appealed for developers to preserve areas where rainwater can soak into the ground and replenish underground reserves.

LEADING construction industry representative Richard Mullings has called for tougher enforcement of Jamaica’s development regulations, warning that builders cannot continue paving over land to maximise profits while complaining about inadequate water supplies to support their projects.

Mullings, who sits as president of the Incorporated Masterbuilders Association of Jamaica, delivered the pointed criticism during a Jamaica Developers Association (JDA) webinar on Thursday, pushing back against an appeal by the National Water Commission (NWC) for developers to preserve areas where rainwater can soak into the ground and replenish underground reserves.

He argued that appeals to developers’ goodwill would accomplish little in an industry driven by commercial interests, insisting that government regulators must do more to enforce standards designed to protect the country’s water resources.

“I don’t believe in just encouragement and well wishes when it comes to things that have to do with profit,” he said.

His comments followed a presentation by NWC Assistant Vice-President for Systems Planning and Water Resource Development Ian Bennett, who warned that the increasing coverage of land with concrete and other impermeable surfaces was restricting the natural replenishment of groundwater, particularly in Kingston and St Andrew.

Bennett’s concern centred on the Liguanea aquifer, a vast underground water resource beneath the Corporate Area that could play a greater role in securing the capital’s water supply but whose potential is already being undermined by contamination.

Presenting findings from the Water Resources Authority identifying potential natural aquifer recharge sites across Jamaica, Bennett urged developers to adhere to existing permeability requirements, which are intended to ensure that sufficient land remains available to absorb rainfall.

He cautioned that when too much land is paved over, rainwater that could otherwise replenish underground reserves instead runs off towards the sea.

“We still have that vast water resource which is available to us, but it simply runs off to the sea because there’s very little permeability,” Bennett told participants.

The NWC official warned that failure to preserve natural recharge areas could eventually force the authorities to invest more heavily in artificial aquifer recharge, a process through which water is deliberately directed underground to replenish depleted reserves.

Bennett pointed to artificial recharge already being undertaken in St Catherine, but said adopting similar measures more widely in Kingston and St Andrew would be considerably more expensive than protecting the land’s natural ability to absorb rainfall.

“If we are to resort to that, it means it’s going to be really costly. It is going to be reasonably effective, but not as effective as if the Kingston and St Andrew basin were able to take on this percolation job naturally,” he said.

However, Mullings was particularly critical of the suggestion that developers should simply be encouraged to preserve permeable surfaces, arguing that stronger regulatory oversight was necessary to counter the commercial pressures to maximise building density, parking spaces, and returns on investment.

He challenged his own industry to recognise the contradiction between demanding reliable water supplies for new developments while pursuing building practices that could compromise the very resources needed to provide that water.

“We as developers, now we’re going to bawl and complain about the availability of water to be able to do our developments and make profit. And then, on the other hand, we’re going to try and pave as much surface area to sell as much, get as much parking spaces to maximise our density. We can’t have both,” he said.

“It’s unrealistic to think that in a competitive environment we are going to just do things on purely social or altruistic motives. The Government, the governance system, the regulators have a critical role to enforce,” Mullings argued.

He maintained that the responsibility could not rest solely with developers, particularly where complying with environmental requirements might mean sacrificing commercially valuable space.

Mullings warned that failures in oversight were also contributing to public resistance to construction projects in communities across Jamaica.

His intervention comes amid continued residential and commercial development in Kingston and St Andrew, where pressure to maximise the use of increasingly valuable land has resulted in greater demand for high-density buildings and associated infrastructure.

Contamination compounds problem

Adding to the challenge is the longstanding contamination of the Liguanea aquifer, where inadequate sewage disposal has compromised groundwater that could otherwise help meet Kingston’s water needs.

During the webinar, questions were raised about households that continue to rely on septic tanks and sewage pits despite public sewerage infrastructure being available in their communities.

The concern is that sewage entering the ground contributes to elevated nitrate levels, limiting the amount of groundwater that can safely be extracted for drinking.

The problem has already affected the capital’s water supply. In March this year, Water Minister Matthew Samuda disclosed that eight major wells in Kingston and St Andrew, with combined production potential exceeding two million gallons daily, could not be used because of contamination linked to backyard sewage disposal systems.

The NWC is now looking to recover some of that potential.

During Thursday’s webinar, Garth Jackson, the utility’s vice-president for engineering and capital projects, disclosed that work was under way to redevelop a well in the Liguanea aquifer where nitrate levels were not high, with the project intended to serve as a pilot for broader groundwater development.

He explained that any major expansion of groundwater extraction would depend on efforts to address contamination and better understand how water moves through the aquifer.

“We believe we can use that as a pilot to do the broader development of the aquifer. But it really is dependent on the aquifer being cleaned up and identifying the flows through the aquifer in order to decide where it’s best to develop groundwater resources,” Jackson said.

He indicated that while groundwater wells form an important part of the NWC’s water supply network, much of that reliance is currently outside the Kingston and St Andrew metropolitan area.

The discussion comes as residents of the Corporate Area continue to grapple with water restrictions despite recent rainfall.

Dr Philippa Campbell-Francis, the NWC’s acting vice-president of operations, disclosed that Mona reservoir was at 43 per cent of capacity and Hermitage dam at 54 per cent, levels that remained insufficient to lift restrictions.

Although the number of water supply systems affected by drought islandwide had declined from 107 to 91, she said the recent rainfall had not provided enough relief to restore normal service in Kingston and St Andrew. The utility was therefore continuing to regulate supply while attempting to rebuild storage levels ahead of the coming dry months.

Costly sewer connections

Restoring the capital’s groundwater reserves, however, will require more than protecting land from excessive paving.

The NWC is also confronting the challenge of getting existing households connected to public sewerage systems, particularly where the cost of establishing a connection has discouraged property owners from abandoning septic tanks and sewage pits.

During the webinar, questions were raised about households located near sewerage infrastructure that are already being billed for sewerage services despite continuing to use private sewage disposal facilities.

Jackson explained that customers located within the prescribed distance of an available sewerage network can be billed for the service, even if they have not physically connected their properties.

He acknowledged, however, that the cost of connecting to the network can be substantial and said the NWC was examining ways to make the process more affordable.

One possibility is to allow homeowners to pay connection costs over several years through their utility bills. The commission is also exploring whether grants or loans could be secured to assist property owners.

Increasing the number of households connected to public sewerage systems could help reduce the contamination of groundwater from septic tanks and soak-away pits, improving the prospects for bringing additional wells into service.

But the infrastructure challenges extend to new developments, where builders have complained about being required to finance sewerage works that would otherwise form part of the public network.

Mullings argued that such requirements add to construction costs and place affordable housing projects at a particular disadvantage.

“Nobody who is trying to build units that are making marginal profit can afford to engage in performing the work for the utility and installing a sewer system. It favours the higher end units,” he said.

The NWC, meanwhile, estimates that approximately $25.7 billion is needed annually to replace ageing infrastructure and upgrade its water supply systems, illustrating the scale of investment required to accommodate future developments while maintaining services to existing customers.

World.title: HAPPY SHE’S BACK!
World.content:
Jamaica goal shooter Jhaniele Fowler (left) catches the ball as England’s Eboni Usoro-Brown (partially hidden centre) and Geva Mentor look on during the Netball World Cup match in Liverpool, England, on July 15, 2019. (Photo: Collin Reid)

NETBALL Jamaica (NJ) President Karen Baugh is confident the senior Sunshine Girls will reclaim the Rhone-Hornsby Trophy, arguing that selectors have assembled a strong and balanced squad for the upcoming Horizon Series against England.

The Sunshine Girls and the Roses are to meet in a four-match series, with the first two contests set for Copper Box Arena in England, on November 21 and 22. The final two matches are slated for National Indoor Sports Centre (NISC) in Jamaica on December 5 and 6.

England were 2-0 winners of the last Horizon Series after both matches in Jamaica were cancelled due to the passage of deadly Hurricane Melissa in October 2025. In the series prior to that, Jamaica claimed a 2-1 victory after one match was tied.

Speaking about the squad for the upcoming clashes, Baugh expressed her full backing of the selection process.

“I think the selectors did a good job of providing us with a balanced team. I know they had a hard time because we had several girls vying for some positions. But, all in all, I think the team is strong and that they will give a good account of themselves in the series,” Baugh said.

The series will mark the return of star shooter Jhaniele Fowler-Nembhard, who missing due to childbirth.

Baugh said Fowler-Nembhard has remained close to the team throughout her three-year absence.

“Well, like I’ve been saying, Fowler-Nembhard never left us. Even though she wasn’t available for selection for obvious reasons, she’s always been with her team members. She’s been there in the background supporting them and so we’re really glad to have her back in camp.

“She will join the team in England and then come home for the home games. So I’m sure Jamaica is longing to see her play. I haven’t seen her play on home soil for a while. So it should be a special occasion,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

“The last time she played for the team was in the 2023 World Cup,” Baugh added.

Baugh also noted that preparations have been progressing well, boosted by the presence of overseas-based players.

“Training has been going well. About more than half of the squad are here, including some of the ladies who play in Australia. They’re here now on their break and so they’ve been training and preparing for this one,” she said.

Baugh is bullish about Jamaica’s chances of bringing the trophy home.

“I’m very confident that we can win back the Trophy. I’m pretty confident that we will. I mean, it all comes down to what happens on the court on those four days. But we definitely have a team that is capable of bringing the trophy back home to Jamaica,” Baugh declared.

On the logistical front, Baugh said final arrangements for the England leg are being finalised, while expressing gratitude to corporate sponsors and leaving the door open for more support.

“Well, we’re still working on the last logistics pieces and of course, we welcome support. If there are sponsors out there who still want to be a part of the series, of course, we welcome them. You know, even though the time is drawing closer. But yeah, preparations are going well and we’ve gotten some support from Corporate Jamaica and we’re very thankful to all of the sponsors on partners who have come on board who recognise the potential and the possibilities of the Sunshine Girls so we’re looking forward to two good days in England and two great days enjoying,” she said.

SQUAD

Shooters — Jhanielle Fowler-Nembhard (co-captain), Shanice Beckford, Gezelle Allison, Azara Wilmot, and Rhea Dixon (reserve).

Mid-court — Crystal Plummer, Nicole Dixon-Rochester, Abigaile Sutherland, Brie Grierson, and Adean Thomas (reserve).

Defenders —

Shamera Sterling-Humphrey (co-captain), Latanya Wilson, Jodi-Ann Ward, Kadie-Ann Dehaney, and Kimone Shaw (reserve).

STAFF — Sasher-Gaye Henry-Wright (head coach), Kerry-Ann Brown (assistant coach), Arleene Findlay (manager), Maureen Brown (assistant manager), Dr Michelle Holt (team doctor), and Nicole Reid (physiotherapist).

World.title: It’s the big 10!
World.content:
Finished in distinctive Essmanngreen with exclusive commemorative badging, the one-of-a-kind anniversary 911 will be up for auction as part of a group of 2026 events celebrating a decade of Porsche in Jamaica.

Porsche Jamaica is celebrating its 10th anniversary as the official importer of the German brand on the island under the theme A Decade of Dreams.

The milestone will be highlighted by a specially commissioned one-of-a-kind anniversary 911 Carrera to be offered through a silent auction, with proceeds benefiting the Bustamante Children’s Hospital.

“When we first introduced Porsche to Jamaica 10 years ago, there were those who questioned whether a brand of this calibre could succeed in our market. A decade later, the answer speaks for itself. We have not only established Porsche as a distinctive presence in Jamaica’s luxury automotive landscape, but we have also built a passionate community of owners and enthusiasts who share our appreciation for extraordinary German engineering, performance and design,” said Adam Stewart, executive chairman, ATL Automotive Group.

Since its arrival in 2016, Porsche Jamaica has established a distinctive presence, setting the standard of Jamaica’s luxury automotive landscape. The journey has seen Porsche Jamaica introduce successive generations of iconic models to Jamaican roads — from the 911 and Panamera to the Macan and Cayenne, while expanding the brand’s offering into electric mobility with models including the Taycan, all-electric Macan, and most recently the all-electric Cayenne.

At the heart of the anniversary celebration is a specially commissioned 911 Carrera, created to commemorate 10 years of Porsche in Jamaica. Finished in distinctive Essmanngreen and featuring commemorative badging, the anniversary 911 is a one-of-a-kind expression of the brand’s heritage, craftsmanship and unmistakable design.

Bidding for the 911 starts at $50 million. Interested individuals wishing to participate and submit a bid can contact a Porsche sales executive at Porsche Centre Kingston or Porsche Centre Montego Bay.

Porsche Jamaica’s 10th anniversary will include a celebration of the anniversary 911, and a series of curated content and brand initiatives throughout the remainder of 2026.

“Porsche has always been about looking ahead without losing sight of what makes the brand unique, our next decade will be about continuing to deliver exceptional Porsche experience while introducing our customers to new technologies, new possibilities, and new ways to experience the brand,” said Stewart.

World.title: 20 things only a Hampton girl would know
World.content:
One of the oldest boarding schools in Jamaica, the Malvern-based all-girls’ Hampton School was founded in 1858, two years after its all-boys brother school, Munro College.

With its motto Suma Virtute Et Humanitate (With Utmost Courage and Courtesy), the school is known for producing well-rounded ladies.

Observer Online spoke with members of the school’s alumni community, who shared fond memories of their time at the institution and some insights on things a person would only know if they attended Hampton.

1. The Quadrangle — While mainly used for devotions, the Quadrangle was the meeting place for the entire school, including teachers, who looked on from the staffroom balcony. Devotions became known as ‘quad’ and were mandatory for ladies to start the morning with the good word. With girls lined up in order of forms, the fifth formers would get exposed to the sun first as it rose higher, but the longer quad went on, especially if it’s a Monday or a Friday, just prepare for everyone to be hot!

2. The ‘sacred’ garden, stairs and blocks — The principal’s garden leading to the front office with its turtle pond was strictly out of bounds for students, and most would only walk through it if they returned after graduation. Similarly, no student was ever supposed to set foot on the steep teachers’ stairs leading to the staff room, and no lower school students should ever be seen on the sixth and fifth form blocks.

3. Blueprint — Blueprint is one of the only all-female steel bands in the country, and Hamptonians will tell you it’s the best! Tickets for the band’s annual show, Echoes, sell out quickly. Founded by the school’s long-time music teacher Alison Morris, Blueprint often performs alongside the school’s celebrated choir.

4. Seniors rule the seats — Hampton was one of the few schools in the country with a fully functional private bus system decades before the new Rural School Bus Programme, and seating charts were no joke. As an informal rule, only seniors were allowed at the back of the bus, and girls would sit in descending order.

5. Late-bugs walk! — Hampton ladies who were late to school would not have the privilege of getting dropped off near the quadrangle; rather, they would have to walk up the long hill leading to the quad in the early morning sun as penance.

6. The green tables — The green (now blue) tables and benches set up across the school grounds hold a special spot in every Hamptonian’s heart; from laughs to trading ‘sus’, they remain a cherished meeting spot for students.

7. Flaming black cake and carolling – This blazing dessert was a speciality afforded to boarding students each year during Christmas celebrations. Students would also be expected to dress warmly and go out carolling in the quiet town of Malvern where the school is situated.

8. Hamptonia — The school’s song, a celebration of its location, creation, ethos and students with its notoriously difficult high notes is learned quickly by all new students if only because it is sung so often at ‘quad’. ‘Vivat floreat Hamtonia, Crescat floreat, Hamptonia, In saecula, per multa Floreat Hamptonia.’

9. Tuck — For boarders, who would only go home every three weeks, tuck boxes were where food and snacks were stored, and students would get access to them on Wednesday evenings and weekends. Opening tuck boxes to trade cup soups, banana chips and Tiggaz was always an exciting prospect.

10.‘Substance’ and cheese/ Sugarbun and cheese — Some older Hamptonians describe it as a cornbread-like cake while other younger ladies remember a brown spiral bun, but whether you called it ‘substance’ or ‘sugarbun ’, the baked good sold with a slice of cheese was always in high demand at ‘bottom caf’ or ‘top caf’.

11. ‘Country’ side and ‘city’ side dorms – Dormitories are split down the middle with a ‘country’ side and a ‘city’ side; the city side consists of the newer pink, green and blue buildings, while the country side consists of older, more traditional dwellings including Villa, Cottage and Ivy Rota.

12. Prizegiving — Held every November, this ceremony is based on academic performance. Only girls with an average of over 75 per cent were allowed to attend along with their families, to be awarded a silver pin (for averages 75 to 84 per cent) or a gold pin (85 per cent and above) to be worn on uniforms or ties.

13. “It’s not Hampton High” (sigh) — Every Hampton girl has, at some point, had to correct someone about the name of the institution, which is Hampton School (for Girls), not Hampton High or Hampton High School, an oft-repeated mistake.

14. The Hampton Clap — Five rounds of five successive claps, a sound distinctive to Hampton and instantly recognisable to anyone who attended the institution.

15. With utmost courage and courtesy — Poise and courtesy are an important part of life at Hampton. Grace, dignity, and composure are emphasised, even after leaving school, you’re unlikely to find a Hamptonian eating while walking or walking with their hands in their pockets. Chewing gum is also not allowed and would never be found for sale in the school’s cafeteria.

16. Dear Munro… — Hampton’s brother school is a 15-minute drive away, and phones are not allowed for lower school students. In order to communicate with their friends (and beaus!) boarders would send specially folded letters delivered by the ‘day-girls’. Written on a single ‘book-leaf ’, the letters would be folded so that the paper became the envelope too, concealing the contents prior to delivery. Aside from letters, the two schools share an intrinsic bond, from excitement about supporting the all-boys school at football and track meets and Schools Challenge Quiz, shared bus routes and pandemonium when they came to visit; Hampton without Munro is like sugarbun without cheese.

17. Chapel — Religion is important for Hampton ladies, and boarders attend services in the school’s historic chapel every Sunday. The attire for these sessions is the same for all students: their bright white chapel gowns.

18. Poui trees — Gracing the grounds of Hampton School are several poui trees, the largest in front of the Information Technology labs. Once these started to bloom with their distinctive yellow flowers, it’s said it would be too late to start studying, as exams are around the corner!

19. Names we can’t forget – The people make the place, and there are some names beloved by students that have been passed down through generations: Mr Singh (hello, get away!), Mr Hall (Biology and Quiz), Ms Reid (History), Ms Quest (Art), Ms Green (Housemother), Ms King (Law), Mrs Taylor (lunch matron), Mr Dwight (cook), Maxine (ancillary staff), Mickey (groundskeeper) and of course Mr Fabian Letman (Security and logistics).

20. Finish the sentence — “Hampton Ladies are…”, “Heads up shoulders back…”, “Hampton ladies don’t set trends…” “If Gold rusts…”

– Dana Malcolm

World.title: Caribbean Cup success showcases strides in local club football, says Ricketts
World.content:
JFF President, Michael Ricketts (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

Kingston, Jamaica — Portmore United and Mount Pleasant Football Academy will contest the Concacaf Caribbean Cup final in December, ensuring that the regional crown will remain in Jamaican hands for the third time in four years.

It follows Portmore’s triumph in 2019 and the successes of fellow Jamaican clubs Cavalier in 2024 and Mount Pleasant in 2025.

Portmore and Mount Pleasant, having progressed to the final, also qualified for the 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup.

It is the first time since 2004, when Harbour View faced Tivoli Gardens, that two Jamaican teams will meet in the final of the Caribbean club competition.

The Jamaica Football Federation (JFF), in congratulating both clubs, hailed their achievements as further evidence of the progress being made by local teams on the regional stage.

JFF President Michael Ricketts said the qualification of Portmore United and Mount Pleasant was a significant accomplishment for Jamaican football.

“I would like to wholeheartedly congratulate Mount Pleasant Football Academy and Portmore United for qualifying for the 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup and also for getting to the final of the Caribbean Cup,” Ricketts said.

“This is the fourth year in a row that at least one Jamaican club is in the final of the Caribbean Cup, so we are very pleased by the strides made by our clubs on the island,” he noted.

“This guarantees that just like in 2024 and in 2025, we will have a Jamaican club lift the Caribbean crown come December 5,” Ricketts added

The 2026 Caribbean Cup champions will receive a bye to the Round of 16 of the 2027 Champions Cup, while the runners-up and third-place team will begin their campaigns in the first round.

The official draw for the 2027 Concacaf Champions Cup is scheduled for Monday, December 21, 2026.

World.title: The Rutte way or the Carney method? Scaramucci says Europe’s Trump strategy is off the Mark
World.content:
“There’s two models of behavior: one is [NATO Secretary-General] Mark Rutte and one is [Canadian Prime Minister] Mark Carney. I think Mark Carney is handling him better. The Canadian people are with him, even if it causes some level of economic hardship,” Scaramucci said.

“Rutte, on the other hand, is making a big mistake. Because when you equivocate or flatter him, when you act in the manner that Mark Rutte has acted, all you’re doing is losing his respect. You’re not gaining anything,” he added.

Rutte has often lauded the U.S. president: “I just like the man. I think what he is doing for NATO is great news,” the military alliance chief said in an interview with POLITICO this summer.

Europe has seemingly yielded to Trump’s wishes on numerous occasions. The EU-U.S. trade deal was criticized as playing in Washington’s favor, while European allies agreed to a 5% of GDP spending target by 2035 at last year’s NATO summit in The Hague, matching Trump’s headline demand.

Carney, by contrast, has been more unwilling to bow to Trump’s pressure. He walked away from U.S. trade talks, saying Ottawa could not accept the offer or the demands — and promised to match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar.

In the interview, Scaramucci also lambasted members of Trump’s own Republican Party. “That is the other side of this story: the cowardice of the political servants that are supposed to check Donald Trump, the members of the Republican Senate caucus and the House caucus,” he said.

World.title: Russian citizen faces spying charges in Poland after photographing railways
World.content:
Police found a large amount of evidence suggesting that the man took pictures of strategic infrastructure systematically. “There were photographs of various places and important communication facilities, not only in Poland,” Łukasz Dutkowiak, a spokesperson for the Lower Silesian police, told Radio Wrocław.

Prosecutors are now investigating “activities for foreign intelligence against the Republic of Poland,” the regional authority added.

Poland has faced multiple sabotage attacks against its military and railway infrastructure over the past year. Prime Minister Donald Tusk accused Ukrainian nationals of “cooperating with Russian services” after a November 2025 attack damaged a rail line close to the Polish-Ukrainian border.

Fires broke out at a drone-components plant in Skarżysko-Kamienna and an aircraft-parts facility in Lublin in late August. In September, a Starlink communications station was set on fire near Warsaw.

“Russia does not even have to cross our border,” Tusk said after the September attacks. “It is already waging a hybrid war against us using drones, acts of sabotage and disinformation on the internet.”

European officials have pointed to an escalation of sabotage attacks from Russia over the past few months, as President Vladimir Putin seeks to disrupt military support for Ukraine and raise the political cost of backing Kyiv.

World.title: Unrest in France is nightmare fuel for Macron’s heirs
World.content:
They are facing a divided field of mainstream candidates on the center and center-right, including two former prime ministers under Macron in Gabriel Attal and Edouard Philippe, and Bruno Retailleau, a former interior minister. These candidates have struggled to settle on a common message in response to the crisis — let alone agree on who the best candidate would be to avoid their nightmare scenario of a runoff between Mélenchon and Le Pen.

‘Out of ideas’

Three officials supporting centrist and conservative candidates told POLITICO that they were concerned the events of the past few weeks would cause lasting damage to their campaigns.

“It’s definitely going to kill us,” said one campaign official who, like others in this story, was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “We cannot be the solution anymore, only the problem.”

A Philippe supporter went as far as suggesting his champion was ill-equipped for the moment. “It’s exactly what he doesn’t need,” the supporter said last week, drawing parallels between the protests and the 2018–2019 Yellow Vest movement under Philippe’s premiership. “He doesn’t know how to do this. He’s not empathetic, and he’s not pretending to be.”

“Honestly, I don’t know how we’re going to get through this. Things are tough, and we’re out of ideas,” a centrist MP said.

The protests have taken place two Saturdays in a row and are expected to continue in the weeks to come. High school students are demanding better learning conditions while the wider public are protesting the cost-of-living crisis. The movement has been marred by scenes of vandalism and looting, especially on Oct. 17, when Macron’s government appeared to have underestimated both the scale of the protests and the potential for violent unrest.

World.title: Former US ambassadors: America must stand with Ukraine
World.content:
Appeasement does not necessarily prevent conflict. It can encourage aggression by convincing dictators the free world lacks the will to resist them. And a ceasefire without effective safeguards could become merely a pause before the next assault. A settlement that leaves Ukraine defenseless would postpone the conflict, not resolve it.

Peace should be measured not by the speed with which an agreement is signed, but by whether it protects Ukraine’s independence and makes another war less likely. And economic pressure is among the most important nonmilitary instruments available to the U.S. in this process, as Russia’s ability to wage war depends substantially on energy revenues, access to international markets and networks that facilitate sanctions evasion.

On Sept.18, U.S. President Donald Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 into law. Then, on Oct. 16, he issued an executive order waiving specified sanctions, restrictions and duties authorized under the legislation, citing the national interest. This order raises a legitimate question about how Washington intends to use the economic leverage Congress provided.

The measurable objectives these waivers are intended to achieve, why they serve American national security and what conditions would trigger their reconsideration need to be explained.

The U.S. needs to enforce restrictions consistently, close avenues for evasion and impose consequences when countries or companies knowingly provide material assistance to Russia’s war effort in violation of applicable law.

This does not require abandoning diplomacy. It requires a coherent policy in which economic relief advances clearly defined security objectives.

World.title: Streeting insists Burnham won’t make ‘arbitrary’ welfare cuts
World.content:
He said: “What I do understand from experience, and I’ve seen this experience borne out under both Conservative and Labour governments, is that when you put in place arbitrary targets to cut welfare without a thought-through plan to do so sustainably and responsibly, the plans fall apart.”

Spending on U.K. health and disability-related benefits has increased sharply since the Covid pandemic, with the bill for working-age disability benefits in England and Wales increasing from £14bn in 2020 to £25bn in 2026.

Former Health Secretary Alan Milburn is leading a report into how to help the estimated one million young people not in employment or education. It is due to be published in November, and the government is also waiting on minister Stephen Timms to make recommendations on disability benefit reform.

A previous bid to reduce welfare under Starmer was scrapped after a revolt among Labour MPs. The row was seen as deeply damaging to Starmer’s authority and a sign that the leadership had lost touch with rank-and-file MPs.

Streeting’s comments came after an extended back-and-forth between ministers and journalists Thursday over whether Burnham’s government will lower welfare spending before the next general election.

Healey was asked by the BBC Thursday whether cuts to the welfare bill would be made before the next election.”There will be a reduction in the benefits bill, we’ll do that in a Labour way,” he said.

World.title: Economy minister warns France could ‘hit the wall’ as new figures show GDP contraction
World.content:
“If we don’t have the budget adjustment we put in the budget, we will hit the wall,” Lescure said.

But France’s fragmented parliament failed to pass budgets before the new year in both 2024 and 2025, and the spring 2027 presidential election may further complicate efforts to seek compromise this time around. That could force Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu to push through the budget using a constitutional backdoor that bypasses a parliamentary vote, but it would expose the minority government to potential motions of no confidence.

Lescure insisted that adopting a budget for next year was key to “reassure markets” and relaunch growth in the last quarter of the year. The French economy contracted by 0.1% in the first quarter of 2026 and recorded no growth in the three months that followed.

That anemic growth will likely complicate the government’s pledge to bring the deficit down to 5.4% of GDP this year, as the target was based on the assumption the economy would grow by 0.5% in 2026.

“The French economy is at a standstill,” Lescure said. “It has to restart.”

World.title: Russian oil refinery suffers major drone attack
World.content:
Fedorischev asked locals not to reveal what was struck, but independent Russian media channel Astra reported a fire at the local oil refinery, which produces jet fuel for the Russian army. Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery can produce about 8.8 million metric tons of oil per year, according to Russian oil company Rosneft.

The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that Kyiv had agreed to pause strikes on Russian oil refineries under pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump. The unofficial halt is expected, according to the report, to last until after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3. Ukraine had paused drone strikes on Russian oil refineries for 72 hours when Trump announced an energy ceasefire earlier this month. But the Kremlin kept bombarding Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

“That didn’t help. There was all kinds of rhetoric, and no one thanked us for those three days,” Zelenskyy told reporters in Kyiv earlier this week.

As of Friday morning, Ukraine has not taken responsibility for the latest strike — though there was some trolling from the Ukrainian military-industrial complex.

“Little drone, how did you end up there? The Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery welcomes guests from Ukraine,” Ukrainian defense company Fire Point — which produces long-range drones used by Kyiv to bomb targets in Russia — said in a morning Telegram post.

Russia also attacked Ukraine with ballistic missiles and more than 100 drones overnight, killing one person in Kyiv and leaving 350,000 people without electricity in Dnipro.

World.title: Elif Eralp und der Palästina-Sumpf
World.content:
Geleakte Anmerkungen in einer Interview-Freigabe setzen die Berliner Linke weiter unter Druck. Wahlgewinnerin Elif Eralp fürchtet einen Terror-Sympathisanten und Teile der eigenen Reihen. Cedric Looks analysiert, wie der Pro-Palästina-Flügel den anstehenden Parteitag kapern will und ob die Entscheidung über einen Ausschluss der umstrittenen Abgeordneten Vanessa Emde noch kommt oder immer weiter verschoben wird.

Der Rückzug von EZB-Chefin Christine Lagarde erwischt Europa auf dem falschen Fuß. Für Kanzler Friedrich Merz bedeutet das eine doppelte Belastungsprobe, weil er sich nun nicht nur mit der Nachfolge für Steinmeier beschäftige, sondern auch mit dem französischen Präsidenten Emmanuel Macron über den wichtigsten Finanzposten einigen muss. Rasmus Buchsteiner ordnet ein, warum Bundesbank-Chef Joachim Nagel dabei wohl nur Außenseiterchancen hat.

Drohen in Deutschland bald französische Verhältnisse? Im 200-Sekunden-Interview warnt der hessische Innenminister Roman Poseck vor einer Eskalation der bundesweiten „Gen Z regelt“-Proteste am Wochenende. Er erklärt, wie ein massives Polizeiaufgebot in Frankfurt am Main verhindern soll, dass Linksextremisten die Demonstrationen für Zerstörung und Plünderungen missbrauchen.
