World.title: Iran’s Revolutionary Guard reports two tankers on fire in Strait of Hormuz as talks continue
World.content:
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Friday, Oct. 30, that two oil tankers had encountered incidents while attempting to navigate routes Tehran considers unauthorized in the eastern and western sections of the Strait of Hormuz. Both vessels were subsequently stopped in the waterway’s southern waters.

 

According to Iranian state media, the Guard claimed the tankers had switched off their navigation and positioning systems and were attempting to leave the strait through routes opposed by Tehran, with the support of the U.S. military.

The Guard said the vessels continued sailing despite repeated radio warnings before encountering trouble in what it described as unsafe areas.

It provided no details about the tankers’ identities, their flags, the precise cause of the incidents or the condition of their crews.

The reports came as Qatari mediators returned to Tehran on Friday to continue efforts to broker an agreement between Iran and the United States.

Uncertainty over the number of tankers damaged

In a separate incident whose possible connection to the Guard’s claims remains unclear, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations, or UKMTO, reported that a small boat approached an oil tanker Thursday evening and attached two explosive devices to its hull above the waterline.

The devices detonated, sparking a fire in the engine room and temporarily disabling the vessel.

The Financial Times identified the tanker as the Louise 1.

The incident occurred about 25 nautical miles (46 kilometers) northeast of Khasab, Oman.

UKMTO said the fire had been extinguished, all crew members were safe and no environmental pollution had been reported. The tanker subsequently resumed its voyage toward its next port.

The attack appeared to mark the first reported successful use of limpet mines against a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz since the U.S.-Iran war began in February 2026.

It was not immediately clear who was responsible or whether the attack was connected to the Guard’s latest claims involving two tankers.

Separately, Oman’s Maritime Security Center reported Friday that the Royal Navy of Oman had evacuated 25 crew members from a Panama-flagged commercial vessel that came under attack and caught fire about 1.6 nautical miles off the coast of Musandam.

The center said the crew members received necessary medical care but did not identify the vessel or those responsible for the attack.

It remained unclear whether the incident was connected to other reported attacks on tankers in the strait.

The Guard’s latest statements followed claims Thursday, Oct. 29, that three tankers had struck naval mines along the strait’s southern route, triggering explosions and fires.

Iran’s regular military also reported Thursday that another tanker had caught fire in the eastern Strait of Hormuz.

According to Agence France-Presse, Iranian officials claimed that all four vessels had been operating in prohibited and unsafe areas.

However, it remained unclear whether the two tankers mentioned in Friday’s Guard statement were additional vessels or were among those involved in the incidents reported Thursday.

U.S. Central Command disputes Iranian claims

Adm. Brad Cooper, commander of U.S. Central Command, reiterated that the Strait of Hormuz’s main shipping lanes had been cleared of Iranian naval mines.

He also claimed that Iran’s navy had been destroyed and that Revolutionary Guard forces were no longer operating in the waterway.

Cooper said U.S. forces remained in the region to keep major shipping routes open and secure.

CENTCOM also rejected a claim made Thursday by the Revolutionary Guard that it had taken control of an American MQM-170 Outlaw drone in the western Strait of Hormuz.

Iranian sources, meanwhile, reported Friday that an American unmanned surface vessel had been destroyed in the eastern Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. military had neither confirmed nor denied that report at the time of publication.

The growing number of maritime incidents comes amid a continuing dispute between Washington and Tehran over the routes used by commercial shipping through the strategic waterway.

Iran has demanded that vessels coordinate their movements with Iranian authorities and use routes closer to the strait’s northern shores. Ships seeking to avoid Iranian control have instead used the southern route.

Qatari mediators return to Tehran amid threats of renewed U.S. strikes

Diplomatic efforts to prevent another major escalation in the U.S.-Iran war are continuing alongside mounting military tensions in the Strait of Hormuz.

CBS News, citing a source familiar with the negotiations, reported signs of progress and said Iran was expected to respond to a revised proposal from Qatari mediators by the end of the week.

The diplomatic initiative is aimed at preventing a resumption of large-scale U.S. strikes against Iran, a possibility President Donald Trump has repeatedly raised in recent weeks.

Axios reported that Qatari-led mediators were seeking common ground on issues including inspections of Iran’s nuclear facilities and sanctions relief.

However, disagreements persisted over the conditions for formally opening negotiations.

Axios also reported that the United States and Israel were considering options for extensive military strikes against Iran after the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections.

The Associated Press reported Thursday, citing two diplomats, that Washington had warned several regional allies about the possibility of renewed U.S. attacks on Iran and potential Iranian retaliation, although Trump had not made a final decision.

Trump, speaking Friday to a Kansas City radio station, said the war with Iran would end "soon," but did not specify whether that would be achieved through a diplomatic agreement or military action.

The U.S. president reiterated that Washington wanted guarantees that Iran would never acquire a nuclear weapon.

His remarks came as there was still no clear indication that Tehran and Washington had reached an agreement on the conditions for ending the war, while the possibility of renewed large-scale military strikes remained on the table.

World.title: UK probes Meta over 'exploitative' new terms for media as global pushback mounts
World.content:
The UK's competition watchdog has launched an investigation into whether Meta is imposing "exploitative" new terms that allow it to use publishers' content for its own products, including AI, without giving media organisations adequate choice.

 

The probe will examine whether the "terms and conditions" from the US technology giant "unfairly harm news publishers and other content businesses", the Competition and Markets Authority said in a statement.

The CMA said the new terms, which the Facebook and Instagram parent had planned to introduce on November 20 before putting it on hold, could amount to an abuse of its dominant position in the market.

The watchdog will determine whether "Meta is abusing a dominant position by imposing exploitative terms on publishers and advertisers".

Meta's new terms could allow it to access and use content from news publishers' websites to develop and provide its own products, including its AI features.

A Meta spokesperson said "we've already committed not to change our terms without consulting publishers and other stakeholders".

"We welcome the opportunity to explain our approach to the CMA," they added.

Thousands of UK businesses rely on Meta to reach customers and audiences, meaning an unfair imposition of the new terms could breach competition law.

"We've heard concerns from news publishers and other businesses and are acting swiftly to investigate whether Meta's proposed changes may breach competition law," said CMA chief executive Sarah Cardell.

European pushback

The British governments effort follow hot on the heels of action taking place across Europe and around the world against Meta's proposed new rules and its practices in general in using media content.

Since May this year, more than 340 local and national news sites including the Guardian, the New York Times and USA Today have blocked internet archive crawler bots to prevent them from collecting data for training AI models.

A Norwegian court this week temporarily banned Meta from enforcing the new user terms after ten media outlets argued it would threaten their rights to their content.

And in France, the country's appeals court rejected on Thursday an attempt by Meta to overturn an order to negotiate in good faith with French media over rights payments for information used on its social networks.

In two rulings, the Paris Appeals Court found that Meta's conduct had caused "serious and immediate harm to the press sector" in France, affirming the position of the country's anti-monopoly body.

The regulatory authority in July ordered the parent company of Facebook and Instagram to "negotiate in good faith" with French media on neighbouring rights payments — a form of copyright payments for use of information on social media platforms.

It said Meta's conduct could be considered "abuse of a dominant position".

Two associations of media groups had complained to the Competition Authority following a lack of progress in talks to renew deals of neighbouring rights payments.

The regulator noted that Meta was continuing to use the content of the media groups but not making payments to them since their deals lapsed.

The Paris Appeals Court found that Meta had in the negotiations with publishers provided only fragmentary, opaque and unverifiable data about its use of media content.

The DVP association of publishers, of which AFP is a member, called the rulings a "major development" and urged Meta to fully meet its obligations to media.

A Meta spokesman said "we are disappointed with the Paris Appeals Court ruling" and was considering what steps to take.

Meta is in the midst of another battle with media over new user terms and conditions that force professional users to give it the right to collect content -- including content behind a paywall -- and use it for AI training among other things.

The company is also facing mounting global pushback against its platform designs and features, especially amid claims of harms against children and teenagers, and is back in court in the US later this month alongside Snap.

World.title: EU to impose €2 fee on all packages entering the bloc as of 1 November
World.content:
The European Union will start charging a €2 handling fee on all packages entering the EU market as of Sunday, as cheap imports from China continue to surge.

 

A €3 duty already came into force in July on small parcels worth less than €150. However, that fee is temporary and will remain in place until 2028, when a new IT customs system becomes operational.

The new measures were deemed necessary as the EU faces a dramatic increase in low-cost imports from Chinese platforms such as Temu, Shein and AliExpress.

The new €2 fee, which comes into force on 1 November, will apply to all packages, regardless of their value, and will cover customs handling costs. It comes in addition to the €3 duty.

“The logic for the duty is the level playing field: all goods entering the EU should pay the due and justified amount of duty,” an EU official said. The official added: “The logic of the fee is to cover the costs of control, as e-commerce represents a disproportionate cost for our customs authority.”

The new fee will be paid by platforms, sellers or carriers and collected by the 27 EU member states. Of the money collected, 75% will go into the EU budget, while the remaining 25% will be retained by EU countries.

The €3 duty introduced in July has already had an impact on import volumes: Between July and September, the number of small parcels entering the bloc dropped by 60%, according to the European Commission. However, 5 million parcels still enter the EU market every day, the EU executive also said.

In 2024, 91% of those shipments came from China, posing fierce competition for European retailers.

Infringements of EU rules on products are also an issue, as the Commission proposed in September a legislation cracking down on imports of illegal products, particularly those sold through online marketplaces, by ensuring that an economic operator in the EU is always legally responsible for non-compliance.

In May, the Commission also fined Temu €200 million for shortcomings related to dangerous baby toys and faulty chargers. Brussels is also investigating Shein over illegal products, including child-like sex dolls.

World.title: PSG to defend Intercontinental Cup title in December as Qatar hosts final stage
World.content:
Paris Saint-Germain will return to Qatar in December to defend their FIFA Intercontinental Cup title, after the country was confirmed as host of the tournament’s final three matches for a third consecutive year.

 

The French club will play in the final on 16 December at Ahmad bin Ali Stadium in Al Rayyan, returning to the venue where they lifted the trophy last year. The other two matches will take place on 9 and 12 December, organisers announced on Thursday.

PSG secured their place by retaining the UEFA Champions League title in the 2025-26 season. Under the competition’s format, Europe’s champions enter directly into the final, while clubs representing the other five continental confederations compete for the remaining place.

Last December, PSG beat Brazil’s Flamengo 2-1 on penalties after a 1-1 draw following extra time, winning their first Intercontinental Cup in front of 42,150 spectators.

Ahmad bin Ali Stadium will host the Intercontinental Cup final on 16 December. Local Organising Committee

Three clubs, one place in the final

Mexico’s Toluca, winners of the Concacaf Champions Cup, will face this year’s Copa Libertadores winners in the Derby of the Americas on 9 December at Jassim bin Hamad Stadium in Doha.

The winners will then meet South Africa’s Mamelodi Sundowns in the Challenger Cup at the same venue on 12 December, with a place against PSG in the final at stake.

Sundowns reached that stage by beating Saudi Arabia’s Al Ahli 2-1 in Pretoria on 19 September to win the African-Asian-Pacific Cup. Al Ahli had opened the tournament with a 1-0 victory over New Zealand’s Auckland FC in Jeddah on 26 August.

The South American representative will be decided in the Copa Libertadores final on 28 November.

The Intercontinental Cup is FIFA’s annual competition for the champions of its six continental confederations. It is separate from the expanded Club World Cup, which is held every four years.

Qatar hosted the final stages of the first two editions of the Intercontinental Cup in 2024 and 2025, having previously staged the 2019 and 2020 editions of the former annual Club World Cup.

This year’s December fixtures will overlap with the closing stages of the Under-17 World Cup, which Qatar is hosting from 19 November to 13 December.

World.title: Nvidia CEO sees Kazakhstan as potential AI hub for Europe
World.content:
Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang has visited Kazakhstan for the first time, saying the Central Asian country could emerge as a major AI computing hub for Europe.

 

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang visits Alem.ai with Kazakhstan's Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev in Astana. Copyright: Alem.ai

Huang made the remarks during a fireside chat with Zhaslan Madiyev, Kazakhstan's Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development, at the Alem.ai International Artificial Intelligence Centre in Astana.

During the discussion, Madiyev said Kazakhstan plans to nearly double its installed power capacity to more than 40 gigawatts by 2035 as the country expands the infrastructure needed to support its growing AI sector.

One of its flagship projects is the Data Center Valley, a large-scale AI computing campus under development in Ekibastuz, one of Kazakhstan's main power-generating centres. Its first 50-megawatt phase is expected to begin operations in 2027, while the project's energy infrastructure could eventually scale up to one gigawatt.

Huang said Kazakhstan's energy resources and growing computing capacity could give the country a significant role in Europe's AI ecosystem.

“Kazakhstan has a lot of real estate. It also has a lot of energy,” Huang said. “You're going to have a lot of compute right here in Kazakhstan. It's going to be a hub, a computing hub, an AI factory hub for all of Europe.”

A fireside chat with Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang at Alem.ai in Astana. Copyright: Alem.ai

Huang described the country's abundant energy resources as a potential competitive advantage in the AI economy, arguing that electricity could increasingly be used to generate computing power and AI rather than simply being exported as energy.

“Kazakhstan has a fundamental advantage because you have so much natural resource already. You have so much energy, and instead of just exporting energy in the future, you could transform the energy into intelligence and export intelligence,” Huang said.

Sovereign AI

But energy alone, Huang argued, will not be enough. Kazakhstan will also need to retain control over another resource — its data.

Madiyev said the country is already developing Kazakh-language large language models based on open-source foundation models and asked whether Kazakhstan should eventually build its own foundation model from scratch.

Huang said building a domestic foundation model “makes complete sense”, describing it as a national security concern.

Kazakhstan's Deputy Prime Minister Zhaslan Madiyev and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during a fireside chat at Alem.ai in Astana. Copyright: Alem.ai

He argued that countries should retain control over both their data and the AI infrastructure used to serve their citizens, comparing it to other essential national infrastructure.

“In the future, you will have your own electric grid, your own internet, your own telecommunications and your own intelligence grid,” Huang said.

The potential of Physical AI

Beyond computing infrastructure and sovereign AI, Kazakhstan is also looking to position itself in the emerging field of Physical AI — systems that can interact with and operate in the physical world.

Pointing to Kazakhstan's industrial base in mining, agriculture, transport and logistics, Madiyev asked whether the country could become a hub for developing and training Physical AI models and robots. Huang called the idea “fantastic”, saying these industries could be among the first to benefit.

“Physical AI is not just robotics,” Huang said. “It includes everything from seismic understanding to mapping mines and wells, to understanding geography and geology — where to mine, how best to mine — understanding material science, the processing of chemicals.”

With the technology still at an early stage, Huang said Kazakhstan has an opportunity to help shape the emerging industry.

Investing in AI startups

The discussion also turned to Higgsfield AI, a Kazakh-founded generative video startup in which Nvidia has invested.

Asked what attracted Nvidia to the company, Huang said the decision ultimately came down to its founders.

“The first thing and the last thing is you invest in people, not companies,” Huang said, describing Higgsfield's founders as “visionary” and capable of competing with leading AI companies globally.

Huang also pointed to the company's presence in both Kazakhstan and the United States, saying it could help bridge the two ecosystems.

Kazakhstan's President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev receives Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in Astana. Copyright: Akorda Press Service

Later that day, Huang met President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, who described the development of artificial intelligence and digitalisation as a national priority.

“This visit is very important for us in terms of giving a serious boost to cooperation with Nvidia,” Tokayev said.

Huang welcomed Kazakhstan's ambition to become an “AI nation” and said the country had the potential to become a global hub for Physical AI.

Huang's first visit to Kazakhstan came at the close of AI Month, a nationwide initiative launched in September as part of the country's Year of Digitalisation and Artificial Intelligence.

World.title: Germany, France, Italy and Spain: Where was inflation highest in October?
World.content:
The eurozone’s four largest economies published fresh inflation data on Friday, offering an early read on what is shaping up to be another hot month for price pressures across Europe.

 

The October's inflation ranking was clear.

Italy came out on top, with prices rising 5.4% from a year earlier. Spain followed at 4.9%, France at 3.4% and Germany at 2.8%.

The more telling story, however, is the direction.

Inflation accelerated sharply in Italy and France, held steady in Spain and fell in Germany, even though all four major economies are dealing with the same surge in energy costs.

So, why are the same pressures producing such different bills, and what does it mean for the European Central Bank?

Italy: Why did prices jump the most?

Italian inflation rose to 5.4% in October from 4.2% in September, according to preliminary figures from national statistics office Istat.

That brings it back to its August 2023 level, and well above the 4.6% economists had expected.

Under the harmonised measure used to compare countries across the EU, Italian inflation reached 5.6%.

Energy did most of the damage. Istat said energy prices were 31.4% higher than a year earlier, up from 22.6%, still shaped by the international geopolitical backdrop.

Regulated energy, the tariffs that are not set freely by the market, rose 59.5% year on year, more than double the previous month’s rate. Prices in this category climbed 18.8% in October alone.

The pressure is also reaching supermarket shelves.

The so-called "shopping trolley," a basket of food, household and personal care products Italians buy most often, rose 2.5%, up from 1.5%. Unprocessed food prices accelerated to 7.5%, and transport services to 3.1%.

Core inflation, which strips out energy and fresh food to show underlying price trends, rose to 2% from 1.6%.

For Italian households, the timing is difficult. Istat also reported on Friday that the economy did not grow in the third quarter.

Melanie Debono, senior Europe economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, wrote in a note that the breakdown due next month is likely to show the energy shock weighed more heavily on consumer spending than monthly retail figures had suggested.

Spain: Why did inflation stop rising?

Spain’s inflation rate held at 4.9% in October, the same as September, according to a flash estimate from the National Statistics Institute (INE). That keeps it near its highest level since early 2023.

Prices still rose 0.6% compared with September. Annual inflation stayed flat largely because fuel was cheaper than last October, when petrol and diesel prices were climbing. Higher gas tariffs offset part of that relief.

FILE. People walk among tents set up by protesters at the Puerta del Sol square demanding stronger laws to protect renters in Madrid, Spain, 17 Oct. 2026 AP Photo/Bernat Armangue

Underlying inflation, which excludes energy and unprocessed food, held at 3.1%. The harmonised rate eased slightly to 4.9% from 5%.

Spain is also the bloc’s strongest big economy at the moment.

Joe Nellis, head of economic research at advisory firm MHA, noted in emailed comments that Spanish output grew 0.6% in the third quarter, supported by stronger domestic demand.

France: Is stagflation setting in?

In France, inflation rose to 3.4% from 3.1%, its highest since January 2024, statistics office Insee said. Economists had expected 3.2%.

Energy prices rose 24.1% year on year, accelerating for a fourth consecutive month, driven by gas and oil products. Services inflation, the largest part of the French basket, picked up to 2.7% as hotel and transport prices rose.

On the harmonised measure, French inflation reached 3.8%.

The figures came alongside data showing the French economy shrank 0.1% in the third quarter.

“France faces stagflation,” Claus Vistesen, chief eurozone economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said in a report.

The term describes rising prices combined with a stagnant economy.

He expects French harmonised inflation to rise above 4% by November.

Germany: Why did inflation fall?

Germany was the exception.

Inflation dropped to 2.8% from 3.3%, below the 3% economists had forecast, the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) said.

The main reason was a cut in fuel taxes that took effect on 1 October and runs until the end of the year. Energy inflation slowed to 12.2% from 14.9%. Consumer prices fell 0.2% from September.

Core inflation, excluding food and energy, eased to 2.1% from 2.4%.

Economists warn that relief may be short-lived. Vistesen wrote that energy inflation is likely to stay subdued through the end of the year, but snap back in January and February if fuel duties rise again.

“The current German core inflation numbers look dovish, but this weakness won’t last long,” he said.

What does this mean for the eurozone as a whole?

Eurostat will publish its flash estimate for the entire currency bloc next week, and Friday’s figures point to another uncomfortable reading.

Before the Italian data, BofA Global Research expected eurozone inflation of 3.7% in October.

After the Italian surprise, Pantheon raised its own forecast to 4%, up from 3.8% in September and twice the ECB’s 2% target.

Paolo Grignani, senior economist at Oxford Economics, said the day’s data paint “a mixed picture for the Eurozone with stagflationary tendencies.”

Energy is still doing the heavy lifting, he said, but there are “worrying signs of the energy shock spreading rapidly to stickier components.”

With eurozone growth holding at 0.4% in the third quarter, Oxford Economics expects the ECB to raise rates twice more.

Will the ECB raise rates again?

On Thursday, the ECB kept its deposit rate at 2.5%, after a hike in September. Christine Lagarde said policymakers had discussed another increase but agreed unanimously to wait.

The meeting was overshadowed by her announcement that she will step down in February, nine months before her term ends.

Matthew Ryan, head of market strategy at financial services firm Ebury, said in emailed comments that a December hike remains “very much ‘live’”.

He added that a drawn-out search for Lagarde’s successor “could inject volatility into markets at an already fragile moment.”

Nellis said the ECB is in a tough position. Years of sluggish growth argue for keeping borrowing costs supportive, but with price pressures mounting, the central bank “may be forced to raise interest rates further at its December meeting.”

Friday’s numbers show both sides of that dilemma.

In Germany, a targeted tax cut was enough to bring inflation down. In Italy, the energy shock is already showing up in what families pay for food and travel.

Which of those two stories spreads across the rest of the eurozone may decide how far the ECB has to go.

World.title: Christa Pike describes 'pain in my mind and in my soul' in first statement after failed execution
World.content:
Christa Pike said she has been in constant pain since surviving a lethal injection in Tennessee last month, but remains grateful for the love and support she has received.

 

“There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul,” Pike said in her first public statement, released through her attorneys on Friday.

Pike dictated the statement to her legal team from the infirmary at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Center, where she is being held.

Pike said she entered the execution chamber prepared to die peacefully, only to wake up alone and confused in a hospital bed. The 50-year-old added that she had never imagined living beyond her scheduled execution date.

“I don’t know why I survived that night. I don’t know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time. And I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone,” she said.

In this image from video provided by WBIR-TV, Christa Pike cries after being sentenced to death on 30 March, 1996 in Knoxville, Tenn. WBIR-TV via AP/WBIR-TV via AP

Pike also criticised the handling of her execution attempt, while expressing sympathy for her victim’s family.

"I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position. I continue to think about my victim’s family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured,” Pike said.

Pike’s lawyers have called on Tennessee Governor Bill Lee to commute her death sentence to life imprisonment.

However, Lee told reporters this week that he expected her sentence to remain unchanged unless the courts ruled otherwise.

“I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts.”

The governor has ordered an investigation into the failed execution and postponed the state's other lethal injection scheduled for this year.

She was initially hospitalised following the failed execution before being transferred back to prison.

World.title: From derelict food market to futuristic Centre of Excellence: inside a Cyprus success story
World.content:
At the very heart of Nicosia, the capital of the Republic of Cyprus, lies a Centre of Excellence (CYENS) specialising in interactive media, smart systems and emerging technologies.

 

The Centre of Excellence is housed in a former food market building in the heart of Nicosia's old city © Euronews

Partially funded by the EU, CYENS employs around 110 people — mostly researchers, developers and technicians — across multidisciplinary research groups, affiliated start-ups and spin-offs. They work across more than 50 projects, mostly European, but also through local, national and industry grants.

For example, computer scientist Panayiotis Charalambous´team is using AI-driven tools and augmented and virtual reality technologies to create a variety of visual content. These include interactive urban maps displaying real-time data on traffic, noise, environment and pollution, along with reproductions of historical monuments where access is limited or restricted.

Computer scientist Panayiotis Charalambous works on an interactive map of the city of Nicosia © Euronews

“Virtual reality is one of those technologies that can enable different modes of interaction with visual elements”, Charalambous, also a Team Leader at the Centre, explains. “One of the things that can enable you [to do] is to be immersed in an environment that maybe it's difficult for you to go to. Either because it's in a remote location, something in a different country, or maybe you also have mobility issues. Being immersed in that environment allows you to feel like, yes, I'm there, right?”.

His team is also developing innovative technologies to allow interactive experiences. One of their recent projects will let children create their own scenarios with actor avatars in a theatre museum.

Avatar theatre actors developed by game programmers, which users can make show emotional states © Euronews

“You can basically give the actors in the scene different emotional temperaments, different actions that they can do and effectively create your own play”, game engineer programmer Ismail Hadjri explains. “There's also the stage designer table where functionally you place the different objects in the space, you tell the actors where they need to go, you put spotlights where they need to be”

Another intriguing technology from the Centre is called Senssos, which involves utilising sensors to monitor interactions between body motion and muscles. This could help musicians reduce imbalances in performance, or physiotherapists propose better treatments for their patients.

Christos Ioannou, co-founder of Senssos spin-off, testing motion sensors © Euronews

“We have developed our own hardware to replace the commercially available systems with something which is cheaper, easy to install and fast. So, it can be easy for consumers to use this either at home or at jobs during rehabilitation, during training, to enhance performance and for rehabilitation reasons as well”, explains Christos Ioannou, research assistant professor and co-founder of Senssos.

The small sensors being tested here are also already helping professional athletes to enhance their performances by measuring real-time cadence, ground contact, heart rate, and many other parameters that could improve their training techniques.

Computer scientist and Darefore spin-off co-founder Panayiotis Kyriakou supervises running tests © Euronews

“Main applications of the technology is for the athlete to have real-time feedback on when they are running, indoors or outdoors, without having a coach with them, or to analyse the data afterwards alone, with a coach or with a clinician,” explains computer engineer Panayiotis Kyriakou, who is also the CTO & Co-Founder of biomechanics company Darefore.

The Centre of Excellence was established with the goal of becoming a regional hub for technology and knowledge transfer. It has now turned into a useful tool to fight against brain drain in Cyprus — a small EU member with highly skilled engineers, researchers and students, claims CYENS´ CEO, Yiorgos Chrysanthou.

Yiorgos Chrysanthou Chief Executive Officer, CYENS Centre of Excellence © Euronews

“Cyprus is a small place, and we cannot really compete with heavy industry or anything else”, he says. “I believe the only way to help the economy and take it forward and move a little bit beyond tourism, which was the main economic driving force for all these years, is to keep this critical mass of talent. And build it and expand it to create an economic activity which relates on technology”.

Software engineer Haris Psallidopoulous, for instance, is working to help farmers improve their farming techniques with AI-driven virtual reality apps.

Software engineer Haris Psallidopoulos helps farmers increase their yields © Euronews

“Farmers were really open to the idea of using AI, extended reality and robots, but they didn't know such technology was available to them, which was actually mind-blowing to me because I am in the tech field: I know they exist”, he says. “Farmers should be using technology more because it's a really helpful tool”.

Other researchers are developing solutions to help cities better map, identify, quantify, protect and manage their trees and urban green spaces.

Researchers behind the “Cyprus Trees Initiative” and “Metacities” projects © Euronews

“We wanted to provide more time to the municipal staff for creative work rather than having to do micro tasks”, explains Penélope Vásquez, project coordinator of the Cyprus Trees Initiative. “It's easier for them to know where they need to go and trim the trees geographically, where they should plant trees because there's something lacking. And also, we combine this platform with other projects that relate to the urban heat island effect, so the rising of temperatures. Now, the municipality will be able to plan with more information and strategically plan to reduce temperatures in the city.”

The City of Nicosia is already actively using some of these solutions.

The Municipality was a founding partner of the Centre; the mayor himself chairs its Board of Directors. The institution, he claims, is a key socio-economic actor in the city.

Charalambos Prountzos, Mayor of Nicosia © Euronews

“We are between Europe, Asia, and Africa. And this is very attractive for people from the wider region to come”, Prountzos says. “The presence of CYENS in Nicosia brings together top-class academics and top-class research together with the municipality, the city, and of course the business community in order to create research that will be used in the sphere of innovation, but also to create applicable solutions.”

These solutions are already in use by municipal services, including this platform DumpMapper, a platform that helps track and report illegal landfills, even tiny ones, across the city.

Associate Professor Andreas Kamilaris and (behind) project manager Marios Zittis have developed the DumpMapper platform © Euronews

“This area is 50 square kilometres, and we have identified through our technology 98 incidents”, Andreas Kamilaris, Managing Director at DumpMapper says while pointing at different points across a map of the city of Nicosia on the computer screen. “Each colour indicates a different type of waste. You can also see a hotspot where most of the waste is located.”

As Managing Director for the DeepCamera research group, associate research professor Alessandro Artusi works with his team to develop new image processing, and computer graphics for a variety of applications.

Researchers from CYENS´ DeepCamera Multidisciplinary Research Group © Euronews

DeepCamera focuses on the development of AI-powered vision pipelines that drive real-time detection, tracking, and decision making across complex environments; “from entertainment to maritime safety”, Artusi explains, while sharing a preview alongside his senior research associate, medical physicist Xenios Milidonis.

Research associate Charithea Stylianides, a PhD student in Mathematics, also works for CYENS on the application of data science and machine/deep learning on patient data for enhanced diagnosis, prognosis and therapeutic outcomes.

Other initiatives promote cultural heritage. Magic Lantern, for example, aims to develop an interactive, augmented-reality-based book designed for museums, galleries, libraries, or archives. The project taps into consumers’ desire to not only witness art and literature, but to connect with it in a more tangible way.

Fotos Frangoudes working on his Magic Lantern technology © Euronews

“The tangible feeling of an actual physical book provides a different sense and a different engagement for the actual user compared to just touching on a screen”, explains Magic Lantern CEO Fotos Frangoudes. “There are a lot of studies and research behind this that [suggest] more tangible technologies can improve overall learning capacity”, he explains.

The Centre has also become a magnet for artists —including Ting-Hun Liu and Leon-Etienne Kühr, who recently experimented with AI’s creative capabilities by asking it to generate its own images without any human prompt.

“We all have the feeling that AI images have this own aesthetic quality to them. And we kind of want to distil this, get only this out of it”, the artistic duo explains. “And what happens if these machines only interact with themselves and there's no more human input? And we can see here, it's very mundane pictures of nature, advertising, and politicians.”

A recent art festival “FLOWS” co-hosted by the Centre of Excellence gathered the proposals of 60 artists from 15 countries.

World.title: US judge narrows Macrons' defamation lawsuit against American podcaster
World.content:
A judge in the United States has ruled that French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte ​could continue their defamation lawsuit against the companies of the American podcaster Candace Owens, but not against Owens herself.

Advertising Read more

Editor’s note: This story was updated at 13:25 on 30 October 2026 to include a statement from lawyers for Emmanuel and Brigitte Macron, sent to us by Ketan Sengupta, who works with the Macron's legal team. It responds to the court’s ruling on Candace Owens’ motion to dismiss the case against her.

In the statement, lawyers for the Macrons said: “We are pleased that the Court rejected Mrs. Owens’ attempt to remove the case from Delaware, where her companies continue to publish and monetize her defamatory falsehoods. As for Mrs. Owens personally, we are keeping all options open to ensure that, in addition to the liability she still faces through her companies, she is held accountable personally.”

***

The Macrons had filed a lawsuit in July 2025 against Owens and two companies, accusing her of helping fan online rumours about whether Brigitte is a transgender woman.

Owens, 37, an influencer with a large following on social media platforms, has claimed that Brigitte was a man.

Delaware Superior Court Judge Sheldon Rennie said in a ruling on Tuesday that Owens could not be held personally liable in the case.

But Rennie allowed the suit against two companies associated with her – Candace Owens LLC and GeorgeTom Inc – to continue.

Question of jurisdiction

Rennie said the Delaware court did not hold jurisdiction over Owens because her residence was in another state, Tennessee.

The ruling means that if the French first couple were to eventually win the case, Owens' personal assets would be shielded.

In their lawsuit, the Macrons said Owens ⁠touted ​false claims and conspiracy theories ​against them "to promote her independent platform, gain notoriety, and make money".

Rennie deferred judgment on Owens' motion to dismiss ‌the ⁠Macrons' litigation until he was briefed on how French defamation law and statutes of limitation intersect with US law.

"I am in the absolute best mood over this Macron dismissal," Owens said on X on Wednesday.

'Centuries of patriarchal history': why trans rumours are wielded against women

Damages to Brigitte Macron

Brigitte Macron, 73, has taken to the courts in France to combat claims she was born a man.

Two French YouTubers, Natacha Rey and Amandine Roy, were convicted in September 2024 of spreading false claims after they posted a video in December 2021 alleging that Brigitte Macron had once been a man named Jean-Michel Trogneux – who is actually her brother.

Rey and Roy were ordered to pay €8,000 in damages to Brigitte Macron and €5,000 to Jean-Michel Trogneux.

The defendants were also given a suspended fine of €500.

Did French media silence enable Brigitte Macron fake news story to go viral?

Brigitte Macron had filed a libel complaint against the two women after their claim went viral, triggering conspiracy theories notably among the far right.

Roy, an online fortune-teller, interviewed Rey, a self-described independent journalist, for four hours on her YouTube channel in December 2021.

The women discussed the unsubstantiated rumour that Brigitte Macron had undergone gender reassignment, with Rey claiming to have uncovered a “state lie” and “scam”.

The claim went viral just weeks before France's 2022 presidential election, spreading even to the US where Owen derided the first lady in a now deleted YouTube video.

World.title: Egypt's mahrganat music: from the streets to five-star hotels
World.content:
Born in Egypt’s working-class neighbourhoods, mahraganat music is loud and raw, and these days it is practically impossible to escape. But for the artists behind it, mahraganat is more than just party music: they see it as the latest chapter in Egypt’s rich musical history.

Advertising

In this third episode of the season, we travel to the Egyptian capital, Cairo, to discover the origins of a genre that has become the soundtrack to urban life, despite receiving no official airtime.

Mahraganat evolved from shaabi: music by the people, for the people. Although it rose to prominence during the revolution of 2011–12, it has since become less overtly political.

It remains the music of happiness, partying, joy, and celebration.

Its fast rhythms and loud beats may be a far cry from the golden age of Egyptian music, but mahraganat has been on the scene since the early 2000s and it isn’t going anywhere, any time soon.

We trace its origins and evolution as we speak to one of the godfathers of the movement, his musical partner and a specialist in the genre.

Mid-East Junction is produced by RFI's English-language service. This episode was mixed by Vincent Pora. Special thanks to Elisa Schouten for her contribution.

World.title: Germany news: Merz calls for Korean reunification at DMZ
World.content:
10/30/2026 October 30, 2026 Munich: Vandals smash Manchester United memorial

A glass cabinet containing memorabilia linked to the 1958 Munich Air Disaster, in which eight Manchester United footballers lost their lives, was smashed and plundered in the Munich suburb of Trudering this week.

The display case on Manchesterplatz forms part of a memorial commemorating the tragedy which occurred when the United team made a refueling stop in Munich while on the way back from a European Cup game in Belgrade, Serbia, on February 6, 1958.

The plane struggled to take off again in the wintery conditions at the old Munich-Riem airport to the east of the city center and, on the third attempt, ploughed off the end of the runway and into a house. Of the 44 people on board, 23 were killed, including eight United players, several journalists and two crew members.

The crash site has become a place of pilgrimage for United supporters and, in 2020, the cabinet was installed on the initiative of the Red Docs Munich – a local Bayern Munich fan club – to house the various memorabilia and tributes left by visitors.

Munich police said the cabinet was broken into on Monday morning between 8 a.m. and 1 p.m. local time (07:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. UTC), with the unknown perpetrators making off with a glass sculpture and several medals.

"They don't understand the damage that they've caused," Ifty Ahmed, chairman of the Manchester Munich Memorial Foundation (MMMF), told the BBC, adding: "Whatever they've taken from inside the showcase, they haven't taken our memories."

The Red Docs Munich arranged for replacement glass to be installed on the same say. The MMMF said Manchester United had offered to pay for the repairs but said the foundation had covered the costs itself.

The joint commemoration of the 1958 disaster and the maintenance of the memorial site has produced extensive and friendly relations between Bayern Munich and Manchester United, who will meet in the Champions League in January.

World.title: Seoul fears being slighted as US reaches out to North Korea
World.content:
With ties between South Korea and the Trump administration strained, the South Korean government worries that Donald Trump's pursuit of a diplomatic breakthrough with Kim Jong Un may come at Seoul's expense.

South Korea's relationship with the North, always strained, seems to be going through a particularly hostile patch in recent weeks.

Last month, Seoul accused North Korea of planting a mine on the southern side of the heavily fortified border. The device exploded, injuring three South Korean soldiers. Pyongyang refused to apologize and insisted this was a false-flag incident designed to tarnish the isolated nation. The North Korean regime has since conducted multiple weapons tests, held its first-ever exhibition of military drones attended by Kim Jong Un, brought up self-propelled artillery units to the border and started preparing loudspeaker systems that will blast propaganda into the South.

On Thursday, North Korea also fired around 10 short-range ballistic missiles towards the Sea of Japan just before a scheduled visit to South Korea by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

On top of South Korea's issues with its arch rival, many in Seoul are growing increasingly wary of their most important ally, the United States. South Korean politicians are worried that the US could push for a diplomatic breakthrough with North Korea at the cost of ignoring South Korea's security, or even leave it exposed to Pyongyang's nuclear arsenal.

Who gets a voice on South Korea's future?

US President Donald Trump famously claimed he and Kim Jong Un "fell in love" during Trump's first term. More recently, Trump has indicated he would like to resume talks and there have been suggestions that a meeting could take place on November 18 in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, where Trump is expected to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.

Why North Korea is now Europe's problem To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The North Korean side has made no official response to Washington's hints, although South Korea's National Intelligence Service informed a closed-door meeting of Seoul's intelligence committee on Thursday that Kim Jong Un discussed the possibility of meeting Trump when he met with senior members of China's politburo in Dandong on Saturday.

Seoul's fears were also fueled by the US proposing three-way talks with Russia and China on the fate of Ukraine, without inviting a representative of Kyiv to attend. The worry in Seoul is that President Donald Trump may similarly bypass Seoul to discuss the future of the Korean Peninsula with China and North Korea.

Washington-Seoul relationship shaken by tariffs, funding disputes

"Right now, there is a problem of trust between the two governments," said Kim Sang-woo, a former politician with the left-leaning South Korean Congress for New Politics and now a member of the board of the Kim Dae-jung Peace Foundation.

A security and trade relationship that was previously considered secure has been rocked by tariffs, trade restrictions and demands from Washington that the South pay more for the US troops stationed in the country, Kim told DW.

President Lee's diplomats have lost access to key decision-making personnel in this White House, he added.

"I do not think this US administration is thinking long-term in the relationship with South Korea," Kim said. "They do not see South Korea as a part of their wider national security network and I do not think they are listening to experts on the importance of allies in the region."

"I also think that Trump is eager to meet with Kim because of his personal quest to obtain a Nobel Peace Prize," he added.

South Korea proposes talks to officially end war with North To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Trump's widely publicized efforts to secure a Nobel have been thwarted so far. However, this might change if Trump somehow manages to formally end the Korean War that was put on hold by the 1953 armistice.

The fear in Seoul is that Trump would trade South's security to achieve this goal.

South Korea eyeing its own nuclear deterrent

"The most serious concern is that the US recognizes Pyongyang as a nuclear power, which would legitimize the North's program and undermine efforts to convince it to abolish its nuclear weapons as well as the broader non-proliferation system," said Lim Eun-jung, a professor of international studies at Kongju National University.

In parallel, she said, there are fears that Trump could reach an agreement with North Korea that requires it to scrap its long-range nuclear missiles — those that are capable of hitting targets in the United States — but permits it to retain short-range weapons that can still easily reach South Korea and Japan.

That would raise questions about the US commitment to defend South Korea in case of a nuclear attack. That uncertainty, in turn, is likely to give credence to voices arguing that South Korea needs to develop its own nuclear deterrent.

"For years, we have depended on US extended deterrence guarantees under the nuclear umbrella, but this US administration is unpredictable and there are more and more people asking why we don't just go it alone," Lim told DW.

"Virtually, all our neighbors have nuclear weapons, and while no-one wants the dominoes to start falling, it could happen," she added.

Merz says Korean security affects Europe

The latest escalation between Seoul and Pyongyang comes amid repeated attempts by South Korean President Lee to improve communication with Pyongyang. The perceived outreach has irritated South Korea's European allies, who are angry over North Korea deploying soldiers and supplying munition and missiles to help Russia in the Ukraine war.

Why Kyiv and Seoul are clashing over North Korean POWs To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Moscow is believed to be repaying for Pyongyang's support with money, military technology and security guarantees.

During his visit to South Korea, Germany's Merz pointed out that "Korea's security affects Europe's security. And Europe's security also affects the security of Korea."

"The world is small — even in war," Merz added.

South Korea needs allies

Berlin, just like Seoul, has been disoriented by the Trump administration turning hostile on many of its allies while seeking reproachment with geopolitical rivals such as Russia and China. During his Asia tour, Merz pushed for an alliance of middle powers to protect free trade and oppose "unilateralism, autocratic power politics and violations of international law."

German Chancellor Merz recently visited South Korea along with Japan and Singapore Image: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

"The fact remains that the United States is shifting its foreign policy, ⁠its foreign economic ​policy, and redefining its interests. As they do so, we must do the same," Merz said in South Korea.

It was not clear if Seoul will respond to Merz's appeal by moving closer to the European Union. At the moment, however, it seems apparent that the South Korean government is struggling to communicate with either North Korea or the US.

"It is a very difficult situation," said Kim Sang-woo. "There is no trust and no connections and that, to me, is very worrisome."

World.title: Bollywood and the underworld — together in the spotlight?
World.content:
A wave of shootings and extortion threats has rattled India's film industry. This time, those claiming responsibility are very different from the Mumbai underworld that had Bollywood in its grip back in the 1990s.

"In the entire film industry, whoever works without aligning with us, or works with Salman Khan, will be killed."

This warning was delivered in an audio message by presumed attackers on Indian actor Tiger Shroff in Mumbai earlier this month, as they claimed responsibility for the shooting.

The apparent perpetrators said they were connected to Lawrence Bishnoi, a student-politician-turned-gangster who has been in prison since 2014. Notably, police have not confirmed the gang's involvement.

The shots fired at Shroff, which injured his driver, were only the latest in a string of attacks targeting prominent figures from the Mumbai-based film industry, popularly known as "Bollywood".

Since 2022, gunmen fired shots at actor Salman Khan's apartment and at the home of filmmaker Rohit Shetty in Mumbai, as well as actor Disha Patani's family home in northern India. Actor Ranveer Singh also reportedly received an extortion demand of nearly $1.1 million (around €980,000).

The attacks have spread to the other side of the globe, with a cafe owned by comedian Kapil Sharma in Surrey, Canada, also hit three times.

For an industry that once lived in the shadow of organized crime, the attacks have revived old fears, harking back to the crime bosses of the 1990s. But experts say the threat facing Bollywood today looks very different from the one it faced three decades ago.

When the underworld ruled Bollywood

In the 1990s, Mumbai's underworld was deeply entangled with the Hindi film industry.

"The mafia was always fascinated with the movie industry," said S. Hussain Zaidi, crime journalist and author of "Dongri to Dubai: Six Decades of the Mumbai Mafia," who has covered organized crime in the city for over three decades.

Gangsters like Dawood Ibrahim, Abu Salem and Chhota Shakeel "were totally obsessed" with Bollywood, he told DW, much like mafiosi who sought a foothold in Hollywood.

During his era, Dawood Ibrahim has been one of the most wanted men in India Image: AP Photo/picture alliance

To the gangsters, films offered glitz and glamor, but also a way to launder their profits. They invested in films "so that they could control the industry and have a legitimate way of making money," Zaidi added.

When producers didn't cooperate, the consequences could be fatal. In 1997, music mogul Gulshan Kumar, founder of the label T-Series, was shot dead. In 2000, filmmaker Rakesh Roshan, father of Bollywood star Hrithik Roshan, was shot and wounded.

Mumbai's streets were "made red with blood" in 1998, Zaidi said, describing the year as the pinnacle of gang killings.

D. Sivanandhan, the former Police Commissioner of Mumbai, who led the crackdown, says 101 businessmen were shot dead in 1998 alone, or one "every third day," mostly over unpaid extortion demands.

Police efforts were reinforced by a tough new organized crime law passed in 1999, which Sivanandhan calls the "ultimate weapon." Security forces used electronic surveillance and preventive detention, and seized some 2,500 illegal weapons.

"A few encounters also happened, but that is not a policy nor a strategy,” he told DW, referring to police shootouts.

By the early 2000s, the gangs' hold had been broken, and a new Mumbai seemed to be emerging.

A gang run from a prison cell

The man believed to be behind the latest wave of attacks is not from Mumbai.

Lawrence Bishnoi was a student politician in the northern city of Chandigarh before gaining notoriety as a gangster Image: Sameer Sehgal/Hindustan Times/IMAGO

Bishnoi, 33, comes from a landowning family in the northern state of Punjab and was studying in Chandigarh when he was drawn into violent student politics. Then, he was arrested, incarcerated and eventually turned to crime, says journalist Jupinderjit Singh, author of "Gangs of Punjab."

"He was introduced to the University of Crime through the jail," Singh told DW.

Bishnoi went on to build what Singh describes as one of the first criminal syndicates spanning several northern Indian states. Investigators say he still directs operations from prison using concealed phones and messaging apps.

Currently, Bishnoi is held in a jail in Prime Minister Narendra Modi's home state of Gujarat.

His network stretches beyond India's borders. In September 2025, Canada designated the Bishnoi gang a terrorist entity. Last month, the FBI added Satinderjeet Singh, popularly known as Goldy Brar, to its Ten Most Wanted list, offering up to $1 million for information leading to his arrest. US prosecutors described him as the alleged leader of Bishnoi's group in North America.

While Bishnoi comes from an affluent landowning family, his shooters are mostly poor. The gang usually recruits them online.

"There are so many youngsters who want to do something… they are just pulled by the lore attached to Lawrence Bishnoi," Singh explained. "Recruiting is no big issue… They offer money, protection, weapons."

Why target film stars?

For Bishnoi, it seems personal.

In 1998, Salman Khan was accused of killing a blackbuck, an antelope revered by Bishnoi's community. Bishnoi vowed revenge, and many of the attacks targeted people close to the actor, including the 2024 killing of politician Baba Siddique, which police have linked to the gang.

Singh sees the feud as a bid for respectability. Criminals "always try to find something that makes them a moral guardian," he says, and this case was Bishnoi's "chance to redeem himself."

Salman Khan was granted bail in 2018 as he appealed a conviction for killing two rare antelopes Image: AFP

But money and intimidation matter too.

"Bollywood has a lot of money," Singh added, pointing that the previous generation of gangsters was no longer in position to take advantage.

"With Dawood Ibrahim and his counterparts away, there was a vacuum, and Lawrence Bishnoi is trying to exploit that."

Sivanandhan explained the old Mumbai gangs ran a whole "basket" of illegal businesses, from smuggling to protection rackets and cricket match-fixing. Their members were "local boys," while the Bishnoi gang has “nothing to do with Mumbai,” he added. It targets Bollywood because the industry is "loaded with money" and a "soft underbelly."

"They are using Bollywood as an ATM," he told DW. "Insert a card and collect your money."

Meanwhile, Zaidi sees the attacks mainly as publicity. "It's a way to grab headlines," he told DW. Within hours of the recent attack on Shroff, someone claimed on social media that he was targeted for being close to Khan, a logic Zaidi called "absolutely illogical and absurd."

But publicity is useful to gangs that live off extortion. "The base material of extortion is: create fear," a security professional responsible for the protection of several Bollywood stars, who asked not to be named because of the sensitivity of the issue, told DW.

Is Bollywood under siege?

Still, experts say its hard to argue that the ongoing violence is comparable to the 1990s crime wave.

"I won't say resurgence, because that would be a bit of an exaggeration," Zaidi said. In the 1990s, several rival gangs fought for control of Mumbai. Today, other than Bishnoi's faction, other gangs are not considered active in Mumbai.

The film industry is also not paying up the way it once did, because the shift to digital payments has made large cash transactions hard to hide, he added.

India's banned film 'Satluj' finds new audiences To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Sivanandhan disagrees. The shootings at walls and gates, followed by quick claims on social media, are "all aimed at collecting… extortion money," he said. In his view, "cash-rich Bollywood would be coughing up so much, which is enough to run an army of people."

At any case, the fear remains real.

And even if violence is not as prevalent, hundreds of thousands of people rely on the Mumbai film industry for their livelihoods.

"If the fear of the underworld continues, leading names may be forced to leave Mumbai," the All Indian Cine Workers Association (AICWA) President Suresh Shyamlal Gupta wrote to Home Minister Amit Shah.

"Mumbai will not be allowed to go back to the underworld days of the 1990s, and Bollywood will not be allowed to work in the shadow of fear," Gupta wrote.

With security forces seemingly on the back foot, gangsters are likely to continue their campaign.

Several Bollywood stars have already stepped up their security.

Edited by: Darko Janjevic

World.title: Bayern Munich's Kenya friendly highlights Africa's growing pull for global sport
World.content:
Bayern Munich are to open Nairobi's new Raila Odinga International Stadium against Ajax as Kenya prepares for AFCON 2027. The match highlights Africa's growing sports ambitions — and questions over cost and legacy.

Bundesliga champions Bayern Munich are to travel to Nairobi, Kenya during the winter break to play a friendly that opens the newly finished Raila Odinga International Stadium in the capital city. The German side will face Ajax Amsterdam as the game acts as part of the country's preparations for the 2027 African Cup of Nations (AFCON), which will be held in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania next summer.

"Bayern has millions of fantastic fans in Africa with whom we feel a close connection – it's a continent with a huge passion for football," Rouven Kasper, Bayern board member for marketing and sales, said in a club statement.

"We will be making a further contribution to raising the profile of the Bundesliga and are very much looking forward to this special event."

Why are global sports rushing to invest in Africa?

The news is just the latest venture into global sports investing in Africa. Earlier this month, Formula 1 announced it was returning to the continent after Rwanda secured the rights for a deal from the early 2030s onwards. In September, World Athletics revealed Nairobi would host the World Championships in 2029. It will be the first time the event has been held in Africa.

Simon Chadwick, a business management and program director at the African School of Economics, believes that over the last two decades the professionalization and industrialization of sports has begun to emerge in Africa.

"Countries like Rwanda, Kenya, Morocco and obviously, South Africa, if we go back to the last decade of the previous century, have increasingly begun to deploy sport as a policy instrument," Chadwick told DW, adding Senegal and Egypt to the list.

"There are these image and reputational benefits which very often are bundled up as soft power. It's about attractiveness and appeal and engagement," said Chadwick.

"It's almost like a kind of professionalization, industrialization and politicization of sport that we're seeing elsewhere in the world has now arrived in Africa. We are seeing a much greater sense of kind of self-determination within Africa to do this," he added.

"This is not just about sport. It is also about diplomacy and bilateral trade, but also about the broader economic and industrial context within which sport sits."

Football has boomed in Morocco, as the development of stadiums like the Prince Moulay Abdellah stadium prove. Image: Emre Asikci/Anadolu/picture alliance

A coup for Kenya sport, but at what cost?

For Kenya specifically, the building of the stadium is in line with the housing and sports infrastructural development that has been so heavily promoted under President William Ruto. Hosting this game is a symbol of the development currently happening in Nairobi.

"The bigger picture is that Nairobi now is positioning itself as a as an alternative sports venue," Richard Wanjohi, Editorial and Research Lead at the African Sports and Creative Institute (ASCI), told DW.

"I think we have seen what Kigali has done over the last number of years. For us to then come back into this conversation as a major city that can host such an event, it's huge. A few weeks later, we'll have the rugby sevens series again and then ultimately, the Africa Cup of Nations in July."

Marathon G.O.A.T Eliud Kipchoge To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Chadwick believes that unlike Rwanda, Kenya's relative stability and pre-existing tourist industry allows for a more natural development of sports investment.

"This is not Kenya trying to build a tourism industry through an engagement in sport. I think it's an extension of what Kenya has been doing for a number of years through sport."

Combined with being a multi-sport country - athletics, rugby, football, volleyball – Wanjohi believes Kenya is ready to make the most of that performance on the field or track.

"It's about time that we also host the world and show them that we can do this from a hosting perspective, but also from developing infrastructure that is ready to host such sports events," Wanjohi said.

"It's beyond just saying that we have the talent that is already in the sport, but it's saying that we have the infrastructure, we have the skills, we have the capability to host this as any other African, if not global nation."

William Ruto (right) is a huge sports fan, in particular football, making his investment into a brand new stadium in Nairobi not very surprising Image: Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images/AFP

Sporting development not free of criticism

However, Ruto's government has been criticized over taxation, unemployment and its handling of dissent. Given that this stadium cost approximately €375 million ($418 million), it is perhaps no surprise that questions are being asked about the decision to invest in major sports infrastructure.

"People are asking, we are a struggling economy. There are a lot of other issues that could be addressed, like the education sector, health and all that. How did we get that money and be able to make that provision? Also interestingly, is that there's an appearance fee that is going to be paid to both Bayern and Ajax," said Wanjohi, who added there was also some frustration that the opening game was not given to local teams or even the national side.

Ultimately, the timing of this also matters. While many sports fans in the country are excited, others are critical.

"The government knows that this is almost like a campaign tool. We have an election coming up in August next year so the government or the president of the day obviously wants to use as much leverage of such an event to milk it for all it's worth," Wanjohi added.

"So the two different schools of thought are: It's a good thing to have, but at what cost are we doing it at and is it in the public interest as well?"

The proof will be in what the legacy of events like Bayern Munich's friendly in Nairobi brings Kenyan football. The feeling in late 2026 though, is largely optimistic.

"I guess the acid test is that many African nations carry with them the baggage from the past that this is just trophy asset investment that is ultimately going to create white, white elephant infrastructure," Chadwick said.

"But having spoken to people in Kenyan sport, in the industry itself, it seems to me that there is a genuine appetite for sports to become a genuine and legitimate driver of economic activity."

Janek Speight contributed reporting for this article.

Edited by: Chuck Penfold

World.title: Italy: Students and workers rally over living costs
World.content:
Students and workers have marched across Italy for more school funding and relief from rising living costs. The rallies follow weeks of school occupations and protests against higher military spending.

Tens of thousands of students and workers marched across Italy on Friday, demanding more education funding and relief from rising living costs.

The rallies followed weeks of student tent camps and school occupations, with a general strike bringing workers into the streets alongside them.

Demonstrations took place in dozens of cities, including Rome, Milan, Turin, Bologna, Genoa and Naples. Police were deployed in large numbers after earlier protests descended into rioting.

Why were students and workers protesting?

Demonstrators criticized Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's right-wing government over low wages, rising fuel prices and military spending. Students demanded more money for schools and universities.

In Rome, university student Beatrice Chilelli said students were "at a breaking point."

"They can't afford to pay exorbitant tuition fees, and rent... which weighs heavily on their parents' shoulders," the 21-year-old told AFP.

Like their French counterparts, students in Italy have been protesting for weeks Image: Marco Bertorello/AFP

The USB trade union called a general strike, with truck drivers, taxi drivers and farmers among those joining the protests. Disruption to public transport remained limited on Friday morning.

Thousands marched from Rome's Termini station past the Colosseum, accompanied by two tractors and a taxi. "We need more houses, not bombs!" one group chanted.

Did the protests turn violent?

Minor scuffles broke out between demonstrators and riot police in Turin at the start of the march. No major clashes had been reported by midday.

In Milan, the procession headed away from the city center, where rioters looted shops, damaged property and clashed with police after a cost-of-living demonstration two weeks earlier.

Authorities also increased protection around landmarks, including Rome's Colosseum and Milan's cathedral.

The student protests have drawn momentum from similar movements in France and Spain. Teachers, retirees and other workers also joined Friday's rallies.

France protests continue despite police crackdown To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: Binance crypto exchange suspends trades over North Korea-linked hack
World.content:
Crypto platform Binance has suspended trading following a suspected hack now linked to North Korea. The disruption has left users unable to trade on the cryptocurrency platform while the suspected breach is investigated.

Blockchain analysts said a North Korean hacking unit was likely behind the theft of more than $6 billion from Binance, the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.

Binance temporarily suspended deposits and withdrawals for security checks and said about $3 billion in affected assets had been frozen.

US-based blockchain intelligence firm TRM attributed the attack to TraderTraitor, which it described as an elite North Korean hacking unit.

"We make this judgment with high confidence," TRM said in a report published Thursday.

Why do analysts suspect North Korea?

TRM said attackers moved approximately $6.36 billion out of Binance wallets across 10 blockchains, most of it within about 20 minutes. It described the incident as the largest cryptocurrency theft on record.

"Several features of this attack match earlier North Korea-linked heists, including the Bybit hack," the firm said.

Bybit lost $1.5 billion in a hack in February 2025. The FBI attributed that attack to North Korea and TraderTraitor.

Jonathan Levin, co-founder and CEO of blockchain analysis company Chainalysis, also said the Binance attack was likely carried out by TraderTraitor.

How to avoid crypto losses To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Experts say North Korea uses cryptocurrency theft and other illicit cyber activities to obtain foreign currency and help fund its nuclear program despite international sanctions.

What has Binance said about the hack?

Binance did not confirm the attribution to North Korea, saying it was "working closely with our law enforcement partners to confirm the identity of the criminals and bring them to justice."

Binance said it worked to secure the affected assets and that it had located and frozen about $3 billion (€2.7 billion) so far. It did not provide information about the remaining $3.3 billion.

"Binance will cover all hacking losses," co-founder Yi He said, without providing more details about the incident.

"Rest assured that user funds are completely safe," a company spokesperson said.

Binance said its initial investigation suggested an attacker had compromised a software infrastructure engineer's laptop, gaining access to an internal service and submitting unauthorized withdrawals. The company said it had found no evidence that wallet private keys had leaked.

Money, power, influence: The Trump family's business empire To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Tether froze around $1.6 billion in its USDT currency, according to CEO Paolo Ardoino, and Circle froze some $800 million-worth of USDC, boss Jeremy Allaire said.

The news of the possible hack sent Bitcoin's value tumbling by 3.2% on Thursday evening, dropping below $79,000.

Who is Binance ex-CEO Zhao?

Zhao, who founded the Binance platform in 2017, said "as a shareholder, I expect all user funds will be fully covered."

He stepped down as CEO after pleading guilty in 2023. to failing to prevent money laundering on his platform. US President Donald Trump pardoned him in 2025.

Zhao and Binance have been key supporters of cryptocurrency ventures by US President Donald Trump and his family.

Edited by Sean Sinico and Karl Sexton

World.title: Germany takes cautious approach on Israeli election results
World.content:
German politicians have been slow to respond as they wait to see who is likely to comprise the next coalition. Many are also hoping for a government without religious hardliners.

Though it has been two days since Israel's parliamentary elections, German politicians are still being cautious to respond, as it is still unclear who will lead Israel's new government.

Although the right-wing bloc, including religious hardliners, led by incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is ahead of the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, neither has a clear path to a governing majority in the Knesset.

Forming a coalition government is likely to be extremely difficult.

Martin Giese, spokesperson for German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, declined to comment at Wednesday's regular government press conference in Berlin.

But he did stress that Germany has been in contact with numerous officials and politicians in Israel via Germany's ambassador. "The Jewish state and Germany are inextricably linked by our history, and we will do everything we can to work well with any future government," Wadephul said.

No clear winner emerges in Israel's election To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Alabali Radovan: 'Winter in Gaza will be difficult'

One concern for the German government is providing aid to the people in Gaza, and protracted coalition negotiations could delay necessary progress.

"Winter is coming, and it will be difficult," Development Minister Reem Alabali Radovan, currently visiting Lebanon, warned in an interview with Politico. She underlined that there must be more opportunities for aid organizations to provide crucial assistance in Gaza and that it cannot wait for coalition negotiations.

In interviews with DW and broadcaster RTL, she spoke about the recent increase in attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians in the occupied West Bank and East Jerusalem.

"The radical settler violence must be stopped. The Netanyahu government remains in office on an interim basis, and this means that this situation must still be brought to an end," she said.

All settlement activity in the occupied Palestinian territories is considered illegal under international law.

More distanced from Netanyahu's government

Relations between Germany and Israel are traditionally close, in part because of Germany's historical responsibility for Nazi Germany's murder of millions of Jews during the Holocaust.

Recently, however, the German government has distanced itself from Netanyahu's policies, at least in its public rhetoric.

Most recently, Wadephul said after a major Israeli military operation near the city of Hebron: "Under international law, Israel is quite clearly obligated to uphold and protect the rights of Palestinians as well." Around 3,000 Palestinians were driven from their homes during the operation, which followed the reported killing of two Israeli soldiers by Palestinians.

In Berlin, there has long been speculation about whether Germany's policy toward Israel might change after Israel's 2026 election.

So far, one thing is clear: Unlike numerous other countries, including some in Europe, Germany does not intend to recognize a Palestinian state for the time being.

Could Arab voters hold the key in Israel's election? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

CDU hoping for a centrist government

At the same time, Germany hopes that the future government will no longer include religious extremists, and in some cases far-right, politicians such as the current Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.

"I think it would be best for Israel to form a government that is closer to the center of the political spectrum," Jürgen Hardt, foreign policy expert for the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in the Bundestag, told DW. "Of course, that's something the people, and above all the elected politicians, will have to figure out. But it's encouraging that so many people participated in the election."
