The Left, a junior partner in Poland’s ruling coalition, has proposed a bill to abolish the Church Fund, which provides state subsidies for the health insurance contributions of clergy. It says it is frustrated by delays in fulfilling a pledge made by most parties in the wide ruling coalition to reform the fund. However, another coalition partner, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), says that it will oppose the bill, calling instead for a system allowing taxpayers to allocate part of their taxes to religious institutions of their choice. Senior church figures also say they have not been consulted. 📣 Lewica składa ustawę likwidującą Fundusz Kościelny. Czas na realizację umowy koalicyjnej w zakresie świeckiego państwa‼️ Co zakłada nasz projekt? ⬇️ ✅ Składki na duchownych przestają być w 80 procentach finansowane z budżetu państwa jak dotychczas. 50% składek pokrywać… pic.twitter.com/syqUMdCugr — Lewica (@__Lewica) October 29, 2026 The Church Fund, originally established in 1950 to compensate religious communities for property seized by the communist authorities, provides state subsidies for the health insurance contributions of clergy, for religious organisations’ charitable activities, and for the renovation of religious buildings. It now supports all legally recognised religious denominations in Poland, including those that did not lose property at the time. Last year, the state spent 275.7 million zloty on the Church Fund. This year it has budgeted 272.6 million zloty. Most of this money is then used to cover 80% of clergy members’ social security contributions. Under the bill proposed by The Left, churches would pay half of the contributions, with clergy covering the other half. For regular workers, such contributions are funded jointly by employees and their employers, Anna Maria Żukowska, the head of The Left’s parliamentary caucus, pointed out, as quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We are introducing the same arrangement for priests and members of the clergy.” At least 17.5bn zloty in state funds went to religious bodies from 2021-23, with over 95% going to Catholic organisations, the state auditor has found. In response, the speaker of parliament has proposed measures to reduce and better oversee such spending https://t.co/IN3dpY4La2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 16, 2025 An exception is made in the bill for members of enclosed religious orders and missionaries, who would have their contributions paid in full by their churches. The cost of maintaining historic churches would be covered by the National Fund for the Protection of Monuments, Żukowska explained. Włodzimierz Czarzasty, who is the leader of The Left as well as the speaker of the Sejm, the more powerful chamber in the Polish parliament, said the party did not oppose religion but wanted clergy to be treated equally under the law. “I would like to remind my coalition partners: our coalition agreement includes a commitment to work toward establishing the principles of a secular state in Poland,” he said, speaking alongside Żukowska. “Our patience is running out”. Ahead of the 2023 election, both the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk and The Left pledged to abolish the Church Fund, while the centre-right Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) proposed replacing state funding with voluntary taxpayer contributions. PSL had no equivalent formal party-wide pledge. In 2024, after the coalition came to power, Tusk announced plans to reform the fund and appointed a government working group led by the PSL leader and deputy prime minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz. The group’s work has since stalled. Kosiniak-Kamysz yesterday dismissed The Left’s proposal, saying it has “not the slightest chance of support in parliament”. His party, the second largest in the coalition with 32 of 239 MPs, sees the existing fund as an inexpensive form of compensation and will oppose abolishing it, he vowed. Instead, taxpayers should be able to allocate part of their taxes to a religious institution of their choice, a system used in several European countries, to “let the Polish people themselves decide whether or not they want to contribute,” he said, quoted by broadcaster Polsat News. Interior minister Marcin Kierwiński, a member of Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO), said that he supported reform, but criticised The Left for submitting the bill without consulting its coalition partners. A long-term decline in trust in the Catholic church in Poland has accelerated over the last year, with only 35% of Poles now saying they trust the church. Meanwhile, the armed forces now enjoy record-high trust of 94% https://t.co/ErCBE4HwWR — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 17, 2025 Religious communities also criticised the proposal for not having been discussed with them in advance. In a press statement sent to PAP, the Polish Episcopal Conference (KEP), the main organ of the Catholic church in Poland, said any solution should comply with the country’s agreement with the Vatican, as well as the constitutional principle that relations between the state and religious communities be regulated by mutual agreement. Bishop Jerzy Samiec, head of the Evangelical-Augsburg Church in Poland, the country’s biggest Protestant body, pointed to the significant costs churches face in maintaining their properties, including care homes and other facilities. The Catholic Church, Poland’s dominant religious institution, has seen a long-term decline in public trust, with only 35% of Poles saying they trusted it in 2025. That has coincided with a series of crises in recent years, in particular over revelations of child sexual abuse by members of the clergy and negligence in dealing with them by the church hierarchy. A variety of surveys, including from the church itself, show that religious attendance and identification have been declining in Poland in recent years. A growing number of Poles are turning away from the Catholic church, but not from religious belief itself. This creates challenges for the church, but also for Polish identity, which has historically been linked to Catholicism, writes Katarzyna Skiba https://t.co/udWGzd0X7F — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 18, 2023 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Polish opposition leader sparks controversy with speech on potential EU exit talks
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Jarosław Kaczyński, the leader of Poland’s largest opposition party, has sparked controversy by appearing to suggest that Poland and some other allied European Union member states could launch the process of leaving the EU if they fail in efforts to reform it. His remarks were condemned by Prime Minister Donald Tusk and other figures from the pro-EU ruling coalition, who have long accused Kaczyński and his national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party of seeking “Polexit” from the EU. However, Kaczyński responded by accusing Tusk of misrepresenting his words, insisting that he wants Poland to reform the EU rather than leave it. Kaczyński pomylił Krynicę z Kremlem. pic.twitter.com/tX0G04krze — Cezary Tomczyk (@CTomczyk) October 29, 2026 The comments in question came in an hour-long speech by Kaczyński at the Krynica Forum, an annual conference bringing together leaders from politics, business and civil society, which he used to outline his vision for sweeping reforms of the EU. Repeating his longstanding criticism of Brussels, Kaczyński warned that there had been a “consistent drive to transform the EU into a centralised state” with too much power over national governments. He also called the European Parliament in its current form a “parody”. But soon, said Kaczyński, “a window of opportunity” for reform may appear because “completely different governments could emerge” in Poland, France and Spain, all of which will hold elections within the year. PiS has previously enjoyed close relations with Marine Le Pen’s far-right National Rally (RN) party in France and the nationalist Vox party of Santiago Abascal in Spain. The EU is preparing a "German plan" that would "annihilate the Polish state", said Kaczyński as Poland marks Independence Day. He warned that the incoming opposition government will "strive to implement this plan" and called on Poles to "fight" against it https://t.co/QDbxmiaazJ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 11, 2023 Kaczyński suggested that Poland, if led by PiS, could work with other like-minded EU governments to push for reform of the bloc by influencing public opinion, identifying breaches of EU treaties, creating a blocking minority in the European Council, and trying to change the EU’s treaties. However, the PiS leader then warned that, “if [those] approaches fail to yield results, the states that want change could conclude a new treaty with the elements we are seeking, but with a delayed entry into force”. Kaczyński then noted that the EU treaties “include provisions specifying the terms under which a state may withdraw from the EU. This all begins with negotiations. And simply begin these negotiations”. “It is a tough approach, a risky one, but the situation is so dire that it is worth employing such a method if all others fail to yield results,” he added. The remarks immediately prompted condemnation from figures in Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right. They accused Kaczyński of effectively calling for Polexit – something they have long claimed he wants, even though PiS has not explicitly called for it before. “Jarosław Kaczyński has just announced that Poland should begin negotiations on the terms of its withdrawal from the EU,” wrote Tusk himself on X. “This is, among other things, what the current struggle in Poland is about – a tough struggle. I do not intend to lose it.” “So they do want Polexit after all,” wrote foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. “Customs borders with Germany, the Czech Republic, Slovakia and Lithuania…An end to subsidies for farmers and investments…And they swore on their lives that they’d never do that.” In a video published later on Thursday, Tusk declared that next year’s parliamentary elections would help decide “whether Poland remains in the European Union or leaves it”. Jarosław Kaczyński ogłosił właśnie, że Polska powinna zacząć rokowania o warunkach wyjścia z Unii Europejskiej. O taką między innymi stawkę toczy się dziś w Polsce walka. Twarda walka. Nie zamierzam jej przegrać, nawet jeśli nie wszyscy zagrają ze mną. — Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 29, 2026 Kaczyński responded by saying that “Tusk is lying as usual”. He emphasised that he believes “the EU is needed but it requires thorough reform” so that it “benefits not the elites, but ordinary citizens”. PiS deputy leader Przemysław Czarnek said on Thursday that his party was “considering all scenarios, including the possibility that the EU will kill itself”. However, he added that the priority remained reforming the bloc and “PiS has no plans to leave the EU”, reports the Polish Press Agency (PAP). When PiS was in power from 2015 to 2023, it regularly clashed with Brussels over a variety of issues, including judicial reform, trade, climate policy, and migration. Since Tusk, a former president of the European Council, took power in 2023, his government has greatly improved relations with Brussels. Tusk jak zwykle kłamie. Najwyraźniej wychodzi z założenia, że dzień bez kłamstwa jest dniem straconym… Unia Europejska jest potrzebna, ale wymaga gruntownej reformy. Kryzys i zapaść w jej obecnym kształcie to efekt rządów Merkel i jednego z jej pomocników, Tuska. Nie ma co się… — Jarosław Kaczyński (@OficjalnyJK) October 29, 2026 Poland has been the largest net recipient of EU funding since joining the bloc in 2004. A study published earlier this year found that the country’s economy is 42% larger than it would have been had Poland not been part of the EU. Opinion polls consistently show a large majority of Poles in favour of remaining part of the EU. However, recent years have seen an uptick in support for Polexit, as well as for anti-EU far-right parties. PiS has increasingly found itself competing against such parties for votes. Regular polling by state research agency CBOS shows that, while opposition to EU membership fell to a record low of 5% in 2022, it has subsequently risen and stood at 14% in the most recent survey. World.title: Polish bishop convicted for failing to promptly report child sex abuse allegations
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. In the first ruling of its kind in Poland, a Catholic bishop has been found guilty of failing to promptly inform the law enforcement authorities about allegations of child sex abuse committed by priests under his authority. Andrzej Jeż, the bishop of Tarnów, was handed a non-custodial sentence that will require him to donate 25% of his earnings for two years to a charity that supports victims of child sexual abuse. However, the verdict can still be appealed, and the diocese of Tarnów has already announced that it “disagrees with the court’s ruling” and that an appeal will be filed. Pierwszy taki wyrok w Polsce. Biskup skazany za zwlekanie z powiadomieniem prokuratury o pedofilach w sutannach Ordynariusz tarnowski bp Andrzej Jeż jest pierwszym biskupem oskarżonym o zbyt późne powiadomienie prokuratury o pedofilii w Kościele. I pierwszym, który który został… — Bartosz T. Wieliński 🇵🇱🇪🇺🇺🇦🇬🇱 (@Bart_Wielinski) October 29, 2026 The case relates to alleged abuse by two priests who worked under Jeż’s authority. They can be identified only as Stanisław P. and Tomasz K. under Polish privacy law. In 2022, prosecutors discontinued an investigation into allegations against Stanisław P. because the statute of limitations had expired, despite concluding that he had harmed at least 95 children and committed “sexual acts” against 77 of them over several decades in parishes in Poland and Ukraine. In 2023, prosecutors decided to charge Tomasz K., who allegedly sexually abused children as early as 2018. However, they have been unable to formally present the charges to him because of his poor health, news website OKO.press reported earlier this year. Though Jeż was not accused of complicity in the alleged abuse itself, he was charged under a 2017 law making it a criminal offence not to “immediately notify the authorities” of “credible information” about sexual abuse of minors. The offence is punishable by up to three years in prison. Investigators say that, although an internal church probe into Stanisław P. was initiated in the 2000s and a decision to remove him from the clergy was made in 2013, Jeż only notified the prosecutor’s office in 2020. In the case of Tomasz K., the bishop notified prosecutors only in 2021. In court, prosecutor Marcin Stępień said that Jeż’s failure to report the abuse promptly had allowed the statute of limitations to expire in the case of some of Stanisław P.’s victims. Stępień also noted that the bishop had only come forward with the information when media coverage brought the allegations against Stanisław P. to light, reports broadcaster TVN. A church commission set up to investigate child sex abuse in a Catholic diocese in Poland has identified at least 50 victims and 29 abusers. It also found that bishops repeatedly failed to take action when credible reports of abuse were submitted to them https://t.co/MRNl5vWp4E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 13, 2026 Prosecutors sought a 10-month prison sentence, suspended for three years, and a fine of 20,000 zloty (€4,550). Jeż, however, denied the allegations against him and sought an acquittal. He argued that he had reported the alleged abuse to the authorities as soon as there was credible information. On Thursday, the court found the bishop guilty, giving him a sentence known as “restriction of liberty” (ograniczenie wolnośći), under which a convict is not imprisoned but required to do some kind of social good. In Jeż’s case, the court ordered that 25% of his salary for two years be donated to the Empowering Children Foundation (Dajemy Dzieciom Siłę), which supports victims of child abuse. He was additionally ordered to pay 20,000 zloty to the Fund for Assistance to Victims and Post-Penitentiary Assistance. In a statement after the verdict was issued, the diocese of Tarnów said that it “disagreed with the court’s ruling” and that, after a written justification from the court was reviewed, “an appeal will be filed”. The Catholic church in Poland has in recent years been hit by a series of revelations regarding historical abuse of minors by members of the clergy and allegations that bishops covered cases up. The Vatican has taken action against a number of Polish bishops over the issue. Most recently, in 2024, the Vatican announced the resignation of the bishop of Łowicz, Andrzej Dziuba, due to his “negligence in handling cases of sexual abuse against minors”. In February, a commission created by the diocese of Sosnowiec following a series of scandals announced that it had identified at least 50 children who were harmed and 29 people suspected of abusing minors, most of them members of the clergy. World.title: Turkish engineer creates live 3D pixel map of adopted hometown Warsaw
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A Turkish software engineer has, with the help of AI and vast quantities of Polish public data, created a precise digital replica of Warsaw, the city where he lives. The map, which can be explored for free online, features almost 200,000 buildings, moving trams that match their real-life schedules, changing light and weather conditions, and over 45,000 accurately placed streetlamps that turn on at night. It is even possible to fly a virtual plane through the city. The person behind the project, Bedirhan Yildirim, was inspired by recent efforts to produce similar maps of New York and London. While he initially considered producing one of Istanbul, his hometown, he decided instead to pick the city he lives in, Warsaw. “It is smaller, mostly flat, and I walk its streets every day,” he explained of his choice. Yildirim then used AI coding agents to create the map through a process of trial and error, constantly tweaking and improving the model. The initial version took only two days to produce and was launched on 22 October, but it has been regularly improved since then based on feedback from users. The work was made possible by what Yildirim says is the “incredible amount of data” Poland’s national mapping office, GUGiK, provides for free, including 3D building models, terrain scans, and even details of almost 2 million trees. Further information, including on parks, streetlamps, and traffic lights, was taken from OpenStreetMap, a freely licensed database. Meanwhile, timetables from Warsaw’s public transport authority, ZTM, and Poland’s national rail operator, PKP, allowed the map to feature accurately timed trams and trains. Current weather conditions are input from Open-Meteo, an open-source meteorological service. But users can also choose to manually adjust the time of day or year, with light and weather changing accordingly. An observation deck at the top of the EU's tallest building, Varso Tower in Warsaw, has opened to the public. Located 230m up on the tower's 53rd floor, the attraction offers a 360° panorama of Poland's capital.https://t.co/VeEapOmh4s — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 9, 2025 The result is an incredible level of explorable detail, from major landmarks, such as the communist-era Palace of Culture and Science and Varso Tower, the EU’s tallest building, down to the seating steps and bars along the Vistula River boulevards. The map also features graveyards reflecting Warsaw and Poland’s diverse past, including Catholic, Eastern Orthodox, Jewish and Tatar Muslim graves. Around 1 November, when Poles visit cemeteries around All Saints’ Day, candles glow around the graves. A final touch Yildirim has added is a flight simulator, allowing users to travel over the city – and complete missions – in a Cessna aeroplane, an air ambulance, a flying car, or even a UFO that takes off from the Copernicus Science Centre and travels to the National Stadium. I turned Warsaw into a flight sim 🛩️ Take off from Chopin, fly through the ring over the Palace of Culture, then land a UFO inside Stadion Narodowy as the roof opens 🛸 Desktop only for now. Can you land it? 👇 pic.twitter.com/DT2fdk1Vem — Bedirhan (@bedcodes) October 27, 2026 Speaking to Notes from Poland, Yildirim says that he moved to Poland in 2022 to pursue a job in IT before starting his own business. Initially living in Kraków, the country’s second-largest city, he then moved to Warsaw in 2025. Asked what his own personal favourite places in the city are, Yildirim points to Warsaw’s parks, such as Skaryszewski, Pole Mokotowskie and Łazienki. His favourite neighbourhood is Saska Kępa on the right bank of the Vistula. The software engineer adds that his project is an example of how AI can be an “amazing tool to do 90% of the job very quickly”. The remaining 10% of human input “is what keeps it from being ‘AI slop'”. Yildirim says that, without the use of AI, the map of Warsaw he created would have needed an entire team to build over a period of months. World.title: Poland detains Ukrainian accused of arson attack in Romania on behalf of Russia
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has detained a Ukrainian citizen who is wanted by Romania on suspicion of involvement in an arson attack on a defence company carried out on behalf of Russia. On Tuesday, the Polish police’s Central Investigation Bureau (CBŚP) announced that anti-terrorism officers had detained the man, who can be named only as Artem S. under Polish privacy law, in Warsaw under a European Arrest Warrant issued by Romania. In the early hours of 14 September, a fire broke out in the city of Brașov, Romania, in the immediate vicinity of premises belonging to Carfil, a manufacturer of military equipment. Carfil is a subsidiary of ROMARM, a state-owned defence company. On Monday this week, the Romanian Intelligence Service (SRI) said it had determined that the fire had been deliberately caused by a “sabotage network coordinated from Russia”. It added that “several citizens of former Soviet states who reside in the EU” had been involved in the arson attack. The SRI also revealed that the group’s activities were not limited to Romania. “Its coordinators in Russia had assigned it a wide range of targets across the region, including state-owned and private arms manufacturing facilities, as well as sites of military and industrial interest.” In a separate statement, Romania’s Directorate for Investigating Organised Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT) confirmed that the suspects were a Ukrainian, who was at large in Poland, and two Belarusians, who had already been detained in Germany, where they “had been preparing to commit similar acts”. Polish broadcaster RMF reports, based on sources, that Artem S.’s role in the Brașov attack was to identify a target and to arrange payment for those involved. A Polish court will now decide whether the 25-year-old should be extradited to Romania. Poland itself has been a primary target for Russia’s campaign of sabotage and other so-called “hybrid actions” in Europe. Many of those detained and convicted have been Ukrainian and Belarusians, though some Polish citizens have also been implicated. Poland is the "primary focus" of Russia's sabotage campaign in Europe, finds a new report by the International Centre for Counter-Terrorism. Among 151 incidents identified since 2022, 31 of them took place in Poland – more than in any other country https://t.co/QXfSI00FD6 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 3, 2026 In some cases, such operatives are amateurs – so-called “disposable agents” – recruited, coordinated and paid through messaging service Telegram. Some have also been pre-existing criminal groups hired by Russia to carry out such tasks. In August, a drone production plant belonging to private Polish arms company WB Electronics was targeted in an arson attack that Poland has blamed on Russia. The following month, a ground station in Poland used by Starlink, Elon Musk’s satellite internet company, was likewise hit by an arson attack that Poland blamed on Russia. Two Turkish men were later detained in Germany on suspicion of carrying out the attack. World.title: Poland and UK sign Warsaw Defence Plan to “deter Russian threats”
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland and the United Kingdom have signed the Warsaw Defence Plan, an agreement to enhance their cooperation on security. The aim, says the British Ministry of Defence, is to “deter Russian threats”. The plan, which follows on from the two countries signing a strategic defence partnership earlier this year, will include joint development and production of defence technologies and military exercises in the Baltic Sea. The UK and Poland share a deep and historical defence partnership. Today, Defence Secretary @WesStreeting signed the Warsaw Defence Plan to bring our two nations’ Armed Forces and industries closer together and help ensure collective security in Europe. 🇬🇧🤝🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/IP98D1Qs1L — Ministry of Defence 🇬🇧 (@DefenceHQ) October 27, 2026 “Poland is one of the UK’s closest allies – from flying together in the Battle of Britain, to breaking the Enigma code, they have been a vital partner for our defence for nearly a century,” said British defence secretary Wes Streeting on a visit to Warsaw. “The new Warsaw Defence Plan honours this cooperation and sets out how we will continue to work together today, building a stronger Europe in a stronger NATO,” he added. His Polish counterpart, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, declared that “the Polish-British alliance has never been as strong as it is now”. Both he and Streeting also emphasised the importance of working together to support Ukraine. Among the aims listed for the plan are collaboration in the development and manufacture of next-generation air-defence missiles, as well as drones and counter-drone technologies. Earlier this year, Poland and the UK, along with Germany, France and Italy, agreed to jointly develop and procure air-defence systems, including missiles and drones. The Warsaw Defence Plan also pledges to “increase defensive maritime activity in the Baltic Sea through exercises and regional coordination, helping British and Polish forces protect vital lines of communication in the sea”. The two countries will also seek to build upon existing cooperation between their defence industries, including Poland’s purchase of CAMM-ER surface-to-air missiles and 100 launchers from MBDA and last year’s strategic partnership on ammunition production between Poland’s PGZ and Britain’s BAE Systems. Poland and the UK have signed a major new defence and security treaty. The agreement includes plans to jointly develop a new air-defence missile, hold large-scale military exercises, and cooperate on countering Russian hybrid attacks https://t.co/cXeYT2u1lw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 27, 2026 This week’s agreement builds upon the Northolt Treaty signed by Poland and the UK in May this year, under which the two countries agreed to cooperate more closely on security. Last year, Poland signed a similar agreement upgrading relations with France. That followed a strategic partnership agreement with Sweden the previous year. In April this year, Poland signed new comprehensive strategic partnership agreements with South Korea and Japan. This year, it has also deepened security ties with Canada and Norway. In November, Poland will host the first military exercises organised by the so-called Coalition of the Willing. Thousands of personnel from the UK, Poland, France and Germany will test operational readiness for a multinational force to secure a potential future Ukraine peace deal. World.title: US chooses Poland to host service facility for Patriot missiles
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The United States has chosen Poland to host a new centre for servicing and maintaining missiles used in Patriot air defence systems, in a decision described as “historic” by both Washington and Warsaw. It was chosen ahead of bids from four other European countries. The new centre, the first of its kind ot be located outside the US itself, will “dramatically shorten turnaround times and further secure critical supply lines”, said the US Department of War, announcing the decision on Tuesday. Undersecretary of War Michael P. Duffey added that the choice of a country on NATO’s eastern front “sends a clear message [that] the Alliance is united, serious about deterrence, and ready to back our words with action”. Poland Selected to Host Historic PAC-3 Missile Maintenance Facility, Strengthening Allied Burden-Sharing and Transatlantic Security – U.S. Department of War – Release | @DeptofWar https://t.co/2caqADRRx8 — US Embassy Warsaw (@USEmbassyWarsaw) October 27, 2026 The decision was welcomed by Polish leaders, with defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz saying that it shows “Poland is a trusted ally and holds an extremely important place on the map of global security”. His deputy minister, Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, said that Poland was chosen ahead of rival bids from Germany, the Netherlands and Norway to host the facility. However, US ambassador to Poland Thomas Rose indicated that Sweden, not Norway, was the fourth candidate. Kosiniak-Kamysz and Sobkowiak-Czarnecka both pointed to the role President Karol Nawrocki had played in securing the deal. On many issues, the government is in conflict with the opposition-aligned president, but the two sides worked together on the Patriot bid. Historyczna decyzja! Centrum serwisowania pocisków PAC-3 do systemów Patriot powstanie w Polsce! 🇵🇱 O europejską lokalizację tej inwestycji rywalizowały cztery państwa, obok Polski – Niemcy, Holandia i Norwegia. Już na etapie składania wniosków polska oferta została oceniona… pic.twitter.com/wUgFhzlzUk — Magdalena Sobkowiak (@magdasobkowiak) October 27, 2026 Nawrocki, a conservative, is a close ally of his US counterpart, Donald Trump. The Polish president’s national security advisor, Bartosz Grodecki, claimed that it was “thanks to a conversation between” the two presidents that the new Patriot servicing centre was being established in Poland. The head of Nawrocki’s foreign policy office, Marcin Przydacz, meanwhile, thanked Washington for choosing Poland to host the new centre. “The Polish-American alliance and the good atmosphere in relations once again yield results,” he declared. “We can see what positive effects the President’s activity brings for Poland.” Poland is one of a number of European countries that operate Patriot air defence systems. Others include Germany, Greece, the Netherlands, Romania, Sweden and Ukraine. The new centre will service the PAC-3 missiles used in Patriot batteries. The competition to host the facility was announced in July, with the selection made by the US government in conjunction with American defence giant Lockheed Martin, the producer of missiles. In its press release, the Pentagon emphasised that, although Poland would host the new centre, its work would “be underpinned by robust, transatlantic industrial cooperation, with critical supply chain integration led by Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden”. Sweden will deploy Patriot air defence systems and around 100 accompanying military personnel to Poland later this year to protect the NATO logistics hub in the city of Rzeszów, which is the main conduit for aid to Ukraine https://t.co/cq9p7OVO7E — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 6, 2026 Global demand for Patriot systems has risen significantly, with the United States expending at least 1,500 interceptors in its war with Iran, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies. Patriot systems have also been crucial in Ukraine’s defence against Russian ballistic missile attacks, although Ukraine’s supply of missiles is now almost entirely exhausted. After Trump recently suggested that he would authorise Ukraine to produce its own missiles, Poland offered to host any such factory, to ensure its security. However, today’s announcement concerns a site for maintaining and servicing, rather than producing, the missiles. Poland has proposed that, if the United States grants Ukraine permission to produce its own missiles for Patriot air-defence systems, the facility could be located on Polish territory to ensure its security https://t.co/jaQng5wtGg — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 28, 2026 The decision cements Poland’s position as one of Washington’s most important security partners in Europe. War secretary Pete Hegseth has praised Poland as a “model ally”, noting that it has for years met NATO’s defence spending targets, unlike many other member states. Poland has also been a significant customer for US defence firms. Between 2021 and 2025, Poland was NATO’s biggest arms importer, with 44% of the equipment it purchased coming from American suppliers. Last year, Poland signed a $2 billion deal for the US to provide logistical support and training for Patriot systems. This year, it was announced that Polish state defence group PGZ would become the first European producer of American Barracuda-500M cruise missiles. Poland will become the first country in Europe to produce cruise missiles developed by US defence firm Anduril Industries The agreement will "transform the continent's defence industry", claims Anduril https://t.co/LPJnwOLfp2 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 7, 2026 Warsaw is also currently lobbying for a new permanent US military base to be established in Poland, with the government and the president once again putting aside their differences to promote the idea. Last month, Nawrocki claimed that the proposed base, which he said would be called “Fort Trump”, was “confirmed”. However, Washington has not publicly announced any final decision. World.title: Germany’s economy minister hails Poland as “example of great success”
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Germany’s economy minister, Katherina Reiche, has praised Poland as an “example of great success”, saying that it offers a model for other countries. Speaking at the fourth Polish-German Economic Forum in Warsaw, which she opened on Monday alongside Polish finance minister Andrzej Domański, Reiche highlighted the deepening trade ties between the two countries. She noted that bilateral trade last year exceeded €180 billion for the first time, up from €25 billion in 2000, reports Deutsche Welle. Germany has been Poland’s biggest trading partner for decades, although recent data suggest that China, for the first time in history, overtook Germany as Poland’s largest source of imports in July this year. Germany has also long been a major investor in Poland. But Reiche welcomed growing recent investments by Polish companies in Germany, which she said was helping to create jobs. Earlier this year, for example, Poland’s largest manufacturer of trains and trams, Pesa, announced the acquisition of German rival HeiterBlick as part of its efforts to expand its operations across Europe. Reiche noted that around 1,000 Polish companies have invested in Germany, while about 1,600 German companies have invested in Poland, reports Reuters. Poland’s largest manufacturer of trains and trams, Pesa, has announced the acquisition of German rival HeiterBlick as it seeks to expand its operations across Europe https://t.co/N1wE1aYL5m — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 12, 2026 Among leading German firms with a presence in Poland are carmakers Mercedes-Benz, which recently invested around €1 billion to build its first electric-only van plant there, which produces its Crafer vans at a plant near the city of Poznań. Reiche also pointed to Poland’s stellar economic performance since joining the European Union in 2004, noting that its GDP has grown by an annual average of 3.8% over that period – twice the EU-wide average. Poland’s economy is on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world, with the country hoping to become part of the G20. Meanwhile, Domański used his remarks at the Polish-German Economic Forum to warn Europe against repeating past mistakes as it confronts a rapidly changing geopolitical landscape. He said the continent faced a “unique” historical moment. “The world is changing faster than ever, and we are facing new geopolitical, strategic, and technological challenges.” Europe would need a strong economy and new sources of growth to meet those challenges, he added, warning against what he called “economic naivety” and urging Europe – and Germany in particular – not to return to its previous approach to Russia. “I would like to state this very clearly: Europe must learn from the past. Under no circumstances can there be a return to the previous approach toward Russia. Poland will never agree to that,” Domański said, noting that this position applied in particular to renewed use of Russian energy imports. “We will only be resilient once we are truly independent of external, unstable suppliers of raw materials,” he added, emphasising that Poland and Germany must “work together to modernise the European energy market, focus on technological change and bear security in mind”. Debata ministra @Domanski_Andrz i minister @BMWE_ Katherina Reiche podczas IV Polsko-Niemieckiego Forum Gospodarczego. 💬 Powinniśmy skupić się na cenach energii, ale potrzebne jest znacznie bardziej zdecydowane podejście do ochrony rynku europejskiego. I nie chodzi tu tylko o… pic.twitter.com/NVPUjwx7jA — Ministerstwo Rozwoju i Technologii (@MRiTGOVPL) October 26, 2026 Following the forum, Domański and Reiche attended a meeting of the Friends of Industry, an informal initiative bringing together EU member states to coordinate positions on industrial policy, competitiveness and the operating conditions for European industry. The meeting was attended by representatives of 21 EU member states and European Commission Vice-President Stéphane Séjourné. Discussions focused on protecting and strengthening European industry’s competitiveness and economic security amid geopolitical challenges. “Today, we are facing the consequences of the fact that, in the past, competitiveness was often relegated to second, third or fourth place. Competitiveness took a back seat to other priorities, with the result that European industry now faces serious challenges,” said Domański. He proposed making competitiveness a core EU policy priority, cutting red tape, strengthening the single market, lowering energy costs, investing in strategic technologies such as AI, and tightening trade protections against unfair foreign competition. World.title: Prague to Begin Winter Maintenance of Roads and Sidewalks on November 1
World.content:
Prague will begin its annual winter road maintenance programme on November 1.

Until the end of March, the Technical Administration of Communications (TSK) will be responsible for keeping roads, sidewalks and other public routes accessible to vehicles and pedestrians.

Maintenance priorities are determined by the importance of individual routes for traffic and local residents. Roads and pedestrian areas are divided into several categories, each with specific deadlines for snow and ice clearance.



Residents can check the designated maintenance routes and the type of work planned for each area through the city’s online Winter Maintenance application (Zimní údržba).

Road maintenance is divided into three priority categories. The first covers 1,399 kilometres of the city’s busiest roads, which must be treated within two to four hours of maintenance crews being deployed.

The second category includes 519 kilometres of roads, with a clearance deadline of 12 hours. The third covers another 346 kilometres, where maintenance must be completed within 48 hours after the first- and second-priority routes have been treated.

Sidewalks, cycle paths and other pedestrian routes follow a separate schedule. The first category includes 1,063 kilometres, which must be serviced within 12 hours. The second covers a further 693 kilometres, with work required by 5 p.m. on the day after maintenance of the first category has been completed.

Altogether, Prague’s winter maintenance programme covers 2,264 kilometres of roads and 1,756 kilometres of sidewalks and other pedestrian routes.

From December 1 to March 31, temporary workers will help clear sidewalks in parts of Prague 6 that are more difficult to reach with standard maintenance equipment.

These include Hanspaulka, Baba, Sedlec, the Šárecké Valley and parts of Ořechovka.

World.title: Prague Appears in Apple’s Latest MacBook Pro Commercial
World.content:
Prague has once again provided the backdrop for an Apple advertising campaign.

The American technology company has released a new commercial promoting its latest MacBook Pro, featuring several recognisable locations across the Czech capital.

The two-minute video centres on the Prague Congress Centre, with additional scenes filmed around Vyšehrad and Karlovo náměstí. Although Apple does not identify the locations in the commercial, viewers familiar with Prague will recognise several of the city’s landmarks.



The Congress Centre plays the largest role in the production. Its glass-walled entrance hall, with views of the Nusle Bridge, features in several sequences.

The commercial also shows people working on laptops at long rows of tables on an upper floor, alongside an overhead view of the building’s spiral staircase and its metal sculpture The Sun, created by Czech artist Vladimír Procházka.

The production also moved outdoors, using the historic fortifications of Vyšehrad as a setting. Another location is the park at Karlovo náměstí, where the monument to Czech physician and naturalist Jan Evangelista Purkyně can be seen.

Not all the Prague scenery in the  is entirely authentic. In some sequences, Apple has used computer-generated imagery to modify the views through the Congress Centre’s windows, replacing the familiar city panorama with skyscrapers and mountain landscapes.

The latest production continues Apple’s history of filming s in the Czech Republic.

Two years ago, the company also used Prague locations for an iPhone 16 Pro campaign, which featured the roof of the Prague Congress Centre and the Vyšehrad area, alongside the sandstone formations of the Prachov Rocks in the Bohemian Paradise region.

The new MacBook Pro introduces a touchscreen for the first time in Apple’s laptop range. The device is powered by the company’s M5 Pro and M5 Max processors. In the Czech Republic, prices start at CZK 84,990, with sales scheduled to begin on November 6.

World.title: Guitar Legend Carlos Santana to Return to Czech Republic in 2027
World.content:
Legendary guitarist Carlos Santana will return to the Czech Republic on July 22, 2027, for an outdoor concert in the Castle Gardens of Slavkov u Brna, near Brno.

The ten-time Grammy Award winner will perform as part of his Planet of Free Will Global Tour 2027, bringing more than five decades of music to the Czech audience.

Known for blending rock, blues, jazz and Latin rhythms, Santana has built a distinctive sound that has influenced generations of musicians and listeners.



His performance at the 1969 Woodstock festival helped establish him as an international star, while early albums such as Santana*(1969) and Abraxas (1970) produced classics including “Evil Ways,” “Black Magic Woman” and “Oye Como Va.”

Santana reached another career milestone with the 1999 album Supernatural, which featured collaborations with artists including Rob Thomas. The record became a global hit, spawning the singles “Smooth” and “Maria Maria” and winning nine Grammy Awards, including Album of the Year.

Over his career, Santana has received ten Grammy Awards and three Latin Grammy Awards. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1998, received the Kennedy Center Honors and was ranked 11th on *Rolling Stone* magazine’s list of the 100 greatest guitarists of all time.

Despite his long career, Santana continues to release new music and perform internationally. His live shows are known for extended guitar solos, Latin-inspired rhythms and a mix of classic hits and newer material.

Tickets will cost CZK 2,000, plus booking fees.

General ticket sales start on October 30, 2026, at noon, through Ticketmaster and Ticketportal.

World.title: Prague Metronome Lets People Donate to Charity for Just 50 CZK
World.content:
Prague’s Metronome is taking on a charitable role through a new initiative that allows people to pay for a minute of illumination while supporting one of six nonprofit organizations.

The project, called Puls města (City Pulse), was launched by real estate company PSN, which operates the landmark on Letná Hill. Donations start at 50 Czech crowns, and participants can choose which organization they want to support.



The new initiative connects its lighting system with fundraising, allowing members of the public to contribute through the project’s website.

Six Colors, Six Charitable Causes

Each participating organization is represented by a different color. Red supports the Tereza Maxová Foundation for Children, while light blue represents the Kapka naděje (Drop of Hope) Endowment Fund.

Yellow is associated with Díky, že můžem, an initiative focused on civic engagement and democratic values. Pink represents Pink Crocodile, dark blue supports the AutTalk Endowment Fund, founded by Kateřina Sokolová, and green is dedicated to the Fund for Endangered Children.

Visitors can select a cause and make a contribution directly through the project’s website.

Donations Start at 50 CZK

Contributions range from 50 to 9,999 CZK. Regardless of the amount donated, each payment purchases exactly one minute of illumination. A larger contribution therefore does not extend the lighting time.

The website also displays the amount raised for each organization, allowing donors to follow the campaign’s progress. A virtual queue shows when each participant’s turn is scheduled, with the expected time provided after payment.

World.title: Prague’s Golden Eye to Host Japanese Brunch With Live Chef Demonstrations
World.content:
Prague’s Golden Eye bar at Fairmont Hotel is hosting a Japanese-inspired brunch combining traditional ceremonies, live sushi preparation, premium food and signature cocktails.

The afternoon will begin with Kagami Biraki, a traditional Japanese sake barrel-opening ceremony often associated with celebrations and new beginnings.



Guests will then be able to watch a live tuna carving, one of the event’s main attractions.

The programme will also include omakase bites, with chefs preparing sushi at a live station. Guests can pair the food with signature cocktails and a curated selection of wines throughout the afternoon.

A live DJ will provide the soundtrack, adding music to the Japanese-inspired dining experience.

The event is designed exclusively for adults, with tickets priced at CZK 7,900 per person. Full prepayment is required to secure a booking.

Reservations can be made through Golden Eye’s online booking page.

World.title: Hip-Hop Star Xzibit Coming to Prague’s Roxy on November 17
World.content:
West Coast rap legend Xzibit will perform at Prague’s ROXY on November 17, bringing his show featuring tracks from his latest album and some of his best-known hits.

Presented by Gotobeat and Enjoy Events, the show will feature music from *Kingmaker*, alongside career highlights including “X,” “Multiply,” “Paparazzi” and “What’s the Difference.”



Xzibit returns with new album Kingmaker

A major name in West Coast hip-hop since the 1990s, Xzibit built his reputation through his distinctive deep voice, forceful delivery and collaborations with some of the genre’s biggest artists.

His albums Restless, Man vs. Machine and Weapons of Mass Destruction helped establish him as one of the defining rappers of his generation. His work with Dr. Dre, Eminem, Snoop Dogg and Ice Cube further cemented his place in hip-hop, while his television career brought him to a wider audience as the host of MTV’s Pimp My Ride.

Released on May 16, 2025, Kingmaker marked Xzibit’s first solo studio album since 2012.

The 20-track record brings together established names and newer voices, with guest appearances from Dr. Dre, Ice Cube, Busta Rhymes, Ty Dolla $ign, Royce da 5’9”, Redman and B-Real.

The album combines the sound that made Xzibit famous with a more contemporary production style, reflecting on his decades in the music industry while introducing his work to a new generation of listeners.

World.title: From Takumi to Gonta, a New Chapter for Japanese Food in Prague
World.content:
For those craving a taste of Japan without leaving Prague, Takumi offers a chance to explore Japanese cuisine in the heart of the city.

Located behind Quadrio, near the moving head sculpture of Franz Kafka, the restaurant recently celebrated its first anniversary this September.

We spoke with co-owner Euntaek Kim about the restaurant’s history, his journey to Prague, and his latest project, Gonta, a Japanese tonkatsu restaurant.



From Korea to Prague

The Takumi franchise was founded in Düsseldorf, Germany, in 2007 by Haruhiko Saeki and Kenjiro Komatsubara. Kim and his business partner, Viet Hung Phung, later partnered with the founders to bring Takumi Ramen to Prague, opening their first branch on Senovážné náměstí in 2019.

Kim’s connection to the restaurant business began long before that. Before he moved to Prague, his uncle owned several Hanil restaurants in Vienna and planned to expand into the Czech market. This led Kim’s family to move to Prague in 2000, when he was just 12 years old.

Later, Kim and his sister took over the Hanil restaurant their parents had run. He eventually sold it to a Korean chef he had worked with for several years.

Over time, Prague became much more than a place to do business.

“Prague has become like my second home. After having lived here for almost 26 years, I feel connected to its culture as well as my own Korean culture. In business settings and everyday life, I always try to find a balance between both,” Kim says.

His decision to open a Japanese restaurant was driven by what he saw as a gap in Prague’s dining scene.

“I felt like something was missing in Prague. Previously, Asian cuisine was close to nonexistent here. I wanted to make a change,” he explains.

Since moving to Prague, Kim has noticed growing interest in Asian food and culture among local residents, reflecting the city’s changing culinary landscape.

Introducing Gonta, a Japanese Tonkatsu Restaurant

Kim’s latest project, Gonta, brings another Japanese specialty to Prague. Located at Jungmannova 750/34, near Můstek metro station, the restaurant focuses on tonkatsu, a Japanese dish made with breaded, deep-fried pork cutlets, typically served with rice and a tangy sauce.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Gonta Prague (@tonkatsugonta.prague)

“When people think about Japanese cuisine, most people tend to think of sushi or ramen. Tonkatsu is a delicious dish that has not yet reached Prague. I craved it a lot,” Kim says, explaining what inspired him to launch Gonta.

The restaurant is scheduled to open in October 2026, adding another option to Prague’s growing selection of Japanese dining spots.

World.title: Why October 28 Is a National Holiday in the Czech Republic
World.content:
October 28th is Czechoslovak Independence Day, marking the establishment of Czechoslovakia in 1918.

Although Czechoslovakia peacefully split into the Czech Republic and Slovakia in 1993, October 28 remains one of the most important dates in Czech history.

It commemorates the struggle for independence and the emergence of modern Czech statehood. It should not be confused with Czech Statehood Day, celebrated on September 28.



Why Czechoslovakia Declared Independence in 1918

Before 1918, the Czech lands and present-day Slovakia were part of the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

Bohemia, Moravia and part of Silesia belonged to the Austrian half of the monarchy, while Slovakia was part of Hungary. For decades, Czech and Slovak political leaders had sought greater autonomy and the right to determine their own future.

World War I, which began in 1914, weakened the empire and intensified nationalist movements. Food shortages, economic difficulties and growing public discontent increased support for an independent state.

Politicians working abroad played a crucial role in the independence movement. Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk, Edvard Beneš and Milan Rastislav Štefánik coordinated diplomatic efforts to win support from the Allied powers. France, Great Britain and the United States recognised the Czechoslovak National Council as a provisional government in 1918.

Czechoslovak legions also fought on several fronts during the war, including in France, Italy and Russia, helping draw international attention to the independence movement.

How Independence Was Declared

On October 18, 1918, Masaryk issued the Declaration of Independence of Czechoslovakia in the United States, known as the Washington Declaration. It outlined the ambition to establish a democratic state based on the right of the Czechs and Slovaks to self-determination.

The decisive events took place in Prague on October 28, as news spread that Austria-Hungary had agreed to armistice terms. Many people interpreted the reports as a sign that the empire was collapsing and gathered in public squares to celebrate.

The Czech National Committee took control and issued the first law establishing an independent Czechoslovak state. October 28 subsequently became the official date of its founding.

Who Founded the New State?

Masaryk became Czechoslovakia’s first president after independence. A philosopher, educator and politician, he had spent years persuading foreign governments to support the creation of a new state.

Beneš was instrumental in diplomatic negotiations and later served as foreign minister and president. Štefánik, a Slovak politician, astronomer and military officer, helped organise the Czechoslovak legions and strengthen cooperation between the Czech and Slovak independence movements.

Politicians working in Prague, including Alois Rašín, Karel Kramář and Antonín Švehla, also helped organise the transfer of power.

What Happened After 1918?

During the interwar period, Czechoslovakia became a parliamentary republic with one of Central Europe’s most developed industrial economies. However, tensions between its different national communities presented ongoing challenges.

In 1938, the Munich Agreement led to the loss of the Sudetenland. Nazi Germany occupied the Czech lands in March 1939, while Slovakia became a separate state aligned with Berlin. Czechoslovakia was restored after World War II but later came under communist rule.

The Velvet Revolution ended communist rule in 1989. On January 1, 1993, Czechoslovakia peacefully split into two independent countries.

World.title: Breaking: Former Fidesz MP István Boldog sentenced to 5 years in prison
World.content:
A Budapest court has sentenced former Fidesz MP István Boldog to five years in prison for his role in a corruption scheme involving EU-funded projects in Hungary. The former politician was also banned from public affairs for five years, fined and ordered to forfeit HUF 6.6 million (approximately EUR 18,000).

The Budapest Metropolitan Court handed down the first-instance verdict on Friday, finding Boldog guilty as an accomplice in several offences, including accepting bribes and agreements restricting competition in public procurement procedures, Telex reported.

According to the ruling, he may be released after serving two-thirds of his sentence at the earliest. The decision is not final, and Boldog had already indicated before the verdict that he would appeal if convicted.

István Boldog. Photo: MTI

How the corruption scheme worked

The court found that an unlawful kickback system operated in Boldog’s former parliamentary constituency in Jász-Nagykun-Szolnok County. Using his political influence, the former MP helped municipalities with connections to him secure EU funding while favouring certain businesses in public procurement contracts.

According to the judge, this was not an isolated incident but a system operating across the constituency. Unlike more conventional corruption schemes involving inflated contracts and documented kickbacks, money was returned in cash to Boldog and people working with him.

The investigation focused primarily on three projects in Cserkeszőlő: the construction of a nursery, the renovation of the Baghy-Szinyei Merse Mansion and energy-efficiency improvements to municipal buildings. However, investigators found indications that other municipalities and contractors could also have been involved.

István Boldog. Photo: MTI

The court also highlighted evidence that a contractor handed HUF 20 million to one of Boldog’s associates, identified as Péter K. The defence argued that the associate had kept the money for himself without Boldog’s knowledge, but the court said other evidence contradicted this explanation.

The judge added that witnesses’ testimonies and intercepted conversations suggested municipalities believed Boldog had decisive influence over which localities would receive EU funding. This influence extended beyond the main regional development programme to other funding schemes, including the Hungarian Village Programme.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Other defendants also receive prison sentences

Boldog was not the only defendant convicted in the case. Petra Fehér, a former Fidesz municipal and county representative who was widely known as one of Boldog’s closest associates, also received a five-year prison sentence. Her time spent in pre-trial detention will count towards her sentence.

Another associate, Péter K., was sentenced to three years in prison and fined. The court found the other defendants guilty as well, with the exception of the ninth defendant, who was acquitted.

István Boldog. Photo: MTI

Boldog denies wrongdoing and plans to fight the verdict

The former MP has consistently denied the accusations, insisting that he never interfered unlawfully in funding decisions or participated in bribery. Before Friday’s ruling, he told Telex that he expected to be acquitted and promised to appeal if the court found him guilty.

At an earlier hearing in February, Boldog again rejected the allegations, claiming that he had spent his entire life fighting corruption. He also questioned the credibility of witnesses, particularly former Kengyel mayor Szilárd Nagy, whose testimony helped launch the investigation.

The case first came to public attention in October 2019, and prosecutors filed charges against Boldog and eight others in 2020. The preparatory hearing took place in June 2021, meaning more than five years passed before the court delivered its first-instance verdict.

Fidesz replaced Boldog as its candidate ahead of the 2022 parliamentary election, after which he withdrew from active politics. He has remained active on social media, describing himself as a national-minded commentator and food blogger.

World.title: Budapest drivers to face weeks of disruption as major junction undergoes renovations
World.content:
Motorists in Budapest should prepare for traffic jams and road restrictions in November, as maintenance work at one of the capital’s busiest junctions is set to disrupt traffic for almost four weeks.

Busy Budapest junction will undergo repairs

Track repairs will take place at the junction of Bocskai Road and Bartók Béla Road, around Kosztolányi Dezső Square, from 7 AM on Monday, 2 November, until 27 November, according to Budapest Közút. During the works, a construction site will occupy the centre of the junction, forcing vehicles to pass around it.

On Bocskai Road, two narrowed lanes will remain open in each direction, while traffic on Bartók Béla Road will be restricted to one lane in each direction. The temporary layout is expected to slow traffic, particularly on Bocskai Road and around Kosztolányi Dezső Square. Drivers heading towards the city centre will also face a change to their usual routes.

Left turns temporarily prohibited

Motorists travelling towards the centre on Bocskai Road will not be able to turn left onto Bartók Béla Road in the middle of the junction. Instead, they must continue straight across Bartók Béla Road and use a temporary left-turn facility near the service road at Kosztolányi Dezső Square. They can then reach Bartók Béla Road via the service road.

Budapest Közút has urged drivers to approach the junction with extra care and use alternative routes where possible.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Tram services and replacement buses

The repairs will also affect public transport. Between 2 and 27 November, trams 19 and 49 will run on shortened routes, terminating at Móricz Zsigmond Square instead of continuing to Kelenföld Railway Station. Replacement buses operating under route number 19 will serve the section between Kelenföld railway station and Móricz Zsigmond Square.

For journeys towards central Budapest, the Budapest Transport Centre (BKK) recommends using metro line M4 or buses 7, 58, 114, 213 and 214. Passengers are advised to check timetables and plan their journeys in advance, using the BudapestGO app for route planning and real-time travel information. The works are scheduled to finish on 27 November, with delays expected in the surrounding area throughout the construction period.

World.title: Hungary raises public transport fines – what passengers need to know
World.content:
Passengers travelling by train, bus and HÉV services in Hungary will face higher penalties from 2 November. The standard surcharge for travelling without a valid ticket will rise by HUF 5,000, while reduced fines for early payment are also going up.

Higher fines on trains, buses and HÉV services from November

Hungary’s MÁV Group has announced an increase in surcharges across intercity trains, buses and HÉV suburban railway services from 2 November.

The standard penalty for travelling without a valid ticket will increase from HUF 25,000 (approximately EUR 68) to HUF 30,000 (approximately EUR 82). The same higher surcharge will apply to various breaches of passenger rules, including smoking on trains or at stations, dirtying vehicles and using discounts without being entitled to them.

Passengers who pay their fine promptly can still benefit from reduced rates. However, these will also increase: on buses, passengers paying on the spot or within three working days will have to pay HUF 15,000 (EUR 41) instead of HUF 12,000 (EUR 33). The same reduced rate will apply on HÉV services for payments made within two working days.

The HUF 50,000 (EUR 137) surcharge for payments made more than 30 days after the penalty is issued will remain unchanged.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Budapest commuters: remember to buy your train ticket before boarding

The MÁV Group is particularly reminding passengers about the mandatory advance ticket purchase zones introduced around Budapest two years ago.

At all stations and stops along the affected railway sections, passengers must have a valid ticket before boarding any train. Buying one from the ticket inspector after getting on is not sufficient to avoid the higher penalty.

The affected routes include connections between Budapest and:

Győr

Esztergom

Székesfehérvár

Pusztaszabolcs

Szob

Veresegyház and Vác

Hatvan

Cegléd and Szolnok

Nagykáta

Pestszentimre

The rule applies to all stations and stops along the listed sections, not just their final destinations.

Passengers should also check whether they need a seat reservation and whether their tickets are valid for the correct train, departure time and entire journey.

If there is no working ticket machine or open ticket office at the station, tickets can be purchased online through the MÁVPlusz mobile app or the official MÁV ticket website. However, the purchase must still be completed before boarding.

Other penalties are changing too

The increase is not limited to passengers travelling without tickets in the mandatory advance-purchase zones.

From 2 November, the HUF 30,000 (EUR 82) surcharge will also apply across intercity trains, buses and HÉV services in cases such as the unauthorised use of travel discounts and breaches of passenger regulations.

On HÉV services, the fee for subsequently presenting a travel pass purchased on the day the penalty was issued will also increase, from HUF 6,500 (EUR 18) to HUF 7,500 (EUR 20.5).

There is, however, one way to reduce certain penalties considerably. Passengers who can prove within 15 days that they already held a valid ticket, pass or travel entitlement at the time of inspection can have the surcharge reduced to an administration fee. This is HUF 2,600 (EUR 7.1) on trains and HUF 2,500 (EUR 6.8) on buses.

Fines on tram-train services will not change.

Thousands of penalties already issued this year

According to MÁV Group data, inspectors issued 5,300 penalties on HÉV services during the first nine months of this year, generating almost HUF 53.5 million in revenue.

The figures were even higher on other services. Nearly 14,700 penalty cases were recorded on trains, generating HUF 88.5 million, while buses accounted for more than 14,500 cases and HUF 97 million in penalty revenue.

The most common reasons included travelling without a valid ticket or pass, failing to provide proof of eligibility for a discount, and being unable to demonstrate that the ticket or pass belonged to the passenger.

MÁV Group says many of these situations can easily be avoided by checking travel documents before departure. From November, that small precaution could save passengers an additional HUF 5,000.

World.title: Gastrodiplomacy brings a taste of Malaysia to Budapest
World.content:
The Embassy of Malaysia in Hungary served up a vibrant display of gastrodiplomacy on 28 October, bringing authentic Malaysian heritage to the heart of Central Europe through an exclusive culinary showcase led by Tourism, Arts and Culture Ambassador for Gastronomy, Dato’ Chef Haji Ismail Ahmad.

Held at the Kuktaparty Cooking School, the event, dubbed “A Taste of Malaysia”, brought together more than 30 distinguished guests, including senior Hungarian government officials, business leaders, culinary educators, media representatives and prominent Hungarian figures.

CDA a.i. during the opening remarks. Photo: Embassy of Malaysia

Guests were treated to an interactive live demonstration of Malaysia’s iconic prawn fritters (cucur udang) by Chef Ismail, followed by a traditional Malay wedding hidang (communal banquet) spread. The curated menu featured regional heritage delicacies, including Johor’s Nasi Biryani Gam, Rendang Tok, Ayam Madu (honeyed chicken), Kari Dhal, Pecal, Lepat Pisang, and Sira Labu (candied pumpkin).

CDA a.i., Chef Ismail, Hungarian Chefs and Perwakilan Wanita Budapest. Photo: Embassy of Malaysia

In his welcoming remarks, Malaysian Chargé d’Affaires a.i. Mr. Norafizan Mustaffa highlighted the power of cuisine as a cultural bridge, noting that despite the geographical distance, Malaysia and Hungary share a profound appreciation for hearty meals, warm hospitality, and essential aromatics like garlic, onions, and red paprika.

Norafizan drew smiles from attendees when highlighting a real-world example of this bilateral connection in Perak, Malaysia, where an eatery operated by a Hungarian-Malaysian couple serves traditional Hungarian fried bread (lángos) topped with Malaysian sambal, anchovies, peanuts, and cucumber.

“If a Hungarian lángos can feel right at home in Malaysia, then our two nations already speak the exact same language, the language of good food,” Norafizan said, stressing those enduring international friendships are often forged over shared meals rather than formal communiqués.

Chef Ismail teaching MATE University Students. Photo: Embassy of Malaysia

He also framed the showcase as an invitation for Hungarian travelers to explore Malaysia ahead of the Visit Malaysia Year 2026 and 2027 campaigns.

Adding a literary dimension to the gathering, Malaysian bilingual writer, poet, and translator Mawar Marzuki recited an original poem dedicated to the occasion. Marzuki is currently in the region undertaking an artistic residency under the Slovene Writers’ Association’s (SWA) Programme in Residence for Literary Mediators in Ljubljana, Slovenia.

Chef with Perwakilan Wanita Budapest. Photo: Embassy of Malaysia

Also present as Guest of Honour was the Hungarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs Deputy Director for Asia and the Pacific, Adrienn Sallai. Other notable attendees included Budapest District 1 Deputy Mayor Artúr Fodor and Hungarian University of Agriculture and Life Sciences (MATE) Vice-Rector for International Affairs Dr. Zoltán Kovács.

The main showcase followed a dedicated culinary masterclass held a day earlier, where Chef Ismail collaborated with six MATE University food science and gastronomy students alongside prominent Hungarian culinary figures such as Chef Péter Korpádi and Chef Lajos Rácz.

Chef Ismail during Live demo, teaching Guest of Honor Adrienn Sallai on how to cook Cucur Udang. Photo: Embassy of Malaysia

Guests were also presented with custom recipe booklets featuring each dish, encouraging them to recreate authentic Malaysian culinary staples at home.

World.title: Hungarian fugitive on Top 50 wanted list caught in the Czech Republic
World.content:
A 28-year-old Hungarian-Ukrainian dual national wanted in connection with robbery and drug possession has been arrested in the Czech Republic following a joint operation by Hungarian and Czech police.

He was recently added to the Top 50 list

The man, identified as Dániel B., was apprehended on 27 October at a factory near Brno, after investigators tracked down his suspected whereabouts and workplace. He had recently been added to Hungary’s list of the country’s 50 most wanted fugitives.

According to Hungarian police, arrest warrants had been issued against him in connection with separate criminal proceedings. The Budapest-Central District Court issued a warrant in February in a drug possession case, while the Budapest-Capital Regional Court issued another in connection with a robbery for which a final conviction had already been handed down.

Convicted over violent robbery in Budapest

Dániel B. was sentenced to several years in prison after robbing a foreign national in Budapest in September 2025. He allegedly snatched the victim’s bag by force and attacked the individual when they tried to recover it. After leaving the scene, the man reportedly returned several hours later and broke into multiple parked cars. A relative of the robbery victim recognised him and managed to detain him until police arrived.

He was supposed to have reported to prison months ago to serve his sentence but failed to do so. Jászberény police began searching for him in September, and European and international arrest warrants were issued in early October. His name was subsequently added to the top 50 wanted list.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Hungarian and Czech police worked together

Given the suspect’s dual nationality, investigators considered the possibility that he had left Hungary. The National Bureau of Investigation’s fugitive-hunting unit joined the search and established that he might be hiding in the Czech Republic.

Hungarian investigators then contacted their Czech counterparts through the European Network of Fugitive Active Search Teams (ENFAST), sharing the information they had gathered. Czech police established that the suspect had previously held a residence permit in the country.

The joint investigation led officers to a factory near Brno, where the man was arrested on the morning of 27 October. He was taken into custody by Czech police. Extradition proceedings are now under way, and a Czech court is expected to decide his fate within days.

World.title: Austria overturns unlawful border closure towards Hungary
World.content:
Austria’s Constitutional Court has overturned a local regulation that effectively closed a border crossing between Hungary and Austria to vehicle traffic, ruling that the decision to create a pedestrian zone was unlawful.

The border crossing was closed in 2023

The crossing connects Ágfalva in Hungary with Schattendorf (Somfalva) in Austria’s Burgenland region. Since 2023, motorists have generally been unable to use the route without special permission, forcing Hungarian commuters and families living on either side of the border to take detours of more than 30 kilometres, writes volksgruppen.orf.

The Austrian court found that Schattendorf’s local authorities had failed to adequately assess whether the pedestrian zone was necessary. They had also neglected to consult those affected by the decision, including cross-border commuters and local businesses. The regulation will formally cease to apply once the Burgenland provincial government publishes the official announcement.

The border back in 2017. Photo: Steindy/Wikimedia Commons

Crossing closed after pedestrian zone introduced

Schattendorf’s municipal authorities decided in early 2023 to establish a pedestrian zone near the local cemetery. The stated aim was to improve safety around the cemetery and a nearby care home, reports Telex. However, the measure was controversial, as the road had been heavily used by Hungarian commuters travelling to work, particularly in the early morning and afternoon. Critics argued that the pedestrian zone was effectively a means of restricting cross-border traffic.

Construction work began on 1 March 2023, bringing ordinary vehicle traffic to an end. By the summer, retractable bollards had been installed in the road to prevent cars from passing. Some motorists were granted exceptions on special grounds, but applicants generally faced strict restrictions. Those seeking permission were reportedly required to pay EUR 160, and most applications were rejected.

Stay up-to-date with Hungary Weekly Briefing: subscribe on Substack!

Previous legal challenge also questioned the closure

The closure significantly affected daily journeys between Austria and Hungary, creating additional travel costs and inconvenience for commuters and residents with family connections across the border. The Constitutional Court’s decision follows an earlier ruling by a court in Burgenland that also found problems with the restrictions affecting Hungarian commuters.

The latest judgment challenges the legal basis of the pedestrian zone, particularly the lack of a thorough assessment and consultation before its introduction. Although the court has overturned the regulation, the practical implications for motorists will depend on the formal publication of the decision by the provincial government.
