World.title: Mother whose son lost sight named WA's Australian of the Year
World.content:
Deeply personal experiences of adversity are behind some of the winners of the 2027 Australian of the Year awards for Western Australia, including a mother whose son lost his sight during the COVID lockdowns.

Telehealth innovator Esther Oh invented specially designed smart glasses and headsets to help frontline medical staff in remote locations connect with specialised practitioners and AI assisted technology.

She developed the technology after her own experiences trying to get help for her teenage son.

The invention, called Agili8, has been used in remote Aboriginal communities, including for a patient who was "was saved from deadly infection and potential amputation in just 15 minutes", according to the award citation.

It said the invention came about after her young son became blind because of delayed treatment during the pandemic.

She was named the Australian of the Year for Western Australia on Friday night.

Eating disorder work recognised

Another recipient who turned her lived experience of adversity into something positive was Phoebe Ho, who has worked to help people with eating disorders recover physically and mentally.

Ms Ho, who has been named 2027 Young Australian of the Year for WA, is a clinical psychologist who has drawn on her own experience of eating disorders to help her patients at the Child and Adolescent Health Service.

Phoebe Ho won the Young Australian of the Year for WA. (ABC News: Stella McGann)

"Her lived experience continues to inform her clinical work and research, including exploring the role it can play as a part of a patient's recovery process," the citation reads.

Lifeline volunteer

Lifeline WA's longest-serving volunteer, Tina Baldwin, 78, has been honoured with the Senior Australian of the Year award for WA.

Ms Baldwin, who with her husband Daniel were Lifeline WA's first volunteer crisis supporters in the mid-1980s, has taken over 33,000 calls from people in desperate situations over more than 40 years.

"In each case, Tina responds with compassion, openness and a willingness to listen," her citation reads.

Indigenous champion

Binar Indigenous basketball association founder Adam Desmond, 47, has been named WA's 2027 Local Hero for his vision in setting up the organisation.

Adam Desmond was named Local Hero for his work with basketball outreach group Binar. (ABC News: Stella McGann)

"Today, Binar provides wraparound support through basketball, education, health, mentoring and cultural identity, creating positive pathways for young people both on and off the court," his citation read.

World.title: Evacuation begins from ravaged Russian-controlled Ukrainian city
World.content:
The evacuation of stranded residents in Oleshky, a ravaged Ukrainian frontline city under Russian occupation has begun as part of a US-brokered ceasefire, officials from Russia and Ukraine said.

Captured by Russia in 2022, locals in the city had faced food, water and medicine shortages for months, with some being forced to hunt and eat pigeons, former residents said.

Officials from Moscow and Kyiv arrived in Oleshky on Friday to oversee the operation.

"Evacuation and distribution of humanitarian aid have begun," Ukrainian negotiator David Arakhamia said on social media.

Yana Lantratova (left) spoke to reporters after sending a video message to announce that many Oleshky residents were leaving. (Reuters)

Russia's human rights ombudsman Yana Lantratova posted a video showing groups of people waiting to board buses.

Some would be taken to Russia, others to Kyiv-controlled parts of Ukraine, she said.

The population of Oleshky has dropped from 24,000 before the war to about 2,000.

Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets posted videos of himself talking to locals, several of whom thanked him, were crying and wiping tears from their eyes.

Groups of residents were seen waiting outside their buildings with bags of belongings ready to leave.

Officials from both countries have said some in the city would choose to stay, even if the fighting resumed.

The ceasefire, announced by US First Lady Melania Trump last week, is due to end on Sunday evening.

Oleshky's population has dropped from 24,000 before the war to about 2,000. (AP)

Now in its fourth day, it is the longest pause in fighting anywhere on the front line since Russia invaded in 2022.

Several other partial ceasefires, for instance, around Orthodox Easter, have been marred by accusations of violations.

Oleshky residents have given harrowing accounts of risking their lives travelling along mine-strewn roads, one known as the "road of death", just to get food and water.

A man rides a bicycle beneath anti-drone nets stretched over a street during the ceasefire in Oleshky. (AP: Evgeniy Maloletka)

Some say they have survived on a cup of rice or buckwheat a day, sometimes with a tomato, cucumber or wild plants added.

Trump's threats to Ukraine It is hard to see Donald Trump's shifting position on Ukraine as a clear strategic change, and not one driven principally by soaring fuel prices ahead of the US mid-term elections.

Despite the brief respite in the conflict around Oleshky, attacks elsewhere have continued unabated.

Some 200,000 households were left without power in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro after Russian attacks overnight.

A drone strike on a train station there a day earlier killed at least 14 people, while an attack on the northern city of Chernigiv killed two teenage girls.

US-mediated peace talks are due to resume next month in Abu Dhabi for the first time since February, as US President Donald Trump seeks to end a conflict he once said he could solve in a day.

A man walks across a road beneath anti-drone nets in Oleshky ahead of the evacuation. (AP: Evgeniy Maloletka)

Russia still hopes that Mr Trump can pressure Kyiv into accepting a deal that meets many of Moscow's conditions, such as full Russian control of Ukraine's Donbas region and a bar on Ukraine joining NATO.

Kyiv wants to ensure that US intelligence sharing continues, along with full access to Elon Musk's recently disrupted battlefield communications system, Starshield, and that European-bought US military hardware, including Patriot interceptor missiles, keeps flowing.

Residents left Oleshky on buses, mini buses and by train. (AFP: David Arakhamia)

The situation with the ceasefire in Oleshky, coordinated with the US, is an isolated case, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Friday on Russian state TV.

It should not be extrapolated to the broader peaceful settlement process in Ukraine, Mr Peskov added.

Wires/ABC

World.title: Police probe Andrew's stay with Epstein at king's castle
World.content:
Scottish police are conducting inquiries into the time then-prince Andrew spent at the king's Balmoral estate with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his associate, Ghislaine Maxwell.

Police Scotland said the investigation was at a "very early stage".

"All inquiries are evidence-led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those inquiries,'' police said in a statement.

" We would never confirm details of ongoing inquiries and it would be inappropriate to comment further. "

The key moments that led to former prince Andrew's arrest Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor has for years faced allegations over his contact with Jeffrey Epstein. These moments led to his arrest.

Images released by the US Department of Justice this year appear to show the former prince, now known as Andrew Mountbatten Windsor, on a shooting trip at the estate with Epstein.

In February Mr Mountbatten Windsor was arrested and held for hours by British police on suspicion of misconduct in public office.

It was the first time in nearly four centuries that a senior British royal had been arrested.

AP

World.title: War of words erupts over Christian group's omission from NT Christmas pageant
World.content:
A decision by Darwin City Council to omit a Christian group from the 2026 Darwin Christmas Pageant has escalated into a war of words between the council and the Northern Territory government.

Darwin City Council (DCC) rejected March for Jesus's application to participate in this year's pageant, citing "intimidating and confronting" behaviour from the group at last year's event.

"People in that organisation were saying things along the lines of 'God is coming for your children because they've been demonised,'" Lord Mayor Peter Styles said.

Peter Styles says the council received complaints about the group's behaviour at last year's parade. (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

DCC chief executive Simone Saunders said the council had received complaints from members of the public about March for Jesus participants allegedly tossing merchandise such as wristbands at spectators who did not want them.

"Where parents were saying, 'I don't wish to take that particular item', there were reports of them being thrown at children," she said.

The council's move prompted swift backlash from a raft of Christian groups, including the Australian Christian Lobby (ACL), which has firmly rejected the accusations.

Nicholas Lay has rejected the accusations against the March for Jesus group. (ABC News: Xavier Martin)

"The group actually filmed the entirety of the event from their perspective, it's on YouTube," said ACL NT director Nicholas Lay.

"When you're confronted with comprehensive evidence that they were well-behaved, I think you'd have to have pretty good evidence to suggest otherwise."

The NT Country Liberal Party (CLP) government, meanwhile, has slammed the council's decision, and said it would take over the Darwin Christmas Pageant from 2027 onwards.

Marie-Clare Boothby has called the council's decision "un-Australian". (ABC News: Pete Garnish)

"Council's decision to ban a Christian group from this year's Christmas pageant can only be described as un-Australian," Major Events Minister Marie-Clare Boothby said in a statement.

"From 2027 the NT government will take back the pageant to ensure it is run properly."

The ABC contacted a March for Jesus spokesperson who was not available for comment.

'Punching bag' tactics

Late this week the debacle exploded into a wider dispute between the DCC and government, with Mr Styles accusing the NT government of making the council a "punching bag".

"Every time there's some sort of an issue they want to divert attention from, they come and punch us," he said.

"That happened after Cyclone Fina with the cyclone clean-up issue; it's happened with this pageant issue."

Earlier this year, DCC and the NT government butted heads over the council's decision to delay and potentially permanently reschedule its pre-cyclone clean-up to May.

Darwin council considering permanent pre-cyclone clean-up move The City of Darwin could soon vote to permanently move its annual pre-cyclone clean-up to May.

The dispute led to several MLAs launching a petition to reinstate the clean-up, and a string of Facebook posts accusing the council of ignoring constituents.

Mr Styles, a former CLP deputy chief minister, has accused the government of sharing misinformation about the pageant and, previously, about the cyclone clean-up.

"We've certainly indicated our displeasure at them putting out information which is misinformation and then the backbenchers putting it all up on Facebook," he said.

The government was contacted for comment on Mr Styles's remarks.

Questions linger around takeover, group's participation

Mr Styles today said that March for Jesus was welcome to take part in the Christmas pageant as long as its participants followed the rules of the event.

"We've negotiated with the senior people in the organisation to get their people to follow [the rules]. A further meeting is also scheduled coming up this week," he said.

"But they've got to be aware certain people in their organisation were performing badly last year, which caused this to become an issue."

The Darwin Christmas Pageant has been running each year since 2022. (ABC News)

Mr Lay said he hoped March for Jesus was involved despite the debacle and welcomed the NT government's announced takeover of the pageant.

"It's a welcome decision, but it's unfortunate that it had to go that far," he said.

"The simple solution was they made a mistake and should have undone it straight away."

Mr Styles said while an NT government "takeover" of the pageant was not within the government's powers, he was happy to negotiate with the government about who ran the pageant.

Ms Boothby was not available for an interview.

World.title: Queensland Land Court approves proposed $1b coal mine
World.content:
One of Australia's largest proposed greenfield coal projects has been given the green light to continue planning after a ruling in Queensland's land court.

Whitehaven Coal's $1 billion Winchester South coalmine in the is expected to produce 17 million tonnes of coal a year.

The project, which is still subject to final approvals by the state and federal governments, would extract mostly metallurgical coal, used to make steel and thermal coal.

The proposal has been on hold while the Land Court of Queensland heard an application from the Australian Conservation Foundation (ACF) and Mackay Conservation Group (MCG).

The court's decision handed down on Friday after a seven-week hearing.

The two groups objected to the open-cut mine because of the potential environmental impacts, climate change and demand for coal into the future.

Whitehaven argued the mine's emissions "would be only a tiny amount within overall global carbon emissions". ACF and MCG said it would influence climate change, according to the judgment.

The open-cut mine, 30 kilometres south-east of Moranbah, would produce mostly metallurgical coal, used to make steel. (Supplied: Whitehaven Coal)

The court was told burning the coal from the project would cause an increase of 0.0003 degrees Celsius of warming, and that the total emissions over the life of the mine would be 557,246,614 tonnes of CO2 equivalent.

In his judgement, Judge Nicholas Loos said the amount of CO2 created was "an extraordinary amount", agreeing that ACF and MCG "advance an eloquent and powerful argument about the frightening consequences of the human driven warming of the planet".

"The proposed mine is going to contribute to those frightening consequences," Judge Loos said.

"But those consequences are going to eventuate with or without this mine … [and] there may be hundred or even thousands of projects proposed, around the world, that will each have the consequence of a 0.0003 Celsius temperate increase.

" This is the wicked problem of addressing climate change. It can only be meaningfully met by cumulative action. "

The mining company said that regardless of future demand for electricity sources, "it should be entitled to carry the risk of future viability" by operating its mine.

Judge Loos said he was unable to agree with ACF and MCG's argument that the project should be refused on their three primary grounds of objection.

The Winchester South project is expected to provide 500 jobs during construction and operation, according to the mining company.

Mackay Conservation Group argued the Winchester South mine would consume valuable grazing land. (Supplied: Mackay Conservation Group)

Judge Loos said the creation of jobs and economic activity for the Isaac region would also be another "key benefit".

He said the local environmental impacts would be serious, but found that Whitehaven's comprehensive plan to manage those impacts was acceptable.

He found that the mine's $696 million in royalties over its life — according to Deloitte calculations — was an "upside" to granting the mine

MCG coordinator Imogen Lindenberg said the groups were considering "their next move" following the court's decision.

"While this decision hurts, this case has achieved so much," Ms Lindenberg said.

"It put the climate impacts of new coal mines under intense legal scrutiny, it forced Whitehaven to answer serious questions in court, and it strengthened the legal arguments around climate harm, community impacts and future risk.

"And it showed, clearly and publicly, that communities in central Queensland are willing to stand up and challenge powerful fossil fuel companies."

What's next for Whitehaven?

Following the court's ruling, the Queensland government will now to decide whether the project proceeds.

If successful, the total mine life would be 35 years, with 28 years of coal extraction and export.

Judge Loos said the project had been "carefully examined" before coming before the Land Court, having already been recommended to proceed by the state's coordinator-general in 2023, subject to conditions and recommendations, following an assessment of its Environment Impact Statement.

The Queensland Department of Environment, Science and Innovation then approved the mine's Environmental Authority (EA) application in 2024.

But before the mine can begin operating an EA and mining lease will need to be issued from the state government before the federal government makes the final decision.

World.title: Joint's promising run in Japan ends with QF exit
World.content:
Maya Joint's encouraging run at the Pan Pacific Open in Japan has ended with a three-set quarterfinal loss on a day when world number one Elena Rybakina pulled out with an injury.

The Australian, ranked 94 in the world, had been impressive in earlier wins over sixth-seeded Romanian Sorana Cirstea and Spain's Cristina Bucsa to book her spot in the quarterfinals at the WTA 500 event against Kamilla Rakhimova.

The Uzbekistani won a tight first set 7-5, before Joint rebounded to claim the second by the same scoreline.

However, Rakhimova romped away in the final set to win 7-5, 5-7, 6-1 in Tokyo on Friday, local time.

Joint took the honours in first serves, landing 66 per cent compared with her opponent's 59 per cent, and serving five aces to Rakhimova's one.

However, the world number 66 was much more effective on her return, converting six of the 12 break points she set up, compared with the three Joint managed.

Despite the loss, the late-season Asian swing has been a welcome confidence boost for Joint.

Ranked a career-high number 28 in February, the Australian's year had been underwhelming until she made the final at last month's Korea Open in Seoul, where she lost to compatriot Kim Birrell.

The signs are certainly promising for the 20-year-old as she plans her assault on the Australian Open in January.

Rakhimova's victory set up a semifinal against Leylah Fernandez.

The Canadian had an armchair ride to the semis when world number one and reigning Australian and US Open champion Rybakina withdrew from their quarterfinal because of injury.

Rybakina said she could not play because of an undisclosed injury. She stepped onto the court in Tokyo and delivered the news to fans and ended by saying, "I hope to see you all next year."

She said she had been struggling for several days "with a little injury" and needs to be ready for next month's WTA Finals in Indian Wells, California.

AAP

World.title: Christmas remained key part of school event, premier told by department
World.content:
The ABC understands a prominent Tasmanian businessman made the original complaint about the renaming of Christmas celebrations at a northern Tasmanian primary school, which ultimately led to a controversial social media post by the state’s premier.

Meredith and Nathan Thurlow – who is the general manager of private fuel distributor Tas Petroleum – are understood to have emailed Trevallyn Primary School leadership and Education Minister Jo Palmer with concerns Christmas celebrations were to be minimised.

Christmas 'culture war' goes against premier's 'nice guy' image A post on social media by Tasmania's premier decrying an apparent attempt to "remove references to Christmas" has spiralled into a culture war.

Pulse Tasmania, which is understood to have been sent a copy of the Thurlows' email, previously quoted an unnamed parent as having written to the school saying they supported inclusion but were worried "in an effort to be increasingly inclusive, the school may actually be moving towards removing or minimising aspects of our own cultural heritage".

"We worry that this approach risks alienating families who value these longstanding traditions and who want their children to feel connected to the cultural practices that have been part of Australian community life for generations," the parent's email reportedly stated, noting it was "important to recognise that families can hold different belief systems while still participating respectfully in one another's celebrations".

Nathan Thurlow (right) with Premier Jeremy Rockliff (second from right) and Liberal MP Rob Fairs (left). (Supplied: Facebook/Tas Petroleum)

The school was planning to change the name of its end-of-year event from "Christmas on the Hill" to "End of Year Extravaganza".

Mr Thurlow is yet to respond to questions from the ABC.

Two-and-a-half weeks later, Premier Jeremy Rockliff posted on social media that he had been told "there had been efforts made to remove all references to Christmas in end-of-year school celebrations".

While the premier did not name the school in his post, and the social media comments were moderated, the name of the school he was referring to – Trevallyn Primary School — was soon revealed.

But a letter tabled in the Tasmanian Parliament yesterday shows that the same day Mr Rockliff made the post, his office was given advice from Education Department secretary Ginna Webster that "Christmas remains an important part of the proposed celebration".

“The school has advised that Christmas carols remain part of the event, with some classes choosing to perform Christmas-themed items, and Santa Claus will be attending,” Ms Webster told him.

Jeremy Rockliff says he was travelling on the day his office received Ms Webster's letter. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Mr Rockliff told the ABC he was travelling on the day the advice was received and he was given a copy the following day.

He said it was clear from the correspondence between the school and family that changes were being made to the Christmas event.

After the premier's post went up, the school was the subject of a social media pile-on and the education union said the school and staff had suffered "distress and harm".

The ABC has now constructed a timeline, revealing how the saga unfolded.

Complaint first lodged

On October 2, 2026, Trevallyn Primary School published its fortnightly newsletter, making a brief reference to the upcoming event.

“We will also be ramping up the planning for our fundraising December Raffle and the 'End of Year Extravaganza!' (formerly known as Christmas on the Hill),” it said.

The same day, the ABC understands the Thurlows emailed a complaint to the school leadership and copied in Tasmanian Education Minister Jo Palmer with their concerns.

Two days later, on October 4, the school is understood to have responded to the Thurlows, with Ms Palmer and school leadership again copied in.

Mr Rockliff was recently asked if the Thurlow family were the only ones to raise concerns about the event, to which he responded: “I don’t mention any constituents publicly."

Trevallyn Primary School was planning to change the name of its end-of-year event. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

The ABC understands that on October 12, Mr Thurlow forwarded this email chain, including his original complaint and the school’s response, to reporters from media outlets Channel 7 and Pulse.

The same day, the premier was on King Island with those reporters, and other journalists.

Two days later, on October 14, Pulse published a story, citing passages from the forwarded email chain.

But it also published an October 13 letter from Mr Rockliff to Department of Education, Children and Young People secretary Ginna Webster, asking her to speak with the school to make sure its practices “align with expectations of the broader school community”.

It is not clear how the media outlet obtained this letter, with the education minister this week telling parliament it had not come from her, her office or the secretary of the education department.

Jeremy Rockliff has not apologised for his post. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

Letter said Christmas would be celebrated

Also in parliament yesterday, the premier tabled the response he received from the department secretary on October 14.

In this letter, Ms Webster said she was satisfied “Christmas remains an important part of the proposed celebration”.

“Rather than remove Christmas, the school is seeking to balance longstanding traditions with an inclusive approach that enables all students and families to participate in a way that is respectful of their individual beliefs and circumstances,” she said.

"I am also advised that a senior executive from School and Early Years will be meeting with the school at the beginning of term four to work through the matter."

She said the school still planned on having Christmas carols, some classes were performing Christmas-themed items and Santa Claus would be attending.

Trevallyn Primary School still plans to incorporate Christmas celebrations in its end-of-year event. (ABC News: Georgia Hogge)

The premier posted on his Facebook page at 8:47pm that night – 14 minutes after the Pulse story was published – that there had been “efforts made to remove all references to Christmas” at an unnamed school’s end-of-year celebrations.

The premier has since told the ABC he did not see Ms Webster's letter until the following day and that it confirmed changes to Christmas were being made.

Over the next five days, other senior ministers, including Felix Ellis, Michael Ferguson, Guy Barnett and Eric Abetz also posted about the alleged “cancellation” of Christmas, a few of which were illustrated with AI-generated images.

Premier 'threw that school under a bus', Greens say

On October 21, the Tasmanian branch of the Australian Education Union held an extraordinary meeting to discuss the distress and harm caused by the fallout.

It then called on politicians not to take part in public school visits for the rest of the year, unless Mr Rockliff apologised.

On October 22, the premier was again asked if he would apologise.

He said he had the right to voice his opinion, and that his "public commentary has been very measured in these circumstances, and will always be very measured".

By October 27, one of the state’s largest public schools — Launceston College — had rescinded invitations to all politicians to upcoming celebrations, due to the "distress and harm" caused by the incident.

Both the education minister and the premier were asked about the incident in parliament this week.

After the premier tabled Ms Webster’s letter, Greens Member for Bass Cecily Rosol said it showed he knew Christmas events were still going ahead before making the post.

“He absolutely knew that Christmas was not being removed from the school, that Christmas carols weren't being ditched and he still went ahead and made that post, and threw that school under a bus,” Ms Rosol said in parliament.

Cecily Rosol says the premier "threw that school under a bus". (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

She went on to allege Mr Rockliff made the post to "shore up his own standing amongst his conservative voters".

"The school has been used as collateral in the premier's own attempts to make himself have a better standing among certain members of the community," she said, before addressing the premier directly.

"Premier, what you have done is unacceptable, it's hurtful and you need to apologise to the school. I call on you to apologise to Trevallyn Primary School."

The post remains online.

The premier has not apologised.

The ABC has texted questions to and attempted to call Mr Thurlow for comment.

It also sent written questions to the premier and education minister.

World.title: Two Australians unaccounted-for after Spain rail disaster
World.content:
Two Australians are unaccounted-for after Spain's deadly rail disaster, with authorities working to confirm their wellbeing.

A statement from the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade says consular assistance is being provided to the family of two Australians in connection with the collision.

"Our heartfelt condolences are with the families and loved ones of those killed, with those injured and all affected by the train collision in Spain," a spokesperson said.

The crash in central Spain on Wednesday killed at least 69 people.

The crash has become one of Europe's deadliest train disasters this century. (AP: Manu Fernandez)

Transport Minister Oscar Puente said the security system on a stretch of track stopped working due to a computer malfunction, causing all trains on that stretch to stop.

Minutes after the order to stop was given, a train from state operator Renfe was told by central command it could run again without speed restrictions, leading it to collide with a train operated by the private Spanish company Iryo.

"The sequence of malfunctions, instructions, and actions eventually led to the collision, in the absence of the necessary mitigating barriers," according to Reuters, citing a preliminary report by the Independent Authority for the Technical Investigation of Accidents and Incidents (AITAT).

It estimated the Renfe train was travelling at a speed of between 160 and 200km/h when the collision occurred.

AITAT said it would not be able to confirm the exact speed of the train until it extracted information from the train's black box.

On Thursday, local time, Spanish media reproduced short audio clips of the controller ordering the train engineer to start moving.

Mr Puente said that the train should never have been told to start moving again since a “stop signal” was still active on that line. And if it had, at least it should have been told to go at reduced speed.

The control centre "had more than enough time to verify the error, and they did not fix it" he added.

The Renfe train was told it could start running again and then collided with the stationary Iryo train. (ABC News: Ryan Boyle)

There were more than 500 passengers on the two trains, according to a regional governor.

Spain's Civil Guard said it had received reports of 64 people missing in what was already Spain's deadliest train accident since 2013, according to reporting by Reuters.

Authorities have carried out 49 autopsies so far and identified five people, three women and two men, Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the Castilla-La Mancha regional government, said on state television network TVE.

"Testing is proceeding slowly, although families will be contacted throughout the day so that they can come and collect their results," Mr Padilla said.

It's unclear how many of the missing were among the bodies still to be identified.

The resulting collision has become one of Europe's deadliest train disasters. Spain has since begun three days of mourning.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who faces a general election on November 29, pledged to establish the cause of the crash.

"We are working day and night not only to support the victims' families, but also to establish every last detail of this tragedy and strengthen safety measures to ensure it never happens again," he said.

The computer system failure saw six trains stopped on just over 60km of track between Madrid and Seville. (AP: Juanma Jiménez/Europa Press)

The crash follows another collision between two high-speed trains in January, which killed 46 people.

In its wake Spain's government faced heavy criticism over the management of the country's railways.

The investigation into the January incident is ongoing.

The January crash was the first fatal incident on Spain's dedicated high-speed rail lines since 1992. According to European Union data, rail fatality rates in Europe have decreased over the last decade.

Between 2022 and 2024, Spain recorded some of the lowest fatalities per million train kilometres in Europe.

World.title: ‘I’m deeply hurt’: Christa Pike releases first statement since botched execution
World.content:
Breaking WorldNorth AmericaDeath penalty ‘I’m deeply hurt’: Christa Pike releases first statement since botched execution Kim Chandler October 31, 2026 — 12:42am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Christa Pike said on Friday that she remains in constant pain and struggles to speak a month after surviving a lethal injection in Tennessee, a failure she blames on “incompetence”. In her first public statement since the execution, Pike said she never contemplated a life beyond her execution date and was prepared to die in peace, but woke up alone and confused in a hospital bed. Christa Pike, 50, survived a double lethal injection in Tennessee on September 30. AP “There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul,” Pike said. Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital as the state tried to execute her on September 30 for the 1995 stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed Slemmer, becoming one of the youngest women to be sentenced to death.



Related Article US midterms The death penalty is making headlines, but this might be its last gasp “I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position,” she said. “I continue to think about my victim’s family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured.” Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has called for an investigation into what happened during the failed execution and postponed the state’s other lethal injection scheduled this year. The state’s prison chief resigned. Pike said she is thankful for the medical workers who saved her life and the people who showed her kindness. “I don’t know why I survived that night. I don’t know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time. And I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone,” she said.



The failed lethal injection left her arms burned and blistered, according to her lawyers. For the first few days of her hospitalisation, Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator. Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on the possibility that a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue rather than entering her bloodstream. Related Article Death penalty Lawyers reveal Christa Pike’s first words after she woke from botched execution Pike’s lawyers have urged the governor to reduce her sentence to life imprisonment. Lee told reporters this week: “I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts.” Friday’s statement was dictated to her legal team from the infirmary at the prison where she is housed. Pike was hospitalised in the immediate aftermath of the failed execution and then moved back to prison at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Centre.

World.title: 2010hvletters2
World.content:
You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Pork-barrelling alive and well

Surely the fact that then Premier Mike Baird’s chief of strategy, “queried why we are giving funding to a clay target association in a … relatively safe seat” amplifies to all that the abhorrent practice of pork-barrelling is alive, well, and, as Berejiklian recently noted, acceptable (“Berejiklian wanted grant hastened: ICAC”, October 20).

Bill Young, Killcare Heights

Government grants awarded before applications close. Majority of high-value grants given through “closed, non-competitive processes”. Over half the grants for rural Australia go to cities (“55% of regional grants go to major cities”, October 20). Voters’ anger over the sports rorts and commuter car park electioneering has led to nothing and never will until a federal integrity agency is established. We deserve better.

Lorraine Hickey, Green Point

Australia deserves, but does not receive, honesty and integrity from its politicians. More than half of federal grants for regional development went to major cities, most favoured Coalition seats, the largest proportion of money was given out just before an election and less than 8 per cent of funding went to remote regional areas. Similar problems occur in NSW, where improper grants were justified by the past Premier as being OK because both parties do it. Government funding for political advantage is not OK, it is fraudulent misuse of taxpayer funds that undermines our democratic process. We will not see honest and ethical behaviour by politicians and the fair election of our representatives until the misuse of taxpayer funds becomes a criminal offence.

Keith Woodward, Avalon Beach

In corporate contract law we had a suite of standard inclusions in our contracts, including a claw back subject to arbitration, for any grant or such like we made if the facts on the ground subsequently changed. The government has left an estimated $27 billion of our money with firms who didn’t need it in JobKeeper, largely a cohort who are Coalition supporters. In contrast, they have claimed for years that transition to clean energy is a cost the economy can’t bear, all the while political donations remain opaque. We should worry about the passive, almost bovine, nature of our democracy if these people win power again.

Peter Spencer, Glebe

Today we read the Auditor-General’s findings that most of the money for regional development goes to capital cities. It would all make perfect sense if Coogee and Campbelltown were in the regions. Now this is something MPs from the regions could be active about once some of them have sorted out energy policy with their colleagues.

Judy Sherrington, Kensington

World.title: Net zero risks being worth precisely that
World.content:
What will we actually achieve with this belated, grudging net zero by 2050 target (“Nats name price for net zero support”, October 22)? Let’s see: ScoMo can go to Glasgow and not get howled out of court and he won’t be too embarrassed the next time he gets to meet the Queen or Prince Charles. All sorts of eye-watering amounts have been promised in the regions. Meanwhile, Australia is still near last on the world league tables. We aren’t likely to get up off the floor during the next crucial decade unless the states and business community take matters into their own hands. Those Nats know how to make hay while the sun shines. About solar power, not so much.

Margaret Johnston, Paddington

What on earth is Barnaby Joyce thinking? Twiggy Forrest among others is leading Australia out of coal and into more profitable job creation via green hydrogen and other renewables. Our world has changed and most people get the message. It has nothing to do with country versus city. Green hydrogen is the future for them. I truly doubt the sanity of some politicians.

Scott Morrison should move with the times and stop his reliance on road maps and start using GPS for his climate change navigation.

London: Police are investigating concerns that young women were “trafficked” to the royal estate at Balmoral when convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein visited the Scottish castle to see his friend, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor. Scottish Police confirmed they received information that led them to launch the inquiry, adding a new investigation to those already involving the former prince. An image that is believed to show Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell at Balmoral in Scotland, released as part of the Epstein files in 2025. US Department of Justice Epstein and his friend Ghislaine Maxwell gained access to several royal estates over many years through their friendship with the prince, as he was at the time. Police Scotland said the inquiries were at a “very early stage” and were ongoing.



“All inquiries are evidence-led, with the needs of victim survivors at the heart of those inquiries,” police said in a statement. “We would never confirm details of ongoing inquiries, and it would be inappropriate to comment further.” An undated photo from the DoJ files shows Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell at a hunting lodge on the royal family’s Balmoral Estate. AP The Scottish Daily Express revealed the police concerns, and said the inquiries were understood to relate to claims that women were “trafficked” to the royal estate in the Scottish Highlands, a favourite retreat for Queen Elizabeth and her family. King Charles responded to years of concerns about Mountbatten-Windsor by removing his title as Duke of York late last year, removing other honours and reaching an arrangement by which his brother would no longer be known as a prince.



Mountbatten-Windsor has insisted many times he is innocent of any wrongdoing. The statement from Police Scotland makes no allegation against him. Epstein was charged in 2006 and negotiated a plea deal with prosecutors that led to most of the charges being dropped. He was found guilty of soliciting a minor for prostitution and spent time in prison and under house arrest before he emerged in 2010. Andrew as a baby in Prince Philip’s lap in a family portrait at Balmoral Castle, 1960 (from left, Princess Anne, Queen Elizabeth and Prince Charles). AP Epstein and Maxwell were photographed at Balmoral during a visit in 1999. One of the young women who worked for Epstein told The Daily Mail six years ago that she had joined him on a visit to Balmoral in the middle of 1999.



Epstein and his entourage visited the Scottish estate as part of a week-long trip to the UK, the Daily Mail reported. The group also stayed at Maxwell’s home in London during the trip. One year later, in June 2000, Epstein and Maxwell attended a party at Windsor Castle hosted by the Queen to mark a series of birthdays for her family, including Mountbatten-Windsor’s 40th birthday. Related Article Analysis

Royal family Andrew is now a pariah. Here’s why he wants to turn the tables on police Epstein and Maxwell were also photographed at Sandringham in 2000, when they went pheasant-shooting at the royal estate. Entries in the infamous birthday book given to Epstein in 2003, when he turned 50, also suggest that he and his friends went to Buckingham Palace. One of Epstein’s assistants at the time, a young woman photographed in a bikini, wrote in the birthday book about meeting Prince Andrew and visiting Buckingham Palace.



Epstein gained access to the royal grounds at Windsor with Maxwell and disgraced movie producer Harvey Weinstein in 2006. The three visitors were photographed at Mountbatten-Windsor’s home, Royal Lodge, during the early stages of an 18th birthday celebration for his daughter, Princess Beatrice, in 2006. The image highlighted the ties between the prince and three people who were later convicted of serious crimes, ranging from Epstein’s guilty plea for sex with a minor to Weinstein’s convictions for multiple sexual assaults and Maxwell’s convictions for trafficking girls. World.content:
WorldEuropeAustralians abroad Concerns for welfare of two Australians after Spanish train crash Jack Gramenz and David Crowe October 30, 2026 — 8:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Australian authorities are working to confirm the welfare of two Australians linked to this week’s deadly train crash in Spain. A high-speed train on Wednesday smashed into the rear of another on the line running south from Madrid, killing at least 69 people and injuring almost 200. Australian diplomats are providing support to the family of two Australians in connection with the collision, the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade said on Friday. Loading A spokesperson expressed the department’s “heartfelt condolences” for all affected by the train crash.



“Owing to our privacy obligations, we are unable to provide further comment,” the spokesperson said in a statement. The Spanish foreign ministry has said that 42 foreign citizens from seven countries were involved in the crash, but it has not named the countries in public statements. While the ministry said on Thursday that one of the foreign citizens was killed and seven others were injured, healthcare workers and officials are facing major challenges in establishing the facts and treating the injured. A crane operates at the site of wrecked train carriages in Spain on Friday. AP Photo/Bernat Armangue The Castilla-La Mancha regional government said it would take time to identify the dead.



“Testing ​is proceeding slowly, although families will be contacted throughout the day so that they can come ⁠and collect their results,” said Esther Padilla, a government spokesperson, on state television network TVE. Spanish Transport Minister Óscar Puente blamed the disaster on human error at a control centre in Madrid that failed to tell the driver of a high-speed Renfe AVE service that another train, run by private operator Iryo, was stationary on the tracks ahead. But the minister’s comments provoked a furore, with rail unions accusing him of “scapegoating” the rail control workers and demanding his resignation, while the train operators offered different accounts of what drivers had been told. The Renfe AVE train had 397 passengers, while the Iryo train was carrying 147.



The accident comes with memories still fresh of another crash between high-speed trains in southern Spain in January involving trains from the same two companies. The Spanish accident authority issued a preliminary report estimating the Renfe train ​was travelling at ⁠a speed of between 160kph and 200kph when the collision occurred. Related Article Analysis

Tragedy Leaked recordings reveal final moments before the Spanish train disaster The public debate about the crash has focused on whether the controller at the Atocha railway station in Madrid told the Renfe driver to “resume normal operations” rather than telling the driver to keep to 40kph because there was a stationary train ahead. “The sequence of malfunctions, instructions, and actions eventually led to the collision, in the absence of the necessary mitigating barriers,” said the report from the Independent ​Authority for the Technical Investigation of Accidents and Incidents (AITAT).

World.title: ‘I’m deeply hurt’: Christa Pike releases first statement since botched execution
World.content:
Breaking WorldNorth AmericaDeath penalty ‘I’m deeply hurt’: Christa Pike releases first statement since botched execution Kim Chandler October 31, 2026 — 12:42am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Christa Pike said on Friday that she remains in constant pain and struggles to speak a month after surviving a lethal injection in Tennessee, a failure she blames on “incompetence”. In her first public statement since the execution, Pike said she never contemplated a life beyond her execution date and was prepared to die in peace, but woke up alone and confused in a hospital bed. Christa Pike, 50, survived a double lethal injection in Tennessee on September 30. AP “There hasn’t been a moment since that night when I haven’t been in pain. My body hurts. My arms hurt. My hands hurt. My throat hurts. I still struggle to speak. And the pain isn’t just physical. There is pain in my mind and in my soul,” Pike said. Pike, 50, survived two doses of pentobarbital as the state tried to execute her on September 30 for the 1995 stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend tortured and killed Slemmer, becoming one of the youngest women to be sentenced to death.



Related Article US midterms The death penalty is making headlines, but this might be its last gasp “I’m deeply hurt by the incompetence that has put so many people in this terrible position,” she said. “I continue to think about my victim’s family and the terrible pain and loss they have endured.” Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has called for an investigation into what happened during the failed execution and postponed the state’s other lethal injection scheduled this year. The state’s prison chief resigned. Pike said she is thankful for the medical workers who saved her life and the people who showed her kindness. “I don’t know why I survived that night. I don’t know what comes next. Some days, finding hope is harder than others. For now, I am trying to heal, one day at a time. And I am holding on to the love and kindness of so many people who have reminded me that I am not alone,” she said.



The failed lethal injection left her arms burned and blistered, according to her lawyers. For the first few days of her hospitalisation, Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator. Medical and lethal injection experts have focused on the possibility that a problem with the IV line caused the drug to pool in her tissue rather than entering her bloodstream. Related Article Death penalty Lawyers reveal Christa Pike’s first words after she woke from botched execution Pike’s lawyers have urged the governor to reduce her sentence to life imprisonment. Lee told reporters this week: “I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts.” Friday’s statement was dictated to her legal team from the infirmary at the prison where she is housed. Pike was hospitalised in the immediate aftermath of the failed execution and then moved back to prison at the Debra K. Johnson Rehabilitation Centre.

World.title: RBA and government must work together on priorities
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters RBA and government must work together on priorities October 30, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Photo: Megan Herbert To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number. No attachments, please include your letter in the body of the email. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. It is a sad fact that the economy drives government priorities when it should be the other way around. Governments should look at what people need and place those needs in some sort of priority order and then decide how they can be funded. The last thing that should be cut are socially critical items of infrastructure and services.

The Reserve Bank, as part of its mandate, is supposed to try to get close to full employment. It prefers around 4 per cent unemployment. This consigns 4 per cent of the employable people to poverty. People are also expected to spend more to stimulate the economy but that becomes difficult with rising interest rates.

So to what should the government and the RBA aspire? Full employment, welfare above the poverty line, affordable interest rates, very low inflation allied with reasonable growth, provision of needed social infrastructure and support, money circulating in the economy, and good gross domestic product (GDP) through overseas trade. But what we are subjected to is a bleak future based on increased unemployment, high inflation and high interest rates, which feed off each other and stoke the cost-of-living crisis.

The government and the RBA need to work out a plan together to deliver what Australians need. They need to work out a way of massaging the economy rather than bludgeoning it into submission using interest rate rises and cuts to important government services. Do they not see what the public is enduring?

Greg Tuck, Warragul Other side of interest coin

Ross Gittins argues, with some cause, that current mortgage interest rates are hurting households with a mortgage (Comment, 28/10). The problem with his argument is twofold. First, using a rule of thumb that a previous RBA governor (Bernie Fraser) outlined – mortgage interest rates should equal the sum of the inflation rate and a margin of 400 basis points. That equals, today, 8.3 per cent. The banks currently ask much less than that. So interest rates for borrowers are low, not high. Second, the banks have money to lend, at least partly, because some people have deposited money with them, for interest. Such people need to be receiving about 5.3 per cent interest to be properly compensated for their saving. They aren’t.

Alun Breward, Malvern East AI, what’s the answer?

One-third of households are mortgage holders, many of whom are under mortgage stress, yet they are expected to carry the load of managing inflation through continuous rate rises. This is such a blunt instrument, and seems incredibly unfair. Surely economics theory has moved on this century? Has anyone asked AI for a better idea?

Fiona White, Alfredton



THE FORUM Tired, but looking ahead

Your correspondent (Letters, 30/10) provides an exemplary overview of Jess Wilson who, she claims, is “surprisingly mired in the past”. Her pledge to dump Victoria’s historic treaty with its First Peoples and her refusal to commit to net zero both mirror One Nation. Rolling back Labor’s energy transition could cost billions and require years to reset. Wilson has (astonishingly) proposed reducing tax concessions for new renewable projects. She should take a look at South Australia, which aims to reach 100 per cent renewables by the end of 2027. Can only imagine what the socially progressive voters of Kew might make of all this. Policy formulation has never been a strong feature of the state Liberals, and I cannot see that changing any time soon. Labor might be a “tired government”, as your correspondent says, but at least its vision is forward looking.

Neil Hudson, East Melbourne Polar climate options

Your correspondent is right: climate and energy policy is vital to our future, and the parties’ plans are worlds apart (Letters, 30/10).

Under Labor’s renewable energy policies, Victoria has gone from 11.6 per cent clean energy in 2015 to 42.4 per cent in 2025. Our wholesale power prices are now among the lowest in the world.

The Liberal Party, by contrast, plans to place unreasonable restrictions on wind farm development, scrap transmission lines and pursue more gas. One Nation is backing coal and nuclear.

The choice between cleaner, cheaper power and costly, polluting alternatives couldn’t be starker.

Larni Dibben, Glen Iris Tax gas exports

Talk about the PM, the treasurer and the budget fails to acknowledge that many financial problems could be resolved if gas exports were taxed. Why on earth is the government giving away our resources like this, free of charge?

Peta Colebatch, Swan Reach ATO, see the light

Surely the ATO would benefit if it absorbed the cost of merchant fees of people and companies meeting their tax instalments via credit card payments. The current arrangements represent a real benefit to the monthly cashflow of any sized business and is ultimately benefiting individual Australians by avoiding potential price increases.

Iain Carmichael, Richmond



Follow the money

Have I got this right? “SRL ‘pause’ would cost taxpayers $1billion” (30/10). Yet if we don’t pause it, it’ll cost taxpayers at least $33.5 billion. As a taxpayer, I know what I’d do.

Tony O’Brien, South Melbourne ABC, SBS independence

The recent report highlighting a “new wave of antisemitism” from progressive critics raises serious concerns about the push for external oversight of Australia’s public broadcasters (“New wave of antisemitism comes from progressive social justice critics: report”, 30/10). Jillian Segal’s assertion that the ABC and SBS are incapable of handling complaints of antisemitism and require an independent, external reviewer lacks objectivity. Given her alignments, Segal cannot be viewed as an independent arbitrator on these matters.

Subjugating our public broadcasters to external review mechanisms would fundamentally undermine media freedom. The ABC and SBS must maintain their internal review systems to safeguard independent journalism from partisan interference.

Paul Caine, Glen Huntly Conflicting figures

On Background’s reporting (30/10) of Liberal senator Sarah Henderson’s questioning of the ABC at this week’s Senate Estimates includes the claim that ″⁣almost 300 (journalists) have been killed by Israeli strikes (in Gaza) in three years″⁣. However, an Israeli terrorism and intelligence research institute has previously found strong evidence that about 60 per cent of killed individuals identified as journalists were members of, or affiliated with, terrorist organisations, primarily Hamas and Palestinian Jihad. Furthermore, even the Committee to Protect Journalists has recently acknowledged that some of those previously on its list of killed journalists actually had such terrorist affiliations.

Geoff Feren, St Kilda East Repeat offenders

Starting a war is a terrible thing to do, but, until I thought about it more carefully, I hadn’t realised just how stupid it is (Letters, 30/10). Since 1900 almost every country that started a war was worse off at the end – the two world wars, of course, the Korean War, Saddam Hussein against Iran and Kuwait, the Falklands War, the Suez Crisis, attacks on Israel. Even when the country ″⁣won″⁣, as in Vietnam and the Second Gulf War, it was a disaster for the winner. Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin, don’t you know that those who do not learn from history are condemned to repeat it?

Aidan Sudbury, Malvern East No o in gulf

On what other planet does a government allocate $6million to upgrade a golf club while crisis accommodation services are offering tents to homeless Australians.

The separation of the sheep from the goats comes to mind: looking out for those who don’t have food, or water or clothing or shelter or are sick – can’t see golf courses in there.

Geoff Sheahan, Glen Waverley



Accommodating data

The article about the Victoria University Data Academy ″⁣One way to turn data centres into a positive″⁣ (30/10) suggests that offering locals faster internet would calm any opposition. That still won’t get rid of the visual bulk of the building, nor the very significant humming noise, that upsets the neighbours.

Another way to make the neighbours happier would be to do what now happens with every major building. There are several basements for cars. As the data centres are usually only about three storeys high, they could be constructed in the ground.

That would give the advantage of sound absorption and would eliminate the bulk of the building. With the top of the building then level with the surrounding ground, it could be turned into a park or a playing field.

Near my home, the same concept has been used, with the local football ground being built as the top of a large reservoir.

Jeffrey Newman, Ivanhoe Fins have changed

After watching the gloom of SBS News I was bemused that SBS felt the need to preface a food show on the Sydney Fish Market with a warning that the program contained “scenes of commercial fishing”. Unsure how to react to this seemingly over-the-top sensitivity, I quickly returned my fish fingers to the fridge and threw a tea towel over the fish tank before any piscine trauma occurred. Thank you SBS.

Stephen Farrelly, Donvale More power to Speaker

The political wrangling over the appointment of MPs’ staff numbers should cease. Additional staff allocation should be outside the domain of the PM. As in The Netherlands, it should be under governance of the Speaker.

Henk van Leeuwen, Elsternwick MPs, lift your game

At a memorial service for Brunswick MP Tim Read this week, the premier led tributes, applauding his integrity, character, commitment to evidence-based policy decisions and willingness to work across the parliament for a better future. He was acknowledged as ″⁣the best of us″⁣, a phrase also used widely to describe Helen Haines. Despite this recognition of the character and commitment of these selfless individuals, we still see too many politicians focused on point scoring, stirring outrage, and prioritising votes and donations over sound policy outcomes. We have a right to expect a lift in behaviour.

Peter Allan, Taradale Photo: Matt Golding



AND ANOTHER THING Politics

Australia may have ″⁣done its bit″⁣ about climate, as Angus Taylor says. But only after his coalition of climate deniers had been sidelined.

Bernd Rieve, Brighton Victoria is on the road to nowhere. Mind the potholes.

Ross McPhee, Seaford Jeff Kennett is right (for once) with his ″⁣sniff of arrogance″⁣ remark (Comment, 29/10). Besides fortuitous timing, what has Jess Wilson actually done to deserve to be elected premier?

Steve Melzer, Hughesdale Bluey, you were certainly dreaming if you thought Pauline Hanson would ever offer an apology like that (Illustration, 30/10).

John Walsh, Watsonia



Pauline Hanson misusing our iconic Bluey in its election material is beyond the pale!

Greg Curtin, Nunawading Your correspondent (Letters, 28/10), rightly, baulks at the use of Alice in Wonderland in political cartoons. But the use of The Mad Hatters’ Tea Party to highlight One Nation’s shenanigans is deliciously appealing.

Jim McLeod, Sale Furthermore

The inflation rate is still about 2 per cent less than when the Labor government was voted in four years ago and is higher across the world. Don’t get too hysterical out there media.

Ross Hosking, Blackwood, SA Had Scott Boland been in the Test team in South Africa instead of Marnus Labuschagne, Australia would have had a stronger attack and probably would have made a higher first innings score.

Les Aisen, Elsternwick I note in next year’s AFL draw, Melbourne play North Melbourne once. The game is in round 23, after they have each played multiple teams twice. Perhaps the AFL would prefer that they didn’t play each other at all.

Greig Morris, Essendon Finally

Would anyone under 50 understand the origin of VicPol’s Operation Furlong campaign title?

Ian Macdonald, Traralgon
