Tech.title: The $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Was Pulled Off in Just 20 Minutes
Tech.content:
Cryptocurrency firms and investigators are racing to freeze and track down billions of dollars of stolen digital cash following what appears to be the largest crypto heist of all time. On Thursday, starting at around 4pm ET, hackers started quickly siphoning around $6.3 billion in cryptocurrencies, spread across multiple blockchains, from wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance.

Following the theft, Binance almost immediately suspended all deposits and withdrawals from its services as part of its investigation into the hack and says it is working to identify who was behind the breach. The company, along with other crypto firms, says it has so far been able to freeze around half of the stolen funds—essentially stopping hackers moving the money further or trying to cash it out. Much of the remaining crypto may not be possible to freeze, however.

Three crypto tracing firms have been quick to link the attack potentially to North Korean hackers. “We think North Korea is likely responsible,” Tom Robinson, chief scientist and cofounder of Elliptic, tells WIRED. “If North Korea is behind it, this one theft would almost double everything the regime has stolen in crypto to date.”

The majority of the stolen crypto was taken in a period of around 20 minutes on October 29, according to analysis by crypto tracing firm TRM Labs. Wallets belonging to Binance across at least ten blockchains—including Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron and Solana—were drained and sent to multiple addresses controlled by a single attacker, according to TRM’s analysis. “Preparation began at least 36 hours before the theft,” TRM says in a blog post. The company says one of the attacker’s wallets received three small withdrawals during a test period, before later expanding the operations.

“Early on October 29, the operator deployed a first piece of code for the attack and tested it on two wallets,” TRM says. “Later that day, it rehearsed the final version on a third wallet, then routed the test funds back to itself. Four hours after that rehearsal, the same code was installed on a Binance hot wallet.” Hot wallets are cryptocurrency wallets that are internet connected and allow crypto exchanges to handle customer withdrawals. Analysts say the funds were drained from hot wallets across the impacted blockchains.

The tactics used in the hack appear to mimic previous methods used by an elite subset of North Korean hackers, known by the name TraderTraitor. Crypto tracing firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis both say they believe TraderTraitor may be behind the attack, while Robinson says Elliptic hasn’t specifically tied it to the group but sees overlaps in the activity.

Tech.title: This App Brutally Shames You by Tracking How Many Hours You’ve Lost to Scrolling
Tech.content:
You know that phone addiction has become a big issue when even Google and Apple are bundling time management tools into their handsets—Digital Wellbeing and Screen Time, respectively. There are now also a plethora of apps looking to help you cultivate a healthier relationship with your device.

One of the newer ones, which takes a slightly different approach to the norm, is Oh My Hours for iOS. (There's no sign of an Android version yet.) Rather than giving you a mass of menus and options to wade through, it simply splits each day into blocks of hours that you can either waste or use productively, then puts a black mark next to the hours during which your phone has distracted you.

It's simple, it's effective, and it just might work. Rather than seeing how long you spent on X and Instagram, you see the hours you've lost to social media algorithms and the infinite scroll. Here's how Oh My Hours works on your iPhone, plus some other apps to check out if you’re looking to develop healthier phone habits.

Moments Lost

You can get started with Oh My Hours for free on iOS. But to really make the most of it, a $10-per-year or $20 lifetime payment is required. This lets you customize what counts as a “lost” hour or day, and it gives you access to month and year views, which provide the best insights into how you're spending time on your phone.

Here's how it works. First, you indicate which apps you consider distractions, either by category (social media apps and games, for example) or by selecting apps individually. If you use any distracting app for a certain amount of time—this can be customized in settings—then that hour of the day is marked as “lost.”

Tech.title: Elon Musk’s Ties to Texas Republicans Go Much Deeper Than the Midterms
Tech.content:
Elon Musk has enjoyed a cozy relationship with top Texas brass for years. And in recent weeks, as the midterm elections approach and Musk’s financial support of the Texas GOP has become virtually limitless, that relationship has gone under the microscope.

While polls suggest that a number of races in deep-red Texas are looking dizzyingly close, Federal Election Commission filings show that Musk has given at least $158 million to super PACs supporting Texas attorney general Ken Paxton’s bid for Senate, and last week Musk explicitly endorsed him in a post on X. “The fate of Texas and America is at stake,” Musk wrote. “Vote for @KenPaxtonTX today.”

Newly released state campaign filings also show that Musk also donated $5,000,000 to Governor Greg Abbott’s bid for reelection, making him his single largest donor.

Abbott’s relationship with Musk has been the subject of public interest for years. State representative Gina Hinojosa, who is running against Abbott, recently sued to view, in full, 1,400 pages of the governor’s correspondences with Musk. Abbott has been trying to block their release for some time; his office has described the communications as too “intimate and embarrassing” to be made public. This week, a judge ruled that Abbott had illegally “obstructed and continues to obstruct” Hinojosa’s right to inspect the documents in her capacity as a state lawmaker and ordered their release to her. Abbott has since appealed; a hearing is scheduled for November 2, one day before the election.

State representative James Talarico, who is running against Paxton for Senate, has campaigned on his opponents’ checkered past. As attorney general, Paxton has been indicted on felony securities fraud charges (which he settled without a plea), was accused by whistleblowers of using his office to benefit the financial interests of a political donor, and was impeached (though later acquitted).

Tech.title: The Best Handheld Translators for Work and Travel (2026)
Tech.content:
Hans Christian Andersen once said, “To travel is to live,” and while that’s a romantic notion, he probably wasn’t careening through Gyeongju, South Korea, at midnight in the back of a taxi with a driver who didn’t speak a lick of English.

A lot has changed since the 1800s, to be fair. Today’s world traveler has it awfully easy when it comes to understanding the local lingo, as even a basic modern cell phone app can offer a pretty good translation of common phrases delivered in everything from Abkhaz to Zulu. Type or speak a sentence or two into the app, tap a button, and out it returns in the language of your choice. Tap another button, and your phone can even speak those sentences aloud. It takes a little doing to turn this into a credible two-way conversation—especially if the cab driver isn’t slowing down—but with some patience and good humor, two strangers can engage in a reasonable discussion this way.

Casual travelers merely in need of directions to the farmacia or who want to know exactly what they’re getting into with a plate of kycklingtallrik can get by with a phone and a translation app, and if you’re going to a place with a fairly common tongue, you may not even need an active internet connection if you download the relevant language file for offline use. Google Translate, Apple Translate, or DeepL Translate will all do the job for free, though Google’s product is widely considered the gold standard for cross-language chitchat.

But what if you want to push past translating menus and asking for extra towels and carry on a conversation with a new friend you met on a trip or the in-laws who are visiting from halfway across the world? That’s where a handheld translator device can prove invaluable. These pocket-sized digital interpreters can help you seem like a polyglot, even if you don't know simple phrases. I have been testing and reviewing handheld translators for WIRED for five years, and I've developed a keen sense of how a good product should work and which ones I'd recommend.

What Do Handheld Language Translators Do? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Handheld translators are exactly that—stand-alone devices that up the ante on language interpretation, and their real value is revealed when you use them for sustained, voice-based conversation. Alongside the spoken word, some have a screen that shows the translation in text, often displaying the other side of the conversation upside down, so you don’t have to constantly pass the device back and forth. Having a translator in a separate piece of hardware has further advantages. Namely, you can use your phone for something else while you’re talking—like snapping pictures or taking notes, for example—instead of tethering it to a translation app. You may also feel more comfortable handing a less costly stand-alone device to someone you don’t know versus trusting them with your $1,000 smartphone. Many handheld translators can operate independently, either via Wi-Fi or with preloaded data plans that generally work worldwide. That means you can take one on a global jaunt and have access to interpretation services without having to pony up for an international plan on your smartphone. Better yet, download all the language packs you want before your trip, and you can use a handheld translator in offline mode, even when you’re in the sticks. Earbud-based translators are the next game changer. These are over-ear devices that come in a pair—one for you, one for your conversation partner. Each of you wears one earbud, and the software on your phone handles the translation, both ways, behind the scenes. The best earbud translators make for the most natural way to communicate with someone in a foreign language that I’ve found to date, though handhelds tend to have more capabilities. (Earbud-based designs seem to be the direction the industry is heading.) When shopping for a handheld translator, watch out for expensive subscription plans. Many devices come with free service, but only for a time, and re-upping after the trial period ends can be pricey. Check the fine print before you buy. Also, make sure the translator you’re considering covers all the languages you need. Note that while some translators support hundreds of languages, they may be limited in the language pairs they can translate between. Who Really Needs a Handheld Language Translator? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Again, if you only need casual translation for occasional or emergency use, you can definitely get by with a free translation app on your phone. Translation devices are best for frequent users who expect to carry on multiple sustained conversations with speakers of other languages over time. Those scenarios could include attending a reunion with your Swedish wife’s extended family or a lengthy workshop series with colleagues from other parts of the world. These tools are also often marketed to first responders who need to quickly assess a situation when human translation services aren’t available. In situations where you may need to communicate with several speakers, each speaking a different language, a portable translator can make even more sense. If you expect your journeys to take you to far-flung areas or off the grid entirely, where internet service may be poor or nonexistent, a translator can be a helpful tool in your travel bag, even if you only expect to use it for emergencies.

The Best Stand-Alone Translator

The Timekettle T1 is a reasonably affordable and very pocketable device that makes for an easy addition to your travel kit. Built for two users to communicate, each with access to half the screen, the T1 translates each side of a conversation—written or spoken—into that user’s own language. Using it can be a little tricky: A color-coded button on the side of the device or a virtual one on the 4-inch touchscreen must be held down to tell the T1 which language to listen for. But once you get the hang of it, the system works pretty well.

Tech.title: Male Insecurity Over Penis Size Is a Booming Business
Tech.content:
As headlines about the male loneliness epidemic were making the rounds a few years ago, which Lombroso felt were “sort of thin and maybe navel-gazy,” he decided he wanted to tell a more “propulsive story” about what was going on with men in America. Around that time, he also started hearing more about penile enhancement and began talking to some of the practitioners offering it as well as the men getting it, including Moore, who invited him to Texas.

Moore fancies himself something of a cosmetic revolutionary. He was among the first wellness professionals in Dallas to use platelet-rich-plasma for hair replacement. In Manhood, his goals remain unwavering: to make his patented penis enlargement technique as commonplace as Botox.

You could say Lombroso, a former editorial producer for The Atlantic and The New Yorker, has a metaphorical hard-on for subcultural deep dives. His first documentary, White Noise, followed white-nationalist groups for three years from Donald Trump’s 2016 win until the end of his first term.

Tech.title: It Sure Looks Like the Department of Education Is Promoting a Right-Wing ‘Harry Potter’ Meme
Tech.content:
At first glance, the Department of Education’s October 27 X post seems like generic Harry Potter-esque slop.

It shows a trio of students walking toward a sprawling Hogwarts-like castle while a young girl with long, flowing white-blonde hair watches them from the foreground, accompanied with the text “There’s Magic in Learning!” and “Make Education Great Again.”

But for a hyper-online, highly radicalized subset of the internet, the state was not just communicating a vague policy stance—it appeared to be adopting the deeply-coded visual language of the “Malfoid.”

The reaction online was immediate. On X, Bulwark reporter Will Sommer quickly diagnosed the situation, posting that the Department of Education was “embracing the ‘malfoid’ meme, a right-wing fan fiction idea about a female Draco Malfoy who Harry Potter could fall in love with.” Others responded with Malfoid art and AI-generated clips, including some featuring President Donald Trump.

The Malfoid concept did not come from conservative think tanks but began in creatively chaotic fan fiction websites like Archive of Our Own (AO3). Gender-bending characters—taking a canonically male character and rewriting them as female or vice versa—is a time-honored tradition in fandoms. However, in these specific stories, the gender-flipped female Malfoy character is not just a narrative experiment for someone’s crackship. She is a potent avatar for toxic elitism, with a ruthless obsession with “blood purity.”

The term Malfoid is a portmanteau combining “Malfoy”—the last name of Harry Potter’s school nemesis Draco—with “foid,” which is short for “femoid” or “female humanoid”—a highly offensive incel term used to describe women.

In the original books, Malfoy is prejudiced against wizards whose heritage is mixed with muggles (non-wizards), but it’s framed as a moral failing to be overcome or punished. In Malfoid fan fiction, however, the character's bigotry is romanticized, transforming her into a right-wing aesthetic vehicle actively propagated by far-right meme channels and Telegram groups. Potter is no longer a traditional hero, but a stand-in for disaffected young men who fantasize about a relationship with a beautiful, cruel silvery-blonde girl.

A quick search of platforms like Reddit and Tumblr for the term brings up a wide range of art, AI-generated and drawn in heavily stylized anime aesthetics, featuring a busty wide-eyed blonde demeaning a blushing and devoted Potter.

The character is also depicted as explicitly anti-queer and anti-trans, as the word “foid” becomes a way for the far right to claim that this gender swapping is correcting an error.

Tech.title: Crematoria Are Being Used to Heat Homes and Swimming Pools
Tech.content:
In 2011, Redditch Borough Council in England tried something that hardly anyone in the UK had heard of before. Staff announced they were going to warm the local swimming pool with heat from a nearby crematorium.

A public firestorm ensued. The plans were met with international headlines, and a labor union official branded them “sick and an insult to residents.” (A spokesman for the union, Unison, says this was not—and is not currently—the organization’s official position.)

“All you’re doing is basically heating a radiator and sending the heat down a tube,” says Guy Revans, of Redditch and Bromsgrove Councils, just south of Birmingham. “But death is always an emotive subject, isn’t it?”

Eventually, the relentless press coverage faded away. The project won a green award, and the crematorium has warmed Redditch’s swimming pool since 2013.

Although extremely rare in North America, European countries have been harvesting warmth from crematoria for years. The total volume of heat available from crematoria is modest, but as people search for ways of reducing the environmental impact of funeral rites, utilizing crematoria waste heat provides a way to lower their carbon intensity.

Tech.title: 140,000 Folds and Counting for the iPhone Duo in Our Fold-a-Phone Testing Machine. How High Will It Go?
Tech.content:
Since Apple’s first-ever foldable phone — the iPhone Duo — launched a week ago, everyone has been examining the hinge and looking for ways to push it to its limits. We braved three hours at the Apple store to snag our own testing model for our lab in Louisville, Kentucky, where I oversee hardware and software testing as director of lab operations.

So, the real question: How many times can we fold the iPhone Duo? At 9:30 a.m. ET on Friday, Oct. 30, we passed 140,000 folds.

Our goal is simple. On Friday, my team and I loaded the Duo into a proprietary machine we built to test foldable phones like Apple’s and Samsung’s rival Galaxy Z Fold 8, which we’ve also already started testing. I’ve overseen the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone. (Read on for how CNET tests foldable phones.)

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone.

Now, my team of engineers and testing experts will watch the iPhone Duo open and close, open and close, to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge.

Product Quiz

Powered by Digioh

CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience.

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo.

Join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube today from 1 p.m. to 5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and watch the Fold-a-Phone do its thing to a Duo.

The importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

Matthew Murray/CNET

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a new-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

In many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

How CNET’s Fold-a-Phone tests foldable phones like the iPhone Duo

Most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.)

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day.

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

We determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

Matthew Murray/CNET

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

We also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test.

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

To secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

There’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

Apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.

Tech.title: Using AI to Vibe Code Your TV Is Stupid
Tech.content:
Recently, some posts on X/Twitter and discussed elsewhere have claimed that AI has helped people “vibe code” their way to a better TV interface. Less clutter, no ads, less tracking and more are all ascribed to AI’s magical powers. Not only is this nonsense, but it’s also stupid.

First, let me say up front that I understand the frustration. TV interfaces have gotten bloated; they often have ads, and their creepy and invasive tracking properties have long been discussed and warned about by me and others.

That said, AI is not doing anything unique here. Not only can you do this without AI, but it’s also probably better if you don’t. Using AI risks potentially TV-ruining issues or worse.

More from CNET

What’s happening

“Vibe coding” is the colloquial term for using AI to assist or fully write programming code for apps, websites and so on. Instead of learning a programming language, people tell AI agents in plain English (or their language of choice) what they want, and the AI does it, or at least something close to it.

In this case, people are claiming they’re using an AI agent, usually Claude, to write a new operating system for TVs. This “new” OS is, they claim, faster, easier to use, has no ads and so on.

Why it’s a bad idea

As with all claims about AI, you should be suspicious. First, TV operating systems are far more complex than they appear. Messing around “under the hood,” especially with no programming knowledge, can easily cause serious problems.

One TV engineer I spoke to for this article, who asked to remain anonymous, literally laughed out loud when I asked him about this. He explained that his engineers will often fix one bug in their software, and it will cause 10 other bugs in random, seemingly unrelated parts of the TV. That’s pretty typical with software development, by the way. There are reports already that people have “bricked” their TVs trying this. As in, they turned their TV into an expensive and unusable brick.

The Google TV interface on a Sony Bravia 9 II. Ty Pendlebury/CNET

There are also a lot of potential issues down the road, even if you have initial success. For instance, will the new vibe-coded OS actually run Netflix and other apps? They might seem to load and then not be able to play anything. What happens if one of the apps needs an update? Will you still be able to? What if that update requires a specific Android version? Maybe you won’t have any issues, but there’s no guarantee of that, and if you don’t have any background in software or coding, can you be sure that more AI vibe coding will fix the issue? Will you be able to perform a factory reset and restore it to the way it was when you bought it? Hopefully yes, but not necessarily.

If you’re not a programmer, how sure are you that the code you’re using is secure? How sure are you that it’s only doing what you want and not exposing your TV to external access? This isn’t as likely as just breaking your TV, but if you don’t know or understand what’s going on “under the hood,” can you really be sure?

And what’s the end goal here? If it’s a faster interface with fewer ads, you can do that already without AI, as I’ll discuss in the next section. If it’s to minimize tracking, maybe changing the OS or interface will help, but not entirely.

Why it’s really stupid: An easier solution already exists

AI can’t invent anything, and you can already change your TV’s interface with just an app install. Android TV launchers, as in the user interface, can be swapped out. So if your TV runs on Android, you can change the interface without any AI vibe coding. These launchers are often far simpler than the stock Google TV interface and are highly customizable.

Projectivy Launcher

Launchers like Projectivity, Monet and TV Launcher Premium Smart UI are some of the top-rated and most popular ones. The AT4K Launcher even makes your Android TV interface look like the Apple TV interface. There are many more options.

If you have a TV with a company-specific operating system, like LG’s webOS, Samsung’s Tizen, Hisense’s VIDAA and so on, the AI vibe coding trick isn’t likely to work anyway. Companies do their best to lock down their operating systems to prevent exactly the kind of thing we’re talking about here.

Monet Launcher

It’s entirely arguable that AI wasn’t doing anything clever in the first place. It was just regurgitating what human programmers had already figured out.

What you can do instead

I think there’s a hilarious irony in not wanting your personal data to be out there, so in order to block your TV from tracking you, you give your personal data to AI. If you don’t understand why that’s ironic, you definitely shouldn’t give your data to AI. As I’ve talked about before, there is no easy way to prevent your TV from tracking you and selling your data. You can minimize it, or go to more extreme measures like Pi-holes and not connecting it to the internet at all, but then you’ll just be switching which device is tracking you. Still want streaming? All the streaming devices track you to some extent (the Apple TV 4K less so).

AT4K Launcher

Using AI to vibe code your way into a better TV experience, however, is a dumb idea. Try a launcher app first and see if that gets you most or all the way to what you’re looking for. Will it be a magical fix to speed up a slow TV? No, but it could be much closer to what you’re looking for, and it’s far less likely to nuke your TV. If you want to go even further, there are apps that give you even more control, but with more potential for issues. Or hey, if you have a TV you don’t mind ruining, and you want to see what you can come up with using an AI that is just stealing from other people’s work, go for it.

Tech.title: AO3 Suffers Major Outage: Possibly No Fanfic for 2 Weeks or Longer
Tech.content:
October has been a rocky month for readers of the fan-run fiction site Archive of Our Own, popularly known as AO3. Now, a routine disruption has escalated into a crisis. What began as an estimated 12-hour unplanned outage has ballooned into a multi-week shutdown, leaving millions of users locked out of the site following a series of intermittent disruptions throughout the month. An outage of this magnitude hit readers out of nowhere, landing with all the subtlety of a Looney Tunes anvil.

The platform is operated by the Organization for Transformative Works. An update posted Thursday to the site’s status page and shared via Bluesky and Tumblr said that service restoration will take at least two weeks, possibly four.

“We are hopeful that we will be able to bring the site back up in a degraded state sooner,” the update said. “If that does happen, there may be times when the site has to be brought down temporarily until this is fully resolved.”

More from CNET

[update] Identified: We estimate that service restoration for #AO3 will take around 2 weeks but it could be up to 4 weeks. We are hopeful that we will be able to bring the site back up in a degraded state sooner. If that does happen, there may be times when the site has … — AO3 Status (@status.archiveofourown.org) 2026-10-29T17:41:58.609Z

That update followed an initial notification, 12 hours earlier, with the announcement that “AO3 maintenance is in progress. We expect it to take at least 12 hours, but it may take longer.”

In response to a CNET request for more information, an OTW representative pointed to a new status update, saying, “The statement confirms that the downtime is a security incident, the scope of which is still being assessed. I can let you know that this is not related to the PHP security issue as the Archive uses Ruby on Rails.”

[update] Identified: Earlier today, we detected evidence of a security incident on AO3. We are still in the early stages of response to this security incident and determining its scope. AO3 will remain down while we continue investigating and addressing what has been fou… — AO3 Status (@status.archiveofourown.org) 2026-10-30T01:27:45.004Z

According to the update, “Earlier today, we detected evidence of a security incident on AO3. We are still in the early stages of response to this security incident and determining its scope. AO3 will remain down while we continue investigating and addressing what has been found so far.”

It emphasizes that no data has been deleted, and while they don’t think user data was compromised, they can’t rule it out and recommend you change your password if it’s not unique to AO3. (It should be if you practice safe password practices.) Donor information resides in a separate, unconnected database.

If you need a stopgap for your fanfic needs, you can try Wattpad or FanFiction. The r/DeletedFanfiction Reddit, Bluesky members and other communities have stepped up to offer copies of works they’d already downloaded and to crowdsource alternatives.

Tech.title: Here’s Why You’re About to See More Ads in Google’s AI Overviews
Tech.content:
If you happened to listen to Alphabet’s quarterly earnings call on Wednesday, you might have heard that searches are up, but ad revenue is down. According to Google Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler, search ad revenue growth slowed in the third quarter of 2026 because user queries are migrating to AI Overviews and AI Mode, which suffer from “lower monetization.”

You actually know how this works. When you type a question into Google, a summarized AI response often appears immediately, reducing the classic ad-clicking behavior further down on the page, which generates Google’s core revenue.

Now, the tech giant is expanding how and where we see ads when using AI Mode during searches. Google is scaling ads in AI Mode to 10 new countries (including Australia, Canada, India, Kenya and Singapore), with plans to launch in Brazil, Mexico and the UK later this year.

More from CNET

In the US, Google is launching what it calls “multiturn ads,” allowing ads to appear directly within follow-up queries in AI Mode when a search or conversation has “commercial relevance.” Take, for example, if you start a search with “How does a smart fridge work,” and follow up with “What are the best-selling smart fridges?” You could then see refrigerator ads in sections labeled “sponsored.”

Google said that “multiturn ads” can better target what a user wants in a product because AI Mode gathers more information during a back-and-forth conversation. Ads can also appear on initial AI Mode queries, not just after follow-up questions, and sometimes ads won’t appear at all if there doesn’t appear to be purchase intent, according to Google.

But as Google relies more on AI Mode and AI Overview, there’ll be less reason to click on content links “below the fold,” meaning content that sits out of view until a reader scrolls down a web page.

Lily Ray, a well-known SEO expert and founder of Algorythmic, told CNET that it’s going to become harder to use Google to find articles from preferred publishers and articles you want to read directly from a website. “You’ll have to dig deeper and look outside of Google’s products,” Ray said via email.

According to Ray, Google’s AI tools aren’t designed to give you the exact link you’re looking for. Still, you don’t have to rely on AI Mode or AI Overviews to get search results. You can also scroll down to the search results the old-fashioned way or use a web filter to use Google as a list of links. She also recommends setting up your favorite publications as “preferred sources” (instructions here) so you can see more of those pages cited in your personalized results.

“Unless you’re satisfied with AI answers directly on Google, you’re going to need to start evolving your own search behavior to find the websites you’re looking for,” Ray said.

AI, advertising and traffic

Google is still the largest search engine in the world, accounting for nearly 90% of the global search engine market. In fact, the company said its year-over-year query volume growth in the third quarter was the fastest over the past five years.

But beginning with the launch of AI Overviews in May 2024, Google’s reliance on AI has slowed advertising.

The impact has been even more devastating for online publishers — ranging from major newspapers and digital media sites to brands and trade associations — driving an unprecedented decline in website traffic. AI Overviews now appear on nearly half of Google search queries, with a corresponding 61% drop in raw traffic volume to other pages. Google is effectively scraping publisher information, summarizing it and satisfying the user before they leave the search results page. That’s why it’s often referred to as the “zero-click” crisis.

“AI Mode and AI Overviews answer questions directly in Google’s interface, so there’s less reason for people to click on publishers,” Ray said.

AI Overviews are summary boxes at the top of a traditional search results page, while AI Mode is a conversational interface designed for ongoing dialogue and research. You can access AI Mode directly by selecting the AI Mode button at the far right of the search bar on the Google home page, or by selecting AI Mode in the horizontal menu near the top of other Google pages.

When you use AI Mode, you won’t get an AI Overview or a long list of links to other websites offering more information. Instead, AI Mode provides “more advanced reasoning and ways of interacting” with a conversational approach. For instance, if I use AI Mode and ask, “Where can I see the northern lights?” I get a map and a list of various locations with pros and cons for each. In regular search mode, I get an AI Overview at the top and, below that, pages of links to websites related to my query.

Ray said that with more ads, there’s going to be an even greater decline in organic click-through rates — in publishing speak, that’s the percentage of people who actually click on a natural, nonpaid search engine result, out of the total number of people who simply saw the headline on the page. Not only will the AI text answer your question, but Google will now aggressively route you toward advertisers rather than publisher links.

“Like many things in Google Search, it means that if you’re not participating in Google Ads, it’s going to be harder and harder to get that traffic organically,” said Ray.

Tech.title: Remember Patrick Stewart by Streaming Star Trek, X-Men and Other Genre-Defining Roles
Tech.content:
Patrick Stewart, the legendary actor known to many as Captain Jean-Luc Picard from the Star Trek universe and Professor Charles Xavier from the X-Men movie franchise, died on Wednesday at age 86. An Instagram post announcing the news says Stewart passed after a brief battle with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia.

When looking back at the slate of work Stewart put out into the world, you’ll find over six decades worth of performances. The actor cut his teeth in the world of Shakespearean stage productions and smaller TV projects, mostly in the UK, before he broke out into mainstream popularity in 1987, leading the crew of the Enterprise in Star Trek: The Next Generation.



More from CNET

Along with Picard, he’s most known for the role of Professor Charles Xavier, the wheelchair-using leader of the X-Men. His final performance as Professor X will be seen in Avengers: Doomsday later this year.

To remember Stewart, you can tune in to many of his projects on various streaming services. Since I’ve stuck to roles that can be streamed, his memorable performances as Ebenezer Scrooge in 1999’s A Christmas Carol, John Thornton in 1975’s North & South and the ghost of Hamlet’s father in 2009’s Hamlet, for instance, aren’t listed.



Star Trek: The Next Generation and Star Trek: Picard (1987-2023)

Patrick Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation. CBS

Stewart made Star Trek an obsession for me growing up, and his performance as Captain Jean-Luc Picard is simply iconic. He starred as Picard in seven seasons of Star Trek: The Next Generation before taking the character to the big screen in four movies in the grander franchise. Stewart reprised his role as Picard in the aptly titled sequel series Star Trek: Picard, which lasted three seasons, with the final one acting as a must-see TNG reunion.

The X-Men franchise (2000-2017)

Patrick Stewart as Professor Charles Xavier in X-Men. Attila Dory/20th Century Fox

After he made a name for himself, boldly going wherever the Enterprise took him, Stewart stepped into an even more legendary role: Professor Charles Xavier in the 2000 X-Men movie. He reprised his role as leader of the X-Men in six installments in the franchise, including the stand-alone Wolverine movie, Logan. In December, audiences will see him one final time in the role in Avengers: Doomsday.

Green Room (2015)

Patrick Stewart as Darcy Banker in Green Room. A24

It wasn’t common to see Stewart in a villainous role, so his performance as Darcy Banker in Green Room is a riveting turn for the actor. The movie takes place mostly inside a bar that caters to a white supremacist crowd, and Darcy is not just the bar owner, he’s their soft-spoken, violent leader.

Moby Dick (1998)

American Zoetrope

Stewart starred as Captain Ahab in the 1998 miniseries adaptation of Herman Melville’s epic Moby Dick. The series follows the quintessential story of Ahab’s hunt for the white whale and delves into his backstory and relationships, introducing his wife, Elizabeth. Costarring in the series are Gregory Peck, Piripi Waretini and Henry Thomas.

Dune (1984)

Patrick Stewart as Gurney Halleck in David Lynch’s Dune. Dino De Laurentiis Corporation

David Lynch’s take on Dune may have been a box office failure, but in the years since it hit theaters, the movie has achieved cult status. Stewart takes on the supporting role of Gurney Halleck, who Josh Brolin played in the new Dune franchise.

The Prince of Egypt (1998)

Stewart had a recognizable, resonant voice, and his voice-acting work appeared in a slew of animated films. The Prince of Egypt featured the actor as Pharaoh Seti I, the film’s antagonist. He was joined by a stacked slate of talent, including Val Kilmer, Ralph Fiennes, Steve Martin and Sandra Bullock.

Extras (2004)

Screenshot by Aaron Pruner/CNET

Sometimes, the best Stewart was the one who poked fun at Stewart. In the first season of the Ricky Gervais comedy series Extras, Stewart appeared as a heightened version of himself. He may have just appeared in one episode (Episode 6, to be exact), but he definitely left an impact.

Jeffrey (1995)

Screenshot by Aaron Pruner/CNET

Jeffrey is a comedy that came out at a time when gay-themed movies were few and far between. The movie stars Steven Weber as the titular character, who decides to become celibate out of fear of contracting AIDS. It should be noted that this is a comedy and Stewart and Weber, along with the likes of Michael T. Weiss, Bryan Bratt, Nathan Lane and Sigourney Weaver, deliver on that front.

The Sheep Detectives (2026)

Patrick Stewart voiced the character Sir Ritchfield in The Sheep Detectives. Amazon MGM Studios

One of Stewart’s final roles is that of Sir Ritchfield, the elder sheep featured in The Sheep Detectives, from Amazon MGM Studios. The movie follows a group of sheep who take it upon themselves to investigate the untimely death of their shepherd, George Hardy, played by Hugh Jackman.

Tech.title: The Massive DHS Breach Is Hacktivist Payback for Government Surveillance
Tech.content:
A Department of Homeland Security breach by an activist group has exposed the personal information of more than 41,000 employees, including Customs and Border Protection workers, Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers and others who work in government cybersecurity.

Information collected from the breach was published online in a searchable repository called Icepick on the Distributed Denial of Secrets website. According to the news leaks site, a hacktivist group called the Department of Peace breached an Okta single sign-on service used by the DHS, stealing employees’ names, contact information and assignments. The group then distributed copies of the database through the leak-hosting group DDoSecrets and to a self-described investigative journalist and cybersecurity researcher from Switzerland known as maia arson crimew, who created an online tool to search the data.

The hacktivist crimew described the leak as an “unprecedented” and “massive” exposure of the DHS’s internal structure. By detailing exact roles, chains of command and agent identities across agencies like ICE, the dataset is a “complete game changer” that leaves the department highly vulnerable to outside investigation for years to come.

More from CNET

The breach appears to be the latest retaliation against government-led surveillance, including ICE’s increasingly tech-driven enforcement tactics and private partnerships with companies such as Flock Security. The Department of Peace directly cited DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin’s July statement about “turning up the heat on the streets” — a reference to ramping up the immigration crackdown and arrests — and responded, “This is what happens to ICE when you do that.” The hackers also attached a note to the files reading, “They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.”

A DHS spokesperson told CNET that the agency “is aware of a potential breach and is actively working to address the situation swiftly and effectively.” The statement went on to say: “We take all security threats against our employees and officers seriously and will work to ensure all are properly protected.”

A massive leak of information

Since the leak, the DHS has been working to take down sites hosting the information, including Icepick’s searchable archive domain. The social network Bluesky opted to block links to DDoSecrets, telling TechCrunch that the platform’s community guidelines prohibit “the unauthorized sharing of personal information and other content that could pose safety risks.”

Much of the attention on the Icepick leak has focused on its size. While the 41,000 affected employees represent only a fraction of the nearly quarter-million people at the DHS, the data goes far beyond basic contact information. Reports indicate the leak exposes office addresses and phone numbers, as well as details on internal work systems and the department’s inner workings.

Because the hackers gained access through Okta, a secure portal for employee login, they also saw the master list of apps connected to that dashboard. That revealed an inventory of surveillance applications used by ICE, including specialized wiretapping and surveillance software, such as Penlink, and popular AI applications like ChatGPT and Gemini, raising questions about how federal agencies feed case files or border data into commercial AI models.

While cross-referencing Icepick data could expose undercover operations, it also risks including unrelated personnel, such as airport security workers. However, DDoSecrets cofounder and journalist Emma Best argued the release is strategic rather than an indiscriminate dump. “Rather than an indiscriminate directory of every DHS employee, Icepick identifies many of the architects and drivers of DHS policy and operations,” Best wrote.

Retaliation against federal agencies

The public response to the breach also points to a crisis of institutional legitimacy, with many viewing the exposure not as a crime but as forced transparency against a federal department that has acted with impunity. In a Facebook comment thread accompanying an NPR story about the incident, many responded with support for the hacktivists: “Not all heroes wear capes,” one commenter wrote, while another said, “Law enforcement identities must be public. Otherwise, it’s just a gang.”

When an agency known for aggressive enforcement and widespread surveillance gets breached, a segment of the population sees it as poetic justice.

There’s also been an escalating operational crisis for any tech company that signs a contract with ICE or DHS agencies. From the outside, hacktivists are targeting their infrastructure (like this recent breach) to unmask federal agents and leak their surveillance toolkits. And from the inside, employees are sounding the alarm, demanding that leadership cancel contracts on moral grounds.

That was the case recently with the robot company Boston Dynamics, after it was reported that ICE planned to spend up to $2 million on Spot robots made by the company. Hundreds of employees signed a petition saying that they can’t be proud working for Boston Dynamics “when that work is being used by a government agency that brutalizes civilians.” The employee noted that friends and family are asking them “in disbelief and horror” how they can work on ICE robots, an indication of broader distrust.

The recent massive DHS breach isn’t a random, isolated cyberattack. Earlier this year, the Electronic Frontier Foundation detailed the spread of “enterprising hackers [that] have started projects to do counter surveillance against ICE,” including applications and web tools geared toward tracking officers’ movements and countering Flock surveillance cameras that can read license plates.

“It’s important to remember that we are not powerless,” wrote EFF’s Senior Staff Technologist Cooper Quintin. “Even in the face of a domestic law enforcement presence with massive surveillance capabilities and military-esque technologies, there are still ways to engage in surveillance self-defense.”

Tech.title: Patrick Stewart, Who Gracefully Steered Star Trek Into Its Next Generation, Dies at 86
Tech.content:
Patrick Stewart, the British actor whose calm demeanor and steely strength led the Star Trek television franchise into its next generation, died Wednesday at age 86. The actor suffered from Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia.

“We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the care of his beloved wife Sunny,” a Thursday post on Stewart’s Instagram account read in part. “We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace.”

Through a long career, Stewart starred in everything from Shakespeare productions to superhero films, but his role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation is firmly cemented in entertainment culture. Show creator Gene Roddenberry didn’t at first think Stewart, who was bald, could play the virile captain he had envisioned for the new Star Trek series. Stewart even had his wife ship his toupee over from London, and he wore it for an audition scene, but executives saw him with both styles and chose the bald look.

More from CNET

Patrick Stewart stands front and center with the cast of Star Trek: The Next Generation. Pictured in the front row are, from left, Marina Sirtis as Counselor Deanna Troi, Stewart as Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Gates McFadden as Dr. Beverly Crusher. Seen in the back row, from left, are Jonathan Frakes as Commander William Riker, Brent Spiner as Lieutenant Commander Data, Whoopi Goldberg as Guinan, LeVar Burton as Lieutenant Commander Geordi La Forge, and Michael Dorn as Lieutenant Worf. CBS Photo Archive/Getty Images

Stewart was stepping into big boots. While the original Star Trek only ran for three seasons, from 1966 to 1969, it soon became a pop culture fixture, and the success of the first Star Wars film in 1977 finally allowed Roddenberry to make feature films using his original cast. The success of those movies led to a new series, Star Trek: The Next Generation, which launched in 1987 and took place about a century after the original show.

With his resonant voice and complete command of the crew, Stewart’s Picard came off as a trained diplomat compared with the more swashbuckling Capt. James T. Kirk, as played by William Shatner on the original Star Trek. But there was no question who was in charge on his bridge, and his crew followed him unhesitatingly. That made later episodes, including the third-season plot where Picard was assimilated by the alien Borg, even more meaningful, as a very human Picard struggled to recover from what had been done to him.

Professor X and more

Star Trek: The Next Generation ran from 1987 to 1994, but Stewart wasn’t done playing leaders. He took on the role of Professor Charles Xavier, or Professor X, in the X-Men superhero franchise, playing a telepathic, wheelchair-using mutant who founded the X-Men superhero team. He portrayed Xavier in multiple films over the span of 17 years, acting alongside his longtime friend, Ian McKellen.

Ironically, McKellen originally advised Stewart not to accept the Star Trek role as Picard, reportedly telling him, “You have too much important theater work to do. You can’t throw that away to do TV.”

Stewart began his acting career on the British stage, working with the Royal Shakespeare Company and winning numerous acting awards.

He was bluntly open about his childhood with an abusive father, writing in the Guardian newspaper in 2009 that the experience never left him.

“As a child I witnessed his repeated violence against my mother, and the terror and misery he caused was such that, if I felt I could have succeeded, I would have killed him,” Stewart wrote. “If my mother had attempted it, I would have held him down.”

Fans and friends remember

Shatner remembered his successor with tenderness and also referenced the death days earlier of Walter Koenig, who played Pavel Chekov on the original Star Trek.

“What a heartbreaking week it has been,” Shatner wrote on X. “Sir Patrick Stewart was a friend, a colleague, and a magnificent actor. From the stage to the bridge of the Enterprise, he brought intelligence, grace, and a deep sense of humanity to everything he did. Captain Picard stood for the best of us, and so did the man who played him. I was filled with affection and admiration for him and his work.”

George Takei, who played helmsman Hikaru Sulu on the original Star Trek, also remembered Stewart.

“Fans across the world mourn the passing of a true and irreplaceable legend,” Takei wrote on Bluesky. “As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before.”

Fans across the world mourn the passing of a true and irreplaceable legend. As Captain Jean-Luc Picard, Patrick Stewart took the starship Enterprise to places it had never gone before. — George Takei (@georgetakei.bsky.social) 2026-10-29T20:08:52.514Z

Wil Wheaton, who played young Wesley Crusher on Star Trek: The Next Generation, posted a photo of the two together, with a broken heart emoji and the words, “Godspeed, Captain.”

Stewart is survived by his wife, Sunny, and two children.

Tech.title: Nvidia Finds Itself at the Center of an AI Spy Saga
Tech.content:
The companies behind powerful AI technology are high-stakes territory for international espionage. A new investigation from The New York Times published Thursday found that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang may have been the target of Chinese spying activity, with the US government identifying a data center executive with whom he had developed a “close relationship” as a possible operative for the Chinese government.

Alice Huang, no relation to Jensen, is a Chinese citizen and an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company. Megaspeed buys chips from Nvidia to run data centers that sell compute to Chinese AI labs, including Qwen AI maker Alibaba. But while US intelligence agencies had her under electronic surveillance for allegedly facilitating the sale of advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of US law, officials discovered she was also allegedly funneling information to the Chinese government in Beijing.

There are no details about what information Alice Huang may have shared with China, or how valuable it might be, though the Times reports that an investigation and surveillance of her are ongoing. Jensen Huang was not given a heads-up by the US government because it could have risked the US’ investigation into the Megaspeed exec, the Times said, citing people with knowledge of the matter.

More from CNET

An Nvidia spokesperson told CNET that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang are “not unusual or unexpected” given that the CEO “talks with thousands of customer executives every year.” Nvidia added that customers like Megaspeed are “no different than many other regional cloud customers” that don’t receive sensitive trade secrets, and the company is “confident that if the US government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.”

This report is the latest incident highlighting how AI technology and infrastructure are a key part of international trade and conflict, underscoring concerns about AI’s capabilities and its outsized share of the global economy. It isn’t even the first time this month that a major AI company has dealt with alleged espionage: The FBI arrested a Saudi Arabian national for planting a recording device in one of OpenAI’s executive conference rooms.

AI and international law

You can’t do AI without cutting-edge computer chips. That’s what has made Nvidia the world’s most valuable company by market cap — $5 trillion this year — because it makes and sells the most advanced computer chips, the kind that AI data centers use. Big Tech companies are hustling to build data centers, in spite of significant environmental concerns and public backlash. It has created a firestorm in the computing industry. With advanced chips in such high demand, the costs of RAM and storage have risen across the board. Many hardware manufacturers are passing the additional cost on to consumers.

The US has tried to control China’s access to these advanced chips for years. The Biden administration banned Chinese sales of a series of advanced Nvidia chips in 2022, but President Donald Trump relaxed those rules in 2025. Now the US government gets 15% of revenue from Nvidia and fellow chipmaker AMD from certain chip sales to China. But reports show that there are still illegal operations underway to smuggle banned chips from the US to China.

Trump has a friendly relationship with many Big Tech leaders, including Jensen Huang, which has resulted in millions in personal donations for the president and relaxed regulations for tech companies. The Times reports that Trump was briefed on the investigation into Alice Huang a year ago and chose not to take any action.

The White House, the US Department of Justice and Megaspeed did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
